"Inequality has fallen sharply. India's Gini index has dropped by over 20% from 29 in 2011 to 23 in 2023," the Prime Minister said in the Instagram post. The Gini index reflects how equitable is the distribution of income or wealth across a population, with a lower number indicating greater equality.
World Bank's latest Poverty and Equity brief, released last week, said that poverty rate in India, defined at $4.2 a day, will decline to 12.1% in 2028 from 57.7% in 2011, having fallen to 16.1% in 2023.
Meanwhile, extreme poverty, defined as spending $3 a day, declined from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023."This progress was mainly driven by strong consumption growth; rising employment, especially among women; and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies. As poverty declined, it became increasingly concentrated among households with lower education, fewer assets, limited access to stable employment and higher dependency ratios. Wage disparities, however, remain pronounced, as median earnings among the top 10% of workers were about 13 times those of the bottom 10% in 2023," the World Bank had said.

Superannuation watchdog warns widespread complaints signal industry 'failures'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
21:19:56 UTC
06:19:56 KST

IN BRIEF
- The watchdog found 25 per cent of super funds weren't analysing customer complaints data to identify systemic issues.
- Experts warn it's a concerning sign of customer and complaints culture, and risk culture across the industry.
Superannuation funds are ignoring warning signs as complaints about the way they treat customers mount, the corporate watchdog says.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission has found superannuation funds wanting in handling members' complaints at a critical time for the $3.4 trillion industry.
As millions of Australians transition from accumulating super balances to withdrawing their retirement income, issues such as timely payment of death benefits have been piling up.
Commissioner Simone Constant said super funds should treat complaints as the "canary in the coal mine", but were often ignoring the warning signs.
"Superannuation is too important for there to be failures now, in terms of member services and complaints," she told AAP.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The death benefit failures were an example of how better complaints-handling could have saved members and their families from harm, the regulator found in a report released on Monday.
The regulator has been cracking down on the industry after finding widespread delays in trustees paying out deceased customers' remaining super balances and insurance payments to family members.
In some cases, loved ones waited years to receive money they were owed.
The regulator reviewed all 45 superannuation trustees and found a quarter were not regularly analysing their complaints data to identify systemic issues, Ms Constant said.
That comes despite a 43 per cent year-on-year increase in superannuation complaints to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority.
Constant said the issue was industry-wide, declining to single out any particular funds for poor complaints handling.
"We see some funds detecting zero or practically zero systemic issues from complaints, despite AFCA identifying complaints [that could be systemic] at twice the rate of the industry," she said.
While complaints growth flattened for a period after the death benefits issues were identified, the regulator has seen it rising again.
That raised real concerns about customer culture, complaints culture, and risk culture across the industry, Constant said.
"When we see several of the funds attributing well more than half of the root causes to the customers, essentially blaming the customer, we're really concerned about whether the industry has used the time, used the processes, and used their complaints data to understand what's really going on with their members in terms of these important services," she said.
Peak body the Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia said the industry heard loud and clear that trustees needed to do better.
"There are clear areas for improvement here, and the sector will use the information ASIC has collected and its recommendations to act quickly to better use complaints to improve how we look after members," the association's chief executive Mary Delahunty said.
"Members reasonably expect super funds to listen to them, and this should be uniform across the industry."

NINGBO, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- China's Pei Xinyi broke world records and completed all six lifts successfully to win the women's 61-kilogram title at the IWF World Championships on Sunday, leading a Chinese one-two finish at the first qualifying event for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Pei, 21, lifted 112kg in the snatch and 142kg in the clean and jerk for a combined 254kg, sweeping all three gold medals. Compatriot Yang Liuyue took overall silver with 249kg, while DPR Korea's Pak Jin Hae claimed bronze with 243kg.
The snatch developed into a three-way contest involving Pei, Yang and Colombia's Karen Mosquera, who twice improved her personal best before finishing with 111kg.
Pei responded with 112kg on her final attempt, equaling the world record held by Yang to take gold. Yang finished third with 110kg after failing at 113kg, while Mosquera claimed silver. Pak missed twice at 109kg and finished outside the snatch medals.
Pei then took control in the clean and jerk, opening at 135kg before lifting 140kg on her second attempt to break the previous world record of 139kg, set by Pak at the Asian Games last month.
That lift also raised the world record for the total to 252kg. Pei improved both marks again on her final attempt, lifting 142kg for a combined 254kg to complete four world-record performances in the session.
Yang lifted 139kg to equal the previous clean-and-jerk world record but failed at 145kg on her final attempt, settling for silver in the discipline. Pak recovered from an opening failure at 135kg to lift 138kg and take bronze.
"I used to be timid and hold myself back, but not anymore," Pei said. "Being steady just means I can go for it on every lift."
Pei, a native of Zhejiang Province, credited the home crowd for helping her deliver under pressure.
"My family all came and cheered so loudly. With everyone behind me, there was nothing to fear," she said.
Yang, the Asian Games champion, said she needed to improve her composure after missing her final attempt.
"I wasn't relaxed enough mentally and my technique wasn't quite right. I'll keep working hard," she said, adding that building confidence would be her next priority.
The championships continue Monday with the men's 85kg competition, featuring China's Chen Shunnan and Lei Jiangqing. ■

====================================================================================================

Explainer: How Poland's Constitutional Tribunal row affects its politics?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-02
05:19:27 CST
06:19:27 KST

WARSAW, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- A leadership dispute at Poland's Constitutional Tribunal has sparked a political confrontation, with the court's top two officials declared suspended and opposition supporters taking to the streets to accuse Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government of trying to take control of the court.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki cut short a visit to Senegal and returned to Warsaw amid the dispute, calling for urgent talks with parliamentary parties. Tusk accused Nawrocki and the main opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party of undermining the rule of law and vowed to ensure that the tribunal could operate independently and in accordance with the constitution.
What has happened in recent days? What triggered the dispute? And what impact could it have?
WHAT HAPPENED?
The row began on Friday evening, when a notice appeared on the Constitutional Tribunal's website announcing the one-month suspension of its president and vice-president and naming judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska to temporarily oversee the court.
A statement subsequently posted on the tribunal's social media account said its website had been "illegally taken over" and accused those involved of staging a "coup."
The announcement prompted opposition supporters to gather outside the court, where some clashed with police. Three protesters who entered the tribunal's grounds were detained, and several people were reportedly injured.
Nawrocki arrived at the tribunal in the early hours of Saturday and became involved in a heated confrontation with several judges. The confrontation escalated into pushing and shoving at the building's entrance.
Nawrocki's chief of staff, Pawel Szefernaker, read out a statement outside the tribunal in which the president accused those involved of violating Poland's constitutional order and taking over a constitutional institution "by force." Nawrocki also called for urgent talks with parliamentary parties to stabilize the political situation and restore constitutional order.
Nawrocki's office said he met representatives of several parties on Saturday, including the Polish People's Party, a member of Tusk's governing coalition, and the opposition PiS. Tusk's Civic Coalition did not attend.
In a televised address on Saturday evening, Tusk accused PiS and Nawrocki of undermining the rule of law, saying no politician, not even the president, had the right to give orders to judges or intimidate them. He pledged to ensure the tribunal's security and provide the conditions necessary for it to function independently.
The dispute will face another test on Tuesday, when Korwin-Piotrowska plans to convene an assembly of judges to discuss the tribunal's budget.
Under Polish law, at least two-thirds of the tribunal's judges must attend for the assembly to adopt valid resolutions. Polish media reported that some judges planned to stay away because they disputed the meeting's legality, potentially leaving it without the required quorum.
WHY DISPUTE ERUPTED?
The dispute stems from Nawrocki's refusal to accept the oaths of five of the eight Constitutional Tribunal judges elected this year by the Sejm, Poland's lower house of parliament, where Tusk's coalition holds a majority. The five, including Korwin-Piotrowska, have not been recognized by the president or the tribunal's existing leadership and have been unable to take part in hearings.
The row is part of a long-running dispute over judicial reforms introduced by PiS, which governed Poland from 2015 to 2023. Changes to judicial appointments and the tribunal's procedures, along with the government's refusal to publish some court rulings, sparked controversy.
Since taking office in 2023, Tusk's government has sought to reverse some of those changes. But tribunal judges serve nine-year terms, leaving some elected under PiS in place at a court that has the power to rule on the constitutionality of legislation.
The government's plans for judicial reform have also faced opposition from Nawrocki, an ally of PiS who became president in 2025. Although Tusk's coalition holds a parliamentary majority, it lacks the three-fifths majority in the Sejm needed to override a presidential veto. The two have repeatedly clashed over major policies.
Inflation and economic pressures linked to the Russia-Ukraine conflict have also fueled public discontent, putting pressure on Tusk's coalition to deliver results before the 2027 parliamentary elections, Wang Hongyi, a researcher at the Center for Central and Eastern European Studies at Beijing Foreign Studies University, told Xinhua.
Wang said Tusk's tough stance in the tribunal dispute was aimed at breaking the deadlock over judicial reform.
WHAT IMPACT COULD DISPUTE HAVE?
The proposed changes to the tribunal's leadership have raised legal questions in Poland. Przemyslaw Rosati, head of the Polish Bar Council, questioned the legal basis for suspending the tribunal's president and whether Korwin-Piotrowska had the authority to assume the post. Marcin Matczak, a law professor at the University of Warsaw, also questioned the legal basis for the move, saying it would "solve nothing" from a legal standpoint.
Li Zhiqiang, a professor at the Center for Polish and Central and Eastern European Studies at Sichuan University, told Xinhua that the dispute could disrupt Poland's judicial system, deepen political divisions, make it harder for the government to carry out its policies and strain unity within the ruling coalition.
The European Commission said on Saturday it was closely following developments and stressed that the tribunal should operate in accordance with Poland's constitution and European Union (EU) court rulings. It also noted that the Sejm has the constitutional authority to elect tribunal judges. The European Conservatives and Reformists Group in the European Parliament, meanwhile, accused Tusk's government of undermining judicial independence.
Judicial independence has long been a source of friction between Poland and the EU, which previously withheld some funding over rule-of-law concerns during the PiS government's time in office. Tusk has sought to improve relations with Brussels since taking office, but the latest dispute could bring fresh uncertainty to those ties, said Li.
Li also pointed out that prolonged political turmoil could divert Poland's attention from regional security issues and hinder coordination between the president and government on foreign policy. ■

====================================================================================================

Judge dismisses Alaska Senate election lawsuit; DOJ vows appeal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
21:18:38 UTC
06:18:38 KST

A federal judge on Sunday dismissed the Department of Justice's extraordinary lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the Alaska Senate election if incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan loses, citing possible voter confusion from another candidate with his name on the ballot.
The ruling came two days before Election Day and two days after the U.S. Attorney for Alaska said ongoing criminal and civil investigations into non-incumbent Dan J. Sullivan's decision to run for the Senate.
The campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola, state election officials and outside advocacy groups had asked Judge Sharon Gleason to dismiss the DOJ's lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Anchorage.
The Department of Justice quickly filed a notice of its intention to appeal the decision to the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals.
Peltola is locked in a tight contest with Sen. Dan Sullivan, whose winner will be determined by a ranked-choice system.
The outcome of the race is one of several contests that determine which party has a Senate majority, where Republicans currently hold a narrow lead.
Neither the other Sullivan nor the fourth candidate on the ballot, Gerald Heikes, is considered a contender.
But voters who rank them as a first choice could swing the outcome by ranking Peltola or Sen. Sullivan second.
Peltola's campaign has been accused of encouraging retired schoolteacher Dan Sullivan to run for the Senate against the incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Peltola.
Her campaign has denied those claims.
"No sham investigation or baseless lawsuit from a weaponized Department of Justice is going to stop Alaskans from electing Mary on November 3rd so she can lower costs for Alaska's working families," Peltola's campaign said in a statement after Sunday's ruling.
"Alaskans will choose their next U.S. Senator – not Dan Sullivan or his DC allies," the campaign said.
In her 20-page decision, Gleason did not resolve whether another Sullivan had been recruited to confuse voters.
Instead, she said the federal government had failed to establish that it had legal standing to file a civil complaint to postpone certification of the election if Sen. Sullivan lost.
In that event, the DOJ wanted an investigation into voter intent and possible confusion from having two Dan Sullivans on the ballot.
"The absence of any explanation from the United States as to how its requested relief could redress its alleged injury while simultaneously maintaining the secrecy of the ballot is telling," Gleason said in her ruling.
She noted that early voting in the state was already underway, and that ballots already cast have been commingled in a way that would prevent officials from linking individual ballots to voters.
"More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," Gleason wrote.
The judge also cited a Supreme Court decision that established the so-called Purcell principle, which "strongly cautions" against courts altering election rules on the eve of election.
She noted that DOJ claimed it was not seeking to alter the "time, place or manner of Alaska's election."
But at the same time, Gleason said, the DOJ was asking her for an order "preventing the State
from certifying the election if certain circumstances occur; a court order requiring the State to segregate and preserve certain ballots; and a court order permitting the United States to conduct an investigation into the intent of those voters who cast ballots for Daniel J. Sullivan."
"These requests certainly involve the time, place, and manner of Alaska's election, which are the responsibilities of the State, not the executive branch of the federal government," Gleason said.
The judge said she would not allow the DOJ to amend the lawsuit, which was revised last week to add a new legal claim under the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution to the first claim under the National Voter Registration Act. The amended complaint also added details of a New York Times article about the alleged recruitment of the second Sullivan.
"The Court finds that further amendment would be futile because this Court lacks the authority to order that certain ballots cast by Alaskans be segregated so that federal law enforcement officials can conduct an unspecified investigation of the voters who cast them," Gleason said.
A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement, "The court dismissed the case on procedural grounds but did not dispute the argument of the United States that Daniel J. Sullivan (a/k/a Decoy Dan) entered the race as a frivolous candidate to confuse voters."
"DOJ plans to file a notice of appeal," the spokesperson said. "Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes."
The White House, when asked for comment, referred CNBC to the DOJ's statement.
President Donald Trump has said he ordered the lawsuit, which was filed Oct. 22.
Trump argued that Peltola and other Democrats had recruited the former school teacher to run in hopes of confusing voters who wanted to cast their ballots for Sen. Sullivan.
Trump, in his first comments after the ruling, said: "So we have two Dan Sullivans. This is voter fraud at the highest level. But the Democrat candidate who is involved in the scheme, Mary Peltola, should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted."
The New York Times on Wednesday reported that Peltola campaign aides and DSCC aides had been involved in efforts to recruit the retiree for the race.
Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied having any involvement in his campaign.
DSCC Executive Director Devan Barber said in a statement, "Today's ruling is a victory for democracy and a clear message to Donald Trump and Senate Republicans: No one, no matter how powerful, can toss out free and fair elections just because they don't like the result."
"We will never stop fighting back against the shameful, brazen efforts from the Trump administration and their weaponized Department of Justice to subvert the U.S. Senate race in Alaska, or any other election as voters reject Republicans at ballot boxes across the country – and we are confident Alaska voters will elect Mary Peltola to the Senate," Barber said.
Sen. Sullivan, in an interview on CNN before Gleason issued her ruling, said he would accept the election results if he lost.
But he also blasted Peltola's campaign and the DSCC.
"Recognizing they couldn't run on their record, so they had to cheat," Sullivan said. "I think a lot of Alaskans, even Democrats, are thinking she is not fit for office; she's continually lying to the Alaskan people, and I guarantee you she's lying right now."
Alaska election officials have pointed to steps they took to avoid voter confusion on the ballots for the race.
The ballots list Sen. Sullivan as "Dan S. Sullivan," with the words "incumbent" and "registered Republican" next to his name.
The other Sullivan is listed as "Daniel J. Sullivan," with no other words next to his name.
Election officials originally had blocked the retired teacher from the primary ballot. But a state judge allowed him on the ballot. Alaska's Supreme Court upheld that ruling.

El-Sayed, standing with Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., and Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., outside a church on Sunday, dismissed Stevens endorsement of his opponent.
"I actually don't think about Haley Stevens," El-Sayed said. "There are families that are preparing to send their kids to schools tomorrow that look like they did 50 years ago. They're worried about what they're going to feed their kids for lunch. They're worried that if one of their kids gets sick, they're not going to be able to pay the bills. Those are the things that matter."
Rogers and El-Sayed are vying for a seat set to become vacant after Democratic Sen. Gary Peters decided not to seek re-election.
In recent weeks, a deepening rift has worsened between El-Sayed and Stevens. At the center of it is U.S. support for Israel, which was a major issue in the primary contest.
Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel; El-Sayed has called the country's conduct in Gaza after the Oct. 7, 2023, terror attacks by the radical group Hamas a genocide.
Stevens' fiancé, Jason Turkish, endorsed Rogers before Stevens' flip-flop, citing what he said was rising antisemitism.
"I'm sorry people are upset," Stevens told reporters at a press conference in Detroit, standing with Rogers, whom she had attended church with Sunday morning.
"I understand that," she said.
Staffers in Stevens congressional office quit following her endorsement.
"As of this morning, many members of our team have resigned, including myself," Justin German, Stevens' chief of staff for eight years, said in a statement obtained by MS NOW.
"We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens' decision to support Mike Rogers," German said, adding that he was speaking on behalf of the team "in wholeheartedly supporting Abdul El-Sayed for Senate," German said.
Stevens had the endorsement of much of the Democratic establishment during the bruising primary, making her endorsement of Rogers even more stunning.
She was the preferred candidate of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York, who on Sunday reiterated his support for El-Sayed and accused Republicans of Islamophobia.
"Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors," Schumer said. "We Democrats [are] equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans."
In a later post to X, Schumer called her endorsement of Rogers "a despicable betrayal from Rep. Stevens."
Peters and Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin both disavowed Stevens for her endorsement.
"[A]nyone who makes an election this important about themselves, and not Michiganders and our democracy, should think hard about whether they are serving the greater good," Slotkin said in a post to X.
Curtis Hertel, the chair of the Michigan Democratic Party, appeared to suggest that Stevens had been kicked out of the party.
"Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future," he said in an X post.
In a Truth Social post, Trump praised Stevens' endorsement.
"Congresswoman Haley Stevens, a Highly Respected Democrat, who narrowly lost in the Primary to Abdul Mohamed El-Sayed, and who has been breathlessly wined and dined by the Dumocrats to help in their Michigan Campaign for the United States Senate against Mike Rogers, has just ENDORSED Mike Rogers for Senate!" the president said.
"Her following is huge, and the level of respect from the People of Michigan, especially our African American and Jewish populations, is virtually unparalleled," he said.

Carney signals progress on Canada-US trade deal talks as midterms loom
Canadian PM Carney announces progress in Canada-US trade deal talks ahead of US midterm elections on November 3.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced progress towards a future trade deal with the United States, which could help ease tensions between the two North American neighbours.
The Sunday announcement came just two days before the November 3 US midterm elections, which will determine control of the US Congress.
“Good conversation with US President Donald Trump on the future of Canada-U.S. trade,” Carney posted on X on Sunday.
Ties between Ottawa and Washington have been strained by an escalating trade war, with Canada and the US imposing billions of dollars in tariffs on each other’s goods in recent months.
“Teams from both countries will be working in the coming weeks to deliver that outcome,” Carney said. “This builds on recent constructive discussions on the outlines of a mutually beneficial trade deal.”
In his second term, Trump has upended global trade by imposing tariffs on many of the US’s allies, including Canada – one of the US’s biggest trading partners.
In August, high-level trade talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down, and Trump imposed a 50 percent levy on $20bn of Canadian goods, or 5.5 percent of its exports. Canada responded with equivalent tariffs on US steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.
Trump said last week that he expected a new trade agreement with Canada to be reached “pretty soon”, but offered no details.
The trade tensions with Canada have become an issue in the midterm elections, particularly in Michigan and Maine, where Republican candidates have faced pressure over tariffs that have hurt local businesses.
Canada has sought to diversify its trade options and recently welcomed a European Union offer to become an “associate member”.
Carney praised the proposal’s ambition, describing his goal as a “unique alliance” rather than conventional EU membership.

Why did Democrat Haley Stevens just endorse a Republican for US Senate?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
21:00:52 UTC
06:00:52 KST

Why did Democrat Haley Stevens just endorse a Republican for US Senate?
Stevens’s endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers comes after a bitter dispute with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
A Democratic congresswoman has thrown her support behind a Republican in one of the most closely watched races in the US midterm elections, just two days before voters head to the polls.
Haley Stevens, who lost Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary in August, announced on Sunday that she was endorsing Republican Mike Rogers over her own party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed.
The decision follows weeks of tension between the two Democrats over Israel and has provoked a backlash within the party as it fights to win control of Congress and limit President Donald Trump’s power.
Here’s what we know.
Who is Haley Stevens?
Stevens is a Democratic congresswoman from Michigan who narrowly lost the party’s Senate primary to El-Sayed, a former public health official who could become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.
Despite a bitter primary battle, Stevens promised to support El-Sayed and said as recently as Wednesday that she still wanted him to win.
That was despite her fiance, Jason Turkish, a Jewish Democrat and civil rights attorney, announcing that he would vote for Rogers. Turkish – who, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) reports, has donated nearly $250,000 to both Democrats and Republicans during this midterm cycle – accused El-Sayed of anti-Semitism, saying his rhetoric about Israel and the war in Gaza had made Jewish voters feel unsafe.
But on Sunday, Stevens changed her position.
Why did Stevens endorse Republican Mike Rogers?
The decision followed weeks of tension over Israel that became increasingly public in the final days of the campaign.
Stevens is a strong supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed has been an outspoken critic of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza and US military aid to the country.
Their differences were also a major issue during the Democratic primary, when a super PAC affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) spent tens of millions of dollars to back Stevens.
But the latest dispute began last week, when an independent group backing El-Sayed, Rebellion PAC, released an advertisement linking US military aid to Israel to Americans’ struggles with the cost of living.
The ad shows a couple shopping for groceries who decide to put back a carton of eggs because they need to save that money for “killing Palestinians”.
Stevens called the ad anti-Semitic and demanded that El-Sayed condemn it. She also accused him of making similar arguments by suggesting that money spent on Israel could instead go towards schools, healthcare and childcare.
El-Sayed said the ad was not produced by his campaign and that he disagreed with its message, adding that Stevens was trying to relitigate their primary rather than focusing on defeating Rogers.
The tensions came to a head on Sunday, when Stevens and El-Sayed were supposed to attend a church service together in a show of Democratic unity, but Stevens was uninvited.
“Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” she said in a video on X, announcing she was going to endorse Rogers.
“And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today.”
But Democratic Congresswoman Debbie Dingell, who helped organise the event, said she was the one who asked Stevens not to attend, telling The Associated Press that “it had become way too distracting”.
Stevens also criticised El-Sayed’s association with political streamer Hasan Piker, whose uncle, Cenk Uygur, founded the PAC that released the ad.
Stevens told reporters on Sunday, with Rogers standing beside her: “We can’t stand with hate. We can’t stand with Hasan Piker”.
She insisted she was still a Democrat and planned to vote for Democratic candidates in 90 percent of the races on her ballot, but said her Senate vote would go to Rogers.
How have Democrats reacted?
Her decision has drawn an angry response from Democrats, including some of the party’s most senior figures.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called the endorsement a “despicable betrayal”, saying Senate Democrats remained united behind El-Sayed.
He brushed off questions about whether Stevens had betrayed the Democratic Party, saying he was more concerned about the issues facing Michigan voters.
“At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he told reporters. “I’m just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all.”
He urged voters to focus instead on healthcare, civil rights and the differences between his campaign and that of Rogers, who is backed by Trump.
The Democratic National Committee (DNC) issued a blistering statement in response to what the organization described as Stevens’ “last-minute political stunts”.
“Haley Stevens’ disappointing decision to endorse Mike Rogers, a Trump ally who would join Republican efforts to sell out working families, is a betrayal of the values of the Democratic Party,” DNC Chair Ken Martin said. “At a moment when Democrats are united in fighting for Michigan families and standing up to Trump’s agenda, we reject these efforts to sow division within our party.”
The local arm of the DNC, the Michigan Democratic Party (MDP), also had strong words for Haley’s endorsement of Rogers.
“Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers … shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about”, MDP Chair Curtis Hertel said. “We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us”.
Stevens’s decision also prompted resignations within her own team. Her chief of staff for eight years, Justin German, announced that he and several other staff members had stepped down over the endorsement.
“We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens’s decision to support Mike Rogers,” German said in a statement first shared by CNN.
Trump, meanwhile, celebrated her decision.
“Wow, this is BIG!” he wrote in a social media post on Sunday before saying, during a rally in Iowa later in the day, he’d “love” if Stevens joined the Republican Party.
“Haley said what few people are willing to say,” Trump added. “It’s a thing called bravery.”
Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson, who flew with Trump to Iowa, also celebrated Stevens, telling reporters he sent the congresswoman a note after her “courageous” endorsement.
“Haley’s a good person. She’s always been very thoughtful”, Johnson said as he described Michigan’s Senate race as a “contrast” election. “She loves her state. She’s served it as best she could. She’s speaking the truth.”
Could Stevens’s endorsement affect the Michigan Senate race?
El-Sayed and Rogers are competing to replace retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters, in a closely contested race that could help determine which party controls the US Senate.
Republicans currently control both chambers of Congress, and Democrats are hoping to win enough seats to challenge Trump’s agenda and increase scrutiny of his administration.
Stevens defeated El-Sayed in Wayne County, which includes Detroit, and neighbouring Oakland County, drawing support from Black and Jewish Democratic voters. Both counties are Democratic strongholds where turnout could help determine Tuesday’s result.
The question now is whether Stevens’s endorsement could convince some of her supporters to back Rogers, or discourage them from voting altogether.
Polling suggests El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support, according to Reuters.
Early voting began on October 24, before the latest dispute erupted.

UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years, UN chief says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
21:57:16 CET
05:57:16 KST

Nov 1 (Reuters) - The 35-year-old UN peacekeeping mission in the Western Sahara region will come to an end after the Security Council failed to renew its mandate, the UN chief said on Sunday.
Morocco, which claims the Western Sahara as its own, welcomed the decision, while its opponents in the Algeria-backed Polisario Front expressed concern.
The Polisario Front has been seeking an independent state in Western Sahara since former colonial power Spain left in 1976.
A peacekeeping mission, known as MINURSO, has been in place there since a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991.
November 1 would mark the start of the “liquidation phase” of the mission, with assets transported back to troop-contributing countries, UN chief Antonio Guterres said in a statement.
The end of the peacekeeping mission comes a year after the UN Security Council adopted a US-drafted resolution that accepted Rabat’s plan to give the territory autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty as the “most feasible” solution to the conflict.
Russia, which abstained in last year’s vote, this year vetoed another US-backed resolution that would have cemented the UN’s preference for the Moroccan plan while scaling back the peacekeeping force.
The Security Council then defeated a competing Russian resolution, leaving the mission to expire without a new mandate.
Besides monitoring the ceasefire, MINURSO was tasked with organizing a referendum that has never taken place due to disagreements over voter eligibility.
Morocco’s Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita told state media that the mission’s reference to a referendum - the “R” in its name - was an “anachronism”.
Rabat had been informed that Russia was going to block the US-drafted resolution, but saw it as “an opportunity to review certain rules of the game”, he said.
Morocco’s royal palace had said the non-renewal of the mission was a “significant development” towards withdrawing the Western Sahara issue from consideration by the Security Council.
Algeria’s Foreign Ministry on Saturday expressed “deep regret” over the non-renewal, blaming the “excessive bias” of the US towards Morocco’s position.
The Polisario said in a statement it was “concerned at the deadlock in the Security Council meeting.”
(Reporting by North Africa Bureau, editing by Alexander Dziadosz and Chizu Nomiyama )

A multi-day ceasefire between Moscow and Kiev in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky has ended with no violations reported by either side.

Longest truce since 2022

Bulgarians abroad feel neither represented nor representative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:48:20 UTC
05:48:20 KST

News
Presidential Election 2026
Bulgarians abroad feel neither represented nor representative
Hristina Karagueorgieva in the Netherlands: Our compatriots expect Bulgaria to stay on its European path
Sunday 1 November 2026 20:55
Sunday, 1 November 2026, 20:55
Hristina Karagueorgieva
PHOTO Private archive
Font size
On 1 November, Bulgaria went to the polls for the second round of its presidential election. Bulgarian citizens living abroad were among those casting their ballots. What accounts for the low voter turnout in this election? What do our compatriots abroad expect, and what challenges will face the country’s next head of state? We seek answers to these questions in a conversation with Hristina Karagueorgieva, who has been living in the Netherlands for many years. She holds a master’s degree in International Relations and Political Science, works as a translator and is a former editor with Radio Bulgaria’s English-language service.
On election day, she had already cast her ballot in Amsterdam, where, she says, everything was well organised. The low turnout in this election, however, raises the question of what is keeping so many Bulgarians, both at home and abroad, from exercising their right to vote. Is it political apathy, distrust in the country’s governance, or the feeling that their vote will make no difference? Here is Hristina Karagueorgieva’s view:
“Although many of the factors you have listed apply equally to Bulgarians abroad and those living in Bulgaria, and another factor is that we are currently voting in a presidential rather than a parliamentary election (the president’s powers being fairly limited by the Constitution), one thing we cannot overlook is that, for decades, numerous political players in Bulgaria have deliberately sought to restrict the vote from abroad. They have done so through legislative and administrative manoeuvres and restrictions on the number of polling stations, or by trying to suggest that, because we live abroad, we do not understand the situation in Bulgaria well enough to vote, or even that we have no moral right to decide who governs the country.
And this has had an effect. That is why, for Bulgarians abroad, a decisive factor is the strength of their civic consciousness: the understanding that every citizen has inalienable rights and that it is our human, civic and, if you will, patriotic duty to keep voting. By voting, we also stand up for ourselves, because Bulgaria’s foreign policy directly affects us; we vote for the loved ones we have left behind in Bulgaria, and, above all, for that hypothetical Bulgaria of the future, to which we might return one day if such a possibility ever becomes reality.”
PHOTO Private archive
There are also generational differences among Bulgarians abroad. According to our interviewee, younger people are showing an increasingly strong commitment to civic engagement:
“Over the past 15 years, I have noticed greater engagement, precisely because of increased international mobility. And this is most evident among younger people,” Hristina Karagueorgieva observes. “On the one hand, this means the emergence of a young generation with an increasingly developed political and civic culture, which, partly thanks to its Western education, is more inclined to vote. This also explains the degree of moral panic among certain sections of Bulgaria’s political elite, because these young people, having experienced a functioning democracy from within, will sooner or later want to reclaim that still hypothetical Bulgaria which has been stolen from them by what we call the status quo.
What do I mean by that? I mean the exploitation of low levels of civic engagement in Bulgaria as a tool for manipulating institutions in order to preserve the feudal reflexes of the past: total political and economic control exercised for the personal benefit of a privileged few. And, as we all understand, not least because in such an environment they would have no opportunity to fulfil their potential if they returned to Bulgaria.”
According to Radio Bulgaria’s interviewee, this presidential campaign has confronted voters with questions that go far beyond domestic political divisions. The war in Ukraine and recent political developments at home have pushed foreign policy and Bulgaria’s place in a changing international environment to the forefront:
“The election debate was largely shaped by two factors: the war in Ukraine and the parliamentary elections, which sent Bulgaria into a foreign policy turn that was not entirely unexpected. Yet those in power have failed to navigate it effectively, given their almost daily political, communication and strategic blunders. These not only create conceptual and political uncertainty, but also replace reality with moral relativism. This could have serious consequences for Bulgaria.
That is why, whereas foreign policy did not play a particularly significant role in electoral choices until recently, today it is a central issue that can neither be ignored nor obscured by petty domestic political disputes. The question is whether voters have the foresight to recognise the threats facing Bulgaria for what they are today and respond adequately to the geopolitical risks that threaten not merely their everyday lives, but also the possibility of preventing a war in Europe,” Karagueorgieva stresses.
In her view, it is precisely the issue of national security that sets this presidential election apart from previous ones:
“The high level of risk to national security and the two very different strategies for addressing the danger, which reflect two fundamentally different worldviews or visions of Bulgaria’s place in the world. This situation, incidentally, is not new. To some extent, it is a re-enactment of a distinctly Bulgarian tragedy.
On the one hand, we have a relatively small middle class, oriented towards Europe and meritocracy, inclined to uphold universal values such as human rights, the rule of law and an international order based on international law, all of which are rooted, broadly speaking, in the ideals of the Western European Enlightenment.
On the other hand, we have a more traumatised form of pragmatism, a culture of poverty and survival, of learned helplessness and moral compromise, in which people bow to those more powerful than themselves. This is a culture that is currently harming Bulgaria.
In this sense, the great divide today concerns where Bulgaria stands in relation to what we need most at this moment: European solidarity. Does Bulgaria see itself merely as a recipient of solidarity, or as a worthy partner in the face of danger?”
PHOTO Private archive
Do Bulgarians abroad, as a rule, have specific expectations of the next president? Do they feel that the country’s institutions listen to them sufficiently? And if not, what needs to be done to strengthen the ties between Bulgaria and its communities around the world?
“Your question about whether they feel heard by the institutions has a very simple answer: no. This is also because they feel that they are neither represented nor regarded as representative at the same time. In my view, the blame lies with the antagonistic rhetoric directed at Bulgarians abroad within Bulgaria itself,” Hristina Karagueorgieva replies.
“As for their expectations, they want Bulgaria to stay on its European path. And when it comes to relations with Bulgarian communities abroad, what is needed is political will in Bulgaria to stop viewing these communities either as something alien or as a resource expected to rescue the country from its demographic crisis. Such instrumentalisation of human beings is cynical, to say the least. We are all equally human, and we are all equally Bulgarian.”
Regardless of the outcome of the run-off, the next head of state will have to operate in a complex domestic and international environment. What, in our interviewee’s view, will be the greatest challenge facing the new president?
“I would say it will be the need to manage several simultaneous crises: geopolitical, economic, foreign policy and a crisis of trust in institutions. All this is unfolding in a complex environment of hybrid and information warfare, in which Bulgaria’s vulnerabilities, stemming from everything that has failed to happen so far, are becoming increasingly apparent,” Hristina Karagueorgieva from the Netherlands told Radio Bulgaria.
PHOTO Private archive

Bulgaria’s acting President Iotova leads in run-off exit polls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:43:33 UTC
05:43:33 KST

Bulgaria’s acting President Iotova leads in run-off exit polls
Iliana Iotova would become the nation’s first elected female president if results confirm her win on Monday.
Bulgaria’s acting President Iliana Iotova is leading the presidential election run-off, according to exit polls in the race overshadowed by drone attacks on ships off the country’s Black Sea coast.
Iotova, who advocates for dialogue with Moscow and opposes military aid to Ukraine, won just over half the vote in Sunday’s run-off, according to three exit polls, reported Bulgaria’s official news agency, BTA.
Iotova had 51 percent compared to about 44 percent for her rival, Andrey Gyurov, who is backed by the pro-Western opposition.
Exit polls put voter participation at about 27 to 29 percent, slightly higher than the first-round race last week, which had a record-low turnout of 23 percent.
Official results are expected on Monday as ballots are counted for the presidency which is largely ceremonial.
If confirmed, Iotova would become Bulgaria’s first elected female president.
The 61-year-old took over as acting president in January, when her longtime ally Prime Minister Rumen Radev resigned to run in, and win, a parliamentary election.
“I don’t like either of the two candidates,” Krassimira Kostova, a 64-year-old teacher in the capital Sofia, who voted anyway, told the AFP news agency.
Petar Doitchinov, a 67-year-old retired engineer, said he had skipped the first round last week because he expected a run-off. He said he voted for “the lesser evil”, as neither candidate matched his “vision of democracy”.
The vote comes as 21 people remain missing following a series of drone attacks last month on commercial vessels off the country’s Black Sea coast. They are suspected to be spillover from the Russia-Ukraine war.
PM Radev has said that the attacks appear to serve Russian interests and summoned the Russian ambassador, though his government said there was no evidence directly linking them to Moscow.
Both presidential candidates have condemned the attacks and called for a diplomatic end to the war in Ukraine.
Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister, criticised Iotova in a television debate for not explicitly blaming Russia. “Russia must stop its aggression so that the next steps can be taken,” he said.
Iotova said “peace can come only through negotiations”. After voting, she said she wanted “Bulgaria to be strong in a strong Europe” and “sovereign in its decisions”.
In the first round of voting last week, Iotova won 35 percent, with Gyurov on 32 percent – a much narrower gap than the 20-point lead predicted by opinion polls for Iotova.
Political analyst Teodor Slavev told AFP that voters were passing judgement on “Iotova’s unconvincing response regarding Russian threats in the Black Sea”.

Bulgaria’s Iotova takes lead in exit polls in presidential runoff
Parallel vote counts following Bulgaria’s presidential runoff on Sunday show Iliana Iotova and her running mate Kiril Valchev leading their opponents, Andrey Gurov and Georgi Kandev, according to preliminary data released by polling agencies, Qazinform News Agency learned from BTA.
Five agencies were registered to conduct exit polls and parallel vote counts: Myara, Gallup International Balkan, Trend, Alpha Research, and Market Links.
The results reported by 9 p.m. local time showed the following figures:
Trend (100% sample):
- Iliana Iotova/Kiril Valchev – 58.1%
- Andrey Gurov/Georgi Kandev – 38.9%
Market Links (100% sample):
- Andrey Gurov/Georgi Kandev – 56.5%
- Iliana Iotova/Kiril Valchev – 40.6%
Alpha Research (100% sample):
- Iliana Iotova/Kiril Valchev – 57.4%
- Andrey Gurov/Georgi Kandev – 39.6%
Myara (100% sample):
- Iliana Iotova/Kiril Valchev – 58.2%
- Andrey Gurov/Georgi Kandev – 38.6%
Gallup International Balkan (75% sample):
- Iliana Iotova/Kiril Valchev – 56.1%
- Andrey Gurov/Georgi Kandev – 39.1%
Earlier, it was reported that the Iotova-Valchev ticket, backed by the ruling Progressive Bulgaria party and the Bulgarian Socialist Party, among others, came on top in the first round on Oct. 25 with 34.76 percent of the votes.
The Gurov-Kandev ticket, supported by the parties We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria, came second among the 27 candidate pairs with 31.95 percent.

Trump's Republicans scramble to stop Democratic midterms wave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:34:28 UTC

Breadcrumb
Trump's Republicans scramble to stop Democratic midterms wave
Republicans made a final push Sunday to prevent a predicted thumping in US midterm elections where Democrats are gunning to win Congress and impose a first political check on President Donald Trump's unprecedented pursuit of power.
Polls show Democrats are all but certain to take the majority from Republicans in the House of Representatives in Tuesday's vote and have a shot at winning the Senate.
But after a decade of Trump defying political gravity and two years of a second presidency in which he has ridden roughshod over every norm, Democrats remain nervous.
"Nauseously optimistic," Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock told CNN to describe the mood.
Those jitters increased Sunday over an ugly party rift in Michigan, a key battleground where a Democratic congresswoman defected to back Republican Mike Rogers against the Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
The consensus among analysts, however, is that Democrats are surging.
Trump is headlining the Republicans' last-ditch charge, holding rallies for candidates in Iowa and Kansas -- states where ordinarily his party should be confident of victory and not require presidential boosts.
Along with making lurid claims that Democrats will turn the country communist, Trump is dangling the promise of $5,000 payments to everyone in the country if his party wins.
"I feel good," Trump told reporters at his luxury golf club in Florida late Saturday. "The country has never done better."
But an NBC News poll released Sunday showed 60 percent of Americans disapprove of Trump's performance, particularly over high prices exacerbated by his now eight-month, sputtering war against Iran.
Curbing Trump
While Tuesday is election day, early voting has already seen a record 54 million people cast ballots around the country, reflecting the intense political fervor.
Trump's second term has featured a relentless expansion of presidential power, aided by an ever-more docile Republican Party.
Trump has torn down part of the White House to build a ballroom, put his image on money and official buildings, disrupted the global economy with sweeping economic tariffs, and threatened to invade or annex allies like Canada and Greenland.
A big Democratic win would kick start the post-Trump era and the start of the race to replace him in 2028.
Winning the House would put Democrats in charge of the budget and powerful committees set to probe allegations of mass corruption, Trump's links to infamous sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and other explosive topics.
The outcome of the contest for the Senate remains in doubt.
Only a third of the Senate's 100 seats are being contested in these midterms and few of the races were seen as favorable to Democrats. However, with surprisingly strong challenges mounted in deeply Republican states like Texas and Kansas, pollsters now say the odds of a Democratic flip are at minimum even.
A Democratic Senate would be able to shut down Trump's lifetime appointments to courts -- especially the Supreme Court.
Will Trump accept results?
The midterms have seen about $11 billion spent on advertising, with large chunks coming from individual mega-donors.
Elon Musk, a close Trump ally who led the so-called DOGE effort in dismantling entire government departments, has given a staggering nearly half-billion dollars to help get Republicans elected.
The campaigns have also been marked by blistering language and insults, led by Trump who falsely accused leading Democrats of being everything from vegans to jihadists.
And hanging over everything is concern that Republicans will refuse to accept a loss, leading to a constitutional crisis similar to Trump's attempt to overturn his 2020 presidential election defeat.
A federal judge on Sunday tossed out an extremely unusual attempt by Trump's administration to hold up a potential victory by a Democratic candidate for Senate in Alaska.
The lawsuit contended that if Democrat Mary Peltola beats the Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, the result should not be certified because there is a third, minor candidate also called Dan Sullivan, allegedly recruited by Democrats to siphon off votes.

Russia's giant new radar in Kaliningrad raises alarm in NATO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:34:00 UTC
05:34:00 KST

Russia's new suspected radar in Kaliningrad could spy deep into Europe
November 1, 2026
The Kremlin is getting closer to opening its 'new eye' on Europe. Construction of a towering radar complex is almost complete in Russia's highly militarized exclave of Kaliningrad, according to reports.
From above, the three radiating arms of the sprawling facility – each more than 500 meters long – look like some sort of alien lifeform has left its mark on an otherwise undisturbed stretch of forested nature reserve. You could actually compare it to a landing platform or launch pad for Moscow's massive intelligence-gathering network.
While Russia has not confirmed it is building the structure, security expert Vaidotas Malinionis said the radar will be so big, it will be able to see beyond the earth's curvature. The retired commander from Lithuania told DW the over-the-horizon (OTH) radar network near Gvardeysk will have a surveillance range of about 3,000 kilometers, allowing Moscow to peer into almost every corner of Europe, as well as right across Ukraine.
The system would reportedly allow Russia to intercept satellite communications and detect aircraft movements and ballistic missiles.
"The goal and the purpose of this radar is observation of long-distance targets and early warning capabilities. We still don't know if it is operationally capable of doing that, but it is definitely being constructed right now," he added.
Mass surveillance system
The British newspaper The Times reports that the systems are primarily intended for the detection and jamming of electronic signals – citing the Finnish-Polish space and defense technology company ICEYE.
"They would be able to use it in offensive operations, to get more information about specific targets," explained Malinionis.
"And if they were able to get an early warning about the movement of NATO troops, in the case of an invasion on NATO's eastern frontier, then they would gain more time for decision-making."
Speaking to DW from the shores of the Baltic Sea, Latvian geopolitical analyst Evija Djatkovica warned there is a significant downside for NATO to this old Soviet technology being revived when it comes to the increased use of new tech in the warfare of today.
"It will help Russia close existing loopholes in detecting low-flying objects, making the rapidly developing integration of drones into regional defense doctrines less effective," she claimed.
Electronic warfare hub
The Times report goes on to say that ICEYE sees Russia's expansion of its OTH radar system as proof that Kaliningrad is being developed into a hub for advanced military sensors and electronic warfare systems.
"The new radar signals an intensifying contest between Russia and NATO for military supremacy and control of the Kaliningrad region," Djatkovica underlined.
"This is a potentially dangerous situation, since further militarization on both sides could be expected and, at some point, a preemptive strike becomes an option to deny the other side an unacceptable advantage over the region,” she warned.
Russia has already alerted NATO it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if the Western alliance attempted to blockade Kaliningrad. The potential flashpoint and Russian outpost is situated on the Baltic Sea, wedged between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania– on the very doorstep of the alliance's eastern flank.
The exclave is only 200 kilometers from west to east and 100 kilometers from north to south. However, from what Malinionis asserted, Russia's smallest federal region or oblast packs a punch.
"According to some sources, they have the capability to deploy up to 100 nuclear warheads in Kaliningrad. And some sources say they have already started deploying some there – although that is yet to be confirmed," the former commander pointed out.
ICEYE claims to have discovered another large circular antenna complex some 50 kilometers west of Gvardeysk, near the city of Chernyakhovsk, according to the German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ). More than 20 signal and electronic warfare facilities are reportedly peppered throughout the Kaliningrad region.
Satellite images also reveal new shelters for fighter jets at the Kaliningrad-Chkalovsk military airfield, according to the FAZ report. Other images show launch pads at the mobile S-400 surface-to-air missile site in Baltiysk, meaning the systems could well be operational.
"These factors clearly depict the strategic importance of territories around Kaliningrad for both Russia and NATO," said Djatkovica. "For Russia, among other things, Kaliningrad's geographic position and nuclear arsenal stationed there allow it to project threats against most European capitals."
This is where the gargantuan radar comes into play, according to her. "Because of the radar's long reach, other European regions from North to West will also become more exposed to Russia's surveillance and military actions."
Motivation for the West
She sighed, saying the good news is that every escalatory step that Russia takes, with repercussions for European countries even further away from its borders, the more the whole continent takes Moscow seriously as a direct threat.
"Russia's malign signals should motivate the West to keep up with rearmament, which, in turn, will make NATO and Europe's collective deterrence more credible."
Djatkovica used the example of Poland, which has been transforming its offshore wind farm in the Baltic Sea into NATO surveillance infrastructure.
In another step towards integrating newer technologies, German arms producer Rheinmetall is building Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites in conjunction with the firm ICEYE. They beam down precise pictures of troop movements and enemy positions, even at night or in bad weather.
The images will be used on NATO's eastern flank and by the Bundeswehr brigade stationed in Lithuania. The first SAR satellites are set to be launched into orbit on a SpaceX rocket in early 2027.
Malinionis agreed that adaptation is the most important lesson to be learnt for European leaders in times of Russian aggression. But he had another point to make. "There is also one disadvantage for this new Russian radar. Because it's so huge, it's a pretty easy target!"

Gyurov Says Bulgaria Must Unite as He Accepts Presidential Election Defeat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:32:01 UTC
05:32:01 KST

Presidential candidate Andrey Gyurov said after losing the runoff that Bulgarian society must seek unity rather than division, while stressing that his political responsibility would continue beyond the end of the campaign.
Gyurov thanked the citizens who voted, including those who supported other candidates, as well as his family, vice-presidential running mate Georgi Kandev, the initiative committee and the political parties that backed their ticket. He also congratulated the winners of the election.
Addressing supporters who might be disappointed by the result, he said he believed their efforts had not been wasted and that the best was yet to come. "We have created a truly good platform that can be built upon," Gyurov said.
He stressed that the end of the campaign did not mean an end to their responsibilities. "We must hold the state accountable, because it ought to work for the Bulgarian citizens," he said.
Gyurov acknowledged that he had not anticipated such a wide margin and said his team would first examine the data before conducting its own analysis. He accepted the outcome despite the differences between exit polls and parallel vote counts, adding that the campaign's initial objective of expanding their support had been achieved.
"This is how the Bulgarian citizens have voted," he said, emphasizing that the results had to be accepted as they stood.
Asked by NOVA whether the gap between him and Iliana Yotova amounted to a failure, Gyurov said it was too early to draw conclusions before reviewing the figures. He added that his team had not yet considered what would happen after the election and that the immediate priority was to analyze the results.
He attributed the defeat to his campaign's failure to set the agenda around the issues raised during meetings with citizens. Nevertheless, he said the campaign had achieved its aim of offering an alternative for Bulgaria, with the first-round results demonstrating that it had succeeded in reaching a broader audience.
Gyurov also rejected the idea that his discussions with political leaders had focused on securing their support. He said the conversations had concerned shared objectives and the campaign itself, rather than political alliances. Asked about his future political plans ahead of the upcoming local elections, he reiterated that his approach was based on common values.
He identified the goals of his political work as building a strong Bulgaria and a dignified state where people could feel secure about their children's future. He warned that the country faced numerous challenges and difficult times ahead, making cooperation around shared objectives particularly important.
Speaking at a briefing after the polls closed, Gyurov also marked the Day of the Bulgarian Enlighteners, greeting those who had helped preserve Bulgarian identity through their dedication to the country's spirit and culture.
Kandev thanked the voters and everyone who had supported their presidential ticket. He said that during the month and a half spent traveling across Bulgaria, the candidates had held numerous meetings and encountered people's hopes, aspirations and everyday difficulties.
"The struggle does not end with this election," Kandev said, congratulating the winners and urging citizens to remain vigilant and check whether the promises made during the campaign were fulfilled. He ended his remarks with a prayer for Bulgaria.
The latest parallel vote counts from polling agencies Trend and Myara showed Yotova and her running mate Kiril Valchev ahead of Gyurov and Kandev by nearly 20 percentage points. With the full samples processed, Trend put the winning ticket at 58.1%, against 38.9% for Gyurov and Kandev. Myara reported 58.2% for Yotova and Valchev and 38.6% for their opponents. The share of voters who selected the "I do not support anyone" option stood at 3% in Trend's count and 3.2% in Myara's.
Alpha Research's 100% parallel count put Yotova at 57.4% and Gyurov at 39.6%.

UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years, UN chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:26:58 UTC
05:26:58 KST

UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years, UN chief says
The 35-year-old UN peacekeeping mission in the Western Sahara region will come to an end after the Security Council failed to renew its mandate, the UN chief said on Nov 1.
Morocco, which claims the Western Sahara as its own, welcomed the decision, while its opponents in the Algeria-backed Polisario Front expressed concern.
The Polisario Front has been seeking an independent state in Western Sahara since former colonial power Spain left in 1976.
A peacekeeping mission, known as MINURSO, has been in place there since a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991.
November 1 would mark the start of the “liquidation phase” of the mission, with assets transported back to troop-contributing countries, UN chief Antonio Guterres said in a statement.
The end of the peacekeeping mission comes a year after the UN Security Council adopted a US-drafted resolution that accepted Rabat’s plan to give the territory autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty as the “most feasible” solution to the conflict.
Russia, which abstained in last year’s vote, this year vetoed another US-backed resolution that would have cemented the UN’s preference for the Moroccan plan while scaling back the peacekeeping force.
The Security Council then defeated a competing Russian resolution, leaving the mission to expire without a new mandate.
Besides monitoring the ceasefire, MINURSO was tasked with organising a referendum that has never taken place due to disagreements over voter eligibility.
Morocco’s Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita told state media that the mission’s reference to a referendum - the “R” in its name - was an “anachronism”.
Rabat had been informed that Russia was going to block the US-drafted resolution, but saw it as “an opportunity to review certain rules of the game”, he said.
Morocco’s royal palace had said the non-renewal of the mission was a “significant development” towards withdrawing the Western Sahara issue from consideration by the Security Council.
Algeria’s Foreign Ministry on Oct 31 expressed “deep regret” over the non-renewal, blaming the “excessive bias” of the US towards Morocco’s position.
The Polisario said in a statement it was “concerned at the deadlock in the Security Council meeting”. REUTERS

Yotova and Radev Hail Election Result as Mandate for More Reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
20:19:46 UTC
05:19:46 KST

Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Bulgaria would not return to backroom political deals and the practices of the transition period after Iliana Yotova and Kiril Valchev won the presidential runoff, describing the result as confirmation of the government's political course and a mandate for more decisive reforms.
Speaking after the polls closed, Radev said Bulgarians had chosen peace, stability and a clear path forward rather than a return to the past. He congratulated Yotova and Valchev for conducting what he called a dignified and positive campaign despite the hostility surrounding them.
* "Today, the Bulgarian people chose the future over the past; they chose peace and a stable, clear path forward,"* Radev said.
Addressing Yotova, with whom he said he had known and worked for 10 years, the prime minister expressed confidence that she would be able to fulfill the responsibilities of the presidency during a difficult period.
* "I am convinced that you will be a worthy president of Bulgaria during these difficult times - a period in which you are called upon to bear this heavy responsibility,"* he said.
Radev thanked Bulgarians who had voted despite the bad weather, as well as Progressive Bulgaria's supporters, party members and youth organizations, crediting them with an impressive mobilization and a strong result achieved in a short period.
He said the outcome confirmed that the government was pursuing the right course and called for more active reforms as the country concluded a difficult election year.
* "We are concluding a challenging election year, but the direction is clear - there is no going back to backroom deals or the shadows of the transition,"* Radev declared.
The prime minister also dismissed suggestions that Progressive Bulgaria's support was declining, pointing to the more than one million votes received by the presidential ticket. He urged political commentators to wait for the final results before drawing conclusions about changes in the party's support.
* "After all, we have secured over a million votes—and this in a presidential election, not a parliamentary one,"* he said.
Radev also addressed the possibility of protests against the government during the debate and adoption of the budget. He said citizens had the right to protest, but argued that public dissatisfaction should not automatically trigger early elections.
* "People protest about the sun, people protest about plants, Asen Vassilev will protest to the bitter end over the budget, but that does not mean we should hold new elections every four or five months simply because some people are protesting,"* he said.
He called on political actors to respect democratic procedures and election results, adding that some who professed their commitment to democracy did not follow its principles.
Newly elected President Iliana Yotova thanked voters for participating in the election and for placing their trust in her and Valchev. She also acknowledged those who had not supported their ticket, saying their concerns and expectations would be examined.
Yotova thanked Progressive Bulgaria, Radev and the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) for their backing, and expressed particular gratitude to the members of her initiative committee.
* "Despite the intense pressure and the hatred, not a single person gave up or betrayed us; they were with us every step of the way. For me, this represents an immense responsibility,"* she said.
She described her campaign as positive and said her team had avoided personal attacks, hate speech and divisive rhetoric, although she claimed the same approach had not been taken by her opponents.
Yotova said her campaign had focused on incomes, peace and the challenges facing the country, adding that voters had understood its message. She criticized Gyurov for conducting what she described as an aggressive campaign targeting her personally.
* "I cannot fathom who misled Mr. Gyurov into launching an aggressive campaign directed personally at me; the people have said, 'That is not the way,'"* she said.
Yotova added that the election result reflected public support for dialogue rather than division and attacks against political opponents. She said she had received a telephone call from Gyurov, who congratulated her on the victory and expressed confidence that she would be a president capable of engaging with everyone.
The newly elected president also referred to earlier statements by Asen Vassilev, who had predicted that his political formation would win an absolute majority in the parliamentary election and later said Gyurov would become president.
* "A few months ago, before the parliamentary elections, Mr. Vassilev claimed that his political formation would secure an absolute majority. A few months later, he stated that Mr. Gyurov would be the country's new president. I leave the rest, and the answer, to you,"* Yotova said.
Asked whether anyone might influence her conduct as president, she said her political experience had left no room for others to dictate her decisions.
* "As for my conduct, I believe that with a political career spanning nearly 30 years, no one has yet come along who could tell me what to do,"* she declared.
Yotova also said she would conduct a detailed assessment of the concerns and expectations of voters who had selected the "I do not support anyone" option.
Valchev, who will serve as vice president, thanked those who had voted for the ticket and said the runoff had brought substantially more support for the prospect of Bulgaria having its first woman president. He also thanked Bulgarians living abroad who had taken part in the election.
He identified engagement with Bulgarian communities overseas, greater participation by young people in public life and improving the country's international image as priorities for his work.
Valchev reaffirmed his commitment to Bulgaria's European identity and democratic principles.
* "I will serve as an additional guarantor, from within the presidency, for Bulgaria’s place in Europe, where it has been for 14 centuries, and for democracy in our country,"* he said.
He also pledged to encourage young people to take part in discussions about the country's future, saying they would be invited to the presidential institution to present their ideas and proposals. Valchev said state institutions should work to overcome divisions and bring more citizens together around common national objectives.
* "Because the most important thing is to bring as many people as possible into the fold of the Bulgarian cause. It is said that a divided kingdom falls into ruin—something we have witnessed in Bulgaria over the last nearly 40 years,"* he added.
Valchev said he would also work to encourage young Bulgarians to remain in the country and those who had left to return.
The final parallel vote counts published by Trend and Myara showed a lead of nearly 20 percentage points for the Yotova-Valchev ticket. Trend put their support at 58.1%, compared with 38.9% for Gyurov and Georgi Kandev, while Myara reported 58.2% against 38.6%.
The "I do not support anyone" option received 3% according to Trend and 3.2% in Myara's count.

Zelensky announces visit by Turkish energy companies to Ukraine
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky said this in an interview with CNN Türk following his visit to Turkey, according to Ukrinform.
“Next week we will host energy companies in Ukraine. And I am sure that joint commitments, productions and projects will be developed with Türkiye in this field,” he said.

Judge orders Trump administration to stop threatening election officials

Judge orders Trump administration to stop threatening election officials
A federal judge has ordered the administration of US President Donald Trump to stop intimidating election officials, who refuse to follow its instructions on handling ballots during the midterms on November 3.
In July, the Department of Justice (DOJ) sent letters to all 50 states warning that election officers, who would knowingly allow non-citizens to take part in the vote, could face criminal liability. Last month, the agency contacted the counties in California demanding them to identify the illegal aliens on the lists of registered voters or face potential legal action.
On Friday, US District Judge Trina Thompson, who is based in California, ruled that the Trump administration was operating outside of its constitutional authority and likely violated the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which prohibits “attempting to intimidate, threaten or coerce” officials, facilitating the election process.
“Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by non-citizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters,” she argued.
The judge issued a temporary restraining order that expires on November 16, almost two weeks after the election day on Tuesday.
The ruling came in response to a lawsuit filed just a day earlier by labor unions and other groups, who blamed the Trump administration for interfering in the administration of the midterms.
Later on Saturday, the Department of Justice challenged Thompson’s decision at the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals in California.
A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement that “the judge issued an order against the federal government without even waiting to hear from the US, while in other cases the Department’s own urgent election claims are delayed by judges until after Election Day.”
On Friday, the Trump administration lost an appeal against an earlier decision by another federal judge, who denied the DOJ’s request for California to block more that 20,000 ballots from alleged non-citizens, arguing that it “violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections.”
The NBC News average of national polls, published on Sunday, suggested that 52% percent of Americans preferred a Democrat-controlled Congress, with 44% being in favor of a Republican one.
