====================================================================================================

How Saintly, the 'horse from heaven', won the Melbourne Cup 30 years ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
18:40:37 UTC
03:40:37 KST

Saintly's 1996 Melbourne Cup win: How 'the horse from heaven' won Bart Cummings's 10th cup
Legendary racing trainer and "Cups King" Bart Cummings rarely showed emotion after big wins or defeats, and he always told people not to get too attached to racehorses.
But even Cummings had exceptions to the rule, and one was the "horse from heaven", Saintly.
The big-striding chestnut gelding with an army of fans gave Cummings a landmark triumph 30 years ago this week in the Melbourne Cup at Flemington.
Going into the big race, Cummings had already won a record nine Cups (his nearest rival at the time was French trainer Etienne de Mestre back in the 1800s), and his campaign to win a 10th proved to be an absolute masterclass.
In his biography, My Life, Cummings told readers there was no particular secret to winning Melbourne Cups.
"There's no magic," he wrote. "There's relentless work, discipline, adherence to your methods and plans, taking a genuine interest in the horse's welfare and above all else, plain commonsense."
Do all this, Cummings believed, and "you make your own luck".
There may not have been any magic, but there was a plan. A 10,000-metre prep plan, to be precise.
Cummings believed horses that ran in the cup should have completed a series of lead-up runs, and have a total of 10,000m or race distance in their legs before Melbourne Cup day.
A run on Derby Day in the Mackinnon Stakes (2,000m) or the Archer Stakes (2,500m) was usually the cherry on top, training-wise, before the Melbourne Cup three days later.
One person who saw this plan in action up close was Joe Agresta, who was trackwork rider for Cummings for 34 years. When he first saw Saintly for the first time, he wasn't overly impressed.
"He was a nice horse but he was a gangly type of three-year-old," Agresta says.
"Then he came out and he just blitzed them in the Carbine Club Stakes [at Flemington].
"He went back [to Sydney], and [Bart] built him up, then he came back and won the Australian Cup."
Cummings had a beautiful property near the Nepean River in Western Sydney called Princes Farm. The great trainer unofficially referred to it as "horse heaven".
Saintly was bred at Princes Farm and was born there in 1992, the year after Cummings's ninth Cup win with Let's Elope.
When Cummings nearly went bankrupt with the collapse of the Cups King syndicate in the late 1980s, Malaysian businessman Dato Tan Chin Nam was among those who helped support him to keep him afloat.
Chin Nam had owned Think Big, which had won back-to-back Melbourne Cups for Cummings in 1974 and 1975.
When Saintly was born, Cummings gave the businessman a half-share in gratitude for his help.
Saintly's three-year-old season included the Carbine Club Stakes win, and then the Australian Cup win in March 1996 marked another win at Flemington, where his long stride had plenty of room to move.
A few more runs in Sydney followed before Cummings gave Saintly a decent spell. He wouldn't return to the track for nearly five months.
Cummings's lesson learned
For his most important campaign, Saintly was running every couple of weeks in Sydney. After three runs, it was clear Cummings had expectations, but what would come next?
By this time, the permanent jockey had long been Darren Beadman, a top operator who had ridden Cummings's eighth Melbourne Cup winner on Kingston Rule in 1990.
It was early October when Saintly had his fourth and fifth runs, over the space of a weekend at Randwick in Sydney.
The chestnut ran second in the Craven Plate on the Saturday and third in the Metropolitan on Monday, although in the latter race Saintly hit the front but was flat at the end, out-finished by Hula Flight and Nothin Leica Dane.
"Bart rang me and said, 'I'm sending Saintly down [to Melbourne]. I want you to freshen up the horse, I've learned something about him,'" Agresta says.
Saintly was quickly jumping out of his skin, but Cummings didn't want to run him in the Caulfield Cup in mid-October. Instead he aimed him at the Cox Plate.
The two most famous races in Australia are the Cox Plate and the Melbourne Cup.
The Cox Plate (run over 2,040m) is known as the weight-for-age championship of Australasia, where the race does what it says on the box. Horses are given a certain weight depending on their age, with female horses (fillies and mares) given a discount because they are racing against males (colts, horses and geldings).
Then there is the Melbourne Cup, which is a handicap run over 3,200m. This kind of race sees horses given a weight (or handicap), decided by a range of factors including age and past performances. Generally it sees more weight for better horses and less weight for less experienced runners.
At least until earlier this century, the point of the exercise was to produce a hypothetical result where every runner finished together.
The reality is usually far different, but that's the aim of the game.
Up to 1996, only three horses (Nightmarch in 1929, Phar Lap in 1930 and Rising Fast in 1954) had won both the Cox Plate and the Melbourne Cup in the same year.
That year, before it was commonplace, Cummings opted for the Cox Plate as the lead-up for the Melbourne Cup, not the grand final.
The Cox Plate
Some thought the Moonee Valley circuit would be too tight for Saintly. Cummings wanted a solid run in the legs of his star horse of the spring.
When the race began, Beadman kept Saintly quiet back in about sixth place near the fence.
The field began to stretch out. At halfway, he was 10 lengths behind the leaders. Saintly was still sixth 700m out when Beadman began to urge his mount forward.
By the 500, Saintly was making ground going five-wide. Rounding the corner, Filante was leading on the fence narrowly from Juggler then All Our Mob. Saintly went four, five then six-wide as he briefly was on the wrong lead leg.
Watching from the stands, Agresta thought that might be the end of his chances, but once Beadman balanced Saintly up, he moved in. As the crowd roared, the gaps narrowed further, and all four horses were in it. It was Filante leading and Saintly closing.
Saintly rattled down the outside, and they called for a photo as the crowd buzzed about the frantic finish. "From where I was I thought he just got beat, but they said he won," Agresta recalls.
The lesson Cummings had learned was that Saintly didn't back up, so instead of running on Derby Day, the trainer had Agresta gallop him at Flemington.
"The clocker was a guy called Des Spain, and he said to Bart afterwards, 'You know that horse ran a quicker time than [the sprinters] go down the straight [for 1,200],'" Agresta says.
"Bart said something silly like his watch must be broken, but that's when he knew Saintly had a great chance in the Cup."
Chin Nam was fascinated with the game of chess, and so his horses ran in eye-catching colours. The black and white checks were like a chessboard, while the sleeves were gold or yellow to represent the sun.
Would the sun rise on another Cummings Cup win?
The Cup itself
Only three years on from Vintage Crop's famous Flemington win, another Irish-trained horse was favourite for the Cup.
Oscar Schindler had won the Irish St Leger, and come third in the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe, so he was seen as the class horse in the race. But would he handle Australian conditions?
Saintly was not a frontrunner, but he drew barrier three for the Cup. This was a simple set-up for Cummings's horse.
"Bart never gave any instructions, but Darren knew he had to bury him [Saintly] away," Agresta says, meaning a spot on the inside.
Cummings didn't want his horse too close to the lead.
Beadman quickly had Saintly out of the ruck and into position on the fence, and by the time the field thundered past the post the first time, the gelding was neatly placed in sixth, right on the fence.
Grey Shot led from Few Are Chosen, Court of Honour and Centico. Not much changed for much of the race.
At halfway Saintly was perfectly placed, still sixth on the fence. The big chestnut had not spent a penny, until about the 800m, when Beadman shifted him off the fence and in a few strides he was into the clear.
"We were up in the stands watching it, and when Darren Beadman pulled out at the 800, he pulled out three-deep, I said, 'This is home,' because there was no way he'd pull that horse out three-deep if he didn't think it was travelling well," Agresta says.
Grey Shot still led at the turn with Nothin Leica Dane coming, but Saintly was in clear air, and he loved the long Flemington straight.
He hit the front at the 300, and soon after moved clear, as nothing could go with him.
"When Beadman let him down, he just sprinted away. It was a great effort by [Beadman and] the horse, and it was probably Bart's greatest training feat. With this horse, everything he did seemed to work," Agresta says.
Flemington erupted, as Beadman rode Saintly past the post, clear of Count Chivas and Skybeau, to clinch Cummings's 10th Cup. Oscar Schindler finished 15th.
It was a sign of Cummings's experience, that even 31 years after his first Cup win, he was willing to go away from his tried-and-trusted plan because of his understanding of Saintly.
"When I first started working for him, we won a couple of Group 1s and we were in the mounting yard jumping around," Agresta says.
"[Bart] said, 'Don't be like those other idiots [celebrating wildly]. We celebrate in our own time.'"
But after another Melbourne Cup win, all bets were off.
"We went to Crown Casino [that night], there were about 30 of us," Agresta recalls.
"Bart and Dato Tan Chin Nam were drinking wine, and they started singing Danny Boy!
"It was a good night. Bart never worried too much about being beaten, but I could see it: the relief and the happiness on his face; it was something special [for him] to win the Cup with Saintly."
'He nearly died': Illness in Japan
The next challenge was overseas, with the Japan Cup in Tokyo, less than a month on from the Melbourne Cup. But Saintly would not get to test himself against the best.
Saintly fell ill the night before the race. Vets would not treat the horse without the trainer's permission, because it would mean Saintly could not run in the Japan Cup. Cummings gave the OK.
"The next morning I was crying," Agresta says. "Bart said, 'What's the matter with you?'
"I said, 'I'm devastated.' He said, 'Don’t worry son, it wasn't meant to be.'"
Asked how serious the illness was in Japan, Agresta pauses and says: "He nearly died."
Saintly came back to Australia, and began another campaign at Caulfield in early 1997 in the CF Orr Stakes. Once again he came from behind, still five lengths back at the 250m mark before storming home to win.
But within a week, he had bowed a tendon in training, and that race at Caulfield proved to be his last.
Agresta says Cummings denied that he had a particular love for Saintly, but his actions say otherwise.
"Living Legends wanted him [Saintly] to come there for them to look after him. He [Bart] said no," Agresta says.
"Graham Salisbury wanted him for the clerk of the course. [Bart] said no, 'He's going to live the rest of his life on my property.'"
And he did.
Saintly lived at Princes Farm, or horse heaven if you prefer, until he died in 2016 at the age of 24.
Cummings himself was already gone, dying at his home a year earlier. He had won two more Melbourne Cups, with Rogan Josh in 1999 and Viewed in 2008. Both horses ran on Derby Day.
Dato Tan Chin Nam died in 2018. He won a fourth Melbourne Cup with Bart, Cummings' final victory with Viewed in the famous chessboard colours.
Cummings' Flemington stables are also gone, turned into apartments. But there is still a Saintly Place, fittingly a section of the Flemington course Cummings made his own, complete with a life-sized statue of him.
And while no-one will ever forget the Cups King, neither will anyone who loves racing forget the "horse from heaven".

traditional bamboo scaffolding and tea-waste panels shape impromptu projects’ pagoda in macau
referencing traditional pagoda forms, the temporary installation integrates a slender bamboo frame and translucent fabric skin along macau's shoreline.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Impromptu Projects erects Bamboo Pagoda along Sai Van Lake
Sited on the shoreline of Sai Van Lake in Macau, Bamboo Pagoda is a 13-meter-tall temporary pavilion designed by local practice Impromptu Projects, led by Rita Machado and João Ó. The installation draws directly from Macau’s vernacular bamboo scaffolding, a building technique listed on the city’s Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2017, reinterpreting construction-grade craft into a contemporary waterfront pavilion for contemplation.
OCTAGONAL SKELETON INTEGRATES TRANSLUCENT BAMBOO FABRIC SKIN
The design by Impromptu Projects studio references classical pagoda geometries and Taoist concepts of equilibrium, structured over an octagonal footprint that tapers as it ascends. Slender structural bamboo culms form the exposed load-bearing skeleton, bound using traditional scaffolding lashing methods. A semi-translucent skin of bamboo fabric wraps the framework, filtering natural light and diffusing the vertical profile. Grounding the structure, the floor surface is laid with composite panels manufactured by Macau-based firm Zence Object Technology (CHAZENCE), composed of recycled tea waste and discarded wood chips. Integrated solar panels power the project’s architectural spotlights off the municipal grid, combining intangible cultural heritage with circular material systems.
project info:
name: Bamboo Pagoda
architects: Impromptu Projects | @impromptu_projects
lead architects: Rita Machado, João Ó, Uieong To, Alexandre Marquês
bamboo scaffolding: Seng Kei Pang Chong
client: Ephemera Public Space Cooperative
location: Sai Van Lake, Macau SAR, China
area: 25 sqm
photographers: Tang Kuok Hou, Gonçalo Lobo Pinheiro

I had a shameful secret only a few people knew about. I still think about it every night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
18:33:43 UTC
03:33:43 KST

Would you tell a friend their partner is cheating? Are you prepared to turn someone's life support off? Should violent prisoners be offered voluntary assisted dying? To find out what happens when you're stuck between a rock and a hard place, watch Insight episode Moral Dilemmas on SBS On Demand.
Last year, I faced a situation that still makes me feel guilty to think about to this day.
My second British Bulldog Oskar bounced into my life as a puppy seven years ago, when my first, Maggie, was almost two — as I wanted her to have a friend when I was at work.
At first, they were in love with each other, and Maggie took on her big-sister role very seriously. But two year later, things changed for the worse.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Oskar, who was always sweet and caring, would become vicious if another dog came close while we were out walking.
Then it started happening at home.
At first, it was a growl here and there towards Maggie, then Oskar started attacking her if she came too close to me.
I was constantly breaking up full-blown dog fights, and I felt completely lost as I couldn't understand the change in his behaviour.
I researched a lot online and sought advice from trainers and a vet behaviourist. I was constantly crying my eyes out at the vet, asking for answers.
I would have to lock up the dogs when people came over because Oskar would not let Maggie near anyone.
We started him on anti-anxiety medication to try to calm him.
It helped a little bit, but it also made him drowsy most of the time; it was not the life he deserved.
'I was walking on glass in my own home'
It all came to a head last year when Oskar started attacking Maggie, who would be fast asleep, the minute I walked through the front door.
At this point, I was walking on glass in my own home.
I was always on edge anticipating the dogs' interactions and living in a heightened state of fear a fight was going to break out.
This is when I started thinking about one of the biggest decisions of my life: did I need to rehome Oskar?
Guilt and embarrassment
I reached out to multiple rescue groups and did not hear back from one.
I felt guilty and embarrassed about my decision.
Would people judge me? In my head raced questions that I thought people might think: 'How could you pick one dog over the other dog? Did you try this? Did you do this?'
I probably would have judged someone back in the day for the same thing. But until you’re put in that position, no one knows what it's like.
Luckily, a vet nurse friend put me in contact with a dog trainer named Michael, who I now refer to as our guardian angel.
After a long phone conversation with him, he offered to take Oskar and retrain him with the goal of eventually rehoming him to a loving one-dog household.
We then had a longer conversation in person at his house and then I made an appointment with my behaviourist vet to make sure I was making the right decision before I relinquished my legal rights over Oskar to Michael.
She said it was probably the best option Oskar would ever have and that he was very lucky to have the opportunity.
'The hardest day of my life'
The day I dropped Oskar off at Michael's house was the hardest of my life.
He was my child, and I felt like I had let him down. To this day, I still feel like this.
Oskar stayed with Michael for six months, and in that time, he became a different dog. And this time, for the better.
Michael and I were very picky with who would get Oskar but eventually, a man with experience with bulldogs and aggressive dogs applied to adopt him.
After a two-week trial, the man decided he would keep him and now Oskar has a forever home where he receives lots of attention from three children and walks along the beach every night.
And as the family live two suburbs away from me, I still get to see Oskar.
With my hand on my heart, I believe he is loved and much happier.
The right decision
Rehoming Oskar is something I still don't really talk about and not many people know about it.
I don't have children but to me, it felt like I had to pick which child to keep. I couldn't cope and I really judged myself for it.
I still replay the situation in my head every night. But at the end of the day, I know it was the right decision.
Maggie is a different dog — she plays with toys again and is no longer on edge. And I am no longer in a high anxiety state needing to keep the dogs separated and watching over them at all hours.
But in my heart, I still have two beautiful bulldogs who I love very much.
I just wish we could all be together.

Saudi-backed Yemeni forces claim to have thwarted advancing Houthis
Yemen has claimed its army has been able to stop an advance by Houthi militants in the southwest of the country.
The hostilities between Yemen and its coalition allies and the Iranian-backed Ansar Allah movement escalated in September when the Shiite group seized the strategically important Red Sea port cities of Mocha and Dhubab as well as Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The Houthis have since also encircled the country’s third-largest city, Taiz, with forces loyal to the internationally recognized government trapped inside.
According to Asharq Al-Awsat newspaper, which allegedly has close ties to the Saudi royal family, the Houthis mounted an offensive along the border between Lahij and Taiz governorates on Friday.
However, Saudi-backed troops reportedly pushed back the advancing militants, with airstrikes and artillery fire disrupting the Houthis’ supply lines, and staged a counteroffensive.
Fighting has also continued around the besieged city of Taiz.
Conflicting reports have been coming in regarding the situation in the north of Yemen over the weekend.
On Saturday, the internationally recognized government announced that its troops had recaptured positions in the northern governorate of al-Jawf, which borders Saudi Arabia. The Houthis, in turn, said that they had thwarted advances in the same governorate, as well as in neighboring Marib.
In recent weeks, the Houthis have claimed responsibility for multiple missile and drone strikes targeting strategic facilities in Saudi Arabia, including the Ras Tanura oil refinery, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, as well as a military installation in Najran region.
In a statement posted on X last Saturday, the Shiite group’s spokesman, Yahya Saree, stressed that the Houthis were conducting such attacks in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes on Yemen.
Ansar Allah’s representative warned that strikes on Saudi territory would continue until Riyadh ended its “aggression” and lifted a blockade it had imposed on the neighboring country.
After the Houthis seized large stretches of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and territory around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in September, government troops mounted a counteroffensive, claiming to have recaptured key positions near the vital shipping route connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.
Meanwhile, Riyadh has stepped up its air support, intensifying strikes on Houthi-held territory.
Yemen has remained locked in a civil war since 2014, with the situation further aggravated by a Saudi-led intervention launched the following year. Large-scale fighting largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022 but flared up again in July after Saudi-backed government forces struck the Houthi-held Sanaa Airport.

The Australian weaving magic with sexy basket movie Wicker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

The Australian weaving magic with Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård
When the trailer dropped for darkly comic fable Wicker, the image of Olivia Colman's fisherwoman in post-coital bliss with Alexander Skarsgård's strawman sent the internet into a frenzy.
So much so that distributors Roadshow pulled its release date forward to please the people.
"It's so funny, because when the internet reaction happened, there was a parallel there to how the villagers behave," says Australian Eleanor Wilson, who co-directed the film with her partner in life and cinema, Alex Huston Fischer.
"There are some people who are horrified by it, like, 'No thank you,' and others who are really horny for it."
The Colman factor
Filmed in rural Hungary, Wicker is a fairy tale-like story in which characters go by their job titles rather than individual names.
Colman plays a fisherwoman who is looked down on by the villagers to whom she sells her wares because of her whiff. Especially by the snooty tailor's wife: Australian actor Elizabeth Debicki.
While the fisherwoman has no interest in the latter's tradwife tendencies — initially refusing to be drawn into a marriage ceremony which pairs off the villagers — the meanness of Debicki's character changes her mind.
She trots round to Peter Dinklage's basket weaver with a handful of coins, asking him to thatch her a buff basket husband (Alexander Skarsgård).
"Olivia made it believable," Wilson says.
"The fisherwoman doesn't care what other people think, but she's also not impervious to being influenced, letting that stuff creep into her.
"Olivia understood that on a gut level and went with it wholeheartedly and instinctively."
Wilson's still pinching herself Colman signed on, given this is only her and Fischer's second feature, following their 2020 low-key alien invasion relationship drama, Save Yourselves!
"She's happy to read a script and take a risk," Wilson says.
Once Colman signed on, the cast blossomed, including Nabhaan Rizwan as the tailor and Richard E Grant as a wildly unprofessional doctor.
"When Olivia's in, everyone wants to be involved, both cast and crew," Wilson says. "She's a magnet for talent."
Crafty people
The willingness to go far out includes the always game Skarsgård.
"We were just so lucky that Alexander's the kind of actor who likes to get weird," Fischer says. "He had just done Pillion right before he came to shoot this, and it's an interesting double feature."
The woven suit worn by Skarsgård was designed by Wētā Workshop, the Kiwi wizards behind Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings movies. They worked hand-in-glove with costume designers Tóth András Dániel and Godena-Juhász Attila, prosthetics guru Joe Dunckley and makeup artist Sarah Rubano to get the look right.
Skarsgård was up for the punishing physical challenge, with the weave taking a minimum of 90 minutes to apply, to be worn for up to eight hours at a time.
"He was sweating profusely," Fischer reveals of the ordeal. "We couldn't have him in direct sunlight."
Skarsgård's Swedish stoicism helped him pull off the demanding character.
"To be able to project the beautiful, subtle performance that he did through this prosthetic was very challenging," Wilson says.
"He had to really exaggerate his facial movements to be able to get the movement across. The work that he's doing underneath that is a completely different style of acting to how one would normally behave in a film."
Sound designer Andy Neil's work helped bring the wicker man to life.
"He achieved the perfectly calibrated creak," Wilson says.
While The Brutalist cinematographer Lol Crawley helped Wicker shine visually.
"He's been such a cheerleader for the film and in mentoring us," Fischer says.
"When he first arrived, we said we wanted to make a comedy that looks like a 17th-century Dutch painting, and he didn't even bat an eyelid."
Eagle-eyed trailer viewers zoomed right in on a momentary flash of the wicker husband's woven wotsit in a stunning scene in which he's waist deep, naked in a river.
But for Fischer it was just a lovely first day of shooting.
"Seeing how the weave patterns interact, how the anatomy comes together, with Lol shooting with the backlight, we were walking on air and couldn't believe how lucky we were," Fisher says.
"There's a lot about this movie that was an impossible technical challenge achieved by these incredible craftspeople."
Hedgehog grease
In getting the village's fraught dynamic right, Wilson was determined to cast Debicki in the pricklier role of the tailor's wife.
"Elizabeth understood she's not there to be a foil to Olivia's character," Wilson says. "She's her own person with a hell of a lot going on, the whole burden of this society on her, and that her position in life isn't really fair."
While Skarsgård was perspiring, Debicki faced her own physical challenges.
"Women worked with their hands so much in those days, and they would break down because they were in water all the time," Fischer says.
A fate faced by Debicki and others on set, but the filmmakers deployed a period-appropriate solution.
"It's gross, but we used hedgehog grease," Wilson says of the old folk medicine that uses literal Erinaceinae fat.
The original trailer that broke the internet greased the wheels in rolling out Wicker to the masses, Wilson says.
"We feel very lucky to be putting out a movie in 2026, because it does seem like an incredible year for wild swings," she says.
Fischer agrees. "Studios have been afraid of it for a long time, because they just assume everybody's a quote unquote normal person. But people are hungry for it. They're freaks."
And Colman was freakishly good, according to the pair.
"That feels like the magic trick of the movie," Wilson insists. "There's obviously a lot of other stuff going on, but if you don't care about the fisherwoman, what do you care about?"
Wicker is in Australian cinemas from November 5.

Transcript: Sen. Bernie Sanders on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 1, 2026

Transcript: Sen. Bernie Sanders on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 1, 2026
The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Bernie Sanders, Independent of Vermont, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Good morning, and welcome to Face the Nation. We are just hours away from voters in 50 states going to the polls for an election that could shift the balance of power here in Washington. We begin with someone who has been on the campaign trail quite a bit, although he is not up for reelection. That's Vermont Independent Senator Bernie Sanders, who joins us from Burlington. Good morning to you, Senator.
SENATOR BERNIE SANDERS (I-VT): Good morning.
MARGARET BRENNAN: I've been told you've hosted telerallies, town halls for Maine and Michigan this weekend. Troy Jackson, Abdul El-Sayed. You're focused as well on Florida and Minnesota. Why Florida, since it is likely GOP according to CBS numbers, and CBS also rates Minnesota as likely Dem. Why focus there?
SEN. SANDERS: Well, I don't take anything for granted. I think Angie Nixon in Florida is running a great grassroots campaign. She pulled off a huge upset in the Democratic primary. I think she has a real chance to win the general election. She is mobilizing working-class people all over this country, and she's talking about the right issues. And those issues are true in Minnesota. They're true in Florida. They're true in Vermont. People are disgusted and frustrated with an economy in which the billionaires have never ever had it so good. Elon Musk now owns more wealth alone than the bottom 53% of American households, while millions of people today are struggling to put food on the table, pay for, you know, pay to fill up their gas tanks, pay for rent. So what Angie is talking about, what Troy is talking about is an economy that works for all. That's resonating.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, out in Michigan, there appears some inner Democratic Party squabbles that are ongoing here around the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. There was a back and forth over the weekend with Congresswoman Haley Stevens. She lost the primary, but she continues to make public her deep misgivings about backing him now, citing concerns about his ads and his views on Israel. Australia expands free GP services to over 4,000 clinics

Australia expands free GP services to over 4,000 clinics
Australian Minister for Health and Ageing Mark Butler said in a statement that 50 percent of all general practices nationwide now exclusively offer bulk billing, compared with 30 percent a year earlier.
Under the bulk-billing system, doctors bill Medicare directly for medical services, allowing patients to receive treatment without out-of-pocket costs.
The increase follows the introduction of the government's Bulk Billing Practice Incentive Program, which provides higher Medicare rebates to clinics where all doctors bulk bill all patients.
According to the statement, more than 97 percent of Australians now live within a 20-minute drive of a general practice that bulk bills all patients.
The proportion of fully bulk-billing practices has more than doubled in South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania and the Australian Capital Territory (ACT) over the past 12 months.
The Northern Territory recorded the highest proportion among states and territories at 80 percent, followed by New South Wales at 58 percent and Victoria at 55 percent, while the ACT had the lowest at 21 percent.
Rural areas saw the largest increase, with the proportion of fully bulk-billing practices rising to 59 percent, while remote areas remained at 77 percent.
Butler said the expansion was helping Australians save hundreds of dollars a year in out-of-pocket medical expenses.
Earlier, it was reported that Australian actor and martial artist Richard Norton died after an injection of unapproved peptides triggered a severe allergic reaction and cardiac arrest, according to a coroner.

UN announces liquidation of MINURSO Western Sahara mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
18:06:56 UTC
03:06:56 KST

Breadcrumb
UN announces start of liquidation of MINURSO Western Sahara mission
The United Nations announced on Sunday the beginning of the liquidation phase of the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO), following the Security Council’s decision not to renew its mandate.
The move marks a significant development in a conflict that has lasted for more than half a century, and comes 35 years after the mission was established.
With the UN’s announcement that MINURSO’s mandate has ended, the peacekeeping operations carried out by the mission since 1991 will come to a halt. However, this does not mean an end to the UN political process or a resolution of Western Sahara’s legal status, as the territory remains on the UN list of Non-Self-Governing Territories.
According to a statement by his spokesperson, UN Secretary-General António Guterres said that the liquidation process would be overseen by a small task force affiliated with the UN Department of Operational Support. The task force will supervise the orderly transfer of equipment belonging to troop-contributing countries back to their respective countries, as well as the disposal of equipment belonging to the United Nations.
He called on all parties to cooperate fully to ensure that the liquidation process is completed in an orderly manner and as soon as possible.
Guterres stressed that the United Nations would continue its efforts to achieve a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution.
The secretary-general warned of the risk of escalating hostilities in the region, urging the parties concerned to exercise the utmost restraint and avoid any steps that could threaten regional stability.
He stressed that the United Nations would continue its efforts to achieve a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution that guarantees the right to self-determination, through his Personal Envoy, Staffan de Mistura.
The announcement comes a day after Morocco’s top diplomat, Nasser Bourita, reaffirmed that his country would seek to move the Western Sahara issue out of the UN General Assembly’s Fourth Committee. In an exclusive interview with Morocco’s Channel 2 late on Saturday, he argued that removing the issue from the committee would be easier than securing the passage of a resolution on it in the Security Council, given the differences in voting procedures between the two bodies.
Bourita made these remarks in the context of his call for a review of how the conflict is managed, arguing that the international community should not simply continue with the UN process in its current form. He pointed in particular to what he described as years of stagnation in dealing with the issue, saying that MINURSO had become part of the political and on-the-ground deadlock.
The Western Sahara issue had entered an unprecedented diplomatic turning point after the UN Security Council failed last Friday to adopt either of the two draft resolutions put forward to extend MINURSO’s mandate. Russia exercised its veto against the US-sponsored draft, after which the Russian draft resolution was itself rejected.
MINURSO was established in April 1991 under Security Council Resolution 690, primarily to monitor the ceasefire and prepare for a referendum on the territory’s self-determination. However, plans to hold the referendum stalled because of disagreements between Morocco and the Polisario Front over the referendum’s conditions and the composition of the electorate.
The mission operates from its headquarters in the city of Laayoune, the largest urban centre in Western Sahara, and maintains 11 locations across the territory and in the Sahrawi refugee camps in Tindouf, Algeria.

Disunity is death, but can the federal government rein in the blame game?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Disunity is death, but can the federal government rein in the blame game?
The problem with delivering a searing political take-down in the modern era is the ease with which it can come back to haunt you. That is the diabolical predicament dogging Treasurer Jim Chalmers.
As shadow treasurer, Chalmers accused then-prime minister Scott Morrison of having "an excuse for everything and a plan for nothing".
"When things are going well in the economy he takes all of the credit, and when times are tough in the economy he takes none of the responsibility," he said in 2022 after the Reserve Bank lifted interest rates for the first time in more than a decade.
Now, if rates go up again on Tuesday, as widely tipped, there will have been 17 interest rate rises by the RBA since Labor came to office. To be fair, there were also three cuts in 2025.
Chalmers attacked the Coalition government for the higher repayments Australians faced, with the following line: "If only you could pay your mortgage with Scott Morrison's excuses."
Now his critics are replaying those attack lines against him, as evidence of hypocrisy. Social media clips feature his attacks on Morrison and contrast them with Chalmers currently pointing to global pressures for spiking inflation.
But it is not just the economic numbers worrying the government.
Yesterday, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher appeared on Insiders and did her best to dismiss claims of internal party tensions.
Labor insiders were in despair over a media report last Friday suggesting Chalmers wanted to go harder on cutting spending, only to be blocked by the PM's allies on the government's Expenditure Review Committee (ERC).
Gallagher, a member of the ERC and a key part of the PM's Praetorian Guard, has long been known in Canberra as crucial to bridging relations between Albanese and Chalmers.
She dismissed suggestions of tension between the two, describing their working relationship as professional, saying individuals come at things from "slightly different perspectives."
Those slightly different perspectives are now the source of feverish speculation.
While Chalmers last week told media outlets he owned his share of responsibility for decision-making, Gallagher emphasised she was part of the government's economic team and also had the job of saying no to her colleagues.
Her message was clear: it wasn't just Chalmers blocking spending requests from ministers hungry for more money — she too was a blocker of largesse.
Pushing back against a growing narrative that Labor is a high-spending government, Gallagher made the point that they are governing in a very different world from Howard and other past governments.
"There should be some acknowledgement of the world in which we are living. NDIS, AUKUS, defence, aged care and interest on government debt; all of these continue to be significant pressures," she said.
"We can't pretend these pressures on the budget aren't coming."
Gallagher's comments offer two insights into the government.
Loading
The first, her pivot to talking about circumstances now being more challenging and complex than past governments have endured, is sensible, reflects the reality and demonstrates that Labor knows voters are fed up with the government continuing to blame far-off conflicts for cost-of-living pressures.
More telling, though, were Gallagher's attempts to downplay division in Labor; she was out this weekend to hose down the raging fire of division talk.
Politics versus policy
While Chalmers rejected any link to last week's media story about him wanting to deliver a more austere set of cuts, his colleagues have told this column they are not convinced.
They see it as an attempt to distance him from the government's big spending that is under scrutiny for putting pressure on inflation.
The thing about stories like this is they become process stories — who is doing the leaking and who is trying to undermine whom?
The premium the prime minister had on unity is eroding, because even if they are sporadic, process stories about internal issues show the media and opposition there is trouble within.
Once this narrative starts to take hold, tensions around the cabinet table become more of a focus than the policy problems before them.
Who leaked what and when is relevant and irrelevant in equal measure. The main problem is that a government that had prided itself on unity — one of Albanese's strongest commodities — is suddenly not looking very unified.
As households continue to grapple with power prices and the cost of groceries and petrol, the government appearing to focus on who said what and where is the quickest way to alienate voters.
Disunity is death for any government, and those in power know this political reality.
Can the creeping disunity narrative be put back in the box now? If the government's senior ministers don't find a way to shut it down, the problems will only grow, and the government will lose any chance of taking control of the story about how it plans to fix the country's economic woes.
Victorians will go to the polls at the end of this month. With Labor on track for a defeat, federal MPs are keen to ensure this election is characterised as a referendum on the 12-year reign of Daniel Andrews and his successors.
They will not want any blame to be attached to the broader economic malaise facing households.
But with process stories starting to appear in the media, a catastrophic Labor result in Victoria will only further stoke tensions in its federal ranks.
A loss in Victoria might be easy to blame on the state government, its governance failures and other scandals. But with New South Wales going to the polls in March, it will be harder for federal Labor to park a second bad result squarely with the state.
The fancy Birdcage at Flemington is where politicians used to go on Melbourne Cup Day to wear fancy outfits and have a punt.
It will be a brave politician who goes near the races on Tuesday when the RBA delivers a decision expected to put another handbrake on Australian households.
Patricia Karvelas is host of ABC News Afternoon Briefing at 4pm weekdays on ABC News Channel, co-host of the weekly Party Room podcast with Fran Kelly and host of politics and news podcast Politics Now.

The brutal redistribution at the heart of the RBA's interest rate policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
The brutal redistribution at the heart of the RBA's interest rate policy
The Reserve Bank has been waging a public relations battle to convince Australians that interest rate policy doesn't primarily work to lower inflation by punishing borrowers.
Economists call this "the cash flow channel", where rising interest rates reduce the free cash households have to spend.
Less spending means less demand for goods and services, which in turn should mean less pressure for prices to rise.
It's the most visible channel by which interest rates affect households, at least for the third who have mortgages.
It's also the most obviously painful one for those households, which is why we've had statements like this from RBA governor Michele Bullock.
"Those who have mortgages, yes, this clearly impacts them and it hurts them. They've got less cash flow, and they've got less money to spend on things," she said at her last press conference.
"But that's not the only way monetary policy works through the system."
Deputy governor Andrew Hauser went even further in downplaying the importance of the cash flow channel at the Citi Investment Conference a couple of weeks ago, drawing on recent research by the RBA's boffins.
"The cash flow effect, probably, in terms of our models, comes last," he said.
"It is first in the public discussion because obviously it's a thing people notice, and we are very sensitive to that."
Indeed.
Borrowers lose, savers win
But there's something the RBA officials talking about the cashflow channel generally neglect to mention.
There is a key reason it has a smaller effect, which is that it is a two-sided coin.
On one side are the borrowers, forking out substantially higher interest payments on their loans.
But on the other are savers, raking in much higher interest payments on their deposits.
To some extent, the two cancel each other out, reducing the cashflow channel's overall impact on consumer demand.
That effectively understates the extent to which borrowers are lent on to dampen demand and, ultimately, inflation.
Calculations done by economists at the Centre for Policy Development, using National Accounts data, show that since rates started rising in 2022, for every extra dollar households paid in interest on their mortgages and other debt, households as a whole received about 72 cents more in interest income.
That number isn't a pure reflection of how the cashflow channel is diluted by savers.
It also captures part of a second transmission mechanism of monetary policy, the intertemporal substitution channel, which as Andrew Hauser said, "is a long-winded way of saying if interest rates go up, [people] actually have an incentive to save more or borrow less".
That's born out in APRA banking data, which shows the total value of outstanding household debt at prudentially regulated banks climbed about 25 per cent between March 2022 and June 2026, while the balance of household deposits jumped 37 per cent.
The latest August banking data shows there are now about 68 cents in household deposits for every dollar of household debt, up from about 61 cents in March 2022, before rates started rising from COVID lows.
A decade-old RBA staff research paper (which doesn't represent official views of the bank) found "the spending of borrowers is at least twice as sensitive as that of lenders to a given change in interest-sensitive cash flows".
That's because a lot more borrowers are living at or very near their financial limits.
Even so, the consumption from the new-found riches of savers blunts the overall cash flow effect, meaning borrowers need to suffer more through even higher rates to make up for it.
Middle-aged mortgagors lose, older home owners win
This differential also has inter-generational effects.
The RBA's 2016 research paper found the median age of net borrower households was 42, where mortgage debts are often at their peak, while the median age of savers was 58.
A paper by RBA researchers Sarah Jennison and Marcus Miller published last year backs up the earlier findings, showing that over-65s overwhelmingly benefited from rising rates, while most people aged 30-54 lost out. The effect was broadly neutral, on average, for under-30s and those 55-64.
Perhaps no surprise, then, that Commonwealth Bank data shows Australians under 55 have been reducing their spending growth over the past year, while those over 55 have accelerated their consumption.
Given that many of these middle-aged households have dependent children and all the expenses associated with them, it is no wonder they are feeling particularly under the pump.
Middle class suffers most from rising rates
Even within this broad group of borrowers, there are those more affected than others.
I bought my home eight years ago, reduced the principal owed on my mortgage and built up a sizeable buffer of offset savings, much of it over the four years post-COVID when I was on a 1.89 per cent fixed mortgage rate.
Two authors of the RBA's 2016 research, Gianni La Cava and Greg Kaplan, recently published a paper showing how financial buffers significantly altered borrowers' spending response to interest rate rises, potentially blunting the cash flow channel of monetary policy.
Loading
In plain English, people like me who built up a lot of savings in our offset accounts and redraw facilities during the low-rate, big stimulus period of the COVID pandemic aren't yet cutting our spending in response to rate rises, because we don't need to.
When you add us to the group of mainly older Australians benefiting from higher interest rates, it leaves a very narrow group of people carrying the burden of the cash flow channel of monetary policy.
These are generally the younger, more recent home purchasers, with the biggest mortgages, the smallest financial buffers, and often the youngest kids, meaning less flexibility to pick up extra work.
This shows up in that 2025 RBA research, which suggests it is households in the middle of the wealth distribution, and those with mortgages at the lower and middle of the income distribution, who suffer the biggest hit to their cashflows from rising interest rates.
Most households at the lower end of the income scale are either renters or retirees who have already paid off their home, while households at the upper end of incomes can generally absorb higher mortgage repayments and have more options to trim discretionary spending.
Loading...
When you look through the studies, no amount of central bank spin can sugar-coat the reality that middle-class mortgage borrowers, many with kids, are bearing the financial brunt of the fight against inflation.
"That cash flow channel, it is a blunt tool. And it's really tricky," the RBA's chief economist Sarah Hunter recently acknowledged on a personal finance podcast.
"And we know some people, especially if you're a first-time buyer and you've stretched yourself a bit to get on the ladder in the first place, and then interest rates go up, that's really tough. We know."
So do they.
Michael Janda is the ABC's business editor.

Watchdog says super funds are failing their members
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Super funds failing members on retirement savings, regulator says
In short:
Australia's corporate regulator warns that super funds are failing to deal with complaints properly.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission says the ombudsman is better at detecting industry-wide issues than the funds.
What's next?
It is threatening legal action against super funds that don't step up.
Australia's corporate regulator says superannuation funds are failing their members in managing their retirement savings, warning that those who do not step up could be staring down future legal action.
The Australian Securities and Investments Commission's (ASIC's) latest review looked at 45 superannuation trustees, covering $1.6 trillion in benefits for more than 12.8 million members.
It found that superannuation members were more likely to get resolutions to their complaints if they went to the financial ombudsman rather than raise it directly with their super fund.
It has prompted ASIC commissioner Simone Constant to hand down a blunt warning to the funds that "blaming customers is not a complaint strategy".
ASIC has long been critical of how super funds handle member complaints over death benefits and disability insurance claims payouts and alleged fraud and misconduct.
In March last year, it called on funds to overhaul the way they dealt with death benefit claims, noting excessive delays, poor customer service and ineffective claims handling were leaving Australians worse off at some of the most vulnerable times of their lives.
In October last year, it criticised superannuation funds over the way they communicated with retirees.
Payouts impact people's lives: commissioner
Ms Constant said superannuation trustees managed $3.4 trillion in Australians' retirement savings.
She said they were dealing with payouts that affect people's lives and the retirement savings they had worked hard to build.
"Super funds must listen to what complaints are telling them," she said.
"When trustees fail to learn from their complaints, small problems left unidentified, unattended or unresolved can snowball into widespread failures.
"That expose[s] members to harm and erode[s] trust in the superannuation system."
Super funds that don't step up could face legal action.
"We're willing and able to bring these actions against funds for not meeting these legal responsibilities,"
Ms Constant said.
Funds not analysing their complaints data
ASIC's inquiries across the industry found close to one quarter of trustees were not analysing complaints data to identify systemic issues on a regular basis.
More than half of trustees reviewed (24 out of 45) identified fewer than five systemic issues from complaints over a two-year period. Of these, 14 trustees failed to identify a single issue.
"We see low levels of systemic issue identification as a potential red flag, not evidence of better performance," Ms Constant said.
"Alarmingly, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority [AFCA] appears better at picking up issues than industry.
According to AFCA, superannuation complaints rose sharply in 2025–26, with the financial ombudsman receiving 8,755 complaints, up 42 per cent on the previous financial year.
AFCA said complaints about super funds refusing to pay claims rose by 80 per cent.
ASIC said during July 1, 2023 and June 30, 2026, more than 19,400 complaints were made to AFCA about superannuation concerning the 45 funds that were part of its whole-of-industry review.
"When comparing the two years of data we collected, AFCA identified systemic issues from superannuation complaints it received at almost twice the rate all trustees identified from the complaints they received," Ms Constant said.
Stop blaming members for faults
ASIC also found several trustees blamed members when they made complaints.
Several of them attributed more than 60 per cent of recorded complaint causes to members.
"Blaming the customer is not a complaints strategy,"
Ms Constant said.
The review noted in one case, a tax-related system problem was raised through complaints for years before the trustee investigated whether other members were affected, with early estimates suggesting about 1,200 members could be impacted.
Another case involved more than 250,000 members being unable to access documents online at different times.
"Trustees need to look behind the complaint and ask whether poor communication, unclear processes, delays or system failures are driving member dissatisfaction," Ms Constant said.
"If a member cannot access their benefit payment, cannot get a timely response, or doesn't receive the support they are entitled to or the services they are paying for, the consequences can be serious."
But the industry said it was working hard to resolve issues.
Financial Services Council chief executive Blake Briggs agreed superannuation trustees had a responsibility to deliver high-quality services to members.
"In recent years, superannuation trustees have undertaken significant work to strengthen their complaints-handling frameworks, including improving processes for identifying and responding to systemic issues," he said.
He said the government, almost two years ago, announced its intention to introduce mandatory service standards across the industry in response to unacceptable failures in how major funds had handled Australians' death benefit and group life claims.
"We support ongoing industry efforts to promptly identify and address systemic issues, learn from complaints and improve processes to deliver better outcomes for members,"
Mr Briggs said.

Multiple people have been arrested and are being questioned as police work to identify the potential shooters, he said, although their possible connection to the shootings is unclear.
The department had increased its staffing in anticipation of Halloween crowds, the chief said. “We had more presence out here, and this was something that we were ramped up for,” Comeaux said.
No officers were injured, police said.
All three incidents appear to have been within about a half mile of one another, along streets checkered with local restaurants, art galleries, bars and concert venues.
The neighborhood refers to itself as “Dallas’ premier arts and entertainment district,” according to its website. Several venues in the area had advertised Halloween events for that night.
It is unclear whether the shootings took place inside any businesses or on the street, Comeaux said.
He praised the department’s “amazing” response time, adding one officer successfully performed lifesaving measures on an injured person.
Victims’ identities and the conditions of the injured were not released Sunday morning as Dallas police continue to investigate the incidents.
The department is asking the public for photos and videos from the area as it works to piece together what happened, Comeaux said in the news conference.
“We’re going to do everything that we need to do to get everyone in custody that’s responsible,” he added.
The overnight incidents took place roughly six months after a pair of overnight shootings within a block of each other in Deep Ellum left a 26-year-old security officer dead and five others injured, according to CNN affiliate KTVT.
CNN has reached out to Dallas police for more information.

Sudan accuses Ethiopia over drone attacks amid fresh strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
17:45:06 UTC
02:45:06 KST

Breadcrumb
Sudan accuses Ethiopia of enabling drone attacks as strikes hit northern power stations
Sudan has accused Ethiopia of allowing its territory to be used to launch drone attacks on civilians and vital infrastructure, as fresh strikes on two northern power stations on Sunday extended a wave of attacks disrupting electricity supplies across the country.
Foreign ministry undersecretary Muawiya Othman told a diplomatic briefing on Saturday that Ethiopia was participating in what he described as a proxy war on behalf of regional actors, particularly the United Arab Emirates, which Sudan’s army-aligned government accuses of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
He alleged that the Assosa base in western Ethiopia had become a hub for supplying the RSF with weapons and equipment and facilitating the movement of foreign fighters into Sudan. He described the alleged use of Ethiopian territory to launch drone strikes as the most dangerous aspect of that support.
Ethiopia denies the accusations and has countered that the Sudanese army is supporting rebels linked to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), an allegation Khartoum rejects.
In a report setting out its allegations, Sudan’s army-led Transitional Sovereignty Council said it had recorded 70 attacks between 15 February and 27 October, involving 187 one-way attack drones and 82 munitions dropped or fired from drones.
The council said the attacks had killed or wounded 484 civilians, and killed 176 Sudanese soldiers and wounded another 200.
The report alleged that armed drones had been launching from Ethiopian territory since February 2026 to strike Sudanese cities and civilians. It identified Assosa airport, the Kurmuk-Gizen border area and Bahir Dar air base in Ethiopia’s northwestern Amhara region as launch sites.
According to the council, the campaign accelerated in recent months, with October accounting for 28 attacks and 97 of the one-way attack drones it recorded.
Fresh strikes hit northern power stations
The accusations came as drones struck the Abu Hamad power station in River Nile state and the Ad-Dabba power station in Northern state at dawn on Sunday, according to local reporting. Witnesses described how the attack triggered explosions and a fire at the facility.
Local media said the Ad-Dabba station had been knocked out of service, cutting electricity to the area, and attributed the attack to the RSF.
Drones also reportedly targeted the headquarters of the army’s 73rd Infantry Brigade and two fuel stations in the Al-Multaqa area of Northern state.
The strikes followed several days of attacks on Sudan’s electricity network, with local reporting putting the weekly total of power stations struck this week at 10.
An earlier strike on the Al-Markhiyat substation in Omdurman left large parts of the capital without electricity for more than 12 hours on Tuesday, disrupting hospitals, bakeries and water services. A further attack on Saturday targeted the Hayya power station, which is still under construction in Red Sea state.
Both the Sudanese army and the RSF have used drones during the war, with attacks hitting markets, hospitals, schools, power facilities and displacement camps.
On Monday, an army drone strike on a crowded market in Nyala, the RSF-controlled capital of South Darfur, killed more than 100 people and wounded 113, according to Emergency Lawyers, a rights group. The group said many of the victims were women and children.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the escalating drone attacks on Saturday, saying through his spokesperson that he was "appalled" by their impact on civilians.
"The secretary-general calls on the parties to spare the civilian population and critical infrastructure and agree without delay to a cessation of hostilities as a first step toward ending this devastating conflict," spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said.

Explainer-How Trump’s noncitizen voter lists could affect the midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
17:26:56 UTC
02:26:56 KST

Explainer-How Trump’s noncitizen voter lists could affect the midterms
Nov 1 - As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday for midterm elections, lists the Trump administration has compiled of possible noncitizen voters could be used to contest the validity of the results.
With US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party fighting to maintain control of Congress, here’s how the lists could affect the midterms.
WHAT HAS THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SAID ABOUT THE LISTS?
The Trump administration has acknowledged sending letters to election officials in five states — California, Washington, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Nevada — as of October 30, saying it identified noncitizens on their voter rolls, according to a Justice Department document seen by Reuters.
In an October 13 letter, the Justice Department demanded California not count ballots from about 20,000 registered voters "who federal agencies reasonably believe are likely noncitizens" without first verifying their citizenship, warning that election workers who processed them could face prosecution. Trump endorsed the warning on social media: “They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!”
State officials rebuffed requests to set aside ballots of people on the lists, which have not been made public. The Justice Department is now suing California to block the state from counting any ballots from the list of 20,000 voters. California says its safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust.
Noncitizen voting is illegal and can lead to jail time, fines and deportation. The White House says noncitizen voting is a significant problem requiring aggressive enforcement to protect election integrity. Trump has long alleged it is widespread, but available evidence indicates it is exceedingly rare. A Reuters investigation in July found just 129 cases in which noncitizens were federally charged with voting illegally since a federal “voting by aliens” statute was created by Congress in 1996; many appeared to stem from confusion or administrative errors rather than intentional fraud.
The Justice Department has since ramped up noncitizens voting prosecutions. “Close elections are not rare, and every illegal ballot cancels out the vote of an American citizen,” a Justice Department spokesperson, Kiersten Pels, said in a statement. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed without evidence in a Fox News interview on Saturday that his agency had found 300,000 noncitizens on the voter rolls.
HOW DID THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION COMPILE THE LISTS?
The federal government has no centralized list of US citizens who are registered or eligible to vote. But the Trump administration has aggressively sought state voter data to expand its role in determining voter eligibility.
States have constitutional authority over federal elections and many states make voter rolls public with private information, such as driver’s license numbers and the last four digits of Social Security numbers, redacted.
The administration has sought unredacted rolls to identify alleged noncitizens. At least 16 states, including Alabama and Texas, have complied voluntarily. Thirty states, including California and New York, as well as Washington, D.C., have not complied and have been sued by the administration for their voter rolls. Courts have rejected 27 of those efforts so far, with many judges finding the federal government has no role in determining voter eligibility.
The Justice Department has appealed many of those losses. “Voters have a right to accurate voter rolls, and states shouldn’t be hiding them from federal review,” said Pels, the department’s spokesperson.
The Department of Homeland Security obtained at least partial voter-roll data from at least 47 states, typically including names, addresses and registration status and, in some cases, additional information such as dates of birth, according to a recent internal DHS email reviewed by Reuters. Federal investigators then matched the voter data against government databases to identify potential noncitizens, the email shows.
DHS did not respond to a request for comment. It has said its investigations are conducted professionally and lawfully to safeguard election integrity.
WILL THE LISTS IMPACT THE MIDTERMS?
The lists could provide a basis for challenging close election results, even if the administration struggles to prevail in court. Under most state laws, only candidates or voters can challenge election results, but a losing candidate could argue that suspected noncitizen votes made it impossible to determine the rightful winner, three legal experts told Reuters. And the Justice Department could pursue other legal avenues to try to block certification of victors. The Justice Department has said it will enforce the law wherever the evidence leads.
Such challenges would face significant legal hurdles, partly because reviews of the administration’s lists of potential noncitizen voters have found that many people on the lists are US citizens.
On October 28, a federal judge in California rejected the Justice Department's bid to block ballots from 20,000 voters it identified as likely noncitizens, saying the move would "wreak havoc" on the November 3 elections and questioning the reliability of the list. A federal appeals court upheld the ruling on October 30, citing a “material risk” of disenfranchising eligible voters.
The Justice Department would “probably” appeal to the US Supreme Court, acting US Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said on Fox News on Saturday. He has acknowledged the California list could include US citizens.
The lists and resulting challenges could cast doubt on narrow Democratic victories and prompt Trump-aligned state officials to seek further review or try to delay certification, though such efforts would face formidable obstacles, the legal experts said. The administration says its efforts are aimed at identifying and prosecuting illegal voting and protecting election integrity. REUTERS

South Korea’s exports hit record $115.3bn in October

South Korea’s exports hit record $115.3bn in October
South Korea's exports jumped 93.7 percent to a record US$115.3 billion in October from a year earlier, driven largely by a sharp increase in semiconductor shipments, data showed Sunday, Yonhap reported.
Strong global demand for semiconductors, coupled with continued investments by major technology companies in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, boosted overall exports, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources said in a press release.
Imports rose 36 percent from a year earlier to $72.78 billion, resulting in a trade surplus of $42.5 billion.
Cumulative exports for the January-October period exceeded $900 billion for the first time, with the ministry projecting that the country's annual exports could reach $1 trillion as early as November if the current trend continues.
By sector, semiconductor exports, a key pillar of Asia's fourth-largest economy, skyrocketed 259 percent from a year earlier to $56.4 billion in October, the release said.
Exports of petroleum products jumped 80 percent to $6.92 billion, while those of petrochemical products rose 27.5 percent to $4 billion.
Cosmetics exports shot up 57.5 percent to $1.44 billion on rising demand in China, the United States and the European Union.
Automobile exports gained 18.1 percent to $6.55 billion, driven by increased overseas demand for gasoline hybrid models.
By destination, exports to China soared 133.6 percent to $26.98 billion, driven by strong shipments of semiconductors and wireless communications equipment.
Exports to China topped $20 billion for the fifth consecutive month.
Shipments to the United States surged 185.8 percent to $24.9 billion, supported by robust demand for semiconductors, computers and electrical equipment used in AI infrastructure.
The monthly report also showed exports to Southeast Asian countries rose 128 percent to $21.33 billion, while those to the European Union increased 56.4 percent to $8.1 billion, with both gains driven by strong shipments of chips and automobiles.
Earlier, it was reported that South Korea’s industrial production recorded its fastest monthly growth in more than 15 years in September, driven largely by a surge in semiconductor manufacturing.

The dedication of Stupa number 76 took place during a ceremony to raise and consecrate 108 stupas in Gelephu Mindfulness City on Sunday.According to news agency ANI, Union minority affairs minister Kiren Rijiju represented India at the ceremony and expressed gratitude to Bhutan for the gesture, describing it as a "huge honour for India". He also conveyed gratitude on behalf of Prime Minister Modi to the Bhutanese King.In a post on X, Rijiju said, "It's a huge honour for India that very sacred stupa 76 is dedicated to Hon'ble PM Narendra Modi ji for his outstanding vision and commitment to friendship between India and Bhutan. On the auspicious occasion of Lhabab Duchen, joined the sacred ceremony in Gelephu Mindfulness City, Bhutan, marking the raising and consecration of 108 stupas, accompanied by the blowing of Dungchens."He further said, "Paid my respects and offered prayers in the presence of His Majesty the King of Bhutan, Her Majesty the Gyaltsuen, H E Dasho Tshering Tobgay, Prime Minister of Bhutan & the people of Bhutan.
A deeply meaningful spiritual occasion, reflecting Bhutan’s rich Buddhist heritage and the enduring bonds of friendship between our two nations."Stupas are sacred Buddhist structures associated with the teachings and life of Gautama Buddha. Traditionally, they were built to preserve the relics of the Buddha and other revered Buddhist figures, including their ashes and remains. Over time, they became important places of worship, meditation and religious devotion.
The 108 stupas in Bhutan are known as Jangchub Chortens, or Stupas of Enlightenment. The number 108 holds special significance in Buddhist traditions and is associated with religious practices, including the use of 108 beads in prayer malas. The structures are intended to promote peace, harmony and spiritual well-being.Rijiju is visiting Bhutan from October 31 to November 2. Earlier on Sunday, Rijiju met Bhutanese Prime Minister Tshering Tobgay in Gelephu. The two leaders discussed strengthening the India-Bhutan partnership and exploring the potential of the Gelephu Mindfulness City project.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV did not broadcast a Real Madrid La Liga match after star forward Kylian Mbappe caused a furore in China with remarks he made about former leader Mao Zedong.
The match between Real Madrid and Racing Santander began at 1515 GMT on Sunday but was not broadcast on either of CCTV's two sports channels.
None of the other matches from the 11th round of La Liga has been broadcast live on public television so far.
A viral video in recent days showed Mbappe referring to Mao as a "dictator", prompting the body overseeing CCTV to say it would halt broadcasts of the top Spanish league.
Mbappe, Real and La Liga later all said sorry for his remarks, and China's foreign ministry said it took the player's apology "seriously".
Asked before the weekend, La Liga said that Chinese television had previously shown all games live, without specifying which platforms hosted the broadcasts.
However, reporters did find live broadcasts of matches on Migu, a digital streaming service owned by the state-owned China Mobile telecom network.
That included Barcelona's 6-1 win over Alaves on Saturday.
However, the Racing Santander–Real Madrid match did not appear to be broadcast on Sunday on Migu.
China Media Group (CMG), which oversees CCTV, had said it had moved on Monday to suspend La Liga broadcasts, adding that apologies from La Liga, Mbappe and Real Madrid were "an absolute prerequisite" for moving past the furore.
The viral video showed Mbappe saying that the funniest internet meme about him he had seen was of his face photoshopped onto that of "some guy — I think he's a Chinese dictator".
This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappe superimposed on an image of Mao.
Mbappe later apologised for his "ill-judged" comments, La Liga said it "deeply" regretted them, and Real followed suit.
CCTV's sports website later reported that CMG had acknowledged the apologies, but it remains unclear whether talks to defuse the situation have begun.
China is a huge market for European football, with CCTV also carrying matches from the Premier League as well as the German, French and Italian top flights.
Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho said on Saturday that the club had "done our part" to put the controversy behind them.
Major Chinese brands cancelled sponsorship deals with Mbappe after his comments.
Various overseas sports leagues and players have found themselves in hot water for comments on topics that are politically sensitive to China.
China effectively cut ties with the NBA for several years from 2019 after then-Houston Rockets general manager Daryl Morey tweeted his support for Hong Kong protesters.

Mokri’s “Black Rabbit, White Rabbit” wins at 63rd International Antalya Golden Orange Film Festival
TEHRAN – Shahram Mokri’s “Black Rabbit, White Rabbit” won an award at the 63rd International Antalya Golden Orange Film Festival, which was held in Türkiye from October 24 to 31.
At the closing ceremony of the festival, the film received the Sungu Capan International Cinema Writers Award, ISNA reported.
“Black Rabbit, White Rabbit,” which had its world premiere at the 30th Busan International Film Festival in South Korea last September, is a joint production of Tajikistan and the United Arab Emirates and deals with three people’s destinies that intertwine through apparently unrelated events.
Chekhov’s famous dramatic adage – if a gun appears, it must be fired – sets the scene for Mokri’s audacious latest, set in Tajikistan and replete with his hallmark virtuosic long takes, wry humor, and interlinking narratives.
A wealthy wife, wrapped in bandages from a car accident, starts to suspect her husband of foul play. On the set of a remake of a classic Iranian film, an experienced armorer fears the prop gun might be real. At an acting audition, a young woman pulls a rabbit out of a hat. These seemingly unrelated stories combine into a playfully intriguing whole, with a healthy dose of magical realism and meta-textuality.
Shahram Mokri, 48, won the Venice Film Festival's Horizons Award in 2013 for Creative Content for his second feature film “Fish & Cat”.
In 2018, his third film “Invasion” was screened at the 68th Berlin Film Festival and was nominated for the Teddy Award.
He also won a silver Hugo medal at the Chicago Film Festival in the main section and the Venice Critics' Best Screenplay Award for his fourth film “Careless Crime”.
The cast of “Black Rabbit, White Rabbit,” Mokri’s fifth feature film, includes Babak Karimi, Hasti Mohammai, Kibriyo Dilyobova, and Bezhan Davlyatov, among others.
The Antalya Golden Orange Film Festival is the second most important film festival in Turkey, held annually since 1963 in Antalya.
Since 2009, the event, which takes place in the autumn months at the Antalya Cultural Center, has been organized solely by the Antalya Foundation for Culture and Arts and has included an international section within the main body of the festival.

De Niro has never been reluctant to make his political views public. Since Trump's emergence as a major political figure, the actor has repeatedly challenged his statements and decisions, becoming one of the most recognizable critics of his presidency in the entertainment industry.
His objections have not been limited to Trump's personality or rhetoric. De Niro has raised concerns about the administration's approach to democratic institutions, freedom of expression and the role of government in public life.

De Niro's objections to the administration have also extended to Washington's military record and its involvement in international conflicts.

His remarks reflected a broader criticism of the human cost of military intervention and the contradiction between Washington's claims to defend freedom and the consequences of its actions abroad.

He also condemned the use of masked immigration officers, arguing that such practices threatened civil liberties.
"I want to love my country again. I want my country back," he said.
By addressing military intervention alongside immigration and social policy, De Niro has presented his opposition as a broader objection to the direction of the country under Trump, rather than simply a personal dispute with the president.
Hollywood's growing political engagement
De Niro's involvement in political debates is part of a wider tradition of American artists using their public standing to address social and political issues. However, his persistent and often outspoken criticism has made him a particularly visible figure in the opposition to Trump.
The actor has used major cultural events, television appearances and public demonstrations to encourage political participation and challenge policies he considers damaging to democratic values.
His appearance at the 2025 Cannes Film Festival was particularly notable, as he used an international cultural platform to argue that developments in American politics have consequences for the wider world.
The continuing confrontation between Trump and De Niro also reflects the deep political divisions in the United States, where actors, musicians and other public figures have increasingly become involved in debates over government policies and the country's place in the world.
For De Niro, the dispute goes beyond the exchange of personal insults. His statements on war, civil liberties and political accountability indicate that his concerns are rooted in a broader criticism of the policies pursued by the US administration and their consequences at home and abroad.
