New Zealand’s two-speed economy poses election dilemma for ruling National party
LOWER HUTT, New Zealand – The campaign for New Zealand’s general election on Nov 7 comes down to the price of everyday life for 70-year-old Liz Hartley, a part-time bus driver.
“You’ve got to work to pay for the extras and to have a few treats,” said Hartley, queuing at a food truck as election volunteers worked the crowd at a riverside market in Lower Hutt, a city northeast of Wellington, the capital.
As a result, Hartley said, she plans a tactical vote in her Hutt South constituency aimed at denying reelection for National Party incumbent Chris Bishop, one of the most senior figures in government.
Three years after urban voters helped the National Party win election on promises to cut inflation and government debt, New Zealand is struggling to fully shake off a recession, though the party says it has laid the foundations for future growth.
In Hutt South, Bishop faces voters battered by a cost of living crisis and expenditure cuts in the capital that eliminated jobs for contractors, and shrivelled spending at shops and businesses.
Voters in the constituency, which spans communities east of Wellington, want a plan to “move the country forward and drive prosperity,” Bishop told Reuters.
“My sense is that our economic plan is beginning to work, and we need more time to see it through,” he added.
As New Zealand emerges from years of sluggish economic growth, its lagging urban sector presents a challenge for the National Party to retain votes in the cities of 30,000 or more that are home to about 65% of a population of 5.5 million.
A shift to National from Labour in traditional left-leaning urban areas in the largest city of Auckland helped propel the party to victory in 2023.
Economic woes
If not for the “economic funk” engulfing most voters, the National Party would have a much easier route back to office, said political commentator Grant Duncan.
“National comes in with this reputation for being the great economic and fiscal managers... and it hasn’t worked out.”
The government was not entirely at fault, but Prime Minister Christopher Luxon also made economic promises ahead of the 2023 election that he could not keep, he added.
New Zealand had endured “shock after shock after shock,” said Kiwibank Chief Economist Jarrod Kerr, which meant that the promise of a recovery has been postponed,
“The cost of living crisis is very real for many businesses and households.”
But rural and urban areas have fared very differently, with tourism and higher agricultural exports supporting the former, especially on the South Island, where second-quarter retail spending was up 8.6% on the year.
In urban locations such as Auckland and Wellington on the more populous North Island, however, consumer spending has lagged, with a smaller corresponding rise of 5.8%.
Jobs also reflect the divergence, with unemployment over the period falling 0.6 percentage points in the South Island but rising 0.7 percentage points in the North Island.
House prices, another key concern for voters, are down almost 30% from their peak in Wellington and 24.7% in Auckland, eroding middle-class wealth, versus a drop of 17% nationally.
“A third of the economy is doing really well, and two-thirds are still trying to find their feet,” Kerr added.
No clear path back to government
Polls show no clear path back to government after the election for any potential coalition, as voters look back at Labour or smaller parties such as the centrist Opportunity Party that could be the first new party in government since 1996.
“People are really looking for something different,” leader Qiulae Wong told Reuters in August, as the party draws urban professionals and voters disillusioned with the left-right divide.
It is getting ever harder to sell National’s message that the programme of fiscal restraint and infrastructure investment is laying the groundwork for stronger growth, said political commentator Liam Hehir.
“National is continuing to promise, ‘We’ve done the hard work, we’re going to get the benefits now, just hang on for a bit longer,’” he said. “You don’t get three years of that.”
A left-wing coalition is pitching a bigger government role to help relieve household pressures, support public services and tackle housing affordability.
But voters still remembered weak economic growth under the previous Labour government, leading them to “shop around” more than in the past, Hehir added.
“The old adage of ‘It’s the economy, stupid’ still rings fairly clear,” for voters, said Infometrics chief economist Brad Olsen.
In Hutt South, Hartley should be enjoying retirement but finds herself working part-time, as rising prices leave very little by the end of the week.
“You don’t have savings anymore, there is no such thing anymore,” Hartley said. REUTERS

The psychological motives driving internet justice and public shaming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
17:00:15 UTC
02:00:15 KST

When internet users publicly shame or expose perceived wrongdoers, their support for these actions is often tied to the pleasure they get from seeing others suffer and a desire to show off their own moral superiority. A recent survey of 1,000 adults shows that people who view internet justice as effective tend to report greater emotional rewards and status-seeking motives. The findings were published in the journal Computers in Human Behavior.
Online vigilantism occurs when internet users band together to expose, criticize, or punish individuals they believe have broken social rules. This behavior often happens completely outside of formal legal systems. Typical actions include public shaming, group harassment, and doxing, which is the act of publishing private or identifying information about someone without their permission. Digital platforms provide unique conditions for these behaviors, offering anonymity and a vast audience. These features allow collective punishments to spread rapidly and permanently, sometimes leading to what researchers call a social death for the target.
Researchers Dosun Kim and Yeon Soo Kim, both criminologists at Dongguk University in Seoul, designed the current study to explore the psychological traits behind these behaviors. While past research has focused on the legal and structural features of internet justice, few studies have explored why individual users actually support these digital punishments. The investigators wanted to see if specific emotional and motivational traits influence how effective people think internet justice is. They focused on understanding the subjective evaluations users make when watching or participating in online shaming.
To do this, they examined two specific psychological concepts: schadenfreude and moral grandstanding. Schadenfreude is a German term that describes the feeling of pleasure or satisfaction someone gets when they witness another person’s misfortune or adversity. In an online context, this might look like enjoying the downfall of a public figure who broke a social rule. Moral grandstanding refers to a person’s tendency to use moral arguments primarily to boost their own social status or self-image. Grandstanding is an effort to manage how others perceive you during public interactions.
The researchers split moral grandstanding into two categories. Prestige-seeking grandstanding happens when someone wants others to recognize them as a good, morally sensitive person. Dominance-seeking grandstanding occurs when someone wants to exert influence, assert authority, or shame those who disagree with them. By examining these traits, the researchers hoped to understand if support for online vigilantism comes from a genuine desire for justice or a personal need for emotional rewards and social signaling.
The investigators recruited a representative sample of 1,000 adults living in South Korea. The participants answered survey questions about their experiences with internet justice, their feelings of schadenfreude, and their tendencies toward both prestige-seeking and dominance-seeking moral grandstanding. The participants also rated how effective they believed internet vigilantism was at achieving social justice, deterring bad behavior, and making up for the limits of the legal system.
The researchers divided the participants into three categories based on their reported behavior. Non-participants had no experience with online vigilantism. Passive participants had viewed or searched for content that criticized rule-breakers. Active participants had taken direct action, such as sharing someone’s personal information, writing accusatory comments, or creating critical posts.
First, the researchers compared the average scores across the three groups. They found that active participants reported significantly higher levels of schadenfreude, prestige-seeking grandstanding, and belief in the effectiveness of online vigilantism than both other groups. Non-participants scored lowest on schadenfreude and perceived effectiveness, but scored slightly higher than passive participants on prestige-seeking grandstanding. The pattern for dominance-seeking grandstanding was slightly different, with passive participants scoring lower than both active participants and non-participants.
Next, the researchers conducted statistical analyses within each group to see how the psychological traits connected to their views on digital justice. Among active participants, the team found that higher levels of schadenfreude and prestige-seeking grandstanding were linked to a stronger belief that internet vigilantism is effective. This means that people who actively participate in online shaming and find it effective often enjoy seeing others suffer and want to be recognized for their moral stance.
The researchers then looked at the passive participants. The findings in this group mirrored the active group. Higher levels of schadenfreude and prestige-seeking grandstanding were associated with viewing online vigilantism as a successful tool. Even though these individuals only consumed the content rather than creating it, their support for the practice was tied to similar emotional and status-seeking motives.
The non-participant group showed a different pattern. For these individuals, schadenfreude was still linked to believing in the effectiveness of internet justice. However, instead of prestige-seeking grandstanding, dominance-seeking grandstanding was associated with their support for online vigilantism. The researchers suggest that some people who do not participate directly might still like the idea of internet justice because it symbolically punishes rule-breakers and affirms their own moral superiority from a safe distance.
Finally, the investigators ran an analysis comparing all the groups together to see if the differences in their motives held up statistically. They found that the overall interaction across the groups was not statistically significant. However, specific calculations within the model suggested that the connection between dominance-seeking grandstanding and support for online vigilantism was stronger among non-participants than among the other two groups. The researchers described this specific result as exploratory, noting that it requires further investigation due to the small size of the non-participant group.
The study relies on self-reported survey data taken at a single point in time, which means the researchers cannot determine cause and effect. It is entirely possible that participating in online vigilantism increases a person’s feelings of schadenfreude, rather than the other way around. Participants might also have adjusted their answers to appear more socially acceptable, a common issue in psychological surveys.
The measure of perceived effectiveness does not mean that online vigilantism actually works to deter crime or bring about justice. It only captures the subjective opinions of the users. The sample was restricted to adults in South Korea, meaning the psychological patterns might look different in other cultural contexts or on different social media platforms.
Future studies could use experimental designs or track actual online behavior over time to clarify how these psychological traits interact with digital shaming. Researchers could also explore whether similar patterns emerge across different legal systems and specific social media networks. This would help untangle the motives behind internet justice in a broader global context.
The study, “Perceived effectiveness of online vigilantism: The role of schadenfreude and moral grandstanding,” was authored by Dosun Kim and Yeon Soo Kim.

Crew from NASA's simulated Mars mission emerges after 378 days in isolation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:53:59 UTC

Crew from NASA’s simulated Mars mission emerges after 378 days in isolation
WASHINGTON, United States – The four members of a crew who took part in a simulated mission to Mars have emerged after 378 days in isolation at the US space agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, an endeavour designed to help prepare for a possible future excursion by NASA astronauts to Earth’s planetary neighbour.
“It’s been a hell of a year – analogue astronauts living in captivity of our own free will,” Ellen Ellis, the medical officer on the Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog, or CHAPEA, mission, said in remarks at Johnson Space Center after emerging with her three crewmates on Oct 31.
The four entered the 1,700-square-foot (158sq m) 3D-printed habitat on Oct 19, 2025, and performed tasks such as growing crops in simulated Martian soil and interfacing with NASA officials with delays recreating those inherent in interplanetary communications.
NASA, which has explored Mars with robotic rovers and orbiting spacecraft, has ambitions for a human mission to Mars as early as the 2030s, with plans before that to return astronauts to the moon for the first time since 1972.
“We have a narrowing window of opportunity to maintain US preeminence in space,” Ellis said.
Ellis mentioned the service academy for space-related operations pursued by US President Donald Trump’s administration and plans for a lunar base.
“Let’s seize the initiative, lead with science that will benefit our economy and ensure our legacy in space for our children’s children,” Ellis said.
The other crew members were mission commander Ross Elder, science officer Matthew Montgomery and flight engineer James Spicer.
“For Mars, the risks are great,” Elder said in remarks after emerging from isolation. “But through seeking understanding, strong vision and leadership, creativity, fortitude, hard work and incredible foundation, the goal of putting humans on Mars is not only achievable, but rather inevitable.”
The crew is set to participate in two weeks of post-mission evaluations and debriefing with NASA scientists. NASA has said it is looking for insight into what it takes for astronauts to adapt to the routines and demands of daily life on long-duration missions beyond Earth to keep them healthy, productive, and connected.
This was NASA’s second CHAPEA mission, with another four-person crew in isolation at Johnson Space Center for 378 days spanning 2023 and 2024.
Vanessa Wyche, director of the Johnson Space Center, greeted the crew members when they exited isolation. Wyche said they managed to live with limited resources, maintain their habitat, and carry out simulated Mars operations.
Wyche also noted how the crew dealt with the simulated interplanetary communications, with lag times between sending messages and receiving responses.
“These delays require patience, careful planning and greater independence – qualities that will be essential for future astronauts travelling millions of miles from home,” Wyche said.
Wyche said the lessons learnt from the CHAPEA crew and their experiences will help pave the way for the missions first to the moon and “one day, Mars.” REUTERS

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has warned of potential military escalation across Western Sahara following the termination of the global body’s 35-year-old peacekeeping mission in the disputed territory.
“The Secretary-General remains concerned about the security situation throughout the Territory and the risk of escalation of hostilities,” spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said on Sunday, urging all parties to exercise “maximum restraint and to refrain from actions that could further increase tensions or undermine regional stability.”
The United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) formally ceased operations after the UN Security Council failed to extend its mandate beyond October 31.
A reduced team under the UN Department of Operational Support began a liquidation phase to repatriate equipment belonging to troop-contributing countries and oversee the disposal of UN-owned assets.
Russian veto
Guterres stressed that the departure of peacekeepers does not diminish or eliminate the “inalienable right to self-determination” of the people of Western Sahara.
He also paid tribute to Special Representative Alexander Ivanko and honoured 20 personnel who lost their lives during the mission, which was established in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front.
While peacekeeping operations have ended, political negotiations will continue under the auspices of the UN chief’s personal envoy, Staffan de Mistura.
The mission’s termination follows a Russian veto on Friday of a US-drafted resolution aimed at renewing its mandate, despite 11 council members voting in favour and three abstaining.
Western Sahara remains a key issue in North African diplomacy.
Morocco has proposed broad autonomy for the territory under its sovereignty, while the Polisario Front continues to seek a referendum on self-determination, a position supported by Algeria.
The dispute over Western Sahara dates back to 1975, when Spain ended its colonial rule of the territory.
It escalated into armed conflict between Morocco and the Polisario Front until a 1991 ceasefire.

John J. Tkacik On Taiwan: “First Island Chain” means “Taiwan”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:43 UTC
01:44:43 KST

The news from General Christopher C. LaNeve, Vice Chief of Staff of the US Army, last month was a low-key 46 pages, but one sentence was arresting: the US Army will “organize, train, and equip against the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) — the ‘pacing threat’ — with the same institutional focus that the Cold War generations brought to the Soviet Army.” Ouch!
The sentence was in an unclassified document entitled “How The Army Fights,” and billed as “Operational Warfighting Guidance” for the Army; it is comprehensive and “multi-domain”; it covers the globe. Despite its breadth, there was no mistaking its focus on the Pacific, and particularly the “First Island Chain” (subtly called the “FIC”). Let me offer some history on the “FIC” concept and also share a thought on the “SIC” (the “second” one, which also unsettles me).
The “FIC” means “Taiwan.” The FIC is meaningless without Taiwan. I learned this 45 years ago from a somewhat flippant aside: “Keep Island Asia out of the hands of Mainland Asia. That’s been America’s strategy since MacArthur.”
Those were words the late William W. “Bill” Thomas put in a letter to my boss, Donald Ferguson, in 1981. Bill was then deputy director of the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) and Don was chief of Taiwan Coordination in the State Department. Bill was responding to a back-channel telegram from Charles W. “Chas” Freeman in Beijing expressing the embassy’s dissatisfaction with our out-of-date “policy” on Taiwan.
At the time, I mistook Bill’s epigram for a general comment on “Asia vs. Pacific,” “Mainland Asia” vs. “Island Asia.” But I soon grasped that Bill’s “Island Asia” was MacArthur’s “Island Chain,” and that the term “Island Chain,” in China policy argot, had been a synecdoche for “Taiwan” since at least April 1951. Indeed, the “Island Chain” as a strategic concept is incomprehensible without Formosa and China.
In a top-secret June 14, 1950, “Memorandum on Formosa” to the Joint Chiefs of Staff (written presciently 10 days before North Korea’s surprise invasion of the South), the supreme commander in Tokyo, General of the Army Douglas MacArthur, wrote: “I have been concerned as to the future status of Formosa and I have been convinced that the strategic interests of the United States will be in serious jeopardy if Formosa is allowed to be dominated by a power hostile to the United States.” It was the latest of several such memos he had sent to the Pentagon and the Department of State warning of the “strategic consequences which would result from the capture of Formosa by the Chinese Communists.” Formosa was, he said, an “integral part” of those “littoral islands” that formed America’s “western strategic frontier.” Its loss would give Communist China and the Soviet Union an “unsinkable aircraft carrier and submarine tender” equivalent to “ten or twenty aircraft carriers” from which they could menace the Philippines and beyond, both by air and under the sea, just as Japan had done in 1941.
MacArthur was well aware that the State Department hoped the US could seduce Communist China away from its new military alliance with the Soviet Union by allowing Mao Zedong’s (毛澤東) forces to occupy Taiwan in the summer of 1950. Secretary of State Dean Acheson was certain that, in contrast to the USSR’s continued occupation of Outer Mongolia, Manchuria and Xinjiang, America’s acquiescence in a Chinese communist takeover of Taiwan would both improve Washington’s relations with Peking and undermine Moscow’s.
MacArthur was dismissive of such appeasement. Formosa’s fate, he said, “largely rests with the United States” … and “unless the United States’ political-military strategic position in the Far East is to be abandoned,” it was obvious that “a line must be drawn beyond which Communist expansion will be stopped.”
It just so happened that the very day the Korean War erupted, June 24, 1950, the JCS chairman, General Bradley, had hand-carried the highly secret memo from Tokyo and delivered it into the hands of then US President Truman. At an emergency National Security Council meeting on June 25 to set US strategy in Korea, MacArthur and Formosa were first on the agenda. Acheson, a foe of MacArthur’s, suggested that “the future status of Formosa might be determined by the UN,” only to be interrupted by Truman, “or by the Japanese Peace Treaty.” General Bradley echoed MacArthur: “We must draw the line somewhere.” The president agreed and Taiwan was saved.
But 10 months later, on April 11, 1951, MacArthur had been fired (ironically, for his stance on Formosa’s possible contribution in the Korean War, a stance far beyond the president’s tolerance). The following week, after an exhausting air voyage from Tokyo, the fired MacArthur arrived at Washington National Airport. Rather than hail a taxi, he and the Mrs. opted for a twenty-car motorcade (with an escort of three dozen police motorcycles) to the Capitol, where he delivered his farewell speech to a Joint Session of Congress. At the center of his address was the “FIC” and Taiwan.
“We control [the Americas and the Pacific] to the shores of Asia by a chain of islands extending in an arc from the Aleutians to the Mariannas held by us and our free allies.” Yet “holding this littoral defense line in the western Pacific is entirely dependent upon holding all segments thereof, for any major breach of that line by an unfriendly power would render vulnerable to determined attack every other major segment … For that reason, I have strongly recommended in the past as a matter of military urgency that under no circumstances must Formosa fall under Communist control.” Moreover, his views “were fully shared by practically every military leader… including our own Joint Chiefs of Staff.” After his address, General MacArthur quietly recommenced his motorcade from the Capitol and processed two miles down Constitution Avenue (lined by a modest assemblage of 300,000 flag-waving well-wishers) to Constitution Hall, where he was greeted by Generals of the Army George C. Marshall and Omar Bradley, respectively Secretary of Defense and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs.
Now, how is all this relevant to General LaNeve’s “How the Army Fights” doctrine of October 2026?
To begin with, Taiwan is still the unnamed FIC silent partner it always has been. The document is chock-full of Taiwan scenarios; one is mooted in the doctrine’s six “Strike” models (along with Ukraine 2025, Gaza 2025, Ukraine 2026, “Nuclear Battlefield” and a nuclear strike on Guam). The doctrine envisages “high-intensity” battle in the “Luzon Strait” and “close battle” over sustained periods in “North Luzon & Batanes Strait, 2027 — Contested Sustainment in the FIC” — none of which include the South China Sea, and all of which require large cached pre-placements of war materiel in hundreds of dispersed locations — presumably in the Philippines and Japan, but perhaps in other unnamed places. Continuous news media commentary over the past seven years has been frank about the strategic challenges of fighting the PLA in the western Pacific. As US President Donald Trump put it, “You know, we’re supposed to travel 9,500 miles [15,289km] to fight a war. I’m not looking for that. I want them to cool down. I want China to cool down.” Meanwhile, the Pentagon reportedly will dispatch representatives from the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy, without oversight by AIT, directly to Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense.
Finally, LaNeve’s “Guidance” posits a most sobering thought: the US homeland is no longer out of reach. In a multi-domain war with China, not only does he presume Guam will be a target of nuclear strikes, but he also presumes America’s infrastructure will come under immediate attack. Cyber and space attacks will be coupled with arson, sabotage, social disorder, disinformation and cognitive warfare of almost unimaginable dimensions. LaNeve posits that US Army deployments in the FIC will not force “escalatory decisions” but, as Tom Lehrer says, “once the rockets are up,” all bets are off. LaNeve’s guidance departs from other Pentagon documents issued over the past 12 months (last November’s National Security Strategy, last Christmas Eve’s Pentagon report on China’s Military Power, and January’s National Defense Strategy) in its overt contemplation of China as the primary adversary. It is unclassified — it is designed to be perused and analyzed by the PLA.
So, if you see any “English teachers” at the Ministry of National Defense, thank them for their service.
One final thought about the “Second Island Chain” or the “SIC”: The US, in conjunction with Australia, France and New Zealand, is spending ridiculous amounts of money, far more than ever before, on infrastructure such as ports, airports and communications in the Mariana Islands, Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM) and across the Pacific. I do not think the Defense Department (or War Department) yet appreciates how China has already penetrated these partners and beyond. For example, on the island of Woleai in the FSM, just over 400 miles from Guam, a Chinese state-owned company began work in September 2025 to rebuild a World War II Imperial Japanese air base. They are not building airstrips in the SIC for frequent-flier miles.
LJohn J. Tkacik, Jr. is a retired US foreign service officer who has served in Taipei and Beijing and is now director of the Future Asia Project at the International Assessment and Strategy Center. He is also on the Advisory Board of the Global Taiwan Institute.

‘Air-con nation’ Singapore eyes alternatives to cool off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:39 UTC
01:44:39 KST

Long dubbed an “air-conditioned nation,” Singapore is experimenting with cooling alternatives from chilled beams to “passive displacement” to curb its thirst for energy-guzzling air-conditioning.
The city-state has the highest per-capita air-conditioner ownership rate in Southeast Asia, with about 99 percent of private residences equipped with cooling units.
Singapore’s local building sector accounts for one-fifth of its emissions, while cooling itself accounts for 40 to 60 percent of a building’s energy consumption, according to studies.
Photo: AFP
A stroll down Orchard Road highlights that dependence. Shoppers are greeted by blasts of cool air that waft into the street as doors swing open — a major draw given that daytime highs hover between 31°C and 33°C year-round.
However, air-conditioning can make the heat problem worse. Compressor units belch hot air back out into the environment, and the electricity that powers the systems can contribute to climate change if generated from fossil fuels.
Some buildings in Singapore are looking at other options, including active chilled beams, which are perforated panels equipped with cooling coils that are mounted on ceilings.
A chiller plant on the building’s top floor cools water down to 9°C, then pumps it into the coils. Simultaneously, air is blasted through small nozzles inside the beams. The jets of air create a low-pressure zone that sucks up warmer air from the room below so it passes over the coils and is cooled before recirculating.
The technology keeps the offices at the eight-story Paya Lebar Green building at a comfortable 24°C.
There is noticeably cooler air flowing from the sleek white panels on the ceiling of the building, described as one of Singapore’s “greenest.”
The system is also quiet, without the constant hum of air-conditioning units.
The system cut energy use by more than 30 percent compared with conventional air-conditioning, DP Architects said, the building’s designers.
A similar system is in use at Singapore’s ports authority maintenance building at western Tuas harbor.
The building uses passive displacement cooling, which taps natural airflow to reduce reliance on mechanical fans. Ceiling cooling coils chill the air, which sinks before naturally rising back to the coils as it warms. This continuous cycle reduces the need for fans, cutting energy use and noise.
Another alternative is radiant cooling, where water chilled to between 14°C and 18°C flows through pipes or panels and absorbs heat radiating from people or objects to reduce ambient temperatures.
The push to find new cooling solutions has government backing.
A 2024 government study identified alternative cooling technologies (ACTs) as a key strategy which found they could save the city up to 48 percent in energy.
By the middle of this year, at least 33 public and 14 private buildings had adopted ACTs, Singapore’s building authorities said.
The city-state has an ambitious goal to achieve net zero carbon emissions by 2050.
The figures are still relatively small, and it can be challenging to find an ACT that is acceptable to users familiar with tried-and-tested air-conditioners.
Supporters of alternative systems acknowledge that they cost more to install than conventional air-conditioning, but say they more than make up for it over time with much lower running costs thanks to big energy savings.
The most popular alternative method remains hybrid cooling — simply turning up air-conditioning to a higher temperature of 25.5°C to 27°C, and pairing it with fans.

The sharing economy is catching up with Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:35 UTC
01:44:35 KST

Shinjuku is moving to restrict minpaku, the practice of letting out apartments and houses for platforms such as Airbnb Inc, following a surge of complaints. Residents of the neon-lit area that is home to the world’s busiest railway station are unhappy about tourists causing noise late at night, jamming apartment building corridors with suitcases and failing to correctly put out garbage. Shinjuku has the most minpaku properties of any municipality in the country, a stock that has more than doubled in just three years.
The mayor, a longtime opponent of short-term rentals, said that the “lofty ideals” of this type of platform — hosts earning a little side money from utilizing unused rooms, perhaps introducing their guests to the neighborhood — simply have not materialized. About 2,000 existing properties would be hit by the changes.
It seems like another black mark against Japan’s sharing economy. Further deregulation of ridesharing, introduced in limited form and to great fanfare in 2024, has stalled. The typical view emerging is that the country has closed ranks to foreign companies to protect entrenched interests such as the taxi lobby.
However, that is far from the full story. Shinjuku’s mayor is right: The “lofty ideals” are often just ways of using technology to sidestep laws. Japan’s approach has long been that if it looks like a taxi or hotel, and operates like a taxi or hotel, then it should be regulated as such, regardless of whether an app sits in between users and providers.
Uber Technologies Inc chief executive officer Dara Khosrowshahi told The New York Times that “Japan is forcing me to be patient,” a persistence that is easy to understand given that Japan is the single largest taxi market in the world. Uber works with existing taxi firms to allow them to utilize its technology, but the move to UberX-style private rides has made little headway.
Individual drivers are in fact a great example. Japan already has a similar system, known as kojin taxi, which is tightly regulated. A license requires years of accident-free, professional driving experience. There is absolutely an argument for loosening those rules, but it should not be simply to convenience Silicon Valley disruptors.
Japan was less skeptical about property rentals, but still resisted getting fully onboard, capping stays at 180 nights a year. Changes this year allow municipalities to further restrict that. Shinjuku’s data indicate that the vast majority of minpaku are investment properties. It is these non-resident owners who benefit, along with tourists, while local residents are stuck with the nuisance, uncollected garbage and pressures that can force rents higher.
Japan is not alone in becoming increasingly skeptical about the sharing economy. New York has regulated Uber more like taxis and cracked down on Airbnb rentals with a law that requires the host to be a resident of the property. Paris has tightened rules on short-term stays; Barcelona is about to shut them down entirely.
Japan is not a great market for disruptors whose advantage comes from exploiting legal loopholes. Most here still expect regulators to regulate, and the government to supervise private business.
That does not mean new technologies cannot be co-opted within existing frameworks. Go Inc, which runs the largest taxi-hailing app and listed earlier this year, operates an efficient platform that reduces payment friction. A forthcoming team-up with Alphabet Inc’s Waymo plans to bring robotaxis to Japan, which needs more rides, especially in rural areas.
Likewise, while Airbnb might be ill-suited to Shinjuku condos, holiday homes in the mountains are another matter. In Osaka’s Nishinari, one of the poorest districts in the country, I was fascinated to see flophouses that once accommodated day laborers now being remade into Airbnbs; less densely populated areas in Tokyo are actually planning to loosen restrictions.
Japan famously has millions of empty homes, but also some of the most cramped apartments in the developed world; rural areas with no taxis, served only by a handful of trains a day, and urban centers with the world’s most crowded public transport. One approach for all is not going to work. The lesson of the sharing economy is not that Japan needs UberX and Airbnbs everywhere. It is that the technology can be useful even when the regulatory model is not.
Gearoid Reidy is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Japan. He previously led the breaking news team in North Asia, and was the Tokyo deputy bureau chief. Do not let algorithms decide the elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:32 UTC
01:44:32 KST

Local elections are at the end of this month, but I have already cast my vote on my phone.
My feed on the social media app Threads has been filled with posts tearing a certain mayor’s entire governing record to shreds. In my mother’s Line group chat, that same mayor is hailed as a flawless hero. My mother and I live in the same place, yet we inhabit parallel worlds. This is not a political divide, but an algorithmic one. The battlegrounds in this year’s elections are not campaign rallies; they are the smartphones in our hands.
As local elections involve candidates that many people might not be familiar with, voters rely heavily on the Internet to stay informed. They turn to Line groups and Facebook, precisely the places where the echo chamber effect is most pronounced.
If you read or search for posts about air pollution, these sites feed you more news about air pollution. For urban development, it might push posts about land justice. Over time, a person’s social media feed could become focused on the issues and opinions the user trained it to find.
Social media have made it easier than ever to target specific groups. The now defunct Cambridge Analytica made headlines for accessing the Facebook data of 87 million users, which it allegedly harnessed to create microtargeted advertising during the 2016 US presidential election.
In Taiwan, a city council candidate could spend a few thousand New Taiwan dollars to target a specific group of voters, potentially with misleading information about a rival. This is not a campaign tactic; it is psychological warfare. Any person could be the victim of paid propaganda, which they then repeat online.
Then there is “deepfake” technology. People used to worry that deepfakes would target the president or a celebrity, but now, even village wardens and city councilors are potential targets.
Imagine a photograph of a candidate accepting a bribe or an audio recording of them saying they would sell off public land suddenly circulating in group chats. Before anyone can even verify its authenticity, voters would already be headed to the polls. Local fact-checking resources are weaker than those at the national level, yet the damage from misinformation is far more direct.
Then nine-in-one elections affect everything from the roads outside our homes to the schools our children attend. We cannot allow algorithms to dictate their outcome.
The Central Election Commission and the Ministry of Digital Affairs must establish lines of defense.
First, require major international platforms to establish a transparency database that discloses advertisers of political content and ad-targeting parameters.
Second, establish an emergency takedown and labeling mechanism for fabricated or manipulated content, requiring platforms to label reported “deepfake” videos and suspend their recommendation within 24 hours in the week before the election.
Third, city and county governments should send text messages to voters debunking disinformation.
Social media can encourage people to take an interest in local governance, but it can also turn them against each another. When we cast our ballots later this month, we should vote for those who serve their communities; we should not cast our ballots out of fear or prejudice fed to us on social media. Do not let algorithms decide who the next mayor is be before we do.
Chang Hou-kuang works in aerospace production control.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

Can Japan beat the  data center backlash?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:29 UTC
01:44:29 KST

Among the nearly 100 pages of risk factors outlined in Anthropic PBC’s landmark initial public offering are the catastrophic threats to humanity that have grabbed headlines. However, it also flagged a more immediate concern that could derail business: mounting backlash against data centers.
Public controversy and regulatory scrutiny over the environmental impact, land and water use as well as consumption of limited power resources threaten to delay or prevent data-center development, Anthropic said in the prospectus. That would raise costs and limit its ability to scale, develop and deploy artificial intelligence (AI) models, it says.
The company is right to worry. Hatred toward data centers has united people across the political spectrum and around the globe. Warning that the technology could create existential risks probably does not inspire anyone to want to give the AI boom a physical address in their backyards.
Illustration: Yusha
Opposition to the build-out has surfaced in Australia, the UK and even rural China. Now, it is starting to fester in pockets of Japan, just as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is pushing massive investment. Meanwhile, Anthropic is reportedly in final talks with NTT Data Group to build one of the country’s biggest data centers near Osaka.
Yet while anxiety around the technology runs high globally, the Japanese are unusually sanguine about it — robots are seen here more as friendly helpers such as Doraemon than The Terminator. For a smaller, relatively insular economy facing acute labor shortages and demographic pressures, the upsides could be enormous.
Many of AI’s strengths neatly address Japan’s acute gaps: translation in a country that has been flooded with foreign tourists, software engineering in a tech industry historically stronger in hardware than coding, boosting efficiency for small and medium-size manufacturers, and easing administrative burdens for the growing cohort of elder caregivers. The list goes on.
For now, Japan’s opposition is scattered and local, hardly close to the organized political movement we are seeing in the US. However, there was little excuse anywhere to be so caught off guard. I have been tracking the AI backlash for a while, and the industry’s implicit threat that this might kill us all or take your job has never been an effective way to greet new neighbors. Outside of the Silicon Valley bubble, data centers as the physical manifestation of an abstract tech revolution have become easy targets. It is more than noise, eyesore or water use. It is about having a say.
This is partly why the US revolt goes far beyond NIMBYism. Nearly three-quarters of Americans oppose having a data center in their community, while two-thirds are against new ones anywhere. It is already having a material impact: In the first half of this year alone, at least 106 projects, representing about US$198 billion in investment, were blocked or delayed, the Data Center Watch said. It offers lessons for Tokyo to not assume these are just isolated groups of Luddites.
Japan has the most favorable environment for data center development among the OECD markets in the Asia-Pacific region, given its established digital infrastructure sector, BloombergNEF assessed. It already has some 2 gigawatts of operating IT capacity, second in the region only to China. Local opposition is a lurking threat, but the more immediate constraint is power.
These facilities guzzle enormous amounts of energy to run servers and cooling, and Japan has never been energy rich. Power demand from new data centers and chip fabs is expected to rise from less than 1 percent of the country’s electricity consumption this year to nearly 7 percent by 2035, SMBC Nikko analysts have said. Addressing this challenge could help catalyze a broader shift toward clean energy.
The government, for its part, seems aware of the problem. Takaichi has pledged a “sufficient and stable supply of electricity” to meet the growing demands from data centers, doubling down on an earlier promise to “take all possible measures” to do so. The policy direction is right, if ambitious, but increasing investments in green energy would help Japan build resilience in the future, not just power these facilities.
Currently, most data center capacity is concentrated in the Greater Tokyo region and Osaka. Mindful of risks in the event of earthquakes or other unexpected shocks, officials have identified potential future sites in Hokkaido, Kyushu and elsewhere. Spreading infrastructure beyond crowded urban areas would also reduce some of the nuisance complaints that have fueled opposition elsewhere.
Japan was initially slow to adopt AI, but usage has finally surged. That delay could become a second-mover advantage that the country cannot afford to squander as investors start questioning the payoff from the expensive, hype-fueled AI infrastructure spree.
The country has long excelled at developing infrastructure that works for people, from trains that run on time to urban design that fosters community. That could be a major advantage. If Tokyo can construct data centers without neighbors bringing out the pitchforks, it could define what comes next.
Catherine Thorbecke is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Asia tech. Previously she was a tech reporter at CNN and ABC News. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Thousands of Indians protest voter list change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:29 UTC
01:44:29 KST

Tens of thousands of Indians yesterday joined a protest led by opposition politicians in New Delhi, renewing demands for the country’s election chief to resign over an overhaul of voter lists they say unfairly benefits the ruling party.
The nationwide revision of electoral rolls has sparked political disputes and street protests over the past month.
The Indian Election Commission said the initiative is necessary to ensure accurate voter lists, but the opposition said it is being manipulated to favor Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Photo: Reuters
The BJP and the commission deny the allegations.
Protesters led by opposition Congress Party leader Rahul Gandhi chanted “vote thief, leave your seat” and beat drums while marching from central parts of New Delhi to Ramlila Maidan, a large outdoor venue.
Gandhi said protesters were “not prepared to accept” the voter list removals.
“It is the theft of the voice of every single citizen of India,” he said. “This protest does not belong to any political party. It is India’s protest to save the democracy and constitution.”
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online youth-led protest movement, has also thrown its weight behind the opposition campaign.
The overhaul of India’s voter rolls has resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings.
Critics said the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.
Members of the BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighboring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.
Election authorities said the revision was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries, and that eligible voters remain entitled to apply for inclusion on the roll.
Minister of Health and Family Welfare and senior BJP leader Jagat Prakash Nadda called the rally “a meticulously planned drama by those who have been defeated and repeatedly rejected by the people.”
“It is a calculated conspiracy to plunge the nation into anarchy,” he said.
Protester Jayshree Roy said the government would have to listen if people “keep asking for their rights.”
“We have to keep showing up in large numbers, that is all that we can do,” the student said. “We have the power of people in our hands. That is all that we have.”

Fuel prices unchanged for seventh straight week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:24 UTC
01:44:24 KST

State-owned oil supplier CPC Corp, Taiwan (台灣中油) on Saturday announced that it would leave its domestic gasoline and diesel prices unchanged this week despite rising international crude oil prices.
Rival Formosa Petrochemical Corp’s (台塑石化) Web site yesterday showed that the company would also keep its fuel prices steady this week.
It would be the seventh consecutive week that CPC and Formosa have maintained their domestic fuel prices at the same levels to reduce inflationary pressure.
Taiwan’s consumer price index rose 2.73 percent year-on-year last month, marking the fifth straight month that the index stayed above a 2 percent alert set by the central bank.
Front-month Brent crude oil futures — a global benchmark — on Friday rose 2.4 percent to hit a high since the end of April amid concerns over potential attacks on Iran after the US’ midterm elections tomorrow. For the week, Brent rose 0.79 percent to settle at US$117.64 per barrel on the Intercontinental Exchange in London.
Under CPC’s floating fuel price mechanism, which tracks a weighted average of 70 percent Dubai crude and 30 percent Brent crude, the average international crude oil price rose to US$117.01 per barrel last week from US$114.83 per barrel the previous week, the company said.
The silver lining was that a stronger New Taiwan dollar, which averaged NT$32.460 against the US dollar last week, compared with NT$32.515 the previous week, reduced CPC’s overseas oil purchasing costs to some extent.
This week, retail gasoline prices are to remain at NT$31.2, NT$32.7 and NT$34.7 per liter for 92, 95 and 98-octane unleaded gasoline respectively at CPC and Formosa stations, while prices of premium diesel would stay at NT$29.9 per liter at CPC stations and NT$29.7 per liter at Formosa pumps, the companies said.

Nuit Blanche brings a night of art to Taipei’s Yuanshan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:23 UTC
01:44:23 KST

Taipei’s 11th Nuit Blanche arts festival wrapped up early yesterday morning following a night of art installations, interactive performances and live music across the city’s Yuanshan (圓山) area.
The overnight event, which ran from 2pm on Saturday until 2am yesterday, was co-organized by the Taipei City Department of Cultural Affairs and the French Office in Taipei, in collaboration with the Centquatre-Paris.
This year’s festival featured more than 30 art installations and 50 performances and sound art programs across Tatung University, Yuanshan Natural Landscape Park, the Yuanshan and Xinsheng (新生) areas of Taipei Expo Park, and areas near Minzu East Road and Qingguang Market (晴光市場).
Photo: Chiang Ying-ying, AP
Among the featured works was Blackcat and Nagashi in Midnight 1972, an interactive theater production that invited audience members to take on the role of employees at a 1970s hot spring hotel investigating a long-standing mystery.
At FreeS Art Space, the artist Chuang Pei-xin (莊培鑫) presented The Method of Entry, an installation using 3D scanning to transform physical bodies into digital models.
The work explored the boundaries between exhibition spaces, offices and theaters, with music and movement transforming the space as night fell, organizers said.
The festival also featured a street dance block party, where dancers took part in open freestyle sessions before competing in a Top 8 battle. Audience members voted for the night’s most outstanding performer, with cash prizes of NT$10,000 for the battle champion and NT$5,000 for the audience-selected Most Valuable Player.
Nuit Blanche originated in Paris 25 years ago, with Taiwan adopting the event 11 years ago, French Office in Taipei Director Frederic Laplanche told a news conference on Saturday.
Attendance at the inaugural Taipei festival reached 200,000, rising to more than 500,000 last year, he said.
The event provided an opportunity for Taiwan and France to promote shared values, including creative freedom and public access to art, Laplanche said.

Laos looks to wind energy for its renewables plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:21 UTC
01:44:21 KST

Rising from verdant ridgelines of southern Laos, 133 Chinese-built wind turbines help power Vietnam’s surging growth and represent part of a regional rush to diversify energy sources.
“The view is beautiful. They’re bigger than trees,” Toukta Phonsala said inside her wooden stilt house in Dak Wai village.
Hydroelectric dams have proliferated across Southeast Asia over the past few years, but production drops off in the dry season and critics lament the ecological impacts.
Photo: AFP
Experts said wind is now set to take off, and point to Laos’ 600-megawatt Monsoon Wind Power Project, which began operating in August last year, as a bankable case study.
Spanning an area the size of Singapore, the US$700 million scheme is the first cross-border wind project in Asia and the largest wind farm in Southeast Asia. Built by a Chinese state firm and owned by a Thai-led consortium, it sells electricity exclusively to Vietnam’s national grid via dedicated transmission lines.
Manufacturing hub Vietnam, Southeast Asia’s fastest-growing economy, was already importing hydropower from Laos, its poorest neighbor.
However, “the economics are moving in favor of wind,” EnergyLab Asia technical program lead Tristan Bellingham said.
“Similar to hydro 20 to 30 years ago, there’s a bit of a rush on to secure concessions and development rights” for new wind projects, he said.
Laos already hosts 90 hydropower plants and there are dozens more in neighboring nations, leaving few optimal sites remaining.
For Toukta, the 18 family members she lives with, and other rice and coffee farmers residing near the turbines, Monsoon has brought new roads and improved access to fresh water and healthcare.
However, what it has not brought to her community is power.
Residents said they still experience outages during heavy storms, as Laos’ electricity infrastructure is outdated and the state utility is heavily in debt.
Still, Toukta is glad Laos can send power abroad, saying: “It’s better for development and can bring prosperity.”
For Vietnam, the project offers a reliable source of less costly energy.
There were severe blackouts in 2023 when drought cut into hydropower supply, and the government warned in September of the risk of electricity shortages from next year due to delays in planned power projects and increasing demand.
Through Monsoon, “wind power is being sold significantly cheaper to Vietnam than what Vietnam is buying wind power for locally,” Indochina Energy Partners managing director Thomas Jakobsen said.
He estimated state utility Electricity Vietnam was paying Monsoon about six cents per kilowatt-hour — two to four cents less than the Vietnamese rate.
The project is also key to Vietnam reaching net zero emissions targets by 2050, National Power Transmission Corporation official Ninh Xuan Hiep said.
By 2030, Laos imports would equal nearly 10 percent of Vietnam’s total installed capacity — its maximum possible production, the official said.
Monsoon Wind plans to boost capacity by 1,000 megawatts and is working to ensure some of this additional power is used inside Laos, general manager Narut Boakajorn said.
“Laos has so much natural resources” — wind, hydro and solar, Narut said. “Not many countries have all the good renewable energy in the same place. Laos has something unique.”
Nobody was forced to relocate because of the project, Narut said, although public dissent is severely restricted in communist Laos.
He said the 1,600 grievances logged, mainly from farmers requesting compensation for construction impacts on their crops, were resolved.
Farmer Phonekhan Sengsopha said he was proud that electricity produced in his country was being sent to its neighbor, also a communist nation.
“Because Vietnam and Laos are like brothers. They help one another,” he said.

Yilan residents file suit to slow HSR review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:21 UTC
01:44:21 KST

Yilan County residents, backed by civic groups, on Wednesday filed an administrative lawsuit to overturn the environmental impact assessment (EIA) approval for the Yilan-bound high-speed rail (HSR) extension.
They filed the lawsuit after the Executive Yuan on Sept. 11 rejected an administrative appeal.
Former Environmental Protection Administration (EPA) deputy minister and lawyer Thomas Chan (詹順貴) said the project’s EIA review was one of the hastiest he had ever seen during his 30-year career in environmental law.
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
Construction of the line would generate nearly 10 million cubic meters of excavated earth and rock, the disposal of which has not yet been explained to the public, he told a news conference at the Taipei High Administrative Court on Wednesday.
Although Chan describe the project as being more than 90km long, the Railway Bureau puts its length at 60.6km.
An earlier Taipei-Yilan direct railway plan for a 36km route through the Feitsui Reservoir (翡翠水庫) watershed with much less excavated soil was rejected during environmental review in 2006, Chan said.
The new project would also involve a proposed 420-hectare district near the HSR Yilan station, for which the precise extent of farmland expropriation remains undetermined, he said.
Such a large-scale agricultural land expropriation seems unnecessary and might attract land speculation, he said, adding that the special district near the Taichung HSR covers less than 300 hectares.
Most land in the proposed station district is within a local special agricultural zone, he said.
The project would affect the agricultural environment and agricultural workers’ livelihoods, but those issues were not addressed in the EIA, Chan said.
Many EIA committee members have expressed concerns over excavated soil disposal, route planning and the impact of the extension on Taiwan Railway Corp’s operations and Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp’s finances, he said.
Nevertheless, the project quickly passed its second-stage EIA review without properly addressing these concerns, Chan said.
The Railway Bureau on Aug. 30, 2019, submitted a comprehensive Taipei-Yilan direct railway plan — in which the line would run parallel to Chiang Wei-shui Memorial Freeway (Freeway No. 5) — to the Ministry of Transportation and Communications, which requested an assessment of the HSR extension option three months later, and on Nov. 22, the bureau began assessing an HSR extension, former transportation minister Hochen Tan (賀陳旦) said.
“That was a crude decision,” he said.
The HSR extension project did not initially undergo a separate feasibility study before comprehensive planning, a procedural choice Hochen criticized, although subsequent reviews involved the National Development Council.
The project also used what he considered disproportionate assessment weighting in comparisons of railway route options.
It gave low weighting to assessment criteria, such as transportation time reduction (0.054), traffic distribution (0.045) or construction costs (0.026), while the weighting for impact on water-source protection areas was disproportionately high (0.145), Hochen said.
He said a 2005 EPA-commissioned study showed that Freeway No. 5 had little effect on water quality in the protected watershed, an interpretation later questioned by the Control Yuan.
“The cross-sectional area of railway is smaller than the freeway’s and would have less of an impact,” he said.

BOOKMAN BILINGUAL 雙語書林： Chinglish or Natural English? 中式英語或道地英語？
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:20 UTC
01:44:20 KST

1. 沒人知道她多麼受苦受難。
ˇ No one knows how much she suffered.
χ No one knows how hard she suffered.
Photo: Adobe Stock l 照片:Adobe Stock
註：可以說 The wind blew hard. / It rained very hard. / He worked hard.，不可以說 *He suffered very hard.，應說 He suffered a great deal / very much.
2. 他成為非常熟練的技師。
ˇ He became a highly skilled technician.
χ He became a high skilled technician.
註：high 既可用作形容詞，也可用作副詞；但 highly 只可用作副詞。high 作副詞時，常用在 to aim high, to hold one’s head high, the bird flew high, hold high the banner of... 等詞組或句子中。Highly 指抽象的「高」，例如：highly amusing, a highly paid officer , to speak highly of someone , to think highly of someone。
He is highly respected.
3. 「昨天你為什麼沒來上學？」老師嚴厲地問道。
ˇ “Why didn’t you come to school yesterday?” asked the teacher sternly.
χ “Why didn’t you come to school yesterday?” asked the teacher strictly.
註：stern, sternly 含有「嚴酷」之意，常用於 a stern look, a stern voice，同義詞是 severe, cruel, pitiless 等。a stern person 的反義詞是 a gentle person。strict, strictly 指要求上的嚴格，常用於紀律、規章制度，例如：
A teacher should be strict, but not stern.（老師要嚴格，不要嚴厲。）
A director may give strict orders.
There is a strict rule against smoking.
Strictly speaking, ... （嚴格地說，……）
4. 他東西一直都亂放。
ˇ He has been leaving things everywhere.
χ He has been leaving things about everywhere.
註：about 在這裏是副詞，作 here and there 解，與 everywhere 重複，應刪去其一。又如：
There are several men lying about (= here and there) on the grass.
5. 我小女兒以她的年紀算是很高了。
ˇ My little daughter is quite tall for her age.
χ My small daughter is quite tall for her age.
註：小女兒可以說 younger daughter 或 little daughter，但不可以說 small daughter。而大女兒可以說 older daughter 或 big daughter，但不可以說 large daughter。
Exercise
A. 我們一直到處找你。
We have been looking __________ for you.
1. anywhere
2. everywhere
3. somewhere
B. 我的老師十分讚賞我。
My teacher speaks very __________ of me.
1. heavy
2. highly
3. well
4. lightly
Answers: A. 2 B. 2

The party is optimistic about turning the tide in Keelung, Yilan County, Hsinchu County, Changhua County and Chiayi City, while candidates in Taichung City and Taitung County are also catching up, the source said.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
While DPP Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) “Ocean Wave” (洋流) has boosted the DPP’s election prospects, President William Lai (賴清德), who also chairs the party, reminded party members to remain vigilant and humble regardless of fluctuations in opinion polls, they said.
Lai urged the DPP, when facing attacks and provocations in the coming weeks, to respond rationally and with restraint.
The DPP’s Central Standing Committee also issued a directive to local branches urging caution in conduct, reminding them that overconfidence leads to defeat, they said.
Party insiders believe that the DPP support remains solid in its strongholds of Kaohsiung, Tainan, Chiayi County and Pingtung County, while Penghu remains a difficult contest, they said.
Changhua County, Chiayi City, Yilan County, Hsinchu County and Keelung are regions where the party hopes for breakthroughs, as divisions within the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), the breakdown of KMT-Taiwan People’s Party cooperation could open the way, they said.
In Taichung, DPP mayoral candidate Ho Hsin-chun (何欣純) has benefited from the “Ocean Wave” effect, drawing support from young voters and raising the profile of policy debates, gradually narrowing the gap with her rival, they said.
In Taitung County, DPP Legislator Asenay Daliyalrep, has continued to advance on the strength of party unity, intensifying grassroots campaigning in indigenous communities to secure 40 percent of the indigenous vote, they said.
The party’s coordinated campaigns in Taipei and New Taipei City have injected momentum into what had been a lackluster election, prompting voters to take a fresh look at candidates’ expertise and policy platforms, they said.
The party plans to extend the momentum to Taipei, New Taipei, Keelung, Taoyuan and other administrative regions by combining publicity campaigns, in-person events and social media initiatives, strengthening appeals for young people to return home and cast their ballots, they said.
In the final stage, the party plans to hold large-scale campaign rallies to mobilize voters, bolstered by appearances from heavyweights, including Lai, former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) and Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴), they said.
Campaign appearances by senior party figures would be coordinated with major events in each administrative region, including the final week of campaigning and election-eve rallies, they said.
As New Taipei City is a pivotal battleground that could influence the overall election outcome, DPP mayoral candidate Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧) has been setting up joint campaign headquarters with city council candidates, completing their grassroots organizational groundwork, Su’s campaign officials said.
The party plans to hold large-scale rallies on four consecutive weekends, each drawing at least 5,000 people, they said, adding that they also plan to have Lai, Tsai, Hsiao and Shen appear onstage, with at least one high-profile figure attending each week.
The rallies would be supplemented by motorcades, street campaigns and social media initiatives to sustain momentum, they said.
Building momentum is one thing, but maintaining that momentum down the stretch is the hardest part, a campaign staffer said, adding that the final month would be a tough battle.
As New Taipei City Mayor Hou You-yi (侯友宜) is campaigning for KMT mayoral candidate Lee Shu-chuan (李四川), the DPP must closely monitor whether the KMT’s local networks fully mobilize, including volunteer police and firefighters, the DPP staffer said.

The TAIEX is expected to face heavy downward pressure today after American depositary receipts of contract chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) on Friday plunged 5.95 percent, tracking a broader sell-off in US tech stocks on Wall Street amid concerns over massive artificial intelligence (AI) spending.
Disappointing sales at some US technology companies spurred the worst drop for stocks since June, with the tech-heavy NASDAQ Composite Index falling 2.86 percent on Friday, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 7.20 percent and the S&P 500 fell 1.8 percent, breaching its 100-day moving average.
Chipmaker Intel Corp and social media firm Reddit Inc fell 29 percent and Sandisk Corp, a chipmaker that has been one of the great beneficiaries of the AI capital-spending boom, dropped 13 percent.
Photo: CNA
Market sentiment remained clouded by concerns over heavy AI spending and growing fears that major cloud service providers might struggle to generate comfortable sales from their massive investments in AI infrastructure, Taishin Securities Investment Advisory Co (台新投顧) chief strategy officer Tony Huang (黃文清) said on Saturday.
Tech stocks worldwide have come under heavy selling pressure since the beginning of last month, and Taiwan’s stock market is unlikely to be spared, particularly as large-cap electronics stocks such as TSMC have been targeted by investors, Huang said.
On Friday, the TAIEX plunged 1,156.50 points, or 2.49 percent, to close at 45,211.83, breaking below the key technical support level of about 45,300 points, which coincides with its 120-day moving average, leaving the benchmark index technically more vulnerable.
Following the latest sell-off in the US market, TAIEX futures also came under pressure, falling 867 points, or 1.91 percent, to 44,433 on Friday, while TSMC futures lost 3.66 percent.
However, the TAIEX appeared relatively resilient compared with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index and the South Korean market, where memory suppliers such as Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc account for a significant share of market activity, Huang said.
More importantly, AI development has not slowed, as major cloud service providers Meta Platforms Inc, Alphabet Inc, Amazon.com Inc and Microsoft Corp have maintained their commitments to substantial spending on AI infrastructure, he said.
Taiwan Stock Exchange’s statistics showed that foreign institutional investors were largely net sellers of Taiwanese shares last month, recording net sales of NT$994.3 billion (US$30.61 billion), by reducing their holdings in major tech stocks such as TSMC, chip designer MediaTek Inc (聯發科) and power management solutions provider Delta Electronics Inc (台達電).
Global markets face additional uncertainty from the upcoming US midterm elections tomorrow and a planned initial public offering by AI safety and research company Anthropic PBC later this month, factors that have prompted large funds to pull money out of Asian markets, analysts said.
Investors would be watching whether the TAIEX will hold above Friday’s intraday low of 44,726 points or record further losses, they added.

Envoy to return to head global drone academy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:17 UTC
01:44:17 KST

Deputy Representative to the Philippines Lee Ting-sheng (李廷盛), a retired air force lieutenant general, is to return to Taiwan and assume the role of chief executive officer at the Global Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Academy (GUAVA), a source said yesterday.
To consolidate resources and maximize operational effectiveness, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ Drone Diplomacy Task Force would also be merged into GUAVA, which would be led by Lee to actively accelerate Taiwan’s drone diplomacy and asymmetric security cooperation, they added.
Lee, 64, graduated from the Republic of China Air Force Academy and is one of the rare US-educated flag officers in the armed forces, having solid flight experience in F-5E and a US military strategic mindset.
Photo: CNA
After retiring from the rank of lieutenant general, he served as the deputy executive director and executive director of the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, and assumed his post as Deputy Representative to the Philippines in September 2024.
During his tenure in the Philippines, Lee facilitated a visit by an active-duty general to Manila, and spearheaded the first official coast guard exchanges since diplomatic ties between the two countries were severed in 1974, the source said.
Lee also assisted in transferring 453-tonne retired the vessel Kinmen to the Philippines for humanitarian search and rescue, laying a solid security foundation for Taiwan-Philippines relations, they added.
Precisely because of his numerous accomplishments on the front lines in Southeast Asia, Lee — who has background and expertise in military strategy, diplomacy and an extensive network — was tapped as the top choice to lead Taiwan’s drone diplomacy, the source said.
Lee had also previously served as deputy commander of the air force and assistant deputy chief of the general staff for communications, electronics and information.
Alongside this appointment, the structural framework for drone diplomacy undergoing a major reform, with the ministry’s Drone Diplomacy Task Force merged into GUAVA, signaling Taiwan’s move beyond bureaucratic constraints toward a more flexible and consolidated operation, the source said.
The official task force, previously restricted by public sector regulations, faced limitations when negotiating commercial opportunities, technology transfers or joint international production, they said.
After merging with the fully privately funded GUAVA, it is to be chaired by Lee Hahn-ming (李漢銘), while Lee Ting-sheng would oversee actual policy execution as CEO, leveraging public-private synergy to break through diplomatic difficulties, they said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:14 UTC
01:44:14 KST

Mexican veteran Saul “Canelo” Alvarez on Saturday produced a commanding performance to defeat French fighter Christian Mbilli and regain his WBC super middleweight title in an emotional victory in Saudi Arabia.
Alvarez won a 12-round decision in Riyadh after exerting his influence in the second half of a fight that went ahead despite the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi movement.
The 36-year-old Mexican was returning to the ring for the first time since he was beaten by American Terence Crawford in September last year.
Photo: AFP
That loss ended Alvarez’s reign as holder of the division’s four major titles.
He faced Mbilli, 31, who was elevated to titleholder in January, but a fight that started off as a tight contest turned into a convincing victory for Alvarez.
The judges scored the contest 115-112, 116-111 and 117-110 in Alvarez’s favor.
The Mexican superstar struggled for words after receiving the belt.
“It’s so difficult to explain, it’s so difficult to explain,” Alvarez said. “It’s something unbelievable. It feels like my first title. Now, after 20, 21 years as a professional — 16 years ago, I won my first title. Now I won the title again.”
Alvarez added another world title to a haul that stretches from light-middleweight to light-heavyweight in a 20-year career.
A host of other sporting events have been called off in Saudi Arabia since the Houthis launched drone attacks and the Saudis intercepted missiles last week.
The Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition event and the final round of the World Rally Championship have been canceled, but the world of combat sports continues to hold events in the kingdom.
Alvarez hinted at the security situation when he thanked his family “who are watching me from afar today for the first time.”
He was the more composed boxer in the opening round in Riyadh, but by round three Mbilli was ripping off combinations and looking the more active of the two fighters.
The Frenchman took the initiative in round five although the bout remained a tactical battle.
Alvarez began showing his class and ringcraft in the sixth, easily winning the round, but it was in the seventh that he really pressed home his advantage, pinning Mbilli to the ropes and delivering a right uppercut that had the Frenchman rocking on his feet.
In the eighth, Mbilli had a point taken away for punching behind the head, and he seemed to lose more momentum from then on, allowing Alvarez to begin dictating the fight in the next round as the wily veteran pulled ahead of his younger opponent.

South Korea’s exports nearly doubled last month, the sharpest jump in more than 50 years, as robust global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) investment boosted shipments of the country’s chips, government data showed yesterday.
Exports from Asia’s fourth-largest economy, a bellwether for global trade, rose 93.7 percent from the same month last year to US$115.28 billion, slightly higher than a median 93.2 percent rise forecast in a Reuters poll of economists.

Photo: Reuters

TTSB urges mandatory reporting of battery fires
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:09 UTC
01:44:09 KST

The Taiwan Transportation Safety Board (TTSB) yesterday called for mandatory reporting of fires involving power banks on public transportation, after a report uncovered 17 incidents in the past three years, including nine last year.
Mandatory reporting of power bank smoke or fire incidents is currently only required on aircraft operated by Taiwan-based airlines, meaning some incidents might not be recorded, the board said.
Authorities should mandate reporting of all power bank smoke or fire incidents to ensure more accurate data for effective safety analysis, the TTSB said.
Photo: Taipei Times
To better track incidents of smoking or burning power banks across different types of transportation, the board on May 26 asked the Ministry of Transportation and Communications and transportation authorities in Taipei, New Taipei City, Taoyuan, Taichung and Kaohsiung to provide data on such incidents.
From 2024 to June, 17 incidents of power banks smoking or catching fire were recorded, including nine last year, according to the data, which covered aircraft, boats, rail and commercial motor vehicles.
Twelve incidents occurred on railways, the highest among transportation modes, it showed.
One incident resulted in three injuries and three incidents resulted in one injury each, while the rest did not result in injury, it showed.
Seven incidents caused equipment damage to vehicles, mostly to seats and flooring.
Two of the power banks were charging when they caught fire or began emitting smoke, while two were not in use and four were connected to mobile phones at the time of the incident, the data showed.
The status of the power bank was not known in the nine other incidents.
On aircraft, flight attendants use water or another nonflammable liquid to cool down and isolate power banks when a fire occurs, the TTSB said.
In maritime, rail and commercial road transportation, crew members, conductors and drivers used fire extinguishers to respond immediately to incidents and promptly evacuated passengers, it said.
Immediate on-site intervention led to a fire being extinguished in most cases, preventing major casualties or further spread of the fire, the board said.
Mandatory reporting of power bank smoke or fire incidents is required for Taiwan-based airlines, but there are no equivalent reporting rules for other modes of transportation, meaning that some incidents might not have been recorded, TTSB Chairman Lin Shinn-der (林信得) said.
To effectively track the actual number of power bank incidents across public transportation, authorities should review their procedures and mandate compulsory reporting, he said.
Power banks are mass-market consumer goods, and managing their risks involves product testing, consumer protection and fire investigation, the TTSB said.
In Japan, power bank fire investigations and data analysis are handled by the Japanese Fire and Disaster Management Agency, while the Japanese National Institute of Technology and Evaluation and the Consumer Affairs Agency address product safety, consumer warnings and market surveillance, to manage risks at the source, it said.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:07 UTC
01:44:07 KST

Chanting and swishing a wooden wand, a Japanese priest on Saturday blessed a cat, a shiba inu and several Yorkshire terriers at a shrine in Tokyo, in a rite usually reserved for children.
The annual “Shichi-Go-San” festival, which literally means “Seven-Five-Three,” traditionally allows families to celebrate the growth of their children at those ages, but with Japan’s population in decline, more and more worshippers are bringing beloved animals to the event instead.
“I came here to pray for my pet’s healthy growth and well-being,” doctor Shoko Kodama said at the Ichigaya Kamegaoka Hachimangu, a Shinto shrine in the capital.
Photo: AF
She said she had spent two months hand-crafting a bespoke, bright-red kimono for her cat, a five-year-old British shorthair named Amber.
“This little one is like my child,” she said. “Just having her around makes all the unpleasant things in life melt away.”
Outside the shrine, other pet owners dressed their fluffy companions in colorful kimonos and posed them for photos to mark the special occasion. They then brought them into the inner sanctuary, where the priest, Kenji Kaji, performed a purification rite with a wand decorated with white paper streamers.
The role of pets in people’s lives had shifted as “the family structure has changed” in Japan, which is grappling with an aging population and a low birthrate, he said.
“I think the number of instances where people who don’t have children, or have finished raising them, and welcome a dog or cat as a member of the family has been increasing,” Kaji said.
His shrine has been accepting about 400 families for each festival since the early 2000s, due to demand from pet owners.
Miyu Shiro, who owns two Yorkshire terriers, said marking the event with her dogs “feels perfectly natural.”
“They’re part of our family,” she said, as she snapped photos of her pups, neatly combed and wearing flower-shaped hair clips.
Data in June showed that Japan’s fertility rate fell again last year to a record low, underscoring the demographic crisis gnawing at the world’s fourth-largest economy.
With a median age of 49.9 years, Japan also has the second-oldest population in the world after Monaco, the World Bank said.
Koichi Ohara who attended the festival with his wife and friends, said his three Chihuahuas gave him “unconditional love.”
“They’re more affectionate than human children. They listen to what we say, too,” he said, adding that he had three kids. “Just like us humans, I hope they can live long and in peace.”
