China harassing shipping with east coast patrol: CGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:07 UTC
01:44:07 KST

The China Coast Guard is harassing shipping off Taiwan’s east coast and trying to exert a fictional jurisdiction, the Coast Guard Administration (CGA) said, adding that it had sent ships to keep watch.
China has stepped up activity off the nation’s east coast since June, sending regular coast guard patrols, which Taiwanese officials said might be practice for a potential maritime blockade, which would use overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets.
Taipei regards the area off its east coast as critical to wartime supply routes in the event of a blockade or conflict.
Photo courtesy of the CGA
The CGA said it dispatched ships, including the Ji An (吉安), to monitor the area, adding that China’s patrols included the Chinese coast guard’s Hushi (CCG 1308) and Meishan (CCG 2303).
Chinese state media showed a video of a ship broadcasting a radio message saying that it was carrying out law enforcement and offering help should any be needed.
It did not say who the message was broadcast to, but showed footage of an unidentified fishing trawler.
The Republic of China (ROC) is a sovereign, independent country, and the ROC and the People’s Republic of China are not subordinate to each other, the CGA said.
China’s “attempts to harass ships at sea through radio communications are a clear expansion of power that violate international law, undermine regional peace and stability, and deviate from reality,” it said.
“Our country holds sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the exclusive economic zone east of Taiwan, and China has absolutely no jurisdiction over any of Taiwan’s waters,” it added.
China is spreading disinformation through political rhetoric, including referring to Taiwan as “China’s Taiwan Island” and describing its activities as “law enforcement patrols,” the CGA said.
The claims distort reality and would never be recognized by the international community, the CGA said, vowing to continue monitoring maritime activity, take all necessary measures to safeguard national sovereignty and ensure the security of Taiwanese waters.
China on Saturday sent another coast guard ship close to Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands (Dongsha Islands, 東沙群島), the CGA said.
Taiwan has so far this year “expelled” China Coast Guard vessels from Pratas waters 13 times, it added.
Security experts see Pratas as vulnerable to a Chinese attack due to its distance — more than 400km — from Taiwan.
Speaking at a security forum in Taipei on Saturday, Ocean Affairs Council specialist Pai Pang-ting (白邦廷) said that, while the Chinese People’s Liberation Army provides a high-visibility military presence, Beijing also uses its coast guard, research and fishing vessels to challenge Taiwan’s maritime law enforcement and administrative jurisdiction.
Beijing is seeking to portray repeated incursions as routine administrative management to gradually narrow Taiwan’s ability to exercise jurisdiction over its waters, Pai said.

CCP communique veils criticism of one-man rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:44:03 UTC
01:44:03 KST

The Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) fifth plenum issued a communique containing detailed discussions of inner-party democracy that amount to veiled criticism of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s (習近平) one-man rule, China observer Willy Lam (林和立) said.
The communique was an important statement outlining the CCP’s goals, with its discussion of issues such as inner-party democracy being “unexpectedly detailed,” said Lam, a researcher with the Jamestown Foundation.
The communique said the plenum had made systematic arrangements for “consistently advancing full and rigorous self-governance of the Party,” emphasizing the need to bolster party members’ political character and strictly implement democratic centralism.
Photo: Xinhua via AP
“Democratic centralism is the Party’s fundamental organizational principle and leadership system, and its implementation is essential to enforcing rigorous Party self-governance,” the communique said.
It also called for improving the systems governing democratic centralism, promoting inner-party democracy and ensuring proper centralization of power.
The communique further said that the party must bolster the centralized leadership of the CCP Central Committee, improve inner-party democracy, enforce rules governing leadership decisions and deliberations, and regulate how “top leaders” exercise their powers.
Lam said that the communique outlined several political reform issues that Xi had refused to consider, including a detailed discussion of inner-party democracy. Given Xi’s reputation for promoting centralized power and his complete disregard for democracy, Lam said that the communique amounted to veiled criticism of his one-man rule.
Xi was only adept at “self-reflection,” Lam said, referring to the CCP’s frequently invoked concepts of “self-improvement” and “self-revolution.” This form of self-improvement did not involve substantive reform, while the communique’s reference to “letting the people supervise the government” could be regarded as a reform, he said.
Although the communique praised Xi’s achievements, saying that the CCP Central Committee with Xi at its core had “fundamentally reversed the lax and weak state of Party governance and eliminated serious hidden dangers within the Party, the state and the military,” it made no reference to principles such as the “Two Establishes” (兩個確立), which Xi has used to demand absolute loyalty from officials, Lam said.
The main outcome of the fifth plenum was that Xi had secured approval to serve a fourth term beginning at the CCP’s 21st National Congress next year, he said, adding that Xi’s outdated model of one-man rule still had come under indirect criticism.
In a commentary published on Saturday, China’s Xinhua said that democratic centralism encompassed democracy and centralization, with the two serving as conditions for and complements to each other, and neither being dispensable.
The commentary said that the party must “uphold and strengthen the centralized and unified leadership of the Party Central Committee, deeply understand the decisive significance of the ‘Two Establishes,’” and ensure that the entire party maintains a high degree of unity with the CCP Central Committee with Xi at its core.

2026 Elections: KMT hopes to mobilize core supporters in run up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:43:57 UTC
01:43:57 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) plans to stick to its strategy of mobilizing its core supporters while reaching out to undecided voters in the run-up to the Nov. 28 elections, KMT deputy secretary-general and head of the party’s Organizational Development Committee Lee Che-hua (李哲華) said.
Lee made the remarks in response to media questions about the intensifying local election campaigns, with attention focused on the Taipei mayoral race and whether the “Ocean Wave” (洋流) effect would spread nationwide.
The “Ocean Wave” — a pun on 洋 (“ocean”) in Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen’s (沈伯洋) name — refers to the campaign movement built around his Taipei mayoral bid.
Photo: CNA
The “Ocean Wave” campaign makes effective use of digital tools and online communities to maximize its reach, Lee said, adding that it remains largely a virtual movement, and its impact might not translate into votes.
“Taipei voters are among the most discerning,” he said. “You cannot take a product that people widely considered poor last year, simply repackage it and expect them to suddenly like it. That would be underestimating Taipei residents’ intelligence.”
The “Ocean Wave” effect has significantly skewed polling figures, leading supporters on both sides to interpret the results differently, Lee said, adding that the pan-green camp sees a boost in morale, while the pan-blue camp feels increasingly uneasy.
Such campaign tactics are normal in elections, and when one side has the upper hand, the other does not necessarily need to confront it head-on, he said.
The KMT’s own polling has also found a decline in the willingness of pan-blue voters to reveal their political preferences, resulting in greater polling discrepancies than usual, he said.
This was only a passing phase, he said, adding that the party assesses the overall election situation as stable.
Supporters on both sides are gradually consolidating behind their respective camps, leaving candidates to focus on winning over undecided voters in the final stretch, he said.
Candidates’ policy platforms and visions, as well as voters’ satisfaction with the government’s performance, would all play a role, he said.
With the election approaching, the key would be each party’s strategy in the final stretch, particularly how they mobilize voters and win over undecided and swing voters, he said.
Both parties are pursuing similar strategies, differing mainly in their timing and pace, he said, adding that the KMT would stick to its timetable, holding joint campaign rallies across different regions in the final weeks to mobilize its core supporters and win over centrist and swing voters.
KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun (鄭麗文) said that Changhua County was the party’s toughest electoral battleground among the administrative regions it governs, while Yilan remained a challenge, but the overall outlook was cautiously optimistic.
The situation in Changhua stemmed from disagreements between Changhua County Commissioner Wang Hui-mei (王惠美) and the party’s central leadership over the nomination process, Lee said, adding that he believed Wang would put the party’s broader interests first during the final campaign stretch.
As for the party’s Yilan County commissioner candidate Wu Tsung-hsien (吳宗憲), Lee said although he had not spent long building a political base in Yilan, voters knew Wu has done more to secure resources and benefits for the county than his DPP opponent, Lin Kuo-chang (林國漳), and that “the voters would make their own judgement.”

Notes from Central Taiwan: An island grab, a Strait-wide crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:43:56 UTC
01:43:56 KST

A February 2023 paper by Andrew Chubb for the Asia Society Policy Institute explores the possibilities and consequences of an attempt by the armed forces of the People’s Republic of China (PRC) to seize an island currently held by the Republic of China (ROC). After discussing the Fujian coastal islands and the ROC-held islands in the South China Sea, Chubb moves to Penghu.
“The most consequential target for a PRC island seizure would be the Penghu archipelago,” Chubb writes.
The Penghu archipelago, with its major port in Makung City (馬公), has long been a stepping stone to Taiwan. The pirate Lin Feng (林阿鳳, Limahong) established a base there in 1574. The Dutch first arrived there in 1604, blown by a storm. In 1622 they began constructing a fortress there. The Ming drove them out, and they retreated to Taiwan. After the Dutch, the pirate lord Zheng Zhilong (鄭芝龍) controlled the Taiwan Strait from bases on the Fujian coast, Taiwan and Penghu. It was in Penghu that the Manchu (Qing) empire crushed the navy of the Zheng family’s statelet on Taiwan in 1683. The French captured the islands in 1885, late in the Sino-French war. When the Japanese invaded in 1895, one of their first moves was to seize Penghu. The Japanese would later use it as the jumping off point for their invasion of the Philippines, just as Lin Feng had done four centuries earlier.
Photo: Taiwanese Coast Guard Administration / Reuters
Chubb’s analysis points to the many problems that the PRC would encounter when attempting to take Penghu. The civilian population exceeds 100,000, and the main island is well defended. But what if the PRC decides to seize an uninhabited island, he asks, using a small force or even a paramilitary maritime militia unit or a “patriotic” organization? An uninhabited island would pose fewer problems than occupying an island filled with people. Taipei would have to respond. Yet, any response could be construed as escalation. I would add that this is especially true because there is a whole world of commentators who treat all responses to PRC expansionism as “escalation.” Chubb also observes that the possibility of US intervention in a Penghu island seizure is also unclear.
COVETING PENGHU
The PRC has long thirsted over Penghu. The US China Aerospace Studies Institute (CASI), recently defunded by the Trump Administration in one of its many suicidal policy moves, translated a “Course Book on the Taiwan Strait’s Military Geography,” intended for masters students at the Academy of Military Sciences. The book’s section on Penghu says: “The Penghu Archipelago is a key point of communication between Fujian and Taiwan, and it controls the throat of the Taiwan Strait, and is known as the ‘key to the southeast,’ and its strategic position is very important.”
Photo: Reuters/Kyodo
The discussion lists, among other things, four airports on Penghu, the two small civil aviation fields on Qimei island and Wangan island, the major modern dual-use airport of Makong city and the old airport at Zhumushui (豬母水) (Wude, 五德) near Makong city, though it ceased operating in 1964.
A more recent piece by Chubb and other scholars in the March edition of The Pacific Review examines the changing Taiwanese public perception of the outlying islands and its consequences for their defense. Based on two waves of surveys in 2023-4, they found that respondents, irrespective of their view of the islands’ importance politically and strategically, “expressed similar levels of approval for militarily defending all of them in the event of a PRC attack or blockade.”
The 2024 survey contained an experiment that found that there was “surprisingly little difference” between Taiwanese willingness to defend Taiwan and to defend the offshore islands. Even Taiwanese independence supporters “express significantly stronger approval of using military force,” they found.
Photo: CNA
Chubb et al contend that this growing inclusion of the offshore islands in the Taiwanese idea of what constitutes “Taiwan” implies that if one is occupied, there will be considerable domestic pressure on the government to recover it. This would go double for the Penghu islands, which have long been treated as part of Taiwan. Indeed, the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) explicitly defines the Penghu (“Pescadores”) as part of “Taiwan” in its list of definitions.
In fact we already have several examples of “patriotic” activists striking at uninhabited islands. Remember this from January 2013? “The voyage was a voluntary action by private citizens.” That was said by Su Chii-cherng (蘇啟誠), the deputy director-general of the Department of East Asian and Pacific Affairs of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA). A group of “activists” had chartered a fishing boat out of Shenao Port (深澳漁港) in New Taipei City (新北市) and headed to the Senkakus (Diaoyutai Islands, 釣魚台) to enshrine a Mazu statue on one of the islands, ostensibly to protect Taiwan’s fishermen. Readers will no doubt know that Mazu is the patron deity of annexation, her cult a key vector of PRC influence in Taiwan.
The fishing boat was escorted by Taiwan Coast Guard ships, but it was intercepted by a flotilla of eight Japanese coast guard vessels, who forced it to turn back.
Photo: Reuters
That incident came a year after “activists” from China, Hong Kong and Macao had slipped into the Senkakus and planted flags representing those three governments, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) flag and the ROC flag. The administration of KMT president Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九) not only publicly cheered the appearance of the ROC flag, but had provided provisions to the boat on its way to the Senkakus on his direct orders.
‘GRAY ZONE’ GRAB
Though Chubb did not discuss them in his 2023 paper, the Senkaku incidents highlight important and scary aspects of “gray zone” island-grabbing. For one thing, the “activists” in 2012 framed their actions as religious. Another issue they raise is cross-border cooperation between subnational actors — the actions of “patriotic activists” coordinate with actions by pro-China groups, or organized crime, in Taiwan. The 2012 crowd carried a multitude of regional flags and had official help from the Ma Administration.
Also shedding light on the “activist” occupation scenario was the run of small boat incursions over the last couple of years that featured PRC citizens entering Taiwan illegally. One of these allegedly planted a PRC flag on a beach in Taoyuan and posted it to Douyin.
Unauthorized entry can already attract up to five years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to NT$500,000. But as an AP round up of these cases last year noted, the penalties are usually not applied if no one is harmed. One thing the government can do is toughen these penalties. This would enhance the government’s ability to treat an activist incursion in Penghu as a criminal law-enforcement matter involving arrests, fines and prison. It should be easy to discredit the operation politically, especially if gangsters are involved. Officials could hint that the op was a sham and the “activists” actually criminals covering the establishment of a base to smuggle drugs and guns into Taiwan.
Whatever decisions about political aspects the government makes, as the small boat incursions show, the government needs to step up the monitoring of the waters and uninhabited islands and areas in the islands in the Strait. What if a Penghu island is seized and nobody knows?
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.
Much attention is being paid to increasing security ties between Taiwan and the Philippines, and rightfully so. The stakes are potentially existential, as explored in “ Donovan’s Deep Dives: Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines need to face the common threat from Beijing” (Sept. 12, page 12). Getting less attention is that across the board the relationship is growing stronger, and both sides appear to be planning to put more of their eggs in each other’s baskets. Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) in August last year confirmed plans to open a second Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) representative

Grant Basile on Saturday scored 37 points, including a team-high 10 in the fourth quarter, to lead the Kaohsiung Aquas past the Taipei Taishin Mars 132-121 in their Taiwan Professional Basketball League (TPBL) home opener.
Basile shot 13-for-20 from the field, including six of 12 from three-point range, and added 13 rebounds, three assists and two blocks at Kaohsiung Arena. He has exceeded 30 points in all three games this season, following performances of 36 and 31 points.
Kaohsiung’s transition attack generated 41 fast-break points to Taipei’s seven, while the hosts also outscored the Mars 60-46 in the paint.
Photo courtesy of the TPBL
“Our coach wants us to play fast, with less half-court offense, more end-to-end basketball and intense pressure,” Aquas wing Su Wen-ju said afterward.
The team’s imports were highly mobile and sometimes outran their smaller teammates, Su added, crediting that mobility for Kaohsiung’s entertaining style early in the season.
Kaohsiung’s other imports also contributed, with Rosco Allen recording 26 points, 11 assists and seven rebounds, while Gabriel Galvanini added 23 points and 11 rebounds.
The Aquas led 73-59 at halftime before a Basile layup about one minute into the third quarter extended their advantage to a game-high 18 points at 77-59. Taipei responded with a 33-15 run to enter the final period tied at 92-92.
The Mars briefly moved ahead in the fourth, but Basile helped restore Kaohsiung’s lead, scoring 10 points on four-for-six shooting, including two three-pointers. The Aquas outscored Taipei 40-29 in the quarter to secure victory.
Adam Hinton, whom the Aquas selected first overall in this year’s TPBL draft, finished with 11 points and three rebounds in 27 minutes and 44 seconds.
He opened the scoring seven seconds after tipoff, driving from beyond the right-side three-point line for a dunk through contact and converting the free throw. Two fourth-quarter free throws completed his scoring.
Hinton scored five points in 10 minutes and 50 seconds in his previous outing, when Kaohsiung was outscored by 24 points during his minutes.
Meanwhile, Benson Lin led Taipei with 26 points, seven assists, five steals and four rebounds.
Kaohsiung improved to 2-1 after finishing last in the seven-team league at 9-27 last season.

People build 108 stupas for Bhutan’s ‘mindfulness’ city
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:43:56 UTC
01:43:56 KST

Tens of thousands of volunteers yesterday took part in building 108 Buddhist stupas in Bhutan, marking the Himalayan kingdom’s ambitious plans for a “mindfulness” city aimed at driving economic growth.
The 15m-tall solid towers — sacred Buddhist monuments found across the Himalayas — stretch along 12km of riverbank near the Indian border, at the site of the future Gelephu Mindfulness City.
More than 40,000 volunteers participated in building the structures in a single day as “a physical form of prayer” after starting work post-midnight, officials said.
Photo: AP
Bhutan is known for its policy of prioritizing “Gross National Happiness” alongside economic growth.
It hopes the city will boost its economy and persuade more young people to stay, attracting investment in sustainable business, green technology, education, tourism and financial services.
Bhutan faces a declining birthrate and an exodus of young people seeking opportunities abroad.
King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck established the special zone by royal charter in 2024, saying its purpose was to “create a vibrant economic hub.”
“This occasion will be recorded in our history for generations to come,” said Nima Gyeltshen, head of the Organisation for Youth Empowerment, which helps young Bhutanese find work.
The sleepy town has a population of less than 10,000, the last census in 2017 showed.
Together, the 108 stupas — a number with significance in Buddhist traditions — stand more than 10 times the height of Egypt’s Great Pyramid of Giza, organizers say, at an estimated cost of US$21 million.
Analysts have questioned whether Bhutan can attract sufficient investment to realize its vision, but Indian billionaire Gautam Adani, head of the ports-to-power conglomerate, joined Gelephu Mindfulness City as a founding member in January.
The site is to be connected to India’s rail network in neighboring Assam, with an international airport slated to open in 2029.
The project is also linked to Bhutan’s cryptocurrency ambitions, with the kingdom mining bitcoin using surplus hydropower and pledging to use digital assets to support the city’s development.

S&P cuts Meta’s outlook to negative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:43:56 UTC
01:43:56 KST

S&P Global Ratings has taken an early step toward potentially downgrading Meta Platforms Inc’s credit rating within the next two years, amid growing pressure on the tech company’s balance sheet stemming from elevated spending tied to artificial intelligence (AI).
S&P on Friday lowered the outlook on Meta’s “AA-” credit grade to negative, it said in a statement.
The company’s rising leverage, a measure of debt relative to earnings, was also a key factor in the decision, the rating firm said.
Photo: Reuters
“Meta’s ability to monetize its AI investments is more limited than that of its peers,” S&P said, adding that it is not clear when its expenditures would start producing material revenue that exceed the rising costs.
The outlook “reflects uncertainty around how long capex will remain elevated and free operating cash flow will be negative,” it said.
The decision signals S&P could downgrade the company within the next couple years, but also means the bond grader is not considering downgrading Meta now. It comes as investors scrutinize Meta’s and other industry players’ ability to generate tangible returns from the massive investments they have been plowing into the AI buildout.
“We respectfully disagree with S&P’s assertion about Meta’s AI monetization capabilities,” Meta spokesman Kamran Mumtaz said in a statement. “We see significant product and business opportunities ahead of us, supporting our very strong credit profile.”
Meta’s “AA-” credit rating is the fourth-highest investment-grade score, and a one-notch downgrade would still leave it solidly in high-grade territory.
Still, the company has been borrowing heavily to fund its ambitions. S&P forecast Meta’s capital expenditure would reach US$140 billion this year, and accelerate to more than US$225 billion next year.
The tech giant’s leverage could climb above 1.0 times as soon as next year, up from about 0.1 times last year, S&P said in the statement.
Last month, Meta disclosed that it has more than US$800 billion in future spending commitments, with almost half tied to leases that have not yet begun yet, largely for data centers and energy infrastructure. Despite some hesitancy from Wall Street, which has pressed Meta on how it aims to make a return on its AI investments, company executives have doubled down on the need for future spending.
“We expect to continue investing aggressively to support both our core business and emerging AI initiatives,” Meta chief financial officer Susan Li said during an earnings call with analysts on Oct. 21.
Overall, the five largest players in the data center race — Meta, Alphabet Inc, Microsoft Corp, Amazon.com Inc and Oracle Corp — have committed more than US$3 trillion in spending over the coming years, pointing to massive ongoing investment in AI infrastructure. That is a mix of short-term spending and some pledges that are as long as decades away.

Chinese ships suspected of spying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:43:56 UTC
01:43:56 KST

Four Chinese survey ships spotted near Taiwan since May are suspected of gathering intelligence on undersea cables, Japanese newspaper the Yomiuri Shimbun reported yesterday, citing data from an intelligence company and Taiwanese authorities.
The four ships have been spotted repeatedly making irregular moves in specific waters around Taiwan close to routes where international undersea cables connecting Taiwan and other areas have been laid, the report said.
The four ships are the Xiangyang Hong 22 (向陽紅22), which belongs to the Chinese Ministry of Natural Resources; the Tongji (同濟號) and Jia Geng (嘉庚號), operated by universities in Shanghai and China’s Fujian Province, respectively; and a vessel whose Automatic Identification System (AIS) identified it as Mushanzi (暮山紫), it said.
Photo courtesy of the Coast Guard Administration via CNA
The newspaper cited analysis conducted by ingeniSPACE, a geospatial intelligence analytics firm based in the US and Taiwan, using data from AIS and other sources, as well as through information obtained by the newspaper from Taiwanese authorities, it said.
The Xiangyang Hong 22 has repeatedly sailed back and forth in specific waters off northern Taiwan since May, frequently slowing down, stopping and making irregular course changes, the report said, citing data provided by the company.
The Jia Geng engaged in similar behavior in eastern waters, and the Mushanzi made similar moves in the Bashi Channel in the south, while the Tongji was spotted repeatedly circling Taiwan proper, and stopping and slowing down at specific locations, it said.
The intelligence firm assessed that the Chinese ships have surveyed undersea cables in a wide area, identifying the routes where major undersea cables have been laid using its own method, the report said.
Based on AIS data, the company concluded that the waters where the four ships slowed down or stopped all coincided with locations where undersea cables connecting Taiwan and other countries have been laid, the newspaper said.
A Taiwanese official told the newspaper that the data and analysis presented by the company was deemed reliable, as they are consistent with the authorities’ understanding of the situation.
Another official was quoted as saying that the possibility of Chinese survey ships collecting information on undersea cables cannot be ruled out.
From 2021 through last year, Taiwan experienced a series of incidents in which undersea cables are believed to have been cut or damaged intentionally by cargo ships and other vessels, the report said.
Taiwanese authorities have pointed to China’s involvement in these cases, it added.
The activities of such Chinese ships could be preparation for sabotaging undersea cables, Keio University professor Motohiro Tsuchiya, an expert on issues related to undersea cables, told the newspaper, citing China’s past moves.
China “may have been surveying not only the location of the cables, but also the seabed topography, water depth and ocean currents where the cables have been laid,” he was quoted as saying.
Activities by Chinese vessels similar to those around Taiwan also have been observed in waters near Japan and the Philippines, ingeniSPACE’s chief operating officer Jason Wang (王柏仁) told the newspaper.
In May, Japan and the Philippines agreed to start negotiations toward the delimitation of boundaries of their exclusive economic zones and continental shelves, the report said.
Objecting to this move, China has repeatedly deployed patrol vessels and survey ships to waters near Taiwan, asserting what it calls “jurisdiction,” it said.
China is using “gray zone” tactics in a wide area along the First Island Chain, which stretches from south of Kyushu to Taiwan and the Philippines, in anticipation of a contingency, Wang was quoted as saying.
Taiwan has been cautious about the “gray zone” tactics by China, which are aimed at causing social disruption through communication outages, such as disguising cable cuts as accidents, the report said.
There has also been a spate of cases in which undersea cables were cut or damaged in the Baltic Sea since 2024, with the involvement of China and Russia suspected, the report said.
Undersea cables, which are used for high-capacity communications, are said to take more than a week to repair if cut in deep-sea areas, it said.

Serbia marks Novi Sad station disaster anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:43:55 UTC
01:43:55 KST

Thousands of Serbs were yesterday expected to gather in Novi Sad to honor the victims of a railway station disaster that launched the anti-government movement which toppled the country’s right-wing ruling party a week ago.
The gathering will mark two years since the concrete canopy at the newly renovated station in Serbia’s second city collapsed, killing 16 people.
Amid nationwide grief and mounting questions over the station’s multi-million-euro renovation, the disaster sparked some of Serbia’s largest protests since the fall of then-Serbian president Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.
Photo: Reuters
“It’s hard to go back to the place where it all happened,” said Dijana Hrka, whose 27-year-old son Stefan was killed in the collapse. “And each time, it gets harder and harder.”
This year’s anniversary falls just a week after the snap election result, with the now-victorious student movement returning to the place that first spawned protests.
Hrka herself became a key protest symbol, and she said the push for justice gave her hope.
“The support of people meant so much to me,” she said, reflecting on the past two years.
“People who support me, who genuinely want us all to achieve justice together,” she said through tears, adding that no one had yet been held accountable for her son’s death.
Demands for a transparent investigation brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets and played a central role in its electoral victory.
The student-backed list won about 140 seats in the 250-member parliament, enough to govern alone.
Hrka hopes the seismic changes in the country will help accelerate investigations into the tragedy.
In the days since outgoing Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic’s party conceded the election, the students have called for progress in numerous corruption and high-profile murder probes, as well as fresh investigations into projects launched by the former government.
The student movement also called for the heads of several key state agencies, including the police and intelligence services, to resign.
Several investigations into the Novi Sad tragedy are ongoing, but no trial has started.
Former Serbian minister of construction, transport and infrastructure Goran Vesic, who resigned days after the collapse, was charged last year alongside 12 others with a serious crime against public safety.
“If we manage to put them behind bars now, this will never happen again,” Hrka said. “I hope this was the last time we had to take to the streets in such numbers because of a tragedy. That’s all I hope for.”

WEATHER
Wind system brings cool
Photo courtesy of the Central Weather Administration
A strengthening northeasterly wind system is to bring cooler weather to northern and northeastern Taiwan starting today, with another surge expected later in the week, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said. Brief showers are forecast for the Keelung north coast, Taipei and New Taipei City, eastern Taiwan and the Hengchun Peninsula, with isolated rain also possible in Taoyuan. Elsewhere, skies are forecast to remain partly cloudy to sunny, it said. The weather is expected to improve as winds weaken on Wednesday and Thursday, it said. Another northeasterly wind system is forecast to arrive on Friday and linger through Saturday, bringing another round of cooler weather to northern and northeastern Taiwan, it said.
ECONOMY
Teahouse raises prices
Taichung-based teahouse chain Chun Shui Tang (春水堂) yesterday said that it had raised prices on more than 80 percent of its menu items by an average of 12 percent, citing rising operating, ingredient and labor costs. The price increases took effect yesterday, the company said, adding that actual prices for individual items are listed at its stores and on its official Web site. Using prices in northern Taiwan as an example, Chun Shui Tang said that a medium-sized bubble tea would cost NT$200, an increase of about 5 percent, while the price of a medium-sized uva black tea would remain unchanged at NT$160. Chun Shui Tang also announced several promotional gift offerings, including a voucher for a small uva black tea, a voucher for a small bubble tea or a small tote bag, based on the amount spent in a single transaction.
ENVIRONMENT
Earthquake strikes in Yilan
A magnitude 5.6 earthquake struck off the coast of northeastern Taiwan at 4:20pm yesterday, the Central Weather Administration (CWA) said. There were no immediate reports of damage or injuries. The epicenter of the temblor was located at sea, 39.4km east-northeast of Yilan County Hall, at a depth of 119.5km. The earthquake’s intensity was highest in parts of Yilan and Hualien, where it measured a 3 on Taiwan’s seven-tier intensity scale, it said. The quake also measured an intensity of 2 across most of northern, eastern and central Taiwan, as well as in Tainan, CWA data showed.
MILITARY
Air force drills begin
The air force is scheduled to begin its annual Tien Lung, or “Sky Dragon,” drills today to test pilots’ combat skills and ground-based logistical support, a military source said yesterday. The drills are scheduled to run through Friday and would test pilots’ air-to-air, air-to-sea, and air-to-ground combat skills using the air force’s main fighter aircraft — F-16Vs, Mirage 2000-5s and Indigenous Defense Fighters — the unnamed source said. The exercises would focus on aerial interceptions and the use of the aerial gunnery target system. They would also simulate pilots scrambling their aircraft at short notice, identifying targets, firing missiles at them and conducting mock “dogfights” with enemy aircraft, the source said. As in previous years, the air force would also select flying aces in different categories, including aerial combat and precision. The source added that the Tien Lung exercises would also include ground-based logistical support drills and test the air force’s joint operational capabilities with the army, navy, and Information, Communications and Electronic Force Command.

Taiwan protests APEC ‘discrimination’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:43:54 UTC
01:43:54 KST

Taiwan has lodged a protest over China’s discriminatory handling of its invitation to the upcoming APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said yesterday.
China, the host of the meeting on Nov. 18 and 19, sent Taiwan a letter, but it was not a formal invitation, an official familiar with the matter said on condition of anonymity.
China did not address Taiwan as “Chinese Taipei,” the nation’s official APEC designation, in the invitation, deviating from established protocol and downgrading the nation’s status, the official said.
Photo: CNA
The government immediately lodged a strong protest against actions by China that undermine Taiwan’s status, to protect the nation’s rights as a full and equal member of APEC, the ministry said.
APEC is an important regional economic cooperation organization, and preparations for Taiwan’s participation are ongoing in accordance with past practice, it said, adding that updates would be provided to the public in due course.
Taiwan takes part in APEC under the name “Chinese Taipei,” which it also uses for the Olympics, and has traditionally sent a representative appointed by the president to the leaders’ meeting.
As an APEC member, Taiwan should be invited with established procedures and conventions, with this year’s arrangements following the same protocol as last year’s meeting in South Korea, they said.
Taiwan’s representative for this year’s summit has already been selected, and the choice had been communicated to Beijing and would be announced by the Presidential Office, they added.
China has hosted the APEC summit twice.
In 2001, under the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) administration of then-president Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁), Beijing sent an unsigned fax notification and rejected Taiwan’s envoy, former vice president Li Yuan-tsu (李元簇), prompting Taipei to boycott the summit.
In 2014, during the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) administration of then-president Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九), Beijing dispatched then-Taiwan Affairs Office deputy director Gong Qinggai (龔清概) to personally hand the invitation to then-Mainland Affairs Council minister Wang Yu-chi (王郁琦) at the Taipei Guest House.
Taiwan was being treated differently again this year, the official said, adding that China only does so with Taiwan, which downgrades and harms the nation’s status.
The government is assessing whether it could accept the arrangements, they said.
When cross-strait relations are bad, China would certainly use the summit to suppress Taiwan, they added.
Even when the KMT was in power in 2014, Beijing had sought to marginalize Taiwan at the summit, they said, adding that the Ma administration had been reluctant to speak publicly about the matter.
Since the DPP has been in power, China has shown no goodwill toward Taiwan and is bound to seek to suppress or belittle the nation at the summit, the official said.
Although previous APEC ministerial meetings had followed established conventions, that does not mean Beijing would refrain from pressuring Taiwan, they said.
China has already chosen to target Taiwan’s representative to the leaders’ meeting by using a discriminatory form of address in its invitation, they said, adding that the government had argued with the Chinese side over the matter.
The key issue this time is whether China’s differential treatment would damage Taiwan’s status, the official said.
Failing to protest against the latest move could allow Beijing to apply the same approach in the future, they added.

N Korea behind US$6bn crypto theft, FBI says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:43:54 UTC
01:43:54 KST

Binance Holdings Ltd (幣安) yesterday said that it had resumed withdrawals after more than US$6 billion in virtual assets were stolen from the cryptocurrency exchange in a major hack the FBI said North Korea was responsible for.
Binance is the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.
The company has offered reassurances it would cover the losses from the attack, saying it has used company funds to buy tokens to replenish 90 percent of what was stolen.
Photo: Reuters
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the attack, but said they would be resumed in phases, the first of which began yesterday.
“First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals,” the exchange posted on social media.
“We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand, so that each network and asset pair can be restored carefully, with stability and security checks completed before access is reopened,” it said.
The US law enforcement agency on Saturday released a statement accusing North Korea of being behind the hack, confirming earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a Pyongyang-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was responsible.
TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a US$1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.
“The Federal Bureau of Investigation is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026,” the statement said.
The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets.”
The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and information technology security protocols.
The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea — which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programs — to find illicit means to capture revenue.

US-based Taiwanese contemporary artist Lin Shih-pao (林世寶) has unveiled an installation art piece titled Glory — Team Taiwan at the Nanshan Art Gallery featuring 600 autographed baseballs and 55 signed bats collected from around the world.
Lin was invited by former World Baseball Softball Confederation Tournament director George Santiago to serve as curator for the initiative to commemorate Taiwan’s historic victory at the confederation’s Premier12 tournament in 2024.
Lin said he hopes to recreate the atmosphere of the tournament and showcase how Taiwan exemplified not only physical strength, but also athletic aesthetics.
Photo: Wong Yu-huang, Taipei Times
The signed baseballs, which Santiago helped collect, include one autographed by baseball legend and home run king Sadaharu Oh (王貞治), alongside baseballs signed by Major League Baseball stars and items from personal collections.
Some of the balls and bats were signed by members of the Taiwan’s 2024 championship team, including coach Wang Chien-ming (王建民) — a star in his own right, having pitched for the New York Yankees from 2005 to 2009 — and Chinese Professional Baseball League president Tsai Chi-chang (蔡其昌).
Born in Taiwan in 1962, Lin graduated from Nanshan High School’s arts and crafts department. He studied in Japan before establishing himself in New York, where he rose to international prominence.
His art spans painting, sculpture, installation and performance art, often focusing on social issues and global cultural trends.
He has received more than 20 international awards and his works have been exhibited at Expo 2005 in Japan’s Aichi Prefecture, the Queens Museum in New York and the Taipei Fine Arts Museum.

Bulgarians yesterday went to the polls to elect a president after a tight race between the two leading candidates failed to produce an outright winner in last weekend’s first round vote for the largely ceremonial role.
Incumbent Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova led over former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, but fell short of the 50 percent threshold in the first round race of 27 candidates that saw a record-low turnout.
Exit polls were to be published after the end of voting yesterday, with a result likely today as the ballot papers are counted.
Photo: AP
The presidential vote comes against the backdrop of a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast in the past month, which have sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine.
About two dozen seafarers are feared dead and the strikes have prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security.
On Wednesday, a Greek container ship sank after being hit by sea drones.
Both leading presidential candidates have condemned the attacks.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who backs Iotova, said the strikes’ outcome “benefits the Russian Federation.” They have both called for a diplomatic end to the war.
A victory for Iotova would make her Bulgaria’s first elected female president. She became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter and win a parliamentary race on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine.
He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as prime minister.
A host of right-leaning political figures, among them former Bulgarian prime minister Boyko Borisov, have expressed support for Gyurov.

The verdict of the voters must be respected — and upheld
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:43:48 UTC
01:43:48 KST

The most important outcome in this week’s midterm elections might not be whether Democrats or Republicans come out on top. It might be whether both parties accept the results.
Judging by the most recent polls, Democrats are likely to make gains in Congress and might win control of one or both houses.
Unfortunately, when asked whether he would abide by the results, the US President Donald Trump has only said: “I will if they’re honest,” leaving voters to ponder his definition of “honest.” The administration also seems to be laying the groundwork for disputing results in several states.
One need not be paranoid to worry about what comes next. In 2020, fake claims about voter fraud and administrative manipulation were used to justify attempts to steal the election, which led to deadly mob violence at the Capitol on Jan. 6.
The obvious lesson from that experience — election fabrications and denialism can lead to disaster — seems to have escaped some congressional Republicans, who continue to tolerate the White House’s efforts to meddle in state election administration and undermine voters’ trust.
Thankfully, most state officials have refused to go along. One expressed “major concerns” with the Republican National Committee’s attempts to alter her state’s ballot procedures. Another blasted the Department of Justice for “aggressive, unexpected, disruptive” conduct after it sent election monitors to polling sites and allegedly attempted to access voting machines. A third called the administration’s actions “gamesmanship” that “keeps me up at night.” And those were just the Republicans.
The courts, too, have thus far been effective checks against election chicanery, repeatedly rejecting the administration’s attempts to interfere with state procedures, including a convoluted and impractical executive order that would have given the US Postal Service a broader role verifying compliance with new ballot-mail requirements. One hopes the administration’s latest gambit — asking the courts to block certification of Alaska’s Senate results if the Republican does not win — would be rejected, too.
Yet, as 2021 proved, the courts can only head off so much danger before serious damage is done. Elected officials have their own crucial role to play in upholding election integrity, as former US vice president Mike Pence did nearly six years ago.
Elections have always been disputed. Tight races occasionally bring legal challenges, a common and acceptable practice that is every candidate’s right. However, in the end, winners, losers and the public have nearly always accepted the results. The sooner that normalcy returns, the better.
The peaceful transfer of power is the sine qua non of democratic societies. It is the “miracle” that has made the US possible, as another Republican president once said. And it should be as universally celebrated and defended as motherhood and apple pie. On Election Day, voters will do their duty. Then it would be up to election administrators and members of Congress to do theirs.

Ministry to expand high-school language subsidies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:43:48 UTC
01:43:48 KST

The Ministry of Education has expanded subsidies for local language programs at public high schools, starting retroactively from Aug. 1, it said on Friday.
Local governments can receive annual subsidies of NT$300,000 to NT$900,000, depending on the number of schools in their jurisdiction, the ministry said.
The funds are for paying the hourly wages of language-teaching support staff, language instructor training and certification, and classroom materials, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Education
Schools with local language programs are authorized to receive subsidies for the hourly wages and transportation costs of part-time instructors, as well as for labor and health insurance, it said.
The instructors’ hourly wages should be the same as the rate for part-time and substitute teachers at public schools, the ministry said.
Transportation subsidies range from NT$2,000 to NT$10,000 per person per year, depending on whether they work in or out of jurisdiction and the number of schools they work for, it said.
Instructors working at four or more townships receive NT$8,000 and another NT$2,000 if one or more of the townships are in a legally designated “remote area,” the ministry said.
The policy does not include transportation subsidies for indigenous language instructors, who are governed by a separate program, the ministry said.
The K-12 Education Administration to provide educators subsidies for taking intermediate or advanced language teaching certification tests, it said.
Teachers who have obtained language teaching certificates and taught classes last year are eligible for a subsidy of up to NT$10,000 for educational materials, student rewards and miscellaneous equipment, the ministry said.
The total amount of subsidies a school could receive under the scheme are capped at NT$50,000 a year, it said.
Each school can receive up to NT$30,000 for field trips related native culture, heritage sites, art and the environment, or professional training classes for educators, the ministry said.

Lai urges passage of extra budget for Taipower, CPC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:43:47 UTC
01:43:47 KST

President William Lai (賴清德) yesterday called for support across party lines for a supplementary budget to subsidize state-run Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) and CPC Corp, Taiwan (台灣中油), which have been absorbing rising energy costs amid geopolitical tensions.
Speaking at the opening ceremony of the Kaohsiung City Medical Association Building, Lai said the president’s responsibilities extend beyond developing the economy and improving life expectancy, and include maintaining social stability and keeping prices under control.
The Russia-Ukraine war, the US-Iran war and tensions in the Middle East have driven up prices in many countries, with some facing fuel shortages and others experiencing sharp increases in fuel costs, but Taiwan has maintained stable fuel and electricity prices, he said.
Photo: Lin Cheng-kun, Taipei Times
The nation’s tax revenue has increased, allowing the government to propose a supplementary budget to help curb inflation, Lai said.
He thanked the public and businesses for their efforts in boosting tax revenue, saying that the additional funds had given the government room to subsidize oil and electricity prices, which would have otherwise had to reflect rising costs worldwide.
It is essential for the government to maintain social stability amid the increasingly serious international geopolitical situation and the significant challenges posed by rising prices for oil, goods and other necessities, Lai said.
The supplementary budget to subsidize CPC and Taipower has been submitted to the Legislative Yuan, he said, urging lawmakers from the ruling and opposition camps to work together to support the proposal.
Lai also called on members of the medical community to encourage opposition lawmakers to approve the budget.
Health insurance premiums should not be raised if possible, but if an increase were unavoidable, additional tax revenue could be used to help cover the costs and prevent higher premiums, he said.
The same principle applied to oil and electricity prices, he added.
Passing the supplementary budget to subsidize CPC and Taipower would help prevent inflation, Lai said, adding that rising inflation could prompt the Financial Supervisory Commission to raise interest rates, which would have significant consequences that could undermine social stability.
Many countries are experiencing fuel shortages amid rising oil prices caused by the war in the Middle East, but motorists in Taiwan can still obtain fuel at relatively stable prices, as CPC and Taipower have been absorbing the rising costs, he said.
However, that has inevitably resulted in a great financial burden for the state-run companies, so the government must allocate additional funds to subsidize their losses, Lai said.
The goal is to stabilize prices, maintain social stability and protect the livelihoods of Taiwanese, he said, urging the public and lawmakers to support the proposal.

Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) on Saturday faced each other in their first televised debate. The candidates debated food safety, urban renewal, child protection, public safety and traffic improvement.
Prior to the debate, Chiang had been criticized for equivocating and sidestepping questions from reporters and city councilors, by giving nonanswers or tasking his aides or city officials to answer for him. He has also been criticized for repeating talking points and avoiding interviews. After Shen’s campaign gained momentum and the legislator’s support rate shot up in polls, the question of the mayor’s evasiveness drew greater attention.
Chiang appeared set on turning his image around in Saturday’s debate, taking an aggressive stance. In his opening remarks, he said that Shen had talked a good game, but failed to deliver on promises. Taking advantage of his incumbency, Chiang went into detail on the city government’s projects, citing statistics to tout his performance. He used specific cases to question Shen, and then followed up by saying Shen did not understand city governance, to frame the legislator as out of his depth.
Chiang also took Shen to task for comments that the legislator had made over the years on drug prevention, the death penalty, the Taipei-Shanghai Twin City Forum and the recall of lawmakers. The mayor sought to force Shen to explain each comment, which at times appeared to have been taken out of context, with the aim of portraying Shen as inconsistent and untrustworthy.
Chiang’s fierce strategy of attacking his opponent, without answering Shen’s questions and even calling them smear attempts and rumors, fulfilled the mayor’s goal of shoring up the KMT’s core supporters. Chiang sought to boost their low morale by striking back at a critic, while playing into his claims of being bullied by the DPP and Shen’s supporters.
Chiang again offered high praise for Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) founder and former Taipei mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲), describing Ko as the target of a DPP witch hunt, an attempt to stir up anti-DPP sentiment among TPP supporters, who Chiang hopes to sway in the election.
However, many of the “accomplishments” Chiang touted were not popular among city residents, and might have been overstated, such as taking credit for Nvidia’s announcement that it would open its Taiwan headquarters in Taipei and the completion of the Taipei Dome, despite water-leakage issues. He also highlighted the city’s free school lunch and milk programs, although those have already been operating in other cities and counties.
Shen has a reputation for being down-to-earth, frequently visiting markets and shops, explaining his policy ideas and giving clear answers to questions from reporters and residents. He is also confident enough to be interviewed by pan-blue-leaning hosts. He is running a positive, innovative and policy-driven campaign, emphasizing hope, while urging his supporters to debate calmly and not give in to emotional provocations.
In Saturday’s debate, Shen demonstrated those traits, expressing concern for Chiang, who called in sick two days before the event, before explaining his platform policies. Shen focused on issues affecting Taipei residents’ daily lives, including time-consuming and hurdle-ridden urban renewal plans, traffic congestion, urban greening, long-term care and child protection. He also reminded Chiang that cherry-picked data do not necessarily reflect the meaningful and heartfelt support that city residents need. Many of the DPP’s policies Chiang criticized are at the central government level, not related to city governance, Shen said, jokingly suggesting that Chiang return to the legislature.
Shen frequently found himself having to explain his or the DPP’s policies in response to Chiang’s selective presentation, while Chiang skipped over questions he found challenging, simply calling them fabrications or rumors. In his closing statement, Shen said his goal is to bring hope back to Taipei with a clear vision for the city, adding that residents should vote for the lifestyles and values they want.
A second televised debate has not yet been confirmed. Saturday’s appeared more like a performance than a focused debate, especially as media questions had been presented to the candidates ahead of the event, and Chiang read from notes when receiving questions from the media. Still, voters have been given a taste of the candidates’ different approaches to how they would govern Taipei.

Iran designates MI6, Royal Navy and RAF under reciprocal measures against UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:41:08 UTC
01:41:08 KST

Iran designates MI6, Royal Navy and RAF under reciprocal measures against UK
TEHRAN — Iran has announced reciprocal measures against the United Kingdom, designating its foreign intelligence service, MI6, as a hostile group and its Royal Navy and Royal Air Force as terrorist organizations, in response to 'Britain's unlawful and hostile actions against the Islamic Republic.'
In a statement issued on Sunday, November 1, Iran's Foreign Ministry condemned the British government's anti-Iranian policies, saying they violated the principles of the United Nations Charter and international law, particularly respect for national sovereignty and the prohibition of unlawful measures against other countries.
The ministry said the measures were intended to safeguard Iran's national security and interests and reaffirmed the government's determination to take all necessary steps to protect the country.
According to the statement, the decision was adopted in response to British actions over the past year, including the country's involvement in the US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran through the provision of military bases, facilities and logistical support.
The ministry also cited Britain's decision on July 13, 2026, to bring Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) under the State Threats Act 2026 as part of the grounds for the reciprocal measures.
The Foreign Ministry said the measures were based on a resolution adopted by Iran's Supreme National Security Council and took effect upon publication of the statement on November 1.
Under the decision, Britain's Secret Intelligence Service, commonly known as MI6, has been designated a hostile group pursuant to Note 2 of Article 1 of Iran's law on intensifying penalties for espionage and cooperation with the Zionist regime and hostile countries against national security and interests.
The Royal Navy and Royal Air Force, meanwhile, have been placed under Iran's law on reciprocal action against the United States' designation of the IRGC as a terrorist organization and will accordingly be recognized as terrorist organizations.
The ministry emphasized that the measures were adopted in accordance with international law and the principle of reciprocity, holding the British government responsible for any consequences arising from its actions.
The decision comes amid heightened tensions between Tehran and London over Britain's role in the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran and its subsequent measures against the IRGC.
Iran has consistently maintained that the provision of military facilities and logistical support for attacks against its territory constitutes a violation of its sovereignty and international law. Tehran has also condemned the designation of the IRGC by Western governments as an interference in its internal affairs and a hostile act against the country's national security.
By extending reciprocal measures to British intelligence and military institutions, Iran has signaled that it will respond to actions it considers hostile through its own legal and security framework.
The Foreign Ministry's statement concluded by reiterating that the British government would bear responsibility for the consequences of its policies and actions against Iran.

The foreign minister said Tehran was making every effort to advance the diplomatic process and expressed hope that Washington would also demonstrate the necessary rationality to prioritize diplomacy over other options.

“Whether the Americans choose diplomacy or another path depends on their own rationality,” he said.

2026 Youth Olympic Games open in Senegal, as Kazakhstan joins parade of nations
Senegal hosted the opening ceremony of the 4th Summer Youth Olympic Games, marking the first time the event has taken place on the African continent, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the National Olympic Committee.
The ceremony took place at Abdoulaye Wade Stadium, which has a capacity of 55,000 spectators.
Organizers prepared an extensive artistic program celebrating Senegal’s history, cultural heritage and traditions, as well as the diversity of African cultures.
More than 1,000 people took part in preparing the show, including over 600 dancers from different regions of the country. The program featured traditional African dances, musical performances, theatrical productions and modern visual effects. Local artisans created around 1,500 costumes for the ceremony.
The performance explored Africa’s history, cultural diversity, traditions and connections between generations. It also highlighted contemporary African culture and youth creativity. The program included two themed productions, La Quête and Alkebulan Live, dedicated to Africa’s history and cultural heritage.
One of the ceremony’s highlights was the parade of national delegations. Judoka Fatima Supygalieva and beach volleyball player Alikhan Agabek carried Kazakhstan’s flag.
Both athletes won gold medals at the 2025 Asian Youth Games in Bahrain. In 2026, Supygalieva also became a world champion in cadet judo.
Another key moment was the lighting of the Olympic flame. It was lit on September 10 at the historic Panathenaic Stadium in Athens before being transported to Senegal.
The Olympic torch relay, held under the motto “Pass the Energy,” covered all 14 regions of Senegal. Among the torchbearers were actor Omar Sy, blogger Khaby Lame and representatives of Senegalese sports.
The final stage of the relay took place in Dakar on October 30. The lighting of the Olympic cauldron at Abdoulaye Wade Stadium marked the official start of the Games.
More than 2,000 athletes are expected to compete at the 4th Summer Youth Olympic Games. Kazakhstan is represented by 18 athletes across 11 sports.
A new athlete admission system has been introduced for the 2026 Games. Unlike previous editions of the Youth Olympic Games, no qualifying tournaments were held. Invitation quotas were allocated by the International Olympic Committee in cooperation with international sports federations, based on established participation criteria.
The competitions will take place across three locations - Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly - and conclude on November 13.
