Transcript: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 1, 2026
The following is the full transcript of the interview with Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, a portion of which aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 1, 2026.
MARGARET BRENNAN: All right. So, Governor, you're campaigning for re-election, and you're also trying to help some of these Democrats get elected to Congress. According to our CBS polling, 57% of likely voters believe Democrats have not offered a clear plan for what they would do if they do win control of Congress. What is it that Democrats are running for, or is it simply in opposition to President Trump?
GOV. JOSH SHAPIRO: Well, certainly for me, it's not about opposition to Trump. I'm running as a GSD Democrat—a Get Stuff Done Democrat. I think what people have seen in my leadership here in Pennsylvania is someone who listens, who goes back to the Capitol, and then delivers, executes for the people of Pennsylvania, and I'm working hard to elect these members of or these challengers to the members of Congress here in Pennsylvania who run on a similar platform, common sense things, making sure people have access to health care, making sure that there is actually accountability in Washington D.C. so that the corruption doesn't take money out of people's pockets here and enrich the folks in D.C. Those are just two examples of the kinds of things I see from our challengers here in Congress. And as I crisscross this Commonwealth, what they're seeing from me is a Democrat who understands how to win, but more importantly, understands how to deliver for them. And that's what these candidates are running on.
MARGARET BRENNAN: How optimistic are you that you're going to be able to take four seats I think you've said?
GOV. SHAPIRO: I mean, look. Right now, it seems like there might even be five competitive congressional districts here in Pennsylvania. Obviously, four have received the most attention. I think we're seemingly ahead in at least three of them. But look, I never pay much attention to these polls. I think it's all a jump ball, and the most important thing is to do what we're doing on this bus: show up everywhere, talk to people, let them know what's at stake, how important it is to not just re-elect their governor, but that we can finally have a check on Donald Trump's chaos, cruelty, and corruption in Washington D.C. If they get out and vote for their candidate for Congress.
MARGARET BRENNAN: And they're still going to have to work with a Republican president for those next two years when they get there. If they get there.
GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah. But there'll be a check on his corruption, and hopefully have real leverage to roll back the Medicaid cuts, to roll back the SNAP cuts, to make sure that there's real responsibility and accountability in Washington D.C. Something we have not had when Republicans have had a trifecta there.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Let me ask you about what's going to happen here in this state in terms of administering the election. Homeland Security claimed earlier this year that as many as 14,576 non-citizens could be registered to vote here. Has the federal government provided enough information to you–
[STOP DOWN]
MARGARET BRENNAN: So Homeland Security said that in this state there are as many as 14,576 non citizens that could be registered to vote in Pennsylvania. Did they provide information to back up that claim? And what did your own investigation find?
GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah, could is the operative word. As soon as we received that from the federal government, we immediately responded and said, "Look, if you have information of illegal voters who are on our rolls, we want that information because we don't want them casting a ballot here in Pennsylvania." I'm very serious about it. Look, I'm the former chief law enforcement officer of this Commonwealth. I have prosecuted election fraud cases. I don't want anyone voting who's not a legal eligible voter–
MARGARET BRENNAN: Did they back that up?
GOV. SHAPIRO: And of course, of course, when we responded to the Trump administration, they provided no backup. So it was a press release designed to get some attention for their false narrative. Listen, the first appointment I made when I was elected governor was the Secretary of State. That's the person that administers elections here in the state. A Republican named Al Schmidt. I chose him, even though I'm a Democrat, because I think the administration of elections should be nonpartisan. Al Schmidt, in his career of running elections, has done more to root out corruption than anything that's ever been done in the Trump administration. We take that very, very seriously, and the Trump administration has never provided a shred of evidence to suggest that there are people on our rolls who are ineligible. If they have it, I want it, and we will act on it immediately.
MARGARET BRENNAN: A recent CBS investigation found Pennsylvania was one of the states where Homeland Security has been going door to door. They've been knocking on doors and asking about the immigration status of people who live there. What can you tell us about what DHS has been doing here? And did the administration coordinate with you as governor in any way?
GOV. SHAPIRO: No. And I want to make very very clearly the Pennsylvania State Police does not do DHS's work for them. Does not do ICE's work for them. We do not ask immigration status. In fact, when ICE came here and tried to bully their way into building two massive detention centers here in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, one in Berks County, one in Schuylkill County, I fought back and won and drove those detention centers out of Pennsylvania.
MARGARET BRENNAN: How many non-citizen voters did you find?
GOV. SHAPIRO: Well, what they said was that there were, whatever the number was, over a thousand people. So we said, great, tell us who they are, so we can check their status. They never told us who they were, and so it is impossible for us to be able to check the people that they claim to have identified. I will tell you, we've got very, very strict guardrails in place, led by Secretary Schmidt, constantly making sure that the people who are on our voter rolls are legal, eligible voters. And if we find that someone is not, if a mistake was made in a county where someone was registering, as an example, we immediately get on that. We work with prosecutors to ensure that they are not in a position to cast a ballot. As I said, I was the chief law enforcement officer of this Commonwealth. I prosecuted election fraud. It was a handful of cases. By the way, some were Republican, some were Democrat. None of it impacted any elections. But still, we can't allow that to happen here in our Commonwealth. And what I would ask of the Trump administration is, instead of sending me a press release, send me actual evidence, actual data, and we will review it promptly.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So you did speak recently with Philadelphia Inquirer's editorial board, and you told them that you think President Trump and his allies are going to try and stop votes from being counted.
GOV SHAPIRO: Yes.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You also said you expect Speaker Johnson to make efforts to delay seating new members if Republicans lose the majority. Why are you raising these concerns now? And do you think at all that you might be undermining faith?
GOV. SHAPIRO: Yeah. Well, respectfully, I was answering their question as to whether or not I thought the Trump administration would take steps to try and undermine our elections. So just to offer some context to that, and I did issue those answers, and I'll tell you why. Because I have lived through this before with the Trump administration. Back in 2020, I was the attorney general, and Trump lost the election here in Pennsylvania and tried to undermine the counting of the vote. In fact, he and his enablers sued me 43 different times to try and throw out the votes of certain Pennsylvanians. Heck, even my opponent went to court to throw out the votes of people in Bucks County. I won every single one of those cases. Went 43 and 0, Trump went 0 and 43. And so we are prepared should they try to do that again this time. In fact, we put together a task force more than a year ago when Trump began to hint at the idea that he would once again take that tack. So we are prepared in the courtroom. Should they go forward and try and undermine the right to vote. Now, more recently, we've seen further evidence of this president trying to undermine the right to vote in signing that bogus executive order, trying to make it so people here in Pennsylvania and across America couldn't vote by mail. I sued him. I won, and we protected the right to vote. So again, this was A) in response to a question, and B) based on a history of dealing with a guy who is constantly trying to undermine the right to vote here in our Commonwealth.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So I want to ask about you. Brian Fitzpatrick, who represents Bucks County, Republican here in Pennsylvania, describes you as a good man, a friend. He said you're smart, competent. I'm competing everywhere for the support of certainly Democrats, but Republicans and Independents as well.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you're laying out an agenda that would require some time to achieve.
GOV. SHAPIRO: I'm not sure I follow your question.

A humanitarian mission was carried out on October 30. Several dozen tons of humanitarian aid - food, hygiene and sanitation products, fuels for power generators, and other daily essentials - were handed out to the city residents, Lantratova said. All those willing to leave the city were given the opportunity to evacuate either to Russia or to Ukraine.

Iran inflicted at least $5 billion in damage on US military bases: WSJ
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:26:07 UTC
00:26:07 KST

Iran inflicted at least $5 billion in damage on US military bases: WSJ
Iranian missile and drone strikes have inflicted at least $5 billion in damage on U.S. military bases across the Middle East, according to a sweeping Wall Street Journal investigation that offers the fullest public picture yet of what the war on Iran has cost American forces in the region.
The Journal's analysis, drawing on satellite imagery, Iranian military statements and interviews with U.S. officials, identified 274 damaged structures at 24 installations with an American military presence during the war's first six months.
The investigation found that Iran increasingly targeted buildings where American troops live and sleep, showing an improved ability to sequence attacks and strike with greater precision.
While the Pentagon has priced the damage to bases at a minimum of $5 billion, according to U.S. officials familiar with the matter cited by The Journal, a separate person briefed on the cost said the figure could reach as high as $15 billion.
The Center for Strategic and International Studies, which reviewed the Journal's findings on damaged buildings, estimated that reconstruction alone would top $4 billion, a figure that excludes replacing the equipment and systems housed inside.
Those repairs come on top of the war's overall cost, which stood at $47.1 billion as of Oct. 16, according to a document viewed by The Journal.
According to an Associated Press analysis, Iran's strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early-warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage.
The AP independently verified damage to American targets using satellite imagery from multiple providers and spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or have firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment.
The Journal also said the human toll has also mounted. More than 20 U.S. service members have died in activity related to the war since it began on Feb. 28, according to Defense Department data, and more than 400 were wounded before a temporary ceasefire collapsed in July. After that, the government stopped publishing casualty figures specific to the conflict.

New airfare rules from next year: No govt intervention except in ‘extraordinary situations’ to prevent spikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:23:53 UTC
00:23:53 KST

Airlines have been asked to give a break-up of tariff in terms of the total amount payable by a passenger and break-up of the same by displaying components like base fare, tax, fees, cancellation charges, refund conditions and any other charge separately.
NEW DELHI: India has adopted new airfare rules where government will not interfere in the process except “in an extraordinary situation (where) it considers it necessary to do so in the public interest.” Notified under the Bharatiya Vayuyan Niyam, 2026, which will be applicable from Jan 1, 2027, government has continued its policy of letting market forces determine airfares without government interference.TOI reported on Oct 17 that India has no plans to regulate or cap airfares in the free market under which airlines here operate under the new airfare policy being finalised. However, it will keep a “strong lever” on airlines to ensure they don’t resort to very sharp surges in “exceptional and extraordinary circumstances” that see demand rising for certain routes.“Every air transport undertaking… shall establish tariff based on factors including cost of operation…. (They) shall submit tariff to the Director General (DGCA) in such form, manner and periodicity as may be specified…. (They) shall publish tariff on their websites… for wider public awareness and transparency,” says the gazette notification published Saturday (October 31).
Airlines have been asked to give a break-up of tariff in terms of the total amount payable by a passenger and break-up of the same by displaying components like base fare, tax, fees, cancellation charges, refund conditions and any other charge separately.
Regarding intervention in “extraordinary circumstances,” it says: “Where the central government is of the opinion that (in) an extraordinary situation it may, by order in writing, issue such directions in public interest…. such directions shall be proportionate to the circumstances and shall remain in force for the period specified only.”

Party releases resolution after plenum on governance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:17:03 UTC
00:17:03 KST

The Communist Party of China (CPC) on Sunday made public a resolution following this week's annual plenary session in Beijing.
The document titled "The Resolution of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China on Certain Major Issues concerning Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance", was released by Xinhua News Agency.
In an explanation of the resolution also published by Xinhua, President Xi Jinping explained that Party building is crucial for the future of the CPC.
Xi acknowledged that the makeup of the Party has changed.
"Over the years, our Party membership is undergoing structural changes, with a steady increase in the proportion of members and officials born after the launch of reform and opening up in 1978. This has raised new requirements for education and management," he said.
"The vast majority of Party members are exemplary, yet there remain a number of problems and hidden dangers that threaten to undermine the Party’s advanced nature, weaken its integrity, and jeopardise its long-term governance.
"In particular, the problems of defects in thinking, organisation, and conduct have yet to be solved root and branch, while some new problems continue to emerge," he explained.
The resolution itself called for stricter monitoring of officials.
"Starting with high-ranking officials, we will tighten all-around management and regular oversight of officials, imposing strict requirements throughout their career and across the whole process of their education, management, and oversight to avoid over-emphasising selection to the neglect of management," it said. 
"The system requiring leading officials to report personal information will be refined. 
"Those with family property and spending far exceeding their normal incomes will be examined, and relevant verifications will be carried out. Regular management will be tightened for the commercial and entrepreneurial activities of leading officials’ spouses, children, and their children’s spouses. Dedicated efforts will be intensified to address nepotism," it wrote. 
Xi in the explanation also said that the nation’s success hinges on the CPC, "especially on the Party’s efforts to exercise full and rigorous self-governance". 
"In the face of complicated international and domestic landscapes and the challenging tasks of advancing reform, promoting development, and ensuring stability, it is essential, in our efforts to ensure steady and sustained progress in Chinese modernisation," Xi said.
The fifth plenum, which ended on Thursday, comes ahead of a major Party congress next year, where Xi is expected to oversee a leadership reshuffle.

Protestors loot shops in Frankfurt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:17:00 UTC
00:17:00 KST

Protestors loot shops in Frankfurt
320,000 hold protests in France as police arrest 770
Protestors looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living.
Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannons to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles, BBC said on its website.
Thousands joined demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organized by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service.
The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday.
On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters.
Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city.
Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organizers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday.
Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion".
She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favor of a fairer distribution of the burden."
On Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed.
The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said.
Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing items like trainers.
Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended.
"We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard.
Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city.
Similar instances took place in other German cities.
In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched.
A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said.
In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested.
The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe.
In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector.
Thousands of police officers were deployed across the country, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests across France during the demonstrations on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail and French prosecutors later launched an attempted murder probe.
Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles.
French protest organizers, the Gilet Jaune, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of stun grenades for policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off.
Protests also took place in Italy, with some clashes between police and demonstrators in Rome and Turin.
In Portugal, police moved to clear a new tent camp that had been assembled after thousands marched to protest against a rental bill that they argue could worsen a housing crisis in the country, where house prices have more than doubled over the past decade.
Mostly young protesters have recently taken to the streets in a swathe of European nations: France, Belgium, Ireland, Spain, Portugal, Italy, Greece, Serbia and Albania.
While the specific demands vary from country to country, the protesters have largely focused on cost-of-living issues, such as access to housing, the quality of education and cuts to public services.

Russian police have arrested a minor in connection with an alleged plot to attack Moscow, Russian news agencies reported, after Russia received a tip-off from the United States.
The US embassy in Moscow published a statement on Saturday saying it was "aware of a credible threat of a mass casualty event at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in Moscow".
The US embassy did not give details on who was plotting the attack.
In a statement quoted by Russian news agencies on Sunday, Russia's FSB security service said it had arrested a minor who had posted photos of himself on TikTok wearing a balaclava, cap and goggles and holding what resembled an automatic weapon.
The unidentified male, who the FSB said was a Russian citizen, had shared photos taken at the Tsaritsyno museum reserve along with the caption "I found a place" and was allegedly subscribed to a "neo-Nazi" Telegram channel, it said.
The FSB did not name the male in question.
"We are grateful to the American side for the information provided," the FSB was quoted as saying.
The Tsaritsyno museum is an imperial palace and park complex in southern Moscow popular with residents and tourists.
Russian Telegram channel Baza, which has reported links to law enforcement, said the park was closed on Saturday and open only for people leaving the grounds.
The US has provided Russia with warnings of planned attacks before, including in March 2024, weeks before a Daesh attack on a Moscow concert hall that killed over 100 people.
Relations between Russia and the United States have thawed in recent months, amid ongoing strain between Washington and Kiev over a US-Russia diesel deal.

Delivering a keynote address at the Botswana-China Friendship Evening event held on Saturday at the Gaborone International Convention Center in the capital, President Duma Boko described his recent state visit to China as "exceedingly successful."
The outcomes of the visit will be translated into "tangible opportunities and benefits for our peoples," said Boko, urging Botswana to learn from China's development experience in skills, expertise, innovation and technology.

Midterms reopen debate over dominance of wealth in US politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:05:21 UTC
00:05:21 KST

Midterms reopen debate over dominance of wealth in US politics
American democracy is drifting away from principle of ‘one person, one vote’ to a system of ‘one dollar, one vote’
TEHRAN – Campaign spending during the current U.S. midterm election cycle has become the subject of intense political and media debate.
It has brought back into focus a fundamental dilemma facing the United States. How can political equality among the public be preserved when a small group of wealthy individuals enjoys extraordinary financial power to fund election campaigns and shape public debate?
While this is hardly a new issue, it has taken on sharper dimensions in 2026 amid soaring campaign expenditures and the growing influence of major donors and special interest groups.
Approximately $8.9 billion was spent on the 2022 midterms. Approximately $11.2 billion for the 2024 presidential election and a projected $11.6 billion for the 2026 midterms.
Donald Trump’s presence on the political scene has played a particularly striking role in highlighting this contradiction.
Having entered the presidential race in 2015, attacking the influence of major donors and presenting his personal wealth as a guarantee of his political independence, Trump went on to benefit, in the 2024 election, from massive financial backing provided by several billionaires and political action committees, most notably those associated with Elon Musk.
The 2026 midterm elections have since witnessed record levels of spending, both during the primary season and in the campaigns leading up to the election.
An investigation published by The New York Times revealed that at least $1 billion in funds linked to donors whose identities remain undisclosed had flowed into the 2026 elections.
The newspaper reported that tens of millions of dollars from unknown sources had been used in efforts to influence Democratic primary contests, particularly in Michigan and Minnesota.
Michigan offered a striking picture of the unprecedented escalation in campaign spending, with expenditures on political advertising exceeding $850 million over the election cycle. Notably, Abdul El-Sayed secured the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate despite being significantly outspent by his rival, Haley Stevens, who received substantial backing from outside funding groups, most prominently the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).
Further evidence of the concentration of campaign financing emerged in a Washington Post report revealing that the 50 largest donors and lobby groups contributed approximately $2.77 billion during the current election cycle. Elon Musk alone accounted for around $446 million, most of which went to political action committees supporting Republican candidates.
The controversy, however, has extended beyond the sheer volume and sources of campaign money to questions about the effectiveness of regulatory oversight.
The Brennan Center for Justice has raised concerns about the Federal Election Commission’s declining ability to carry out some of its core responsibilities, after the agency spent more than a year without the quorum required to make certain official decisions.
The center warned that this situation heightens the risks associated with opaque campaign financing, particularly as spending on digital advertising and social media influencers continues to expand, areas that do not always fall under the same disclosure and oversight requirements as traditional media.
The current elections have therefore exposed a debate that goes beyond record-breaking campaign expenditures.
At its heart lies a more fundamental question: how freely can political parties and voters choose their representatives when wealthy individuals and corporations possess enormous financial resources with which to influence the electoral process?
This dilemma was explored earlier by legal scholars who offer a critical examination of the American democratic experience, focusing on the contradictions between the principles underpinning the country’s political system and the way those principles are put into practice.
Among the central issues examined are economic and social inequality, the influence of money and private interests, equality in the political process, the role of constitutional and judicial institutions, and the gap between America’s proclaimed democratic values and its conduct on the international stage.
Specifically addressing campaign finance, criticism has been aimed at the U.S. Supreme Court’s 1976 decision overturning key restrictions on campaign spending because they violated the constitutional protection of freedom of speech. That ruling became one of the legal foundations of the campaign finance system that operates in the United States today.
Many critics argue that the distinction between political contributions and campaign expenditures opened the door for wealthy individuals, corporations, and lobbying groups to exercise disproportionate political influence, thereby threatening the principle of equality on which a supposedly democratic society is based.
The arguments closely echo warnings voiced by prominent American thinkers, writers, and politicians who represent a broad intellectual and political current that views the growing influence of money as a genuine threat to the electoral process and to the principle of political equality.
Among the most prominent is Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz, who has drawn a direct connection between wealth inequality and disparities in political influence.
He has warned that American democracy is drifting away from the principle of “one person, one vote” and moving closer to a system of “one dollar, one vote.” In Stiglitz’s analysis, wealth and political power reinforce one another in a self-perpetuating cycle: wealth enables its holders to influence legislation and public policy, while those very laws and policies, in turn, help consolidate their fortunes and political influence.
Along similar lines, a widely cited academic study by researchers concluded that economic elites and business-oriented interest groups exercise considerable influence over American policymaking, while ordinary citizens have little independent influence on political outcomes.
Studies have sparked widespread debate about whether the political system genuinely reflects the will of the majority or instead grants economic elites influence far beyond their share of the electorate.
These warnings and academic findings have emerged against the backdrop of a lengthy judicial and legislative trajectory that has progressively expanded the scope for unlimited political spending, building on the foundations established by the Supreme Court’s 1976 ruling.
Since 2010, a series of Supreme Court rulings, beginning with Citizens United v. FEC, has dismantled campaign finance restrictions, granting lobby groups, wealthy individuals, and political parties greater freedom to spend money on elections. The result is a system that increasingly treats political spending as constitutionally protected free speech rather than a force to be regulated.
U.S. politics has become a system where money speaks louder than votes, and wealth, not the majority, ultimately decides who rules.

====================================================================================================

Study finds a specific emotional route from feeling humanized to political compromise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:00:03 UTC
00:00:03 KST

When voters believe their political rivals see them as full human beings rather than mindless brutes, they become more willing to negotiate, compromise, and work across party lines. New research published in Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin suggests this effect works mainly by reducing feelings of disgust toward the opposing party, and that it is especially relevant when people feel political divisions threaten the fabric of society.
In many Western democracies, political disagreements have increasingly become personal and moral clashes. Psychologists call this affective polarization, the tendency of partisans to distrust and dislike members of the opposing party, not merely disagree with their policies. Rather than seeing opponents as fellow citizens, partisans often view them as morally corrupt or even less than human.
Part of this hostility may stem from meta-perceptions, or beliefs about how one’s own group is viewed by outsiders. Partisans often experience meta-dehumanization, the belief that the other party sees them as subhuman, irrational, or animalistic. A 2020 study of American political partisans found that Democrats and Republicans both substantially overestimated how much the other side disliked and dehumanized them, and these exaggerated beliefs predicted stronger support for spiteful actions that harm democratic norms.
Feeling dehumanized can set off a cycle of retaliation. A 2016 series of studies on intergroup conflict indicated that people who feel dehumanized by a rival group tend to dehumanize that group in return and support aggressive policies against it.
The reverse belief, known as meta-humanization, may help repair relations between groups. In a 2021 study of Muslims and non-Muslims in Canada and the United Kingdom, the same two researchers behind the new paper found that perceiving the other group as seeing one’s own group as fully human reduced prejudice and encouraged friendly contact, even when tensions were high. But a 2024 study in post-conflict Kosovo found that feeling humanized by former adversaries did not reliably make people more willing to negotiate with them, suggesting the effect may depend on how immediate and threatening the division feels.
Less is known about how feeling humanized changes people’s emotions toward their opponents. Moral emotions shape how people treat other groups. Anger typically stems from perceived injustice and sparks confrontation, disgust is tied to a sense of moral contamination and motivates avoidance, and empathy encourages perspective-taking and care.
To examine which of these emotions explains the benefits of meta-humanization, and how they interact with fears that society is fracturing, the researchers conducted five experiments with a total of 1,541 participants in the United Kingdom, the United States, and Canada. The work was led by Melissa Pavetich, an assistant professor at Heriot-Watt University in Dubai and a member of the SOCIAL Impact Lab, together with Sofia Stathi of the University of Greenwich.
“A lot of research on polarization focuses on what partisans think of each other,” Pavetich told PsyPost. “We were interested in a different question: what people believe the other side thinks of them.”
“We wanted to know whether that belief matters in politics, and if so, why,” she said. “In particular, we wanted to identify the emotional route that links it to whether people are willing to reconcile.”
Across all five experiments, the researchers statistically controlled for frequency of out-partisan contact on a 1-to-5 scale, accounting for how often participants already encountered members of the rival party in everyday life. The first study, conducted in February 2021 via the online platform Prolific, included 353 British adults (average age 36, 61.1 percent female, 79.9 percent White), split between Conservative Party supporters (52.0 percent) and Labour Party supporters (48.0 percent).
Participants were randomly assigned to read fictional social media posts, styled as messages from Twitter (now X), supposedly written by supporters of the rival party. In the meta-dehumanization condition, the posts referred to the participant’s party as “animals and brutes lacking in self-control,” whereas in the meta-humanization condition, the posts described them as “sophisticated.”
After reading the posts, the British participants rated their feelings and attitudes on 7-point scales, where higher numbers meant stronger agreement or intensity. Both Labour and Conservative supporters who read the humanizing posts reported lower anger, lower disgust, weaker intentions to hurt or humiliate opponents, and greater comfort with close social contact, such as having a doctor from the opposing party.
Among Labour supporters, those in the meta-humanization group reported lower disgust (an average of 2.14 vs. 3.21 in the meta-dehumanization group), lower anger (1.94 vs. 2.61), lower hostility (2.05 vs. 2.55), and less desire for social distance (3.50 vs. 3.75). Conservative supporters showed a similar pattern when comparing the humanizing and dehumanizing conditions for disgust (1.68 vs. 3.09), hostility (1.82 vs. 2.32), and social distance (2.77 vs. 3.05), alongside a pronounced drop in anger (1.64 vs. 2.77).
Because the first experiment did not include a baseline control group or a measure of empathy, the authors designed Study 2a to add both elements while testing how moral emotions connect to broader political reconciliation and whether perceived threat to social cohesion alters the process. Threat to social cohesion refers to the worry that political divisions are eroding shared community values, mutual trust, and collective belonging. The remaining four experiments were preregistered on the Open Science Framework, with materials and data posted publicly.
Conducted one week before the 2024 U.S. presidential election, Study 2a recruited 301 American Republicans (average age 47, 63.8 percent female, 83.1 percent White) through Prolific. Participants first rated their perceived threat to social cohesion on a 7-point scale, reacting to statements such as “The values in our society have gone seriously off track,” and were then randomly assigned to read humanizing X posts from Democrats, dehumanizing X posts from Democrats, or no posts at all in a control group.
They next rated their anger, disgust, and empathy toward Democrats on 7-point scales, and evaluated how civilized and evolved they considered Democrats to be on a slider from 0 to 10. Finally, they completed 7-point scales measuring affective polarization and four conciliatory attitudes: support for cross-party negotiation, willingness to compromise, support for bipartisan teamwork, and openness to future contact with Democrats.
Republicans who read humanizing posts felt much more humanized by Democrats (an average of 5.31 out of 7) than those in the control group (3.91) or the dehumanizing group (1.52). Statistical modeling indicated that feeling humanized by Democrats lowered Republicans’ disgust, which in turn led them to view Democrats as more human and civilized, predicting lower affective polarization and higher support for negotiation, compromise, teamwork, and contact. This indirect pathway held across all outcomes under moderate perceived threat to social cohesion, compared to both the meta-dehumanization and control groups, and extended to high threat for several outcomes. The pathways through anger and empathy were not statistically significant.
Study 2b mirrored this setup in the same pre-election context in the United States, examining 302 American Democrats (average age 46, 66.6 percent female, 79.9 percent White) reading fictional posts attributed to Republicans. Democrats in the meta-humanization group scored an average of 5.73 out of 7 on feeling humanized by Republicans, compared to 3.43 in the control group and 1.70 in the meta-dehumanization group.
Just as with Republicans, disgust was the sole emotion that linked meta-humanization to viewing the opposing party as human and adopting more conciliatory attitudes. This chain reaction through reduced disgust held most consistently under moderate perceived threat to social cohesion, where it predicted lower affective polarization and greater support for negotiation, compromise, and contact compared to both other conditions (and teamwork compared to the control group), while extending to low threat for several conciliatory outcomes when compared to the meta-dehumanization condition and to high threat when compared to the control condition. The pathways through anger and empathy were not statistically significant.
To test whether these patterns held outside the intense atmosphere of a U.S. presidential election, the researchers replicated the experiment in Canada using Qualtrics Panel. Study 3a surveyed 310 supporters of the Conservative Party of Canada (average age 46, 55.4 percent male, 73.1 percent White), evaluating their reactions to supporters of the rival Liberal Party. Canadian Conservatives who read humanizing posts felt more humanized by Liberals (an average of 4.55 out of 7) than those in the control group (3.81) or the dehumanizing group (2.92).
Consistent with the American findings, feeling humanized reduced disgust and increased how human Canadian Conservatives viewed Liberals to be, which in turn predicted more conciliatory attitudes. This indirect effect emerged under moderate threat to social cohesion for conciliatory outcomes such as compromise and teamwork and extended across all outcomes, including reduced affective polarization, when perceived threat was high. The pathways via anger and empathy were not statistically significant.
Study 3b completed the series by surveying 300 supporters of the Liberal Party of Canada (average age 49, 51.5 percent male, 71.1 percent White) regarding their attitudes toward Canadian Conservatives. Liberals in the meta-humanization condition reported feeling more humanized by Conservatives (an average of 4.64 out of 7) than those in the control group (3.91) or the meta-dehumanization group (2.64).
Among Canadian Liberals who reported low to moderate threat to social cohesion, feeling humanized by Conservatives again reduced disgust and increased outgroup humanization, predicting lower affective polarization and stronger support for negotiation, compromise, teamwork, and contact compared to both other conditions. Uniquely in this fifth experiment, heightened empathy also served as a parallel bridge toward reconciliation alongside reduced disgust, though only when comparing the meta-humanization group to the control group under low to moderate threat.
Taken together, the five experiments suggest that learning one’s political group is respected as human promotes compromise mainly by disarming disgust rather than by soothing anger or sparking empathy. Because disgust functions as a psychological barrier that motivates people to avoid perceived moral contamination, lowering disgust removes a major obstacle to treating political opponents as fellow citizens worthy of dialogue.
“How we think the other side sees us shapes how we treat them,” Pavetich explained. Across the five studies, she said, “when people feel seen as human, they feel less moral disgust toward the other side, and that makes room for reconciliation.”
“I expected empathy to do much of the work, since it’s so often discussed as the path to bridging divides,” Pavetich noted. “Instead, disgust stood out as the main pathway. This suggests that reducing a negative moral reaction may matter more than building positive feelings.”
The researchers also noted a difference in how perceived threat operated across political camps: the pathway through reduced disgust was most consistent at moderate threat across groups, extending to high threat among conservative participants and to low threat among liberal and Democratic participants. The authors suggest that because conservative voters are often particularly attuned to threat cues, seeing goodwill from the opposing party when threat is elevated may be especially reassuring to them or create a psychological tension that resolves by warming toward the outgroup.
As a competing explanation, the authors note that low threat may simply allow people to feel safe and open enough to benefit from humanizing messages, whereas high threat can push people into a defensive posture that blocks reconciliation.
“We were also interested to find that these processes were strongest when people saw a moderate level of threat to social cohesion,” Pavetich said. “Feeling some stake in the conflict seems to make how you’re perceived matter more.”
“The effects were small to moderate,” Pavetich added. “Effects like this won’t erase partisan hostility on their own. They were consistent across countries and outcomes, though, and they come from people’s beliefs about the other side.”
“That matters because those beliefs are often inaccurate and can potentially be corrected,” she said. “Small shifts in how people think they’re seen could add up across many everyday political interactions.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Although the researchers experimentally manipulated the social media posts that participants read, participants’ emotional reactions, their humanization of the opposing party, and their willingness to compromise were all measured at the same time through survey questions, meaning the study cannot prove that a drop in disgust directly causes someone to become more open to political negotiation.
“These findings don’t mean people should simply be told ‘the other side sees you as human’ whether or not it’s true,” Pavetich cautioned. “Meta-perceptions work best when they reflect genuine signals from the other group.”
“Perceived threat was measured as an existing attitude rather than manipulated experimentally, so we’re more cautious about interpreting its role,” she added. “Finally, humanization was measured with a widely used but debated scale, the Ascent of Man scale. Future work using a range of measures would strengthen the conclusions.”
In addition, the experiments took place in three Western nations where politics largely revolves around two dominant rival parties, meaning the findings might not apply to countries with multi-party coalitions or entrenched violent conflicts where partisans have little desire to reconcile. Future work could test whether combining humanizing messages with face-to-face collaborative problem-solving helps partisans build lasting trust across the political aisle.
“One direction I’m especially keen to pursue is the role of disgust itself,” Pavetich said. “Disgust is closely tied to how people judge right and wrong, so I want to understand why it emerged as the key pathway here. Does it reflect seeing the other side as morally contaminated or as violating core values? And can that response be reduced directly?”
“Alongside this, I’m examining how intergroup contact interacts with meta-humanization,” she added. “We’re testing whether the quality and type of contact, both face-to-face and through media, strengthens the benefits of feeling humanized. I also plan to extend this work beyond Western two-party systems to multi-party contexts and regions that are underrepresented in this research.”
“I’d love readers to remember that polarization isn’t only about disagreement over issues,” Pavetich concluded. “It’s also about feeling looked down on. Signs that we see the other side as fully human, even when we disagree strongly, may do more to lower the temperature than winning the argument.”
The study, “Bridging the Political Divide: Meta-Humanization and Moral Emotions Shape Partisan Reconciliation,” was authored by Melissa Pavetich and Sofia Stathi.

RAF Chinooks Take to Sea with HMS Queen Elizabeth on Exercise Hathi Pol
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:00:00 GMT
00:00:00 KST

Royal Air Force Chinook crews and support personnel embarked on HMS Queen Elizabeth (QNLZ) to undertake Exercise Hathi Pol, a key maritime aviation training activity that sustains critical operational capability for future global missions.
Led by 27 Squadron, with support from personnel from 7 Squadron, the exercise saw two RAF Chinook helicopters and 80 personnel operating from the Royal Navy's flagship in the Western Mediterranean and Eastern Atlantic region.
The training focused on delivering Deck Landing Qualification (DLQ) and Embarked Aviation Qualification (EAQ) training, enabling aircrew to gain or revalidate the specialist qualifications required to operate safely and effectively from maritime platforms.
The exercise provided valuable opportunities for engineers and support personnel to develop and maintain the unique skills needed to sustain aviation operations at sea, strengthening the RAF's ability to deploy rapidly alongside our partner services wherever required.
Operating a large support helicopter from a moving aircraft carrier presents a distinct challenge, demanding close integration between RAF and Royal Navy personnel. Through joint planning, flying and engineering activity, the exercise enhances interoperability between the Services and reinforces the UK's ability to project air power from the maritime domain.
Memorably, Ex Hathi Pol coincided with the (221st) anniversary of the Battle of Trafalgar. On 21 October, QNLZ was sailing approximately 100 miles west of Cape Trafalgar, close to the waters where Nelson secured his famous and final victory in 1805.
"27 Sqn’s deployment on Ex Hathi Pol marked a significant milestone for both the Sqn and HMS Queen Elizabeth. Chinooks from 27 Sqn were the first embarked aviation to operate from QNLZ in over two years, providing an important opportunity for aircrew and Ship’s Company to work together and refresh their embarked maritime experience.
Departing the familiar training areas of the English Channel, QNLZ sailed south towards  Gibraltar. During the passage, Chinook aircraft were dispatched ashore to embark the essential equipment required to support at-sea replenishment from a UAS, the first fixed-wing aircraft operated by the ship since her return to sea." 
Squadron Leader Grahame, Deputy Officer Commanding 27 Sqn RAF Odiham
Detachment Commander on Ex Hathi Pol
The recent embarked training contributes directly to maintaining Defence readiness for a range of future operations, including Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief missions, Non-Combatant Evacuation Operations and wider contingency tasks around the world.
The activity reflects the RAF commitment to maintaining a Warfighting Ready force, investing in its people and strengthening the UK's integrated Defence capability through close collaboration with the Royal Navy.
By training in the maritime environment, Chinook crews gain experience operating from sea-based platforms, extending the flexibility and reach of the UK's heavy-lift helicopter force.
The exercise reaffirms the RAF remain ready to respond to emerging crises and support operations across the globe, demonstrating the value of a highly trained, adaptable and integrated Joint Force capable of delivering effect wherever and whenever required.

Russia's FSB says minor detained over park attack threat after US tip-off
Nov 1 - Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) said on Sunday that a Russian minor had been detained over a threat to carry out a terrorist attack in a Moscow park following a tip-off from the United States, news agency Interfax reported.
On Saturday, the FSB said it had received information from the US through established partner channels about preparations for an attack in Moscow and was taking appropriate measures.
The minor had posted photographs of himself on TikTok wearing tactical clothing and a balaclava, holding an object that looked like an automatic weapon, as well as photographs taken at Moscow's Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve with the caption: "I found a place," Interfax cited the FSB as saying.
"We are grateful to the American side for providing the information," the security service was quoted as saying in its statement.
It said officials searching the minor's home found the clothes and accessories seen in the social media posts, while his phone showed a subscription to a neo-Nazi channel on the app Telegram and “a significant number of searches concerning terrorist attacks, mass killings and other acts of violence,” according to Interfax.
Russia's Investigative Committee is considering what legal or procedural action to take, the FSB said.
Tsaritsyno, a palace museum and park complex in southern Moscow, was temporarily closed on Saturday following the US tip-off. REUTERS

- Prosecutors said around 15 gendarmes and police were targeted; one officer suffered burns, and no suspect has been arrested.
- More than 770 people were arrested nationwide, while shop damage was lower than before, though retailers fear harm before the holiday season.
AI generated
PARIS – France has launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at security forces during a weekend protest in Paris, prosecutors told AFP on Nov 1.
On Oct 31, clashes erupted in the capital and some other cities after hundreds of thousands of people staged a third weekend of protests against soaring living costs.
The Paris police prefecture said that several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles, including a Molotov cocktail. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has decried an “extraordinary” level of violence from some rioters.
“Explosive devices were thrown at around 15 gendarmes as well as police officers,” the prosecutor’s office said on Nov 1.
Gendarmes are military police officers who are part of the French armed forces.
Prosecutors said an investigation had been opened for “attempted murder of persons vested with public authority”.
Dramatic images, including AFP photos and video, showed a homemade incendiary device exploding at the feet of a security officer in eastern Paris, engulfing his lower body in flames.
An assessment of the injured was ongoing, prosecutors said, adding that the reported injuries include second-degree burns.
Initial complaints were expected to be filed on Nov 1.
The gendarme struck by the Molotov cocktail told French television of the burns he suffered, describing “skin that stings” and a “rain” of projectiles thrown at his unit.
Fewer shops damaged
The gendarmerie said that 13 members of the officer’s unit were injured, according to RTL.
No suspects “have been arrested at this stage in connection with the incident”, the prosecutor’s office said, adding that investigators were working to identify those responsible.
The protests come in a tense political climate, with presidential elections six months away and front runner Marine le Pen vowing to restore law and order if elected in 2027.
The leader of the far-right National Rally party said those responsible for the firebomb attack must be “punished with the utmost severity”, in a post on X.
Both she and Bruno Retailleau, head of the right-wing Republicans, described images of the officer in flames as “unbearable”.
The right-leaning Le Figaro said: “The days of the May 1968 riots are a far cry from today, when gendarmes facing the most violent protesters wore... ties.”
More than 770 people were arrested during weekend protests in France, the Interior Ministry said on Nov 1. It added that there had been “no major incidents” late on Oct 31.
A total of 159 members of law enforcement were injured during protests and Halloween celebrations, it said.
The number of shops damaged on the sidelines of the Oct 31 protests was significantly lower than during previous weekends, with some 20 businesses affected, according to France’s Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).
But CCI France voiced concern about the impact of the protests on retail activity ahead of the year-end holiday season, a peak period for businesses. AFP

‘Less than a minute’: Hong Kong travellers praise Japan’s new tax refund at airports
Visitors now pay 10 per cent consumption tax either at self-service airport kiosks or via Visit Japan Web instead of upfront at cash register
Hong Kong tour groups returning from Japan have praised a smooth roll-out of the country’s new tax refund arrangement that requires travellers to complete refund procedures at airports or ports rather than at shops.
Under the “pay first, refund later” scheme, which took effect on Sunday to curb illicit domestic reselling and tax evasion, international tourists must now pay the 10 per cent consumption tax upfront at the counter.
Travellers are now required to complete customs verification before checking in their luggage, either at self-service airport kiosks or via the website Visit Japan Web. After verification, most will be cleared automatically, while some may be selected for customs inspection and asked to present their purchases.

US midterm campaign enters last weekend as ballot fights heat up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:42:26 UTC
23:42:26 KST

Breadcrumb
US midterm campaign enters final weekend as Alaska, California ballot fights heat up
President Donald Trump's administration pressed a criminal investigation into Alaska's pivotal US Senate race and said on Saturday it would likely take its fight over thousands of California mail-in ballots to the Supreme Court, as the midterm campaign for control of Congress entered its final weekend.
In Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating whether aides to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola helped to recruit a retired schoolteacher, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to run because his name is similar to the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan. The closely contested race is seen as crucial to Democrats' hopes of taking the Senate in Tuesday's vote.
It is one of 35 Senate races, along with all 435 House seats, that will decide whether Trump's Republicans keep control of Congress for his final two years in office.
Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority and a narrow edge in the House.
Early voting has set a record. More than 51 million Americans have already cast ballots in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day at the last midterms in 2022.
In California, a federal appeals court this week ruled 2-1 that the Justice Department had failed to justify its emergency bid to force the state to set aside mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters it alleges are likely noncitizens.
"I hesitate to give a final answer, but I think probably the Supreme Court's next on this one," acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter told Fox News on Saturday, adding that any request for Supreme Court consideration would come before Tuesday's election.
Trump has been on a campaign blitz in multiple states over the past month but is spending Saturday at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. He returns to the campaign trail on Sunday in Kansas and Iowa.
Alaska probe intensifies
The Justice Department's top prosecutor in Alaska, US Attorney Michael Heyman, said at a Friday press conference that a recent New York Times article claiming there had been an effort to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had driven a "surge" of FBI resources onto the case.
Heyman said he had assigned several prosecutors to it and that investigative steps were taking place "intensely and swiftly."
Peltola and the campaign committee have denied involvement in any effort to recruit the second Sullivan. The retired teacher has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign.
Voters in Alaska have largely dismissed the fight over the ballot.
"I knew which Dan Sullivan was which Dan Sullivan, you know? It's very clear on the ballot," Anchorage resident Mickey Buster, 36, said as he stood outside a polling place on Saturday.
But another Anchorage voter, Carol Riggs, 52, said she was disappointed by the entire situation and the possibility it "muddies the water for some voters, potentially."
Michigan rift
In Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers in another closely watched Senate race, El-Sayed's feud with the rival he beat in the primary, US Representative Haley Stevens, flared again.
El-Sayed's campaign asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as "not to distract from the central issues of the campaign," a person familiar with the matter said. Stevens has backed El-Sayed but demanded he condemn an outside group's ad blaming Israel for high grocery prices and apologise for past rhetoric about Israel.
"It's certainly unhelpful to the El-Sayed campaign to have continued visible division within the party just before Election Day," said Matt Grossmann, a political scientist at Michigan State University. Polls show El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support.
Trump's pressure campaign on states
Beyond its bid to block the counting of ballots from more than 20,000 California voters it alleges could be noncitizens, the administration has sued roughly 30 states and the District of Columbia seeking unredacted voter rolls.
The legal manoeuvres have alarmed state election officials. Under the Constitution, states have primary authority over how they run elections.
On Friday, a federal judge ordered the Justice Department to stop threatening to prosecute California election officials who defy its directives.
California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, warned the state's top federal judges on Saturday that the Justice Department may seek warrants to seize ballots before results are certified, though he said he did not know of any pending request. Newsom said in a letter to the judges that the only reason to seize ballots "would be to interfere" in the count.
Sean Morales-Doyle of the Brennan Centre for Justice said the efforts, while unlikely to win in court, aim at "creating uncertainty, sowing fear, distrust, chaos," in hopes of pressuring officials such as Alaska's lieutenant governor "to do something that they're not supposed to do."
Even so, 76 percent of US voters are confident their ballots will be counted accurately, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted from 30 September to 5 October, with confidence about equally high among Republicans and Democrats.

Serbians mark railway disaster that led to rise of victorious student movement

Crowds converged from across the city of Novi Sad on the main train station, where the concrete awning crashed down shortly before noon on Nov 1, 2024, killing 16 people.
Mourners observed 16 minutes of silence before laying wreaths, flowers and candles near the site.

“I hope we have finally realised that we shouldn’t wait... years to change what is bad, especially when it costs human lives,” said Jelena Trajkovic, 32, an academic from Novi Sad.
On Oct 25, the Student List – a group that includes academics, professionals, farmers, actors and activists chosen by student assemblies – secured 141 seats in the 250-member Parliament, according to a preliminary tally. ====================================================================================================

Why AI is boosting Meta's ad business while hurting Google search
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:31:29 UTC
23:31:29 KST

Google and Facebook have dominated the internet for the past two decades, turning billions of eyeballs into trillions in advertising dollars over that stretch. But with the ChatGPT era altering how consumers engage online, the companies are diverging.
In the third quarter, Meta's ad business grew more than twice as quickly as Google's Search and other unit, backing up Mark Zuckerberg's claim that his company's investments in artificial intelligence are leading to better targeting tools for brands to promote goods and services across Facebook and Instagram.
Google's problem is that chatbots are becoming an alternative to search, leading consumers to click far fewer blue links and hurting Google's ad revenue. Anthropic's Claude chatbot and Meta's recently launched Muse assistant are adding to the mix. Meanwhile, users are spending more time scrolling on Instagram, giving Meta more advertising opportunities.
"It's a double-edged sword, because as AI revolutionizes discovery, people might come across tools they like better than Google," Nate Elliott, an analyst covering AI at Emarketer, told CNBC in an email. "If ChatGPT or Claude or Muse is better at helping them find what they're looking for, people's search habits might change for the first time in a generation. That's potentially catastrophic for Google's ad business."
Meta's ad revenue rose 26% in the quarter to $63.1 billion, up from $ 50.1 billion a year earlier, compared with 12% growth for Google's search division, which brought in $63.4 billion. That 14-point growth gap is the widest in Meta's favor since 2021, and it puts the two businesses neck and neck by size, though Google got an additional $11 billion in third-quarter revenue from YouTube.
Following its disappointing third-quarter earnings report on Wednesday, Alphabet had its worst day ever on the stock market, plunging more than 12% and wiping out about $500 billion in market cap. Meta isn't exactly a Wall Street darling at the moment either, as the stock fell 14% in October for its worst month since October 2022. That followed a 27% surge in September, which was its best month since November of that year.
Investors' reactions reflected market jitters surrounding the companies' AI buildouts, which have pushed both businesses into negative free cash flow territory. Questions are swirling about whether their historic spending on AI infrastructure will generate enough revenue.
Meanwhile, both Meta and Google are aggressively trying to diversify their revenue streams. Meta, which still relies on ads for nearly all its revenue, is pouring money into AI models and agents to build a subscription business. Google already has a great and rapidly expanding cloud computing division that just reported over 100% growth to $31 billion in quarterly revenue, driven by demand for its infrastructure and its custom AI chips called tensor processing units, or TPUs.
Post-Apple revival
The boon in online advertising, and the hefty margins that come along with it, catapulted the two companies into leadership positions and brought their market caps into the trillions.
Meta needed AI to breathe life into its ad business after Apple's iOS privacy change in 2021 severely limited the company's ability to target users on iPhones. The following year, Meta's revenue fell for the first and only time in the company's history.
Late 2022 brought the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT and ushered in a new era of generative AI technology. While Meta initially struggled to find a consistent AI strategy and fell far behind OpenAI and Anthropic in developing frontier models, the company has successfully infused AI into its ad products, giving brands advanced tools to reach users more efficiently.
A year ago, the company unveiled the Meta AI business assistant, which advertisers can plug into the Ads Manager system to help build campaigns and improve performance. Meta CFO Susan Li said on last week's earnings call that advertisers adopting the system's recommendations "drove almost 5% more conversions" and "increased their advertising investment by 9% compared with similar non-adopters."
Li gave the example of syrup producer Simply Organic Maple, and said the company, in using the assistant, saw a 57% increase in purchases and a 36% decrease in cost per purchase. She added that in the third quarter, almost 10 million advertisers used at least one of its AI tools.
Google has a similar opportunity with AI in ad products across its properties, including YouTube.
Philipp Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said on the earnings call that the company is deploying its Gemini models "across our entire ads infrastructure," adding tools for advertisers and improving ad quality.
However, Google's search engine is competing directly with ChatGPT and Claude by surfacing more results through AI Overviews and AI Mode, where users primarily get summaries rather than links to other sites. Search queries hit a record high in the quarter, Google said, but revenue growth is slowing.
"That's going to bring Search cannibalization fears right back to the forefront, made worse by META's ad strength this quarter and the lingering Muse/agent threat," analysts at UBS wrote in a note after Google's results.
Both companies are so bullish on AI's potential that they're pumping hundreds of billions of dollars into the infrastructure needed to build new models and services. Google projects up to $205 billion in capital expenditures this year, while Meta expects to spend up to $145 billion.
Advertising remains key, but both are investing in a future that could look very different. Google is much further along on diversification, as ads now account for less than two-thirds of its revenue, while Meta still counts on ads for 98% of sales.
Still, analysts at Wedbush see Google's search monetization as critical to the investment thesis.
"GOOGL shares are unlikely to work until the search narrative changes," the analysts wrote in a report on Thursday. "And it will likely require new ad products and proof points that it can monetize in the evolving AI era as it did in the past."
— CNBC's Jonathan Vanian and MacKenzie Sigalos contributed to this report.

Ask LLOG: Convenant?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:28:05 UTC
23:28:05 KST

Ask LLOG: Convenant?
« previous post |
From L.J.:
Could you explain the real pronunciation of "covenant"? In American English, the first vowel is not like that in British English as shown in the Oxford English Dictionary. Please see the attachment. However, theoretically, a word cannot have three schwas because the stress cannot be assigned. Could the first vowel be actually a longer one?
I'll answer the question, while indulging in a short rant about the faults of the International Phonetic Alphabet (and the worse faults of its use, in dictionaries and elsewhere).
To start with, here's the OED's audio for its two top-row pronunciations
"British English" /ˈkʌvənənt/ and "U.S. English" /ˈkəvənənt/
Curiously, the two non-IPA spelled pronunciations are identical, both
KUV-uh-nuhnt
…which is actually fine, since I perceive no difference in perceptual vowel quality between the first syllables of the two (audio) versions.
(If there's a standard term for non-IPA spelled pronunciations of that general kind, I don't know what it is — so I'll call them "lah-lah-lah".)
Even more curiously, the alternative "British English" pronunciation (given in IPA as /ˈkʌvn̩ənt/ instead of /ˈkʌvənənt/, and in lah-lah-lah as "KUV-uhn-uhnt") is actually bit-wise identical in audio waveform samples to the first British pronunciation — that is, the audio is the exact same file, decorated with a (therefore empty) claim about a difference in syllabification.
OK, now we get to the question, about how stress can be assigned to one of the three schwas in /ˈkəvənənt/.
The background problem is a fundamental equivocation about what "schwa" means.
Many (not all) unstressed vowels in English are "reduced", which means that they have a unrounded central quality if pronounced in a hyper-articulated syllable-by-syllable style, plausibly represented by IPA [ə] ("schwa"). However, in actual speech these vowels can be deleted (= reduced to non-existence), raised or lowered, fronted or backed, rounded or unrounded, nasalized or not, etc., depending on the sounds around them, and the phonetic realization principles of the speaker's idiolect.
IPA offers no symbol to represent this situation, so most people (phoneticians, dictionary editors, dialect coaches, whoever) use [ə] ("schwa") to fill the gap. This then creates an ambiguity. Does [ə] mean an unstressed-and-reduced vowel, whose actual quality might be [ɪ] or [ɛ] or [ʌ] or etc., depending on circumstances? Or does it mean an unreduced (and perhaps stressed) vowel , in the phonological category that J.C. Wells assigns to the STRUT lexical class, and whose phonetic quality in a particular case might be perceived to correspond best to IPA [ə]?
For most people — though apparently not (some of) the OED's editors — the solution is to reserve the use of [ə] for the meaning "unstressed reduced vowel", and to used [ʌ] to represent the pronunciation of stressed STRUT vowels. This is obviously not what the OED editors have done, though their choice is undermined by their own lah-lah-lah transcriptions and by the phonetic quality of the audio clips they provide.
For comparison, see the entries for covenant from Merriam-Webster, Wiktionary, Cambridge, and so on.
As etymological background, see the Wikipedia entry for Hebrew "shva".
And in place of a longer IPA rant, you can take a look at
"Why I don't love the International Phonetic Alphabet", 1/2/2008
"How truck starts", 8/9/2011
"On beyond the (International Phonetic) Alphabet", 5/19/2018
"Farther on beyond the IPA", 1/18/2020
"First novels", 2/13/2022
"Pronunciation evolution", 3/15/2022
"More post-IPA astronauts", 3/16/2022
"What 'IPA' means now…", 9/28/2022
"Steele v. Monboddo", 7/12/2025

Agreement between the Italian Embassy and the University of Tokyo to Strengthen Cooperation
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:22:39 CET
23:22:39 KST

Strengthening academic, scientific, and cultural cooperation between Italy and Japan: this is the objective of the letter of intent signed in Tokyo by the Italian Embassy and the University of Tokyo, in the year marking the 160th anniversary of bilateral diplomatic relations. The document was signed by Ambassador Mario Vattani and the university’s president, Teruo Fujii, in the presence of Giorgio Mulè, vice president of the Chamber of Deputies.
                                    
The agreement provides for joint research projects, academic exchanges, and mobility programs for students, faculty, and researchers. In addition to supporting Italian cultural and academic activities in Japan, it will promote new Japanese scientific initiatives in Italy, opening up opportunities for collaboration on research programs.
                                    
The agreement was presented during an event at the university dedicated to the Japanese archaeological project in Somma Vesuviana, in the province of Naples, attended by students, researchers, journalists, faculty members, and representatives of the international academic community. “The agreement reflects the depth of the academic and scientific ties between the two countries and represents a strategic investment in the younger generations, in line with the priorities of the 2024–2027 Bilateral Action Plan,” stated Vattani. The ambassador cited the Somma Vesuviana project as an example of scientific cooperation capable of uniting research, culture, and the preservation of historical heritage. Launched in 2002, the project is considered one of the most significant examples of humanities collaboration between the two countries and involves institutions, local authorities, archaeologists, researchers, and students.
                                    
The excavation campaigns have unearthed important Roman-era artifacts, including monumental structures that have strengthened the hypothesis that the villa where Emperor Augustus spent the last days of his life once stood in the area. Speakers at the event included Professor Masanori Aoyagi, founder of the project and former commissioner of the Japan Agency for Cultural Affairs, and Professor Mariko Muramatsu, director of the excavations.
                                    
The special guest was Mari Yamazaki, author of the manga ‘Thermae Romae’ and ‘Plinius,’ which have introduced millions of Japanese readers to the history of ancient Rome. Yamazaki will help raise awareness of the project among the Japanese public by supporting the outreach and fundraising initiatives promoted by the embassy. Among these is the annual celebration of the Founding of Rome on April 21 at the ambassador’s residence in Tokyo, attended by institutions, businesses, and private supporters. The first edition will take place in April 2027, coinciding with the 150th anniversary of the founding of the University of Tokyo.
