"They're alive, but weak": UAnimals reports on the fate of animals evacuated from Oleshky – videos
Pets and stray animals were evacuated to Ukrainian-controlled territory alongside residents of occupied Oleshky, which has been gripped by a humanitarian crisis.
Source: UAnimals, a Ukrainian animal rescue and welfare organisation, in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda.Zhyttia (Life).
Details: UAnimals reported that specialists are examining the cats and dogs to assess their condition. Although no owners have yet collected their pets, some have already contacted the organisation to ask about them.
The organisation said it began making arrangements to help the animals a day before they were evacuated from Oleshky. The organisation did not know exactly how many animals to expect, what species they were or what condition they were in, so it was "preparing for various scenarios".
Quote: "We made arrangements for wild animals to be transferred to a rehabilitation centre and for pets to undergo veterinary examinations before being placed in shelters if necessary.
We coordinated with veterinary clinics and shelters and prepared food, water, cages, pet carriers and other essentials."
Details: Two UAnimals teams, comprising four staff members and a vet, set off to meet the buses carrying the evacuees and their animals.
After the convoys crossed the border from Belarus, the dogs and cats were collected and taken to a veterinary clinic.
The latest figures show that more dogs than cats were evacuated. All the animals are now receiving the care and food they need.
Quote: "All the animals have been settled in and given food and water. Vets began examining them today. All are alive, although some are weak. We'll be able to provide more details about their health and the care they need once the examinations are complete.
We've already counted the animals and drawn up a list. The next step is to digitise the records for each animal so that we can work with the human rights commissioner's office to reunite those who have families with their owners."
Details: The organisation does not yet know exactly how many animals have been evacuated, as more are still arriving after their owners took them along to hospital.
Quote: "This is a complex humanitarian operation: new information continues to arrive and we're taking it into account in our further work. We will share details about the condition of the animals and assistance provided to them on our social media pages."
Background:
- On 31 October, the mission to evacuate the residents of Oleshky concluded. Evacuees were transported by bus from the occupied city, then flown to Belarus before reaching Ukrainian-controlled territory.
- Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights, reported that residents took their animals with them during the evacuation, including dogs, cats, a parrot and even a raccoon. A specially equipped vehicle with cages was brought in to transport them.
- The oldest person evacuated from Oleshky is 94 and the youngest is just over a year old. The evacuees came not only from Oleshky but also from neighbouring settlements. They sang Ukraine's national anthem on the buses.

Iran’s 40-Day War Changed How People Travel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:18:53 UTC
23:18:53 KST

Iran’s 40-Day War Changed How People Travel
Travel disruption can change more than the number of journeys people make. It can affect how far ahead they book, which transport options they consider and whether they travel at all.
MrBilit’s report on travel behaviour during the 40-day war examines these changes through activity on its platform. Its findings offer a picture of passengers responding to uncertainty, with different patterns .emerging across booking times, transport modes and destinations
The report provides insight into MrBilit as a platform influencing users’ travel decisions. Its figures should be understood as platform-level evidence, rather than a comprehensive measure of tourism across Iran
The Initial Shock: Cancellations and Falling Travel Demand
MrBilit recorded a 40% year-on-year decline in trips during the reporting month spanning February 20 to March 20, 2026. The report also shows that 75% of tickets purchased before the war were cancelled.
These figures illustrate two different aspects of disruption: a contraction in travel activity and the reversal of plans already made. For travel businesses, that distinction matters. Supporting passengers with existing bookings becomes an immediate operational priority, even as demand for new journeys falls.
Cancellations also require careful interpretation. A cancelled ticket confirms that a particular booking did not proceed; it does not necessarily establish whether the passenger later travelled by another route or means of transport.
Last-Minute Bookings Became More Common
The share of purchases made less than 24 hours before departure increased from 40% to 60%, a rise of 20 percentage points.
This shift suggests a shorter planning horizon among passengers using the platform. More purchasing decisions were concentrated close to departure, leaving less time between choosing a journey and taking it.
For travel providers, the practical implication is that booking lead time deserves attention alongside sales volume. The same number of bookings can present different operational challenges depending on whether they arrive weeks before departure or within the final day.
The figures do not, on their own, explain every passenger’s motivation. They do, however, show a measurable change in when users committed to their journeys.
When Flights Were Disrupted, Travellers Reconsidered Their Options
Among passengers whose flights were cancelled, MrBilit reports that 84% cancelled their journeys and 16% switched to overland travel. Bus ticket sales increased 200% on the first day of the war.
Alternative transport therefore helped some passengers continue travelling, while many others did not proceed with their journeys. Increased demand for buses should consequently be read alongside lost air journeys, rather than treated as evidence of growth across the entire travel market.
For travellers planning a new journey, checking available flight tickets on MrBilit can be a starting point for assessing air travel options. Before purchasing, passengers should review their itinerary and the ticket’s cancellation and refund conditions.
Where another transport option is available, comparing total journey time, departure and arrival points, and any required connections can help travellers assess whether it meets their needs.
Travel Demand Returned Unevenly Across Destinations
Tehran–Qom and Tehran–Mashhad were among the fastest-recovering domestic routes identified in the report. Southern destinations, including Kish, Qeshm, Bushehr and Chabahar, had not fully recovered demand when the report was prepared.
The contrast highlights the importance of examining individual routes. A rebound in one part of a booking platform does not establish that demand has returned equally across destinations.
It is also important to distinguish travel from leisure tourism. Tickets may be purchased for work, family visits, pilgrimage or other purposes. Without a breakdown of passengers’ motivations, recovering ticket demand cannot automatically be described as a recovery in holiday travel.
For destination businesses, transport bookings provide one useful signal. Accommodation demand, visitor spending and the purpose of travel would add further context when assessing the local tourism economy.
What the Findings Mean for Travel Planning
MrBilit’s findings demonstrate why travel disruption needs to be examined through several measures. Cancellations reveal what happened to existing plans. Booking lead times show when passengers committed to new journeys. Transport choices and route-level demand indicate how travel activity changed.
For passengers, the practical response is to assess the whole journey before making a purchase: the available service, its timing, any connections and the conditions attached to the ticket. This is particularly relevant when plans may need to change.
For the industry, the report offers a basis for asking more precise questions about recovery. Which journeys are returning? How close to departure are passengers booking? Are alternative transport options meeting their needs?
Answering those questions requires keeping the scope of the evidence clear. MrBilit’s report documents behaviour observed on its platform during a period of disruption. Its contribution is a detailed view of changing travel decisions, with lessons for how services can respond to passengers’ needs.

China's logistics sees improved performance as industrial upgrades support growth
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:17:04 CST
23:17:04 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- China's logistics demand maintained steady growth in the first three quarters of the year, supported by industrial upgrading and resilient high-end manufacturing, official data showed Sunday.
The total value of national social logistics reached 280 trillion yuan (about 41.7 trillion U.S. dollars) in the January-September period, up 4.9 percent year on year, according to data from the China Federation of Logistics and Purchasing.
In the first three quarters, the value of industrial goods logistics rose 5.3 percent year on year, contributing 78 percent to the growth of the total.
Within this growth, equipment manufacturing and high-tech manufacturing played a prominent leading role, with their shares rising to 37.6 percent and 18.3 percent, respectively, according to the federation.
Logistics volumes for new products such as smart wristbands, 3D printing equipment and sensors surged 77.1 percent, 62.5 percent and 16.4 percent year on year, respectively, highlighting an accelerated shift toward new and upgraded industrial logistics demand, the data showed.
From January to September, the total cost of social logistics reached 14.8 trillion yuan, up 4.2 percent year on year. The ratio of total social logistics costs to GDP stood at 13.8 percent, down 0.2 percentage points from the same period last year.
"The dividends of logistics cost reduction continue to be released to the real economy," said Liu Yuhang, chief engineer of the federation.
Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, Liu said that with the arrival of the e-commerce peak season and the year-end production rush, logistics demand is expected to be released in a concentrated manner.
High-quality logistics development will provide strong support for the recovery of the real economy and the achievement of the full-year economic and social development goals, he said. ■

Interview: China offers South African fruit growers opportunities to diversify exports, says industry representative
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:17:00 CST
23:17:00 KST

by Ntandoyenkosi Ncube
JOHANNESBURG, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- China offers South African fruit growers an opportunity to diversify their export markets and reduce reliance on traditional destinations, while its vast consumer market holds significant long-term growth potential, an industry representative has said.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Pieter-Steyn de Wet, information manager at Hortgro-Cherries, which represents commercial cherry growers in South Africa, highlighted China's potential as a major export destination, noting that the country imported approximately 586,900 tonnes of cherries in 2025.
South Africa and China have signed a protocol on phytosanitary requirements for fresh cherries, paving the way for South African cherries to enter the Chinese market. The fruit could also benefit from China's zero-tariff treatment for qualifying products from African countries with which it has diplomatic relations.
"Zero-tariff access enhances the competitiveness of South African cherries by reducing landed costs for Chinese importers," de Wet said.
"While zero-tariff access is an important advantage, it will not be sufficient on its own," de Wet said, warning that exporters must compete through "efficient logistics, consistent quality, reliable supply, and competitive pricing."
Beyond the immediate trade prospects, access to China could support the continued expansion of South Africa's burgeoning cherry sector. "Access to China provides a critical outlet for our scaling production and will encourage continued investment in orchards, packhouse capacity, and cold-chain infrastructure," de Wet said.
However, he cautioned that "investment and export growth will ultimately depend on market demand, sustained profitability, and our international competitiveness."
Beyond cherries, China could also serve as an alternative destination for South Africa's broader range of stone fruits, buffering growers against logistics bottlenecks and geopolitical disruptions affecting shipping routes through the Middle East.
"South African stone fruit offers promising avenues in China," de Wet said, noting that protocols governing the export of peaches, apricots, plums and nectarines had already been signed, with commercial shipments expanding.
"Continued investment in market development, consumer insights, product quality, and reliable supply chains will be essential to unlocking this potential," de Wet said.
To capitalize on these opportunities, establishing a lasting presence in China will require South African exporters to navigate stiff competition from established suppliers, high transport costs, logistical bottlenecks and stringent phytosanitary requirements, he said.
Describing the Chinese market as "highly discerning," de Wet emphasized that long-term success also hinges on strict adherence to local consumer preferences and quality expectations.
Closer cooperation between South Africa and China in agricultural research, post-harvest technology and trade promotion could further deepen bilateral agricultural ties, he said.
"Our long-term objective is to build a diversified, competitive, and sustainable agricultural export sector that delivers fair returns for producers, creates jobs, and contributes meaningfully to economic growth," de Wet said. ■

Feature: Dragon boat races return to Cambodia's Takeo, reviving vibrant, centuries-old regatta tradition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
22:16:30 CST
23:16:30 KST

TAKEO, Cambodia, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Under the blazing sun in southern Cambodia's Takeo province, a sprawling lake came alive this weekend as hundreds of locals raced dragon boats, reviving a vibrant, age-old regatta tradition for the Water Festival.
Framed by cheering crowds that lined the shores of Daun Keo city's Takeo Lake, 36 dragon boats and their crews turned the two-day weekend spectacle into a theater of pure speed. The banks erupted in roaring excitement each time a favored boat surged across the finish line, leaving its rivals in the wake.
For 22-year-old spectator Huch Sreynea, the spectacle was an electric bridge across the centuries. She told Xinhua on Sunday that she felt thrilled to see the vibrant boat races, adding that this regatta was held to honor Cambodia's naval forces of ancient times.
That living history dates back to the late 11th century during the ancient Khmer Empire, when naval forces honed their skills on the water.
Celebrated in the Southeast Asian nation, the Water Festival also marks the end of the annual rainy season and the unique seasonal reversal of the Tonle Sap River's flow, which connects the Tonle Sap Lake with the Mekong River.
For 20-year-old university student Chhin Lida, the festival does more than just keep ancient legacies alive -- it acts as a powerful magnet for tourism.
"This event also helps boost the provincial economy by attracting more tourists," she told Xinhua.
Walking through the bustling fairgrounds, Lida noted that the festival offered a rich tapestry of local flavors and sights -- from lively food stalls and "One Village, One Product" showcases to traditional arts and night-time fireworks.
At its heart, Lida reflected, the festival is a deep breath of gratitude: a salute to resilient ancestors who defended the realm, and a quiet "thank you" to the rivers and rains that sustain the land.
The excitement on the water was shared by the athletes themselves.
Ly Sophal, a 37-year-old dragon boat racer competing in Takeo province for the first time, proudly led a crew of 12 members.
"The regatta is an age-old tradition deep within the heart of the Cambodian people and a prime occasion to attract both national and international tourists to Takeo," he told Xinhua. "I am absolutely thrilled to see such massive crowds of spectators cheering us on."
Leang Chanthon, another 37-year-old competitor, echoed the fierce pride of the day. To him, every stroke of the paddle is a tribute to the past.
He explained that the regatta stands as a living monument to the Khmer naval forces who fought and triumphed over their enemies on these very waters centuries ago.
"It is vital for us to preserve this uniquely beautiful tradition for our younger generations," Chanthon told Xinhua. ■

COLOMBO, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka's fuel imports expenditure from January to September 2026 increased by 51.5 percent from the same period last year, according to data released by the Central Bank of Sri Lanka.
The bank's latest External Sector Performance report, dated Oct. 30, showed that the country spent 4.49 billion U.S. dollars on fuel imports during the first nine months of 2026, compared to 2.96 billion dollars on fuel imports during the same period in 2025.
Fuel import spending, however, declined slightly in September. Sri Lanka spent 415.1 million dollars on fuel imports during the month, down 5.8 percent from 440.7 million dollars in September 2025. September 2026 also marked the country's fifth consecutive month of fuel imports expenditure decline.
Despite the downward trajectory, the overall fuel import bill remained significantly higher than during the same period last year, said the bank.
The increase came amid higher domestic fuel prices following an escalation of conflict in the Middle East.
Disruptions to global energy supply chains, including restrictions affecting petroleum shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, also pushed up crude oil and petroleum product prices, as well as freight and insurance costs. ■

International Digi Yatra trials to begin at 7 airports for Indian nationals this year for wider rollout in 2027: Government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:12:03 UTC
23:12:03 KST

File photo: India will trial Digi Yatra for international passengers at seven airports over the next three months
NEW DELHI: Travelling abroad from India could soon be a seamless experience just like taking domestic flights with Digi Yatra (DY). India will hold trials for international passengers at seven airports in the three months of this year, allowing eligible Indian nationals holding e-passports to use DY at designated airport touchpoints while travelling on select flights operated by Air India and IndiGo.The aviation ministry said trials are being conducted at Delhi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Cochin, Mumbai, Chennai and Amritsar airports. “Eligible passengers will be able to use the facility at terminal entry points, security hold areas (SHA) and boarding gates, wherever the required infrastructure is available. Feedback received during the trial period will inform the planning of a wider rollout in 2027,” it said in a statement.To access this facility, eligible Indian nationals will need to create an e-passport-based “verifiable credential” (VC) through DY mobile application. “The process involves scanning the machine readable zone (MRZ) of e-passport, reading the embedded chip using the near field communication (NFC) feature of a compatible smartphone, capturing a selfie and verifying the details. The credential is stored in the passenger’s Digi Yatra wallet on the device and can be used at airport touchpoints enabled for the trials,” the statement said.
The facility will complement, and not replace, existing travel processes. “Passengers must continue to carry their travel documents and complete all mandatory airline document checks, immigration procedures and other applicable travel formalities,” it added.IndiGo said eligible passengers can upload their boarding pass to the Digi Yatra app. After completing mandatory document verification at airline check-in counter, they can proceed through the security hold area and boarding gates using DY biometric face authentication.IndiGo chief digital and information officer Neetan Chopra said: “At IndiGo, we are committed to redefining air travel by making it more seamless, efficient, and customer centric, and we believe that technology can be a key catalyst in this evolution. Having been a key part of the technical proof of concept earlier this year, we are pleased to partner with Digi Yatra for the launch of these international passenger trials. Expanding secure digital identity and biometric technologies to international departures is a significant step forward for Indian aviation. We are committed to delivering a seamless travel experience for our customers at every touchpoint. The successful deployment of this technology marks an important step in reimagining the airport experience, combining enhanced security, convenience and operational efficiency. As the aviation industry continues to evolve, such innovations will play a key role in shaping the future of passenger travel.”Digi Yatra Foundation CEO Suresh Khadakbhavi said: “Digi Yatra has demonstrated how digital identity can simplify domestic air travel. With the start of international passenger trials, we are taking an important step towards extending this experience to eligible Indian nationals travelling internationally.
Interoperability with global frameworks such as IATA’s One ID and ICAO’s Public Key Directory (PKD) will be an important part of this journey, helping explore how e-passport-based digital credentials can enable more seamless and secure passenger journeys across borders, while keeping passenger consent, privacy and security central to the experience.”Digi Yatra platform has over 2.6 crore users at present and has enabled more than 11 crore journeys across 39 domestic airports, serving domestic airlines. A further 25 domestic airports are planned to be covered by 2027. “The aviation ministry remains committed to leveraging technology to improve airport operations and facilitate seamless air travel, in line with govt's vision of Digital India and ease of flying.”

French school blockades to restart from Nov 2: Student group
PARIS – The head of a student group said a campaign of high school blockades would restart from Nov 2, adding the government’s proposals did not go far enough.
On Oct 31, hundreds of thousands of people, including high school and university students, took to the streets across France for a third consecutive weekend of protests.
Some high schools will be blockaded from Nov 2, when students return from a two-week holiday, said Pierre Sourzat, head of the “Lyceens!” group.
“It will be more significant from Tuesday, but we know that some schools will be blocked as early as tomorrow,” he told broadcaster RMC on Nov 1.
“We support all our comrades who are blocking their schools from tomorrow,” he added.
France’s protest movement against soaring prices emerged from weeks of demonstrations by high school students protesting deteriorating learning conditions and inequality.
On Oct 26, the government announced a series of measures aimed at addressing student protesters’ demands, including replacing the university admissions platform and providing loans for school renovations.
Students said the proposals did not go far enough.
On Oct 31, Sabrine Kharbach, spokeswoman for the Union Etudiante (Student Union), said blockades of universities and high schools would take place on Nov 2 and 4.
President Emmanuel Macron has called for classes to resume in a calm manner, arguing that “young people have been heard”.
Sourzat countered that “the president hasn’t listened to us”.
“It’s smoke and mirrors,” he said. “There’s a bit of polish on the surface, but once you scratch beneath it, there’s nothing there.”
Sourzat said the proposed overhaul of the university admissions platform, long criticised for its lack of transparency, failed to address the shortage of places in higher education.
He also dismissed the government’s plan to reduce class sizes as insufficient, noting that it would apply only to 10th-grade classes.
“We were asking for all year groups,” he said.
With the euro zone’s second-largest economy on the brink of recession and under pressure to rein in its debt, the government has limited scope to appease student protesters through additional spending. AFP

Estrogen therapy linked to fewer signs of Alzheimer’s disease in brain tissue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:00:55 UTC
23:00:55 KST

Women who use estrogen-only hormone therapy during menopause may have a lower risk of developing the brain changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease. A large analysis of patient data found that those who used the therapy had less physical evidence of the disease in their brains and better memory test scores. The research was published in the journal Neurology.
Alzheimer’s disease disproportionately affects women, who make up more than two thirds of all patients worldwide. Researchers have investigated whether the natural decline of estrogen during menopause contributes to this disparity. Estrogen helps regulate physiological processes that keep the brain healthy, including inflammation and the integrity of the blood brain barrier. This barrier is a cellular filter that shields the brain from harmful substances in the bloodstream.
Past research on whether menopausal hormone therapy helps protect against dementia has yielded mixed results. Some trials suggested a protective effect, while others found either no benefit or an increased risk of cognitive decline. Variations in the timing of the treatment, the specific chemical formulation used, and the genetic backgrounds of the patients have made it difficult to draw a definitive conclusion.
To understand the relationship better, Stanford University psychiatry and behavioral sciences researcher Jennifer L. Bruno and colleagues examined records from thousands of older women. The research team wanted to see if they could link the use of estrogen-only hormone therapy to physical indicators of Alzheimer’s disease in the brain. They also looked at clinical diagnoses and memory test results.
The researchers analyzed information from two independent, large databases. The first was the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center, which collects data from dozens of research centers across the United States.
The team focused on a specific group of female participants aged fifty and older. They separated these women into two categories: those who reported using estrogen-only menopausal hormone therapy and those who had never used it. Women who used a combination of estrogen and progestin were excluded from the main analysis.
Using this first database, Bruno and her team looked at autopsy records for 2,959 deceased women. Of these participants, 258 had used estrogen-only hormone therapy. The researchers compared the two groups based on a standardized scoring system that measures three distinct signs of Alzheimer’s disease in brain tissue. These signs include the buildup of amyloid proteins and the presence of tangled nerve fibers, both of which disrupt normal brain function.
The team found that women who had used estrogen-only hormone therapy had a measurably lower chance of exhibiting advanced Alzheimer’s disease pathology at the time of their death. The autopsies also revealed that these women had fewer signs of cerebrovascular disease, such as small strokes or damaged blood vessels in the brain. A secondary analysis of the autopsy data showed that the lower odds of brain pathology were specifically linked to a formulation called conjugated estrogens, rather than a different formulation known as estradiol.
Next, the researchers evaluated the clinical records of a large group of living patients from the same national database. This group included 1,841 hormone therapy users and 17,561 non-users. The researchers found that women in the hormone therapy group had lower odds of receiving a clinical dementia diagnosis. These women also showed fewer symptoms of general memory and functional decline compared to those who had not used the therapy.
To understand how hormone therapy might influence brain health while patients are still living, the researchers turned to a second database. The Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative contains detailed biological measurements from living participants. From this dataset, the team identified 110 women who used estrogen-only hormone therapy and 1,948 who did not.
The researchers examined biological markers in the participants’ blood plasma and cerebrospinal fluid, which is the liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord. They measured the levels of amyloid proteins, which can clump together and form the plaques characteristic of Alzheimer’s disease.
Women who used the hormone therapy had higher levels of a specific amyloid protein, amyloid-beta 42, in their blood and spinal fluid. In these fluids, higher levels indicate that less amyloid is being deposited as plaques in the brain, so this pattern points to less Alzheimer’s-related amyloid buildup. Brain scans using a technology called positron emission tomography did not show a difference in amyloid accumulation between the two groups. The blood and fluid tests are generally more sensitive to early protein changes than the brain scans, suggesting that hormone therapy might be associated with lower levels of early stage amyloid buildup.
The team also reviewed cognitive test scores from the imaging database participants. They found that hormone therapy users scored higher on tests measuring immediate verbal memory and learning ability.
The researchers conducted exploratory analyses to see if genetics played a role. They separated the participants based on whether they carried the APOE e4 gene variant, which is a known risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease. The autopsy data showed that the hormone therapy was associated with less brain pathology only in women who did not carry this high-risk gene. The clinical benefits, such as a lower chance of a dementia diagnosis, were visible in both genetic groups.
Because this was an observational study, it cannot prove that the hormone therapy caused the improved brain health. It is possible that women who choose to take hormone therapy are generally healthier or have better access to healthcare to begin with. Unmeasured lifestyle factors could also contribute to the observed differences between the two groups.
The type of therapy examined in the study also limits how broadly the results apply. Estrogen-only hormone therapy is typically prescribed only to women who have had their uterus removed, because taking estrogen without progesterone can increase the risk of uterine cancer. Most women who undergo menopausal hormone therapy take a combined estrogen and progestogen regimen. The protective associations seen with estrogen alone might not extend to the combined treatments that are far more common in everyday medical practice.
The average age at which women in the study reported using hormone therapy was around seventy. Current medical guidelines usually recommend starting hormone therapy during the onset of menopause, typically in a woman’s late forties or early fifties, and stopping by age sixty. The researchers noted that a small subset of women in their data who started the therapy before age sixty also showed a lower chance of developing Alzheimer’s pathology, though the result was not statistically significant due to the small sample size.
Future research will need to follow patients over time in controlled trials to better evaluate how menopausal hormone therapy impacts physical markers of Alzheimer’s disease. Such studies could help medical professionals weigh the risks and benefits of prescribing the treatment to older women.
The study, “Association between menopausal hormone therapy and Alzheimer’s disease neuropathology,” was authored by Jennifer L. Bruno, Jacob S Shaw, and S.M. Hadi Hosseini.

AI reality check triggers $2 trillion tech stock rout
Unknown

AI reality check triggers $2 trillion tech stock rout
An estimated $2 trillion in market value was wiped from the tech-heavy Nasdaq-100 during October as investors grow increasingly skeptical that enormous spending on artificial intelligence will ever pay off.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.9% in its biggest one-day fall since June. Over the whole month, the Nasdaq shed about 5.2%, its worst showing since March 2025, while the S&P 500 slipped 1.2%, and the Dow – which includes many traditional businesses – still finished October up 1.5%.
Among the hardest-hit companies was Google owner Alphabet, whose shares plunged 12.6% on Thursday in its worst day on record. The slump was triggered by its earnings showing slower growth in search advertising, its core business.
While search advertising revenue still grew 12%, Google executive Philipp Schindler acknowledged that its AI Mode brings in less ad revenue per search than traditional results. At the same time, Alphabet is spending heavily on AI infrastructure, putting further pressure on its cash flow. The company’s net profit also slid 25% year-on-year, largely due to investment-related losses, while Thursday’s share plunge erased nearly $500 billion from its market value.
Amazon reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the preceding 12 months, largely due to AI investments, with its shares falling 1.4% on Friday. Chipmaker Intel came out worse, plunging 28.6%, its worst day since 1974, after forecasting weaker profits amid trouble in its PC and manufacturing businesses. 
Nvidia – which produces powerful chips used to train and run AI systems – slipped 4.2%, becoming the biggest drag on the S&P 500, while rival AMD dropped 10.9%.
Commenting on the slump, Globalt Investments senior portfolio manager Keith Buchanan, described the current state of the market as “scrutinizing” and “discerning”. “Last year was hope. This year is: At the end of day, how does this all work in real-world terms, like how to finance [it] and who gets the economics. Those questions are much more difficult to answer,” he told CNBC.
Enormous spending on AI and data centers has become a staple of US tech giants in recent years. Together, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Alphabet are projected to spend more than $700 billion on data centers, computing equipment and other long-term investments in 2026 alone, and much of it is AI-related.
According to various estimates, global AI-related investment is valued at between $900 billion and $2.7 trillion dollars this year, depending on the methodology. Companies are also borrowing more to finance expansion, fueling concerns among investors.
Market analysts meanwhile warn of further near-term losses. Bank of America strategist Michael Hartnett expects weakness until mid-November, while Morgan Stanley’s Mike Wilson says the S&P 500 could fall even further within weeks before recovering by year-end.
Other major tests for the US market are the midterm elections on Tuesday, which could reshape AI regulation, as well as quarterly results from Apple, Nvidia, AMD and Palantir, and Friday’s jobs report.

UK flies Protector drone on first home operation against Russian frigate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:46:01 UTC
22:46:01 KST

- An RAF Protector RG1 flew its first operational sorties in UK airspace, providing more than 10 hours of surveillance over the English Channel.
- The aircraft supported HMS Dauntless and HMS Tyne as they tracked the Russian frigate Neustrashimy between Oct. 1 and Oct. 14.
An RAF Protector RG1 remotely piloted aircraft has flown its first operational missions in UK airspace, giving the Royal Navy more than 10 hours of surveillance over the English Channel while warships tracked the Russian frigate Neustrashimy, the UK Ministry of Defence said.
The unarmed Protector flew alongside military and civilian air traffic while the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless (D33) and offshore patrol vessel HMS Tyne (P281) monitored Neustrashimy and accompanying merchant ships through the Channel between Oct. 1 and Oct. 14. The ministry did not say how many sorties the aircraft flew, which sensors it used or how much of the frigate’s transit it covered.
“Protector’s first operational sorties in UK airspace demonstrate the significant value this capability brings to UK Defence. Working alongside Royal Navy vessels, it provided persistent intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance coverage, highlighting its ability to operate seamlessly across military and civilian airspace in support of maritime security, NATO commitments and wider UK tasking,” said Wing Commander Sam Haley, officer commanding XIII Squadron.
Protector is the RAF’s version of General Atomics’ MQ-9B SkyGuardian, flown from RAF Waddington in Lincolnshire by 31 and XIII squadrons. The UK Military Aviation Authority issued it a military type certificate on April 29, 2025, clearing it to fly without geographic restrictions in UK airspace, and it entered service in June 2025 as the first remotely piloted aircraft authorized to do so. The MQ-9A Reaper it replaced never flew in UK airspace during its RAF career. The first of 16 Protectors arrived at RAF Waddington in 2023.
The RAF lists the aircraft’s endurance at more than 30 hours and its ceiling at up to 40,000 feet (12,200 m), with full-motion video, infrared imagery, synthetic aperture radar and ground target tracking among its sensors. In June 2026, a Protector flew from Waddington to RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus through European civil airspace, covering more than 2,000 nautical miles in about 13.5 hours.
The Channel mission was one of several Royal Navy operations against Russian ships between late September and mid-October. Merlin helicopters from Royal Naval Air Station Culdrose deployed to Glasgow Prestwick Airport under Operation Iceblast, a test of how quickly the Merlin force can operate away from its home base. From Sept. 29 to Oct. 8, they tracked the Vishnya-class intelligence-gathering ship Viktor Leonov near the Outer Hebrides, where NATO’s Exercise Strike Warrior was underway with more than 2,000 personnel from six nations.
From Oct. 11 to Oct. 14, HMS Tyne and a Wildcat helicopter from 815 Naval Air Squadron followed the Ropucha-class landing ship Aleksandr Shabalin, the cargo ship MV Energy-2 and the tug Proton through the Channel as they headed for the Baltic.
“HMS Dauntless monitored the movements of RFN Neustrashimy during her transit through the English Channel, contributing to the wider maritime picture and supporting UK maritime security,” said Commander Neil Skinner, commanding officer of HMS Dauntless.
Royal Navy activity monitoring Russian movements rose 25% in the first seven months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, the ministry said. Most of that work falls to patrol ships, frigates and helicopters; in January, HMS Mersey, HMS Severn and a Wildcat shadowed a Russian corvette and tanker through the same waters in a two-day operation coordinated with NATO allies.
“For the first time, Protector has joined Royal Navy warships and helicopters monitoring activity around our shores, demonstrating how we are constantly innovating to monitor and deter threats and irresponsible provocation,” said Defence Secretary Wes Streeting.
The ministry tied the operations to £298 billion (about $399 billion) in planned defense spending over the next four years and a commitment to reach 3% of GDP on defense in 2030. It also pointed to £330 million (about $442 million) over four years to protect undersea infrastructure and to Atlantic Bastion, a Royal Navy effort combining warships, patrol aircraft and autonomous systems against Russian submarines in the North Atlantic.

EU urges Poland to uphold legal standards amid tribunal crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:45:14 UTC
22:45:14 KST

The EU has called on Polish authorities to ensure that the country's Constitutional Tribunal functions in accordance with the constitution and European legal standards amid an escalating political crisis.
"The Commission is following the recent developments closely," a European Commission spokesperson told Anadolu on Sunday.
"It is for the Polish authorities to ensure that the Constitutional Tribunal can function in accordance with the Polish constitution and in respect of the relevant case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union," she said.
The spokesperson noted that appointing eight new members of the Constitutional Tribunal falls within the constitutional powers of the Sejm, the lower house of Poland's parliament.
She cited an October 13, 2026, opinion by the Venice Commission confirming the Sejm's authority to make the appointments.
"Also, on May 5, 2026, the European Court of Human Rights issued interim measures obliging the competent Polish authorities to refrain from hindering the taking up and exercise of judicial duties by judges appointed by the Sejm in March 2026," she added.
Political crisis escalates over tribunal control
The European Commission's remarks followed a sharp escalation Friday, when the Constitutional Tribunal announced the immediate suspension of its president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and vice president, Bartlomiej Sochanski.
Control of the tribunal was transferred temporarily to Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, an appointee of the current parliamentary majority.
Police were deployed around the building after Korwin-Piotrowska warned of threats to judges and staff and possible public disorder.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki cut short an official trip to Senegal on Friday night and returned to Warsaw, heading directly to the tribunal's headquarters.
Media footage showed tense confrontations inside the building between presidential aides and newly appointed judges.
After leaving the tribunal, Nawrocki declared the situation a violation of Poland's constitutional order and called for urgent consultations among parliamentary leaders.

Norwegian frigate deal shaped new offset policy
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:35:08 GMT
22:35:08 KST

The Chancellor has cited Norway’s own requirements as an example of the thinking behind Britain’s new offset policy, telling reporters that Norwegian industry is part procuring the frigates being built on the Clyde and that Britain will now ask the same of foreign suppliers in return, according to remarks made at a press huddle in Glasgow.
John Healey was asked what role Scotland will play in the Defence Investment Plan, in manufacturing and jobs, and what impact the plan will have in Scotland specifically.
He said: “Defence is our number one priority. We also announced today the defence secretary and policy, where people have seen this is a government that will direct our defence investment first and foremost in British jobs and British businesses. But there will be things that we need to buy from abroad and from allies.
“So Norwegians, for instance, are part procuring some of this portion behind us, and they will require us because they have a policy that we’re now introducing for the first time ever in Britain, which we call an offset policy. We will buy some of the things the Norwegians produce that we can’t here.
“Now, in future, when Britain places contracts abroad, we’ll make sure that those we place those contracts with invest in Britain as well, jobs, business support, innovation, so that we can make sure that every pound of British taxpayers’ money works twice. It works for the national security of this nation, and it works also to reinforce jobs and businesses in the future of this country, including across the UK here in Scotland.”
Norway ordered five Type 26 frigates from Britain in a £10 billion deal that supports 2,000 jobs on the Clyde, the largest warship export in a generation, and Norwegian industry expects work in return under arrangements of exactly the kind Britain is now adopting. Oslo has run an industrial cooperation requirement for decades, obliging foreign suppliers of significant defence equipment to place work with Norwegian firms.
Under the British policy published today, contracts above £50 million placed with overseas companies will be considered for offsets, and suppliers can be required to deliver benefits worth up to the full contract value through jobs, apprenticeships, factories, investment in British suppliers or transfers of technology. A central Offset Authority will agree, value and monitor each arrangement, and the policy applies to a select number of procurements from April 2027.

Following a mandatory medical examination and the acquisition of a transit remand, he will be taken to Raipur and produced before the CBI Special Judge Monday.Chandrakar is wanted in two CBI cases, in which chargesheets have already been filed, as well as an Enforcement Directorate (ED) case where a prosecution complaint has been submitted and several properties in India and abroad have been attached.The investigation into the Mahadev Online Book cases was taken up by the CBI at the request of the Chhattisgarh government.
The probe revealed that the syndicate operated as one of the country's largest illegal online betting networks run from outside India, facilitating unlawful betting on cricket, football, card games, and other events through a widespread system of franchised "panels" and "branches."Proceeds from the illegal betting network were funneled through numerous mule bank accounts, layered via multiple transactions, and moved overseas through hawala channels.
CBI investigations also established that a portion of the illicit funds was used to pay protection money to public servants to ensure the unhindered operation of the syndicate.Chargesheets in the matter have been filed under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, provisions of the Indian Penal Code relating to criminal conspiracy, cheating, and forgery, as well as the Chhattisgarh Gambling (Prohibition) Act, with Chandrakar named as a key accused.
Chandrakar was initially located and detained by the Royal Oman Police following a Red Corner Notice issued against him. Subsequent extradition proposals, accompanied by gathered evidence, were submitted by the CBI and ED, and pursued in close coordination with Indian government agencies, the Interpol National Central Bureau, and Omani authorities.The CBI expressed gratitude to the Government of the Sultanate of Oman and the Royal Oman Police for their cooperation, highlighting the strong bilateral relations and mutual commitment to combating international crime. The extradition represents a key milestone in India's ongoing efforts to hold foreign-based fugitives accountable under Indian law, CBI said.

Column: Small producers, big markets -- the CIIE story
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
21:29:13 CST
22:29:13 KST

by Maya Majueran
At a time when global trade is increasingly disturbed by tariffs, protectionism and geopolitical competition, a different story is emerging from Shanghai's exhibition halls.
It is not about multinational giants or the strategic interests of major economies. It is about Peruvian artisans, Kenyan avocado farmers and Malagasy herders -- ordinary producers seeking access to international markets and opportunities to improve their livelihoods.
The China International Import Expo (CIIE) is helping turn "inclusive globalization" from a diplomatic slogan into economic reality by creating market opportunities, generating employment, and improving livelihoods.
For many developing countries, the greatest obstacle to international trade is not a lack of products or entrepreneurial ambition, but limited access to markets, financing, logistics and commercial networks. Through targeted support, dedicated exhibition areas for least-developed countries, and direct connections with Chinese buyers, the CIIE seeks to reduce these barriers.
The objective is not charity, but meaningful participation in global trade.
The CIIE's significance also lies in its continuity. Through its "6 days + 365 days" model, the expo connects temporary exhibitions with year-round trading platforms. Bonded warehousing, cross-border e-commerce, and buyer matchmaking help businesses turn initial orders into sustained commercial relationships.
In July 2025, Burundi shipped 38.4 tonnes of Arabica coffee directly to China for the first time, followed by contracts exceeding 900 tonnes worth over 5 million U.S. dollars.
At the seventh CIIE in 2024, 13 of 16 participating Nigerian companies reportedly secured agreements, including a cocoa contract worth over 1.2 million dollars.
The eighth CIIE last year recorded 83.49 billion dollars in one-year intended deals, up 4.4 percent from the previous edition and hitting a new high.
Smaller economies face structural disadvantages in international trade. Regulatory compliance, logistics, marketing, and distribution impose disproportionately high costs on low-volume exporters. By connecting buyers and sellers and facilitating market entry, the CIIE helps reduce these barriers.
The CIIE offers one practical model for smaller economies to access international markets. For artisans in Peru, farmers in Kenya, and herding communities in Madagascar, the benefits can extend beyond export contracts to employment, household incomes and local development.
Inclusive globalization should be measured not simply by how much trade expands, but by how widely its opportunities are shared.
It is an approach worth drawing on.
Editor's note: Maya Majueran serves as the director of the Belt and Road Initiative Sri Lanka, an independent and pioneering organization with strong expertise in Belt and Road Initiative advice and support.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect those of Xinhua News Agency.

Practical conservation workshop held at ruined Sassanid palaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:19:20 UTC
22:19:20 KST

Practical conservation workshop held at ruined Sassanid palaces
TEHRAN - A practical training workshop on emergency conservation and restoration at the Palace of Ardashir and Qal'eh Dokhtar (“Maiden Castle”) near Firuzabad, southern Iran, has brought together heritage conservation specialists and university students to provide hands-on experience in protecting historic structures.
Afshin Ebrahimi, director of the Sassanid Archaeological Landscape of Fars World Heritage Site, said the workshop was held on Friday, October 30, with the participation of the World Heritage site management team, facilitators from Isfahan University of Art and 12 students.
He said the program aimed to familiarize students with practical procedures for heritage conservation, monitoring, documentation and emergency restoration, while bridging the gap between academic knowledge and field experience at historic sites.
During the workshop, participants learned about the site's specialist conservation activities and periodic monitoring procedures. They also took part in practical exercises, including surveying, preparing detailed sketches, mapping and assessing damage to selected wall surfaces at Qal'eh Dokhtar, and completing conservation monitoring records.
Ebrahimi said training in the proper identification and documentation of structural damage was essential to the effective conservation of historic monuments. Participants were also introduced to monitoring forms and the technical information required to assess and record the conservation conditions of historic buildings.
Another part of the program focused on emergency conservation work at the Palace of Ardashir. Students, working under the supervision of specialists, participated in repointing sections of the palace's walls and preparing a gypsum witness to help monitor changes in the structure.
Ebrahimi said continuing such workshops could strengthen the technical capabilities of the next generation of conservation professionals, facilitate the transfer of practical experience and promote scientifically grounded approaches to safeguarding Sassanid heritage.
The Palace of Ardashir, also known as Ardashir Papakan Palace, dates to the early third century and was built by Ardashir I, founder of the Sassanid Empire. Located near Firuzabad, the monument is distinguished by its domed chambers, monumental iwan and stone-and-mortar construction.
Qal'eh Dokhtar, another major Sassanid-era monument in the Firuzabad area, is a fortified structure traditionally attributed to Ardashir I. Its architectural features include vaulted halls, arches, domes and stairways.
Both monuments form part of the Sassanid Archaeological Landscape of Fars Region, which was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2018. The property encompasses archaeological remains in Firuzabad, Bishapur and Sarvestan, illustrating the development of Sassanid architecture and the early history of the empire.

Qeshm launches multimedia documentation project to preserve island’s intangible heritage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:19:06 UTC
22:19:06 KST

Qeshm launches multimedia documentation project to preserve island’s intangible heritage
TEHRAN - Qeshm Island has launched a multimedia documentation project to record and preserve its indigenous knowledge, oral history and intangible cultural heritage, with the aim of passing the island’s traditional knowledge and cultural practices on to future generations.
Seyyed Mehdi Mousavi-Ojagh, deputy for cultural, social and tourism affairs of the Qeshm Free Zone Organization, said the initiative involves conducting multimedia interviews with local cultural figures and tradition bearers to document their knowledge, experiences and accounts of the island’s cultural heritage.
According to the official, the project focuses on several aspects of Qeshm’s traditional culture, including indigenous maritime knowledge, local stories and narratives, traditional knowledge related to water heritage, and other elements of the island’s oral history.
He stressed that much of a community’s intangible heritage is preserved in the memories, skills and personal experiences of local people, warning that valuable knowledge could disappear permanently if it is not documented before its bearers pass away.
The initiative seeks to prevent the loss of indigenous knowledge and facilitate the transmission of previous generations’ experiences and cultural practices to younger people, ensuring their continued recognition as part of Qeshm’s historical and cultural identity.
Mousavi-Ojagh also identified community-based cultural tourism as one of the expected benefits of the project, saying that documenting local narratives, skills and traditional knowledge could help introduce the island’s cultural attractions more comprehensively and encourage tourism rooted in local identity and authenticity.
Located in the Persian Gulf, Qeshm is Iran’s largest island and is known for its distinctive combination of natural, geological and cultural heritage. Its cultural traditions include traditional wooden boatbuilding, known as Lenj construction, Bandari embroidery and mat weaving, as well as distinctive local customs and oral traditions.
The island is also home to the Hara mangrove forests and the Qeshm Island UNESCO Global Geopark, which encompasses 26 geological sites and was the first geopark of its kind in West Asia.
The documentation project is intended to turn the knowledge and experiences of older generations into a lasting cultural resource, supporting heritage preservation, education and the development of cultural tourism, the official underlined.

Sasanian-era rock carvings of human hands discovered in Marvdasht
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:09:59 UTC
22:09:59 KST

Sasanian-era rock carvings of human hands discovered in Marvdasht
TEHRAN - Archaeologists have identified previously undocumented Sasanian-era rock carvings depicting human hands without accompanying figures in the historic Marvdasht Plain in Fars province, southern Iran.
The unusual engravings, found alongside a Sasanian-era prayer inscription in Middle Persian (Pahlavi), may shed light on ancient practices of prayer, oath-taking and religious rituals.
Archaeologist and historian Abolhassan Atabaki announced the discovery during ongoing archaeological surveys and documentation in the Marvdasht Plain, Ana news agency reported on Sunday.
He said the newly identified carvings depict human hands together with parts of the forearms, engraved directly onto rock surfaces without any accompanying human figures. Their artistic style and visual characteristics suggest that they date to the Sasanian period (224–651 CE).
Atabaki noted that although hands frequently appear in Sasanian rock reliefs as symbols of respect and homage, their independent depiction also has precedents in seals and seal impressions from the period.
Examples held in collections at the British Museum, Bandar Abbas, Takht-e Soleyman, Tell Abu Shaaf in Iraq and the University of California, Berkeley, demonstrate that Sasanian artists sometimes depicted hands independently of other parts of the human body.
Studies of Sasanian art suggest that the hand motif was associated with concepts such as greeting, goodwill and benevolence. In some instances, researchers have also proposed connections with covenants, the deity Mithra and religious ceremonies.
One notable example is a seal impression discovered at Takht-e Soleyman, which depicts a hand accompanied by a Pahlavi inscription reading abestan o yazdan, meaning “seeking the assistance of the deities.”
In that regard, Najmeh Ebrahimi, a historian, said the available evidence suggests that the independent depiction of hands may have served as a symbolic means of expressing prayer, oaths, covenants and wishes for good fortune.
She explained that because the hand plays a central role in carrying out such acts, depicting it independently could have conveyed the intended meaning without the need to portray the entire human figure.
Ebrahimi said the Marvdasht carvings may likewise have had a devotional purpose, possibly representing prayers or appeals for divine assistance.
She added that this interpretation is reinforced by the discovery of a Sasanian-era prayer inscription beside one of the hand carvings.
The depiction of part of the forearm, ending in a straight edge, together with the distinctive positioning of the fingers, gives the newly documented carvings particular archaeological and artistic significance.
Researchers say further examination and documentation will be needed to establish more precisely the meaning and function of the unusual motifs.

U.S. Marine Corps attack helicopters set for major upgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:02:58 UTC
22:02:58 KST

- The U.S. Marine Corps is refining the SPINE upgrade for AH-1Z and UH-1Y helicopters using data from two test aircraft at Patuxent River.
- PMA-276 and Bell are preparing the Amarillo plant to begin modifying operational fleet helicopters in fiscal 2027.
The U.S. Marine Corps’ H-1 program office is using flight test data from the first two upgraded AH-1Z Viper and UH-1Y Venom helicopters to lock down the SPINE configuration, with modification of the first fleet aircraft set to begin in fiscal 2027. Naval Air Systems Command’s Light/Attack Helicopter Program Office, PMA-276, said test points flown so far are feeding into the final aircraft configuration and the technical drawing package for Phase 3.0, the stage that moves the upgrade from test aircraft to operational helicopters.
SPINE, short for Structural and Power Improvements for NextGen Effects, strengthens the airframes to carry heavier loads and adds electrical generating capacity so the helicopters can take on new weapons and mission systems. The Marine Corps lists SPINE among its H-1 lethality priorities in its 2026 Aviation Plan. The program office did not say how many test points remain, when the configuration will be frozen or how much additional power the upgrade provides.
Developmental testing continues at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland, with Air Test and Evaluation Squadron 21, Bell Textron and PMA-276 working as an integrated test team. Bell finished the two test aircraft, one AH-1Z and one UH-1Y, in March 2026 after 19 months of structural and electrical work at its Amarillo Assembly Center in Texas. The effort was known as the Structural Improvement and Electrical Power Upgrade, or SIEPU, until early 2026.
PMA-276 and Bell are now preparing the Amarillo plant to take in operational helicopters. The work includes buying parts, setting up manufacturing and production lines, readying support equipment and specialized tooling, planning how aircraft will be moved to and from Texas, and aligning SPINE with other H-1 modifications so the work can be done in the same visits. The two organizations are also choosing which aircraft go first and scheduling inductions to keep squadrons supplied with helicopters and to keep the fleet’s configuration consistent.
“H-1 modernization is critical to maintaining a capable and ready force for aviation-delivered fires in support of Marine Air-Ground Task Force crisis response,” said Lt. Col. Benjamin Carlton, capabilities and combat relevance pillar lead for PMA-276. “SPINE will provide greater flexibility for utility mission kits and a digital weapons bus capable of integrating advanced lethality systems, including AIM-9X and other digital weapons.”
The contracts for that first batch are already in place. In July, the U.S. Navy awarded Bell $33.6 million for SPINE Phase III hardware, including A-kits, D-kits, power generation components and drivetrain assemblies. Bell described the award as a base contract with three option years covering up to 49 aircraft, 28 AH-1Zs and 21 UH-1Ys, with work in Amarillo starting in mid-2027 and first deliveries in 2028. In October, the U.S. Navy exercised a $114.7 million option for 15 A-kits, four mission kits and nine aircraft installations, all due by June 2028.
Fiscal 2027 began on Oct. 1, 2026, and runs through September 2027, so the first inductions would fall inside the window Bell gave for the start of work in Amarillo.
A digital weapons bus is a data connection between the aircraft’s mission computers and its stores stations. It lets the helicopter exchange data with smart weapons before launch, which analog connections cannot do, and new weapons can be added largely through software. That matters for a fleet that is no longer being built: U.S. production of the UH-1Y ended in 2020 and of the AH-1Z in 2022, and the Marine Corps operates about 189 Vipers and 160 Venoms. The two types share about 85% of their components, so one set of SPINE changes covers both.
The Marine Corps is already testing missions that will draw on that capacity. On May 13, during an exercise at Twentynine Palms, California, Marine Light Attack Helicopter Squadron 169 used UH-1Ys as airborne control nodes for Neros Archer first-person-view drones, launching one from a helicopter in flight and taking over another launched from the ground.
“Government and Bell SPINE teams are continuing developmental testing while preparing for Phase 3.0 modifications in FY27,” Carlton added. “The team has prioritized critical test points before the first installations and maintained close coordination throughout engineering reviews. By addressing critical test requirements early and incorporating refinements as the program progresses, the team is delivering enhanced capability to the fleet sooner.”
Bell and PMA-276 are also working to keep a common technical baseline for the upgraded aircraft, combining Bell’s role as original equipment manufacturer with PMA-276’s program management, so the modified airframes and mission systems can be supported for the rest of their service lives.

====================================================================================================

Genes may explain about a third of earnings differences, according to a study of 44,500 U.S. twin pairs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:00:52 UTC
22:00:52 KST

A massive analysis of census and tax records indicates that inherited genetic factors account for nearly one-third of the variation in earnings among steadily employed Americans in their late 20s and 30s. At the same time, the research suggests that standard twin studies may overstate the genetic component of career success, partly because same-sex twins are unusually likely to end up working at the same company. The findings were published in PNAS.
Why do children from certain families consistently earn higher paychecks in adulthood than children from other families? Social scientists examine this question using a statistical concept called heritability, which measures the proportion of differences in a trait across a population that can be traced to inherited genetic variation rather than environmental conditions.
To estimate heritability without directly sequencing DNA, researchers have traditionally relied on the classical twin design. This method compares identical twins, who develop from a single fertilized egg and share 100 percent of their genes, with fraternal twins, who develop from two separate eggs and share about 50 percent of their genes, just like ordinary brothers and sisters.
Because both types of twins grow up in the same household, researchers attribute any extra similarity between identical twins to their shared DNA. This rests on what is known as the equal-environments assumption, which holds that identical and fraternal twins share their home environment to the same degree.
Sorting out genetic inheritance from family upbringing has proven challenging in economics. For instance, a 2008 study of American brothers and sisters found that siblings’ adult earnings are moderately correlated, indicating that family background accounts for a sizable share of economic inequality. But ordinary sibling comparisons cannot separate shared DNA from parental wealth and parenting styles.
Twins offer a way to separate those channels. A 2012 review of genetics and economics indicated that long-term income appears roughly as heritable as personality traits or many medical conditions. The review’s authors also warned that separating true genetic effects from social influences remains difficult.
Complicating matters further, a person’s paycheck is not determined solely by the individual skills, education, or personality they bring to the labor market. Labor economists separate wages into two main parts. The first is a portable worker component, which reflects an individual’s earning capacity across different jobs. The second is an employer pay premium, the extra pay or discount a specific company gives to all of its staff.
In a 2013 study of West German workers, study co-author David Card and colleagues found that growing differences between workers and in company pay premiums, along with the increasing sorting of high-earning workers into high-paying companies, accounted for much of the rise in wage inequality. Whether access to these high-paying companies reflects inherited traits, personal connections, or simple luck has remained an open question.
Because population registries rarely record whether twins are identical or fraternal, previous twin studies of income have typically relied on small survey samples. To investigate how genetics and social interactions shape both individual earning power and workplace pay premiums on a national scale, Card and Jesse Rothstein of the University of California, Berkeley, along with Moises Yi of the US Census Bureau, analyzed administrative records covering the full population of young adult twins in the United States.
Unlike physical traits such as height, career outcomes depend heavily on social choices, including where a person wants to work and who else works there. The authors reasoned that if twins influence each other’s job choices or prefer working together at the same workplace, standard twin comparisons could mistake that social coordination for genetic inheritance.
The researchers linked household records from the 2000 United States Census to quarterly wage records from state unemployment insurance tax filings. These records cover formal wage and salary jobs, and the team used data from 2018 through the first quarter of 2023. They omitted the last three quarters of 2020 to avoid labor market disruptions caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.
The sample tracked biological children of household heads who were between 9 and 17 years old in 2000 (born between 1983 and 1990). Twins were defined as children in the same household born within two days of each other, and non-twin siblings as children born at least nine months apart. The employment analysis encompassed 87,000 twin pairs (60,000 same-sex and 27,000 opposite-sex) and 2,168,000 non-twin sibling pairs (1,072,000 same-sex and 1,096,000 opposite-sex).
For the detailed wage analysis, the authors focused on pairs in which both siblings maintained stable full-time work. This meant having at least eight quarters in which they earned more than $3,800 from one employer (roughly full-time minimum-wage pay), excluding the first and last quarters of each job spell. That restriction yielded 44,500 twin pairs (31,500 same-sex and 13,000 opposite-sex) and 1,007,000 non-twin sibling pairs (507,000 same-sex and 500,000 opposite-sex).
Because census files do not record whether twins are identical or fraternal, the researchers relied on biological sex. All opposite-sex twins are fraternal, whereas same-sex twins are a mix of fraternal and identical twins. Identical twins made up an estimated 58.7 percent of same-sex pairs in the sample.
Families may also treat sons and daughters differently. To filter out that possibility, the team used a statistical technique called difference-in-differences. They subtracted the similarity gap between same-sex and opposite-sex regular siblings from the similarity gap between same-sex and opposite-sex twins.
The team analyzed average quarterly earnings using a logarithmic scale, a standard economic measure that captures proportional differences in pay. They also used a statistical wage decomposition model to split each worker’s pay into two parts: their portable individual earning capacity and the average pay premium of the companies they worked for. The model controlled for work experience and calendar time.
That employer pay premium was further broken down into three pieces. These were a geographic location premium (the average employer pay premium among companies in the local commuting zone), an industry premium (the average employer pay premium among companies in that industry), and a remaining workplace-specific pay premium.
Across the full wage sample, same-sex twins showed a correlation in average earnings of 0.543 (on a scale where 0 indicates no relationship and 1 indicates that one twin’s earnings perfectly predict the other’s). By comparison, the correlation was 0.317 for opposite-sex twins, 0.386 for same-sex non-twin siblings, and 0.265 for opposite-sex non-twin siblings.
The researchers also examined non-twin siblings separated by age gaps of one to three years, excluding pairs born less than a year apart to avoid adoption or recording errors. Earnings similarity barely faded as the age difference grew, and the gap between same-sex and opposite-sex siblings remained steady. This pattern supported the assumption that shared family and gender influences do not change drastically for siblings born close together.
Based on their extended twin model, the researchers initially estimated that inherited genetic factors accounted for 36 percent of the variance in overall earnings. Genetic factors also accounted for an estimated 23 percent of the variance in having any employment and 32 percent of the variance in the number of quarters employed.
When the researchers separated earnings into individual and workplace components, portable individual earning power had an estimated heritability of 40 percent. The employer pay premium had an estimated heritability of 21 percent.
Within the workplace component, the industry pay premium had a heritability estimate of 26 percent and the remaining workplace-specific premium had an estimate of 20 percent. The geographic location premium (18 percent) was not statistically significant, because most siblings remained in the region where they grew up.
Finding heritability in employer pay premiums even within regions and industries made it look on the surface as though genetic factors affected not just workers’ skills, but also their access to high-paying companies. Because the 21 percent estimate was roughly twice as large as what skill-based hiring alone would produce, the authors examined whether twins were ending up at the same establishments.
The employment records showed that 11.4 percent of same-sex twin pairs worked at the exact same establishment at some point between 2018 and 2023 (not necessarily at the same time). That was double the rate for same-sex non-twin siblings (5.7 percent), triple the rate for opposite-sex twins (3.8 percent), and more than five times the rate for opposite-sex non-twin siblings (2.2 percent).
The researchers then re-estimated their model after removing all twin and sibling pairs who ever worked at the same establishment. The estimated heritability of the employer pay premium dropped by two-thirds, from 21 percent to 7 percent, and was no longer statistically significant. The heritability of the industry premium fell from 26 percent to 12 percent, and that of the workplace-specific premium fell from 20 percent to essentially zero.
The remaining link between genetics and employer pay premiums fit what would be expected from high-paying companies hiring high-skilled workers alone. Excluding coworkers also lowered the estimated heritability of portable individual earning power from 40 percent to 35 percent. The estimated heritability of overall earnings fell from 36 percent to 31 percent (a relative decline of about 15 percent), and the authors regard these lower figures as their best estimates.
Even with that downward adjustment, the finding that genetics account for roughly a third of individual earning differences aligns with a recent German study, which found that higher cognitive ability at age 23 predicted higher socioeconomic status at age 27 largely due to shared genetic factors. That study looked at educational attainment and occupational prestige in young adulthood rather than wages, but both point to a substantial genetic influence on socioeconomic outcomes.
“The results show that estimated heritability is clearly present, as one would totally expect, but the effect depends a lot on whether the twins work at the same firms,” said Felix Bittmann, a postdoctoral researcher at the Leibniz Institute for Educational Trajectories and the University of Bamberg who was not involved in the research. “It’s an interesting aspect that deserves more attention. Clearly, the paper shows that even well-done genetically informed studies cannot partial out ‘pure’ genetic effects as social interactions will always be present and can influence the findings strongly.”
“While this study is done with twins, its implications extend a lot further: in the social sciences, it is an important question to understand how success is determined (nature vs. nurture),” Bittmann noted. “Twin designs are usually an elegant way to attempt to account for both factors, which classical research designs (surveys) cannot capture at all, as genetic transmission pathways are usually not measured; often, even proxies are lacking (like IQ tests for both children and parents).”
Sociologists often try to separate what they call primary and secondary effects: how family background shapes a child’s academic performance, and how families make choices about continuing education. Those two pathways are harder to separate when genetic inheritance goes unmeasured.
“Especially in sociology, when primary and secondary effects are to be separated, genetic pathways are usually ignored, which is a biasing factor,” Bittmann said. “This research can help to estimate how large such a bias could probably be.”
“The research design is clever, as they exploit a huge US database with official statistics,” Bittmann told PsyPost. “These databases do not contain information about twins, so this information is lacking, but they can reconstruct it from birth dates, which is a good idea. While they need to make some assumptions and correct for the aspect that same-sex twins can be identical or not …, they can account for this statistically; I think this part is fine.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. A heritability estimate of 31 percent describes variation across a population. It does not mean that 31 percent of any one person’s paycheck comes from their genes, or that an individual’s earnings are biologically fixed at birth.
Even when genetic differences influence earnings, they can operate through indirect or social pathways, such as how parents’ genetic traits shape the home environment they create for their children. In addition, the wage analysis only included sibling pairs in which both people held stable, full-time wage and salary jobs. That leaves out self-employed workers, federal employees, and adults with minimal attachment to the labor market.
Model assumptions can also pull the heritability estimates in opposite directions. The baseline model assumes parents pair up randomly with respect to genes related to earnings. If spouses instead tend to share genetic traits tied to education and earning potential (known as assortative mating), regular siblings and fraternal twins would share more than half of those relevant genes. The authors calculate this could make the estimates about 16 percent higher than reported (for example, roughly 36 percent rather than 31 percent).
On the other hand, even after removing siblings who worked at the same company, the remaining estimates for portable earning power may still be inflated by unmeasured social interactions. Twins might, for instance, influence each other’s education choices or decide to attend the same college.
The authors suggest this kind of sibling influence could be one contributor to the “missing heritability” problem in genetics. Studies that directly analyze DNA using polygenic scores (scores that add up the small effects of many genetic variants) estimate lower heritability for social outcomes like education and income than twin studies do.
“I’d say the paper confirms known aspects with a larger and better sample size and is generally trustworthy,” Bittmann said. “When it comes to disentangling nature vs. nurture, the paper contributes but can, of course, not give a definite answer. Maybe other researchers can use the same research plan on other databases from other countries to add more insight and external validity.”
The study, “Heritability and social interaction in labor market outcomes: Evidence from the population of twins in the United States,” was authored by David Card, Jesse Rothstein, and Moises Yi.
