Top Trump Officials Are Hitting the Campaign Trail Ahead of the Midterms. Are They Allowed To?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

Top Trump Administration officials have taken to the campaign trail to boost Republican candidates ahead of the pivotal midterm elections as the party battles to retain control of Congress.
Last month alone, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr, and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum appeared alongside President Donald Trump to support Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in his tight reelection fight against Democrat Mary Peltola at a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on Oct. 13. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth appeared in Wisconsin alongside GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden on Oct. 20 to speak to manufacturing workers during a Pentagon tour highlighting U.S. defense production. Last Monday, Vice President JD Vance and Burgum spoke at a rally in Topeka, Kansas. And on Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio briefly joined Trump on stage, at the President’s urging, during a rally in Corpus Christi, Texas.
Cabinet members and other leading Trump officials have been wading into the midterms in these and other ways for months. In August, for instance, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy endorsed Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan.
Legal experts and advocacy groups contend that in making such moves, members of the Administration have violated a decades-old law: the Hatch Act, passed by Congress in 1939, which places restrictions on certain political activities for federal executive branch employees.
The Administration has argued that the officials have participated in political events in a strictly personal capacity, which is permitted under the Hatch Act, and that their actions have been cleared by lawyers and ethics officials.
But several top Trump aides—including at least nine of his 15 Cabinet secretaries—have been hit with formal complaints that their actions have violated the law.
“The number of Hatch Act violation complaints is extreme and abnormal for election time, especially for complaints against senior officials,” Kedric Payne, the head of ethics at the Campaign Legal Center, a legal non-profit that has filed a complaint against the Trump Administration for using taxpayer money to fund political ads, tells TIME.
“We are seeing with the Trump Administration why the Hatch Act is so important,” Payne says, “because when it is not enforced quickly, it can be abused.”
Here’s what to know about the Hatch Act, and the accusations that Trump officials have violated it.
What is the Hatch Act?
The Hatch Act is an 87-year-old federal law that prohibits certain government employees from using their “official authority or influence for the purpose of interfering with or affecting the result of an election,” among other limits it imposes on officials’ political activity. It states that such interference applies to “an activity directed toward the success or failure of a political party” or candidate.
The law was established to ensure that “federal programs are administered in a nonpartisan fashion, to protect federal employees from political coercion in the workplace, and to ensure that federal employees are advanced based on merit and not based on political affiliation,” according to the Office of Special Counsel (OSC), which enforces it.
Many of the Hatch Act complaints against Trump officials on the campaign trail have centered around one specific aspect of the law that says federal employees cannot use or identify with their official title while engaging in political activity. In a handful of such complaints against members of the Administration, legal and press advocacy groups have pointed out that they were introduced at rallies by their Cabinet positions.
“Political activity must be conducted purely in your personal capacity, without using your official title, without implying endorsement of the United States government. In your personal time at your own personal expense,” Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer under George W. Bush and a professor at the University of Minnesota law school, tells TIME.
The Trump Administration has pushed back on the accusations, saying that its members were acting in a personal capacity at the times in question.
How Trump Administration officials have been accused of violating the Hatch Act on the campaign trail
A number of complaints have been filed against the Trump Administration for violating the Hatch Act in recent months.
Two advocacy non-profits, The Democracy Defenders Fund and Reporters Without Borders, filed a complaint in October over the rally in Alaska that featured Trump, Lutnick, Burgum, and Carr. The groups claimed that Carr “impermissibly mixed his official work into his personal remarks” and requested that the OSC open an investigation into each Trump official’s conduct at the rally.
In September, the two advocacy groups also filed a complaint against Duffy for his appearance in Michigan and his endorsement of Rogers.
Chief Counsel at the Democracy Defenders Fund said in a statement that Duffy’s conduct “crossed the legal and ethical line” and more broadly stated that it was “part of a broader pattern of this administration playing fast and loose with the law.”
Spokespeople for the Interior and Transportation departments have denied wrongdoing on the part of their respective leaders to media outlets. The FCC and Commerce Department did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for comment.
These complaints are among many more that have been filed over Administration officials’ participation in campaign activities.
“We haven't seen since the first Trump Administration this number of complaints against officials, and I've lost track, but I do think it's well over 20 complaints just in recent weeks,” Payne says.
In addition to complaints over officials’ appearances at campaign rallies, others have similarly alleged that Trump officials used their official titles in efforts to influence the midterms through social media and television network appearances.
CREW, a nonprofit government watchdog organization, has made several such claims. In one complaint from earlier this month, it argued that White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller violated the Hatch Act during an interview on Fox News in which he spoke against specific Democratic candidates running for office and urged voters to support a “pro-American Trump agenda.” The group has also filed complaints against Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Federal Bureau of Investigation Director Kash Patel for comments made while speaking to Fox.
“These accusations are baseless and amount to a manufactured political attack," the Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement. "Secretary Kennedy takes his ethical obligations seriously, follows federal ethics laws, and consults HHS career ethics officials to ensure his activities comply with the standards governing public service.”
The Department of Department of Justice, which houses the FBI, did not immediately respond to TIME’s request for comment regarding the accusations against Patel.
When asked about the various Hatch Act complaints against Administration officials, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis tells TIME that “it has long been established that senior administration officials are allowed to discuss current events, policies, and the candidates involved with those policies in order to advance the agenda of the administration.”
Complaints allege further Hatch Act violations
Top Trump officials have additionally been accused of violating the Hatch Act through other means than direct statements and appearances in support of—or opposition to—midterm candidates that complaints allege may also affect the outcome of upcoming elections.
Payne and his colleagues filed a complaint accusing several Administration officials of using taxpayer money for political ads which the complaint describes as “touting partisan and political rhetoric” to influence the outcome of the midterms. The complaint cites three ads: one that promotes Trump’s actions in Iran, another that decries socialism, and a third that features Trump speaking at Mount Rushmore. The Campaign Legal Center in its complaint quotes parameters set by the OSC that say the Hatch Act is designed “to prevent the use of federal power and taxpayer resources to shape electoral outcomes and to preserve public confidence in the nonpartisan administration of the law.”
“Voters deserve to know that elected officials are campaigning using their own money and not taxpayer dollars,” Payne says. “Clearly these advertisements that were paid for by U.S. taxpayer dollars were intended to promote the Republican Party and influence the upcoming election.”
The complaint specifically requests an investigation into Trump officials including Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, and White House Appointments Secretary Natalie Harp for their involvement in putting together the ads.
“There’s a statute that prohibits use of government funds for publicity or propaganda, unless expressly permitted by Congress,” Painter says. “Those ads that Trump was paying for with taxpayer dollars that said ‘paid for by the White House,’ that was propaganda. That violated that statute.”
Trump has defended the ads by saying he was “only promoting the country,” rather than specific candidates. “That’s an ad for the spirit of our country,” he said when asked about the ads in the Oval Office in September.
A Hatch Act complaint was also filed against the Administration by the Democracy Defenders Fund over the raid federal agents conducted at Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home in Minnesota in October. The raid was reportedly part of an ongoing Department of Justice investigation into potential immigration fraud. Omar has denied all wrongdoing.
“The timing of this outrageous action against a long-time target of Trump’s evinces illegal political intent,” Norm Eisen, the co-founder of Democracy Defenders Fund, said in a statement. “Staging a public raid on the home of a sitting member of Congress weeks before a consequential election is an abuse of power.”
Trump has maintained that he has “nothing to do” with the investigation, but has continued to levy public attacks against Omar, including calling her “crooked.”
The flurry of recent complaints against the Trump Administration are far from the first instances in which the President and his aides have come under fire for alleged Hatch Act violations.
An OSC report from 2021, for instance, found that in 2020, at least 13 senior Trump Administration officials violated the Hatch Act.
What is the penalty for a Hatch Act violation?
Following an investigation by the OSC, disciplinary measures for Hatch Act violations are determined by the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB), an independent judicial agency within the Executive branch. For Cabinet or senior officials, OSC refers its findings to the President, who determines disciplinary action.
“The potential of those consequences happening under this President are small because it is up to the President usually to hold members of the administration accountable when they violate the Hatch Act,” Payne says, noting that in some cases, officials may be required to only issue a public apology for their violation, or face no consequence at all.
Federal officials who have previously been found to have violated the Hatch Act under Trump largely have not faced repercussions because the President either declined to punish them or because the OSC reported the violations after Trump and the officials in question left office.
After one OSC report from 2018 found Kellyanne Conway, a former counselor to Trump, had violated the Hatch Act, for example, Trump declined to fire her, telling Fox & Friends at the time that “it looks to me like they’re trying to take away her right of free speech and that’s just not fair.”
The OSC itself has meanwhile acknowledged that it was reporting other violations at a point when disciplinary action could not be taken. “Though discipline is no longer possible once subjects leave government service, OSC is issuing this report to fully document the violations, highlight the enforcement challenges that OSC confronted in investigating the violations, and to deter similar violations in the future,” one OSC report from 2021 reads.
Federal employees can face several civil penalties if they are found to have violated the Hatch Act, however, including a fine, a suspension, or a letter of reprimand. For a criminal violation, up to three years in prison may be imposed as a penalty if an official is found to have “intimidate[ed], threaten[ed], command[ed], or coerce[ed] … any employee of the Federal Government … to engage in, or not to engage in, any political activity.”
“If President Trump or anyone overreaches the point of trying to coerce someone in the government to engage in partisan conduct, that's a violation of the criminal provision of the act, but all the rest of it's civil,” Painter explains.

The Hollywood Color Nerd Who Shot ‘Knives Out’ Explains His Viral iPhone Camera App
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Steve Yedlin is a certified color nerd. He almost immediately starts explaining “the math” behind his passion for color science.
But I didn’t call to chat about psychophysics or color theory. I called to talk to Yedlin about his Chromagraph Camera app, newly released, virally popular, and available only on the iPhone.
Yedlin is a longtime collaborator with director Rian Johnson, shooting his films like Knives Out and Star Wars: The Last Jedi. The duo teamed up again for this launch. “I write all of my own image processing that we use on the movies,” he says. The Chromagraph Camera app brings a taste of Yedlin’s special sauce to your smartphone camera.
Instead of the iPhone’s built-in image processing, this app shoots RAW image data and processes it with a similar formula to what he uses in film production. After Johnson promoted Chromagraph Camera on social media in late October, it quickly became the top paid download in the iOS store. The app costs a one-time fee of $13 and only shoots still photos. (There’s no video support yet.)
I am far from the resident photography nerd on WIRED’s gear team. (That award goes, in part, to my wonderful editor, Julian.) I’m often just whipping out my iPhone and snapping a picture with the default settings. Even so, I really enjoyed capturing some of San Francisco’s fall vibes using the Chromagraph Camera. Although Apple gives iPhone owners plenty of built-in tools for adjusting the color on your own images, I loved this app’s ability to capture highly stylized shots without me needing to fiddle with anything at all.
When you open the app, what you see in the viewfinder before snapping the shot is not what the Chromagraph Camera will spit out. The photo is essentially “developed” in the app after you capture the image. This is because the app needs a moment to run its unique processing for the specific tone, color, and grain effects. You can also alter how an image looks in the app after it’s processed, if you want to tweak the overall exposure or texture of an image.
Yedlin is adamant that he’s not attempting to replace your iPhone camera app or release a professional tool for editing everything. It’s all about that color, man. “It's just this curated app that takes the pictures the way we like,” he says. Yedlin and Johnson teamed up with programmer Eric Cameron to build the app centered around their color tastes, experimenting with it for a couple of months before launch.
Even after all of this custom image processing, Yedlin still sees the iPhone as a fundamentally limited device. “This idea that you can actually have the control that a professional camera would have is not really true anyhow,” he says. Software can only do so much to change how hardware works, especially when developing an app within Apple’s parameters that limit how far the software can push the phone’s hardware.
As advances in computational photography and generative AI have renewed discussions about what a smartphone photo even is anymore, Yedlin’s approach isn't an attempt to find a sense of neutrality. He doesn’t see any image as a literal rendering of what exists. It’s always an interpretation, whether that's a stylized, artful depiction or a more stagnant shot. He says that the look of the Chromagraph Camera app is consciously “opinionated” and specific.
“You can describe how the different rendering looks in words, but you just have to look at it,” he says. The color speaks for itself.

There’s a Free Video Editor Inside Google Drive That Anyone Can Use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Mention the online apps available as part of Google Workspace, and most people will immediately think of Google Drive, Gmail, Google Docs, Google Sheets, and Google Slides—those speedy, lightweight office apps that let you get work done from any browser tab.
There's more to the suite of Google Workspace tools than you might have realized though, including an online video editing package called Google Vids. Originally launched in 2024 for business and enterprise users, the app was made available to individuals in 2026 and continues to get regular updates from Google.
Since it's both free to use and designed to run in a web browser, it's not capable of pro-level, high-resolution, multitrack video editing. But for personal and hobbyist use, it works well, and it won't take you long to learn the basics.
The Google Vids Interface
Finding Google Vids isn't difficult: You can either open Google Drive on the web, then click New and Google Vids, or head straight to the Google Vids app page and click the + (plus) button under Start a new video. (Any videos you've previously made are shown here, too.)
Besides beginning with a clean state (the Blank vid option), there are plenty of other ways to get started: You can generate AI videos with the Veo 3.1 model, turn a slideshow into a video, work from a template, upload an existing video as a starting point, create an AI music track, record a video using your camera, produce a video with an AI avatar, or create a storyboard outline. Note you can also pick the video orientation at the top.
Most of these options use a similar layout, and we're going to focus on the traditional video-making approach here—though the AI options are well worth exploring, too, if you don't have source material to work with. If you're new to Google Vids, then picking Templates from the opening splash screen will ease you in gently.
When it comes to picking a template, the topic isn't as important as the layout. Look for something that matches what you want to create as closely as possible (hover over any of the thumbnails to see an animated preview). The next dialog lets you choose whether you want to use the entire template or just selected scenes. After that, you're into the video editing interface proper.
Most of the elements should be relatively familiar if you've ever used a timeline-based video editor in the past. At the bottom you've got your video and audio tracks, while the main window shows the currently selected segment of your video. The panel on the right lets you edit whatever's currently selected.
Down the right side of the interface you've got all the options for loading in new content. You can record webcam clips, create AI videos, import footage from Google Drive and Google Photos, add voiceovers, and drop in text, images, music, and shapes. If you've started with a template, some of these elements will be styled to match.
Along the top of the Google Vids interface are more editing and formatting tools. These menus are where you should head to change transitions between scenes, to manage how elements are arranged in a particular scene, to drop in new scenes, and to manage your video project as a whole.
Building Video Projects With Google Vids
To begin building your projects, you'll probably want to load in audio, video, and images via the buttons on the right. On the most basic level, you can click the + (plus) button on the timeline to create a new scene, then drag in a photo or video from the right-hand panel to fill the scene you've just created.
A whole host of options present themselves when you right-click on the timeline. You can, for example, mute the audio track imported with a video, then add a voiceover or some different music. You're also able to split scenes (if you only want to keep half a scene maybe) and duplicate scenes (for quickly expanding the running time of your project) with a right-click.
Keep your eye on the panel on the right, which changes depending on the context. With audio tracks, you can apply fades, and with video clips you can choose from different transitions. If your scene has several elements (like shapes that scroll over a video), you're able to adjust how they look and behave.
Let's say you have a video scene and want to put some text over it. Select the scene in the timeline, click the Text button on the right, then click Add a title to do just that. If you then select the title in the scene itself, you can change the text and its styling.
Using the handles around the text box you can change its position, size, and rotation. There are also three buttons underneath on a floating toolbar: Animation lets you animate the text, Resize will resize the text box to fit the text you've entered, and Format options brings up a panel where you can change text size, padding, rotation, and so on.
Click and drag on elements inside a scene to reposition them, and right-click for more options—including Cut, Copy, Paste, and Delete. If you need more material to work with, choose the Stock option on the right, which gives you a library of material you can make use of in addition to your own content and anything created with AI.
There's a lot more to Google Vids, but that should be enough to get you started—try experimenting with a few of the templates to see what else is possible. As with the other Google Drive apps, all your edits are saved instantly, and up in the top right corner you've got a Play button for viewing your work in progress, and a Share button for when it’s ready for the world to see.

London Bridge gets early review to test structural condition

London Bridge gets early review to test structural condition
LONDON – London Bridge is undergoing an earlier-than-planned engineering review as concerns grow over the state of the British capital’s ageing river crossings.
The assessment will deepen “understanding of the condition” of the cables within the bridge, the City Bridge Foundation, a charity that manages five crossings over the River Thames, said in its 2025-26 report.
Initial investigations found no defects, it said in an emailed statement.
The bridge charity brought forward the review after a railway bridge in the German city of Dresden collapsed into the Elbe River in September 2024.
The dramatic failure left engineers searching for answers and led the foundation to accelerate its assessment of London Bridge.
Like Dresden’s Carola Bridge, the building of London Bridge was completed in the early 1970s and shares some design features.
London’s river crossings are facing growing attention after Westminster City Council warned that Waterloo Bridge could be forced to close unless it secures funding for needed repairs.
Structural reviews are also planned for Blackfriars Bridge, Southwark Bridge and Tower Bridge, according to the bridge charity.
London Bridge, which commuters walk every day on the way to work in the City of London financial district, is already closed to general traffic on weekdays from 7am until 7pm to reduce congestion.
The latest evaluation follows essential maintenance completed in 2020 that helped waterproof the structure, the City of London Corporation said at the time.
The foundation, which has about £1.5 billion (S$2.5 billion) in funds, will continue to manage only crossings under its existing mandate despite pressure to take on more, Chair Paul Martinelli said in a recent statement.
The five bridges the foundation manages “cost the taxpayer nothing. Today they are open, safe and in good condition,” Martinelli said.
“London’s other bridges belong to other organisations. We can’t take on the whole river.” BLOOMBERG

COP17: Nations chart ‘Yerevan Pathway’ to speed up action for nature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

COP17: Nations chart ‘Yerevan Pathway’ to speed up action for nature
At the halfway mark to 2030, countries meeting in Armenia have agreed a roadmap to accelerate action for nature, after a global review found the world off track to meet its biodiversity targets.
Agreement was formalised through the Yerevan Pathway as the UN Biodiversity Conference (COP17) closed in the Armenian capital on Saturday.
It sets out priorities for the four years left to deliver the 23 targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
Mixed message
“We cannot protect nature while continuing to finance its destruction,” said Astrid Schomaker, Executive Secretary of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD).
The pathway calls on countries to tackle subsidies that harm nature and to increase financial, scientific and technical support for developing countries.
It also calls for national budgets and economic decisions to be aligned with the framework, and for stronger monitoring and reporting.
“Over these two weeks we have demonstrated that differences can be bridged, commitments can become decisions and cooperation can deliver,” said COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan.
Progress made
Parties adopted nearly 50 decisions, covering areas including protected areas and forests, wildlife management, invasive alien species, marine and coastal biodiversity, and synthetic biology.
After intensive negotiations, they also agreed the Sevan Guidelines.
These set the rules of operation for a new permanent body strengthening the role of Indigenous Peoples and local communities in shaping global biodiversity policy.
Funding boost
Nearly $2 billion in new biodiversity funding was announced. This included $560 million under the Global Environment Facility’s latest replenishment and $500 million through the Species Recovery Alliance.
Another $330 million is going to the Value Nature Fund, which aims to mobilise private capital for nature.
Other initiatives included a new biodiversity bond and investment incubator launched by the Asian Development Bank, and new indicators to improve biodiversity monitoring and accountability.
Spirit of compromise
“In Yerevan, we saw environmental multilateralism prevail once again,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP).
“Countries came together, found the spirit of compromise and allowed us to agree important decisions that will support real progress for people and for planet.”
The next conference, COP18, will be held in Ecuador, with two years remaining to achieve the targets.
“Ultimately, the test is not what governments agreed in Yerevan, but what they change when they return home,” said Ms. Schomaker.

Western Sahara: UN ‘stands ready’ to keep supporting peace efforts as MINURSO mission ends
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Western Sahara: UN ‘stands ready’ to keep supporting peace efforts as MINURSO mission ends
The UN remains committed to supporting a just, lasting and mutually acceptable political solution in Western Sahara that provides for the self-determination of its people, Secretary-General António Guterres said on Sunday, as the UN peacekeeping mission there began to wind down.
The departure of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) “does not abrogate” the people’s “inalienable right to self-determination”, his statement said, delivered by his Spokesperson.
It called on all parties “to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara.”
The mission’s mandate expired at midnight on Saturday, after the Security Council failed on Friday to agree on its future.
A draft resolution from the United States was vetoed by Russia, while a rival Russian text failed to win the nine votes needed for adoption.
Although MINURSO’s operations have now ended, the UN will keep working towards a peaceful resolution through the Secretary-General’s Personal Envoy, Staffan de Mistura.
Orderly withdrawal
Mr. Guterres recognized the “central role” MINURSO has played since 1991 in helping to monitor the ceasefire and in creating conditions for the pursuit of a political solution.
He expressed his “deepest gratitude” to the mission’s personnel, including the Special Representative for Western Sahara, Alexander Ivanko. Mr. Ivanko led the mission through a “particularly challenging period" after hostilities resumed in 2020.
The UN chief also paid tribute to the 20 MINURSO personnel who lost their lives during the mission’s 35 years in the territory.
When its mandate ended, the mission was headquartered in Laayoune, with nine team sites – four west of the berm and five east of it – and a liaison office in Tindouf.
It had about 200 civilian staff, military observers and staff officers from over 35 countries, and a dedicated mine action capability.
Sunday marks the start of a liquidation period. A smaller team reporting to the UN Department of Operational Support will oversee the disposal of UN equipment.
Mr. Guterres called for the full cooperation of the parties so the process can be completed in an orderly way as soon as possible.
‘Maximum restraint’
The Secretary-General said he remains concerned about the security situation throughout the territory and the risk of hostilities escalating.
He urged all concerned “to exercise maximum restraint and to refrain from actions that could further increase tensions or undermine regional stability.”
Divided council
The US delegate in the council on Friday said his country’s draft would have supported the principle of self-determination and “moved the 50-year conflict forward”, calling the status quo unacceptable.
Explaining the veto, the Russian delegate said the text would have imposed one-sided solutions, describing his vote as “a life-saving veto, so to speak”.
Russia’s alternative, a one-year extension of the mandate to 31 October 2027, failed to attract enough support from the 15 nation body.
MINURSO was established under Council resolution 690 (1991), in line with UN-Organization of African Unity settlement proposals accepted in 1988 by Morocco and the Frente POLISARIO.
These provided for a referendum in which the people of Western Sahara would choose between independence and integration with Morocco. While the referendum never took place, MINURSO continued to carry out the tasks entrusted to it by the council.
In 2007, Morocco put forward an Autonomy Proposal as a basis for negotiations. It envisages the territory as self-governing under Moroccan sovereignty.
In closing, the statement said that while MINURSO’s peacekeeping operations had concluded, “the United Nations stands ready to continue supporting efforts to advance dialogue and pursue a peaceful resolution of the conflict.”

NEW DELHI: BJP on Sunday mocked the INDIA bloc's rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan, calling it a "super flop" event and claiming that around 40% of the ground was empty. BJP MP Sambit Patra took a swipe at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and other opposition leaders, questioning their claims of a massive turnout and asking where the 10 lakh people they had expected to gather were."Rahul Gandhi is speaking and empty chairs. Super Flop rally," Patra said, sharing a video of the gathering.Speaking to reporters, Patra said the BJP had been watching the rally since morning and listening to Gandhi's address, but felt it had ultimately been a "complete waste of time".
"Where were the 10 lakh people? Show us. No one becomes a leader or Prime Minister through such tricks. PM doesn't just mean Prime Minister. P stands for Paseena (sweat) and M stands for Mehnat (hard work). A Prime Minister is made through sweat and hard work. Despite bringing together so many parties and flags, they could not manage to gather 10 lakh people," he said.
Accusing the opposition of using camera angles to create an impression of a larger gathering, Patra dismissed the visuals as "trick photography". He also took a swipe at Gandhi, saying, "Rahul ji, Hindustan is not your abujan’s property.

Here, even a chaiwala can become the Prime Minister, and that is what bothers you."The INDIA bloc rally was organised to protest alleged electoral irregularities and raise the issue of 'vote chori'. Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:55:46 UTC
20:55:46 KST

Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Augsburg
- Summary:
- Scientists have built a groundbreaking molecular motor that spins in either direction using electricity, inspired by a machine invented more than 2,000 years ago. Even more remarkably, its rotation can boost electrical conductivity by up to 100 times, potentially transforming the future of molecular electronics.
- Share:
Scientists have developed a remarkable new molecular motor that spins when electricity passes through it. Inspired by an ancient invention, the tiny machine can even reverse its direction when the electrical voltage is switched. The achievement marks an important step toward creating working machines at the smallest possible scale.
Molecular machines are widely seen as a promising next frontier in miniaturization. Nature already provides examples inside living cells, where molecular motors use energy to produce movement. Researchers have spent decades trying to recreate these remarkable biological systems artificially, and progress in this field was recognized with the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
An Ancient Invention Inspires a Molecular Motor
Scientists first developed molecular motors powered directly by electricity in 2011. However, those earlier designs operated on surfaces and relied on the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope to drive their movement.
The new motor takes a different approach, borrowing its basic design from the Archimedes screw, one of the oldest machines in recorded history. Traditionally used to move water uphill, this simple device relies on a rotating spiral to transport material.
Researchers adapted that principle to the molecular scale. Instead of moving water, their design allows electrons to travel through a spiral-shaped molecule, causing it to rotate as electrical current passes through.
A Tiny Molecular Screw Suspended Between Gold Tips
The motor's central component is a specially designed spiral molecule created by the research group of Prof. Michael Pittelkow at the University of Copenhagen. Measuring only a few millionths of a millimeter, the molecule can attach to gold surfaces through sulfur atoms.
At the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel, researchers led by Prof. Oren Tal and Dr. Anil Kumar Singh positioned individual molecules between two gold tips sharpened to atomic dimensions. By carefully changing the separation between these electrodes, the team could stretch or compress the molecular screw.
When the scientists applied an electrical voltage, measurements revealed that the molecule began rotating. Even more importantly, they could reverse its direction simply by changing the voltage's polarity.
This represents the first demonstration of a molecular motor that is driven by electrical current, firmly connected to two metal electrodes, and capable of rotating in a controllable direction.
How Electricity Makes a Single Molecule Spin
The driving force comes directly from electrons traveling through the spiral molecule. As they move, they transfer angular momentum to the molecular structure, producing rotation in much the same way that moving air turns a wind turbine.
The spiral's shape determines how it responds to this flow, similar to the difference between screws with right- or left-handed threads. Once the applied voltage exceeds a certain threshold, the movement becomes continuous rotation.
But the experiments revealed another intriguing effect. The rotating molecule conducted electricity much more efficiently than it did when stationary, raising an important question about what was happening inside the tiny machine.
Scientists Discover a Surprising 100-Fold Electrical Effect
To investigate this unexpected behavior, Prof. Dr. Fabian Pauly and his PhD students Léon Martin and Yuta Ito, working at the Chair of Theoretical Physics I at the University of Augsburg, used quantum mechanical simulations on the LiCCA supercomputer.
Their calculations revealed a close relationship between the molecule's rotation and its ability to carry electrical current. Conductivity changes dramatically depending on the angle of the molecule, increasing by as much as two orders of magnitude, or 100 times, during rotation.
The reason turned out to be particularly surprising. Some of the molecular positions that allow electricity to pass most easily are also positions that the molecule naturally avoids when it is not moving. Rotation makes those highly conductive arrangements accessible.
"The surprising thing is that it is precisely the positions that the molecule avoids when at rest that conduct electricity best. It is only the rotation that makes these positions accessible," explains Léon Martin.
The finding demonstrates that molecular motion does more than simply consume electrical energy. The movement itself can strongly influence how electricity flows through the machine.
International Collaboration Solves the Mystery
The researchers then worked with theoretical physicists Per Hedegård of the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen and Jing-Tao Lü of Huazhong University of Science and Technology in Wuhan.
Using the simulation results, the scientists developed a simplified theoretical model that successfully recreated both the rotation observed in the experiments and the accompanying increase in electrical current.
This combination of experimental measurements and theoretical calculations was essential to understanding the mechanism. Although researchers could measure the current passing through the molecule, they needed simulations to determine what was happening at such an extraordinarily small scale.
"In the experiment, you only see the current. Our calculations allow us to glimpse what is happening inside the nanocontact. It was only through close collaboration between experiment and theory across several countries that the mystery of the current increase could be solved," says Yuta Ito, a PhD student originally from Japan.
A New Frontier for Molecular Electronics
The achievement could eventually contribute to the development of molecular electronic components and technologies involving spintronics, which uses properties of electrons beyond their electrical charge. It may also offer possibilities for microfluidic systems, which manipulate extremely small quantities of fluids.
Beyond these potential applications, the motor provides scientists with a new way to investigate physical processes at the atomic scale. Its ability to convert electricity into controlled rotation, while allowing that rotation to influence electrical current, introduces a new principle for designing extraordinarily small machines.
"We have shown that an electric current can be used to generate a directed rotation and that this rotation, in turn, controls the current. This is a new operating principle for machines at the very limits of miniaturization," explains Pauly.
The work at the University of Augsburg received funding from the German Research Foundation (DFG) through Collaborative Research Center (SFB) 1585 (project number 492723217). The computational research was conducted using the University of Augsburg's LiCCA supercomputer (DFG project number 499211671).
Additional support for the collaborating institutions came from the European Research Council (ERC, Horizon 2020, Grant 864008), the Israel Science Foundation (2129/23), the Minerva Foundation, the Villum Foundation, the Novo Nordisk Foundation, the Independent Research Fund Denmark (DFF), the National Key Research and Development Program of China, and the National Natural Science Foundation of China.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Augsburg. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Anil Kumar Singh, León Martin, Matea Sršen, Freja Schou Guttesen, Bing-Zhong Hu, Yuta Ito, Stephan Korsgaard Pedersen, Fadhil Suleiman Kamounah, Fabian Pauly, Michael Pittelkow, Jing-Tao Lü, Per Hedegård, Oren Tal. Current-Driven Molecular Machine with Rotation-Enhanced Conductance. Nature, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11312-x

Feature: Myanmar star elephant's 73rd birthday brings back generations of memories
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
19:39:02 CST
20:39:02 KST

Children wear elephant headbands during the celebrations of the 73rd birthday of Momo, a female Asian elephant, at the Yangon Zoological Gardens in Yangon, Myanmar, Nov. 1, 2026. (Xinhua/Myo Kyaw Soe)
YANGON, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- At 73, Momo, a renowned female Asian elephant at Yangon Zoological Gardens, was once again the center of attention as children, parents and elderly visitors gathered on Sunday to celebrate her birthday.
As children and other spectators sang the song "Happy Birthday," Momo gently swayed her trunk and moved her legs, seemingly joining in the celebration. Later, she chomped on an assortment of fruits and vegetables arranged in the shape of a cake.
For some visitors, it was their first time seeing the gentle giant. For others, the occasion brought back fond childhood memories of visiting Momo at the zoo, memories they are now passing on to their own children and grandchildren.
For 11-year-old Thuta Nyan Kywal, visiting the zoo with her mother and sister was an exciting opportunity to see elephants in real life rather than simply reading about them in textbooks.
"In the past, I only saw elephants in textbooks. Now I can see them in real life and learn how they behave and what they eat. I did not know about Momo before coming here, but today I learned about her and am very happy to join her birthday celebration," she said.
"I wish Momo a long and healthy life. Happy birthday, Momo!" she added.
For 60-year-old Thida Soe, seeing Momo again was like taking a journey back to her childhood.
"I have known Momo since I was young and used to visit her at the zoo. Seeing her brings back so many childhood memories," she said.
"Although Momo is an animal, people treat her like a human being and celebrate her birthday. She is very gentle. She has changed as she has grown older and cannot be as active as she once was, but she has lived to 73. Not everyone, even among humans, gets to live that long," she said.
According to Than Myint Tun, warden of Yangon Zoological Gardens, Momo was donated to Yangon Zoo in 1961. Over the decades, she has grown from a young performing elephant into a much-loved grandmother figure and one of the zoo's most recognizable residents.
During her younger years, Momo entertained visitors with performances and dances. She also took part in significant national events, including the opening ceremony of the Shwedagon Pagoda stairway, he said.
"Momo stopped performing when she turned 60 in 2013. Since then, we have celebrated her birthday every year. Now she has turned 73," he said.
"Momo is loved by the public and is one of Yangon Zoo's trademarks. By celebrating her birthday, we can also raise public awareness about elephants and their nature," he added.
For more than four years, Momo has been under the care of her keeper, Thant Sin Tun, who inherited the responsibility from his senior colleagues.
"Momo is polite and gentle. As she has grown older, she has become less patient. She does not like being scolded, so we have to speak to her softly," he said.
"When we call her name, she responds. When we ask her to dance, she dances," he added.
Momo loves cleanliness. If her food falls on the ground and gets mixed with sand, she refuses to eat it. She also likes drinking tap water and enjoys scrubbing herself when taking a bath, he said.
Age, however, has brought some physical challenges. Her eyesight has become blurry, and she can no longer chew hard food as easily as before. Apart from these age-related changes, her keeper said she has no major health problems.
At the zoo, Momo receives regular medical attention and care. Unlike elephants in the wild, she does not have to search for food herself or face some of the dangers associated with life in the forest, he said.
"If she could speak, I think she would say that she wants to live longer here because so many people love her and we take care of her health," he said. ■

Over 4,000 Australian GP clinics now offer free consultations to all patients: gov't
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
19:38:26 CST
20:38:26 KST

CANBERRA, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- More than 4,000 general practitioner (GP) clinics across Australia now provide free consultations to all patients under the country's Medicare system, up from 2,300 a year ago, the government said on Sunday.
Australian Minister for Health and Ageing Mark Butler said in a statement that 50 percent of all general practices nationwide now exclusively offer bulk billing, compared with 30 percent a year earlier.
Under the bulk-billing system, doctors bill Medicare directly for medical services, allowing patients to receive treatment without out-of-pocket costs.
The increase follows the introduction of the government's Bulk Billing Practice Incentive Program, which provides higher Medicare rebates to clinics where all doctors bulk bill all patients.
According to the statement, more than 97 percent of Australians now live within a 20-minute drive of a general practice that bulk bills all patients.
The proportion of fully bulk-billing practices has more than doubled in South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania and the Australian Capital Territory (ACT) over the past 12 months.
The Northern Territory recorded the highest proportion among states and territories at 80 percent, followed by New South Wales at 58 percent and Victoria at 55 percent, while the ACT had the lowest at 21 percent.
Rural areas saw the largest increase, with the proportion of fully bulk-billing practices rising to 59 percent, while remote areas remained at 77 percent.
Butler said the expansion was helping Australians save hundreds of dollars a year in out-of-pocket medical expenses. ■

In France, protests continued largely peacefully for a third weekend after extensive riots and looting on October 17 damaged shops, public buildings and businesses.

Prices on gaming laptops are out of control. The ongoing memory shortage has made laptops more expensive across the board, but it's hit gaming laptops especially hard. Some manufacturers have even resorted to launching “new" gaming laptops in 2026 with the RTX 4050 as the starting configuration—and that graphics card is more than three years old.
Given this landscape, there's really only one gaming laptop under $1,500 that I feel comfortable recommending. That's the Lenovo LOQ 15. It's not the thinnest or most powerful gaming laptop in the world, but for this price, there's nothing else like it.
It's not that the price of the LOQ 15 hasn't gone up over the past year alongside its gaming-laptop brethren. (It certainly has.) For the first few months of 2026—the good old days—it was selling for less than $1,000. But even then, it was technologically ahead of its rivals in a number of ways, offering strong performance paired with a high-quality IPS display. So many cheap gaming laptops come with pitifully desaturated screens that put a damper on the gaming experience. That's really what sets the LOQ 15 apart from the competition.
Also significant is the fact that, right now, you can buy the LOQ 15 with an RTX 5060 for just $1,300. That's not any cheaper than it normally has been (at least not for the past few months). However, the RTX 5060 is a big upgrade over the RTX 5050, especially with the 100 watts of power that the system can throw at it. Every game I tested could play at well over 60 frames per second at the medium preset, including heavier games like Black Myth: Wukong and Monster Hunter Wilds. You can always push frame rates higher by adjusting settings further or by adding a dash of upscaling.
Amazon has the RTX 5060 configuration, which also comes with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage, for $1,300, but Lenovo also has a killer deal on the RTX 5050 configuration that's about as cheap as it gets: $999 for an RTX 5050 (and otherwise identical specs). I've tested a number of other gaming laptops that sell for around this price, such as the MSI Cyborg A16 and the Acer Nitro V 16, and none can compete with the LOQ 15. I've also tested the Alienware 15 and Lenovo LOQ Essential 15 recently, and both suffer from the same problem.
As much as I wish I could recommend a budget gaming laptop that's newer, none I've tried have successfully dethroned the Lenovo LOQ 15. While you could wait until Black Friday to see if prices dip further, note that I haven't seen much fluctuation over the past few months. For example, it wasn't on a deeper sale during the October Amazon Prime Day—and yet, it was still the best gaming laptop deal you could get.

Binance covers 90% of $6.3 billion hack losses, but what about the rest?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:28:51 UTC
20:28:51 KST

Binance covers 90% of $6.3 billion hack losses, but what about the rest?
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance says it has replenished 90% of the assets stolen in a $6.3 billion cyberattack, but replacing the remaining funds could take longer because some cryptocurrencies are harder to obtain, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the company's latest recovery update, the proportion of replenished assets has increased from 80% to 90%, with Binance continuing to purchase replacement tokens through public markets and over-the-counter transactions.
The exchange confirmed that 10 major cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Tether (USDT), BNB, Solana (SOL), USD Coin (USDC), XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and Zcash (ZEC), are now fully backed by reserves.
Why is the remaining 10% taking longer?
Binance explained that the outstanding assets consist of less liquid cryptocurrencies, meaning they are not as readily available for purchase in large quantities.
Unlike widely traded cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, these tokens may require additional time to acquire without disrupting market conditions.
The company said it is working with industry partners to secure the remaining assets and intends to continue purchasing replacement tokens until all affected cryptocurrencies are fully backed.
Importantly, replenishing stolen assets does not mean the stolen funds themselves have been recovered from the attackers. Binance is using its own financial resources to replace missing assets while separate efforts to trace and recover the stolen cryptocurrency continue.
Where is the replacement money coming from?
Binance identified three sources of funding: its Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a portion of its Futures Insurance Fund, and corporate funds.
SAFU, established in 2018, serves as an emergency reserve designed to protect customers during exceptional incidents, including security breaches.
The company also pledged to replenish SAFU to approximately $1 billion after using part of the fund to cover losses.
Binance announced that it had taken a new Proof of Reserves snapshot on October 31, providing updated information about assets held by the exchange.
The company said preparing the complete cryptographic proof would take approximately 40 to 50 hours because of the computational resources required.
Once published, the results are expected to allow customers holding the 10 fully backed cryptocurrencies to independently verify that their assets are supported by reserves at a ratio of at least 1:1.
The complete verification results are expected by November 3.
Binance also identified restoring withdrawals as a priority, with services scheduled to resume in phases from November 1, subject to security checks.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that investigators had linked the $6.3 billion Binance hack to a North Korean state-backed hacking group, with stolen assets transferred across multiple blockchain networks.

These tattoos can magically disappear—here’s how they work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:25:41 UTC
20:25:41 KST

How handy would it be if you could make your tattoos invisible for a job interview in the morning, and reveal them again for a party in the evening? This sounds like science fiction, but it may soon be reality.
Researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder have developed invisible tattoo ink than can be revealed with a UV torch and stays visible until switched off with white light. They have published their research in the journal Matter & Light.
They created different motifs with this ink ranging from a lantern that reveals its light when activated, to multicolored scales like those in the much-loved children’s book The Rainbow Fish.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The pigments used in these inks are so-called photochromic dyes(from the Greek “photos”, which means “light” and “chroma”, which means “color”). In other words, they are compounds that change colour when exposed to light. These dyes have been used for years in color-changing sunglasses.
Light carries energy, and photochromic compounds are designed in such a way that this energy is enough to cause a chemical change that alters the shape and therefore the properties of the molecule.
In the case of the “invisible” tattoo ink, two or three seconds of bright ultraviolet (UV) light is enough to form a new ring in the dye molecule, which switches a colorless pigment to a colored one. A variety of colors are available depending on the exact structure of the molecule.
A blast of bright white light reverses the reaction, breaking the ring and turning the colour off again. For a long time, the challenge with this chemistry was that the colored form of the dye was relatively unstable and quickly reverted to the more stable, colorless form—especially at higher temperatures.
Another issue was fatigue: after a certain number of on-off cycles, the dyes degraded and took on a permanent coloured hue. Have you ever bought transition lens sunglasses and noticed that they became less effective over time? This is due to the same deterioration of photochromic compounds in the lenses. But thanks to recent research efforts, remarkably stable dyes have been designed that reliably hold their colour for months and can undergo over 10,000 activation and deactivation cycles without degrading.
Carson Bruns’ team at the University of Colorado Boulder showed that these pigments could be formulated into tattoo inks by encapsulating them in poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), a polymer approved for medical use in bone cement, dentures and intraocular lenses. This family of inks is known as PhotoTat.
Time to market
So, when will you be able to get one of these switchable tattoos? A red pigment was already launched in 2024 under the name Magic Ink by Colorado-based biotech company Hyprskn. A 2 millilitre (ml) vial will set you back £77, which is about 100 times more expensive than regular tattoo ink due to the specialised dyes and formulation process required. The ink is fully compliant with the EU’s Reach (Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals) safety regulations.
Now, Bruns’ research team has developed three more PhotoTat inks – blue, magenta and yellow – that can combine into 16 other colours. “So far,” Bruns says, “the only person who’s tested this ink is me. I actually have hundreds of these tattoos on my legs now and they’ve all gone really well.”
Some challenges remain though: direct sunlight contains enough UV radiation to activate the tattoos unless they are protected by sunscreen. Indoor light will slowly switch them off over a period of several days.
In addition, the blue ink currently degrades after only 10–100 activations, leaving a permanent, purple-coloured mark. Most importantly, the inks need to undergo thorough toxicity and safety testing before they can be rolled out to tattoo shops for general use, which will likely take several years. Don’t get your hopes up just yet about your new “business during the day, party at night” look.
When Hyprskn launched Magic Ink, the reception in the tattoo community was mixed. While some tattoo enthusiasts viewed it as a revolutionary creative tool, others thought it was an overpriced gimmick. Bruns does not only see his photochromic tattoo inks as fashion accessories, however.
He also envisages medical applications, for example for patients who need permanent skin markings to guide radiation therapy or identify sites for biopsies. Bruns argues that these markings “become a permanent reminder of a traumatic experience” which can be mitigated by making the tattoo invisible once it is no longer needed in a clinical setting.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

Tehran, New Delhi hold talks to deepen ties in technology sector
TEHRAN – Iran and India have discussed ways to expand cooperation in information and communication technology (ICT), promote specialized exchanges, and strengthen coordination in international forums.
ICT Minister Sattar Hashemi and India’s Ambassador to Iran, Vishwesh Negi, held a meeting on Saturday to explore the two countries’ capacities for joint initiatives in the sector, Mehr News Agency reported.
 
The discussions focused on identifying opportunities for cooperation between government bodies and private-sector ICT stakeholders, enhancing professional interactions, and making greater use of the two countries’ scientific, technical, and technological capabilities.
Given the respective capacities and the regional and international standing of Iran and India, both parties underlined the need for the promotion of cooperation and coordination within specialized international forums and organizations, particularly those related to the ICT sector.
The officials also highlighted the importance of harmonizing views, participating in ongoing consultations, and strengthening joint initiatives to ensure a more effective presence on the international stage.
The two sides agreed to continue discussions, follow up on the discussed issues, and enhance ties in areas of mutual interest.
Tech ties with India in key sectors
In February, Hashemi, in a meeting with Indian Minister of Electronics and Information Technology, Jitin Prasada, voiced the country’s readiness for the expansion of scientific and technological ties with India in key sectors, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity, and the digital economy.
The officials met on the sidelines of the India AI Impact Summit 2026, being conducted in person at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi, from February 16 to 20, IRIB reported.
During the meeting, Hashemi highlighted the capabilities of the two sides in emerging technologies. Referring to Iran’s strong scientific and human infrastructure, he said the country has taken great strides in advancing modern technologies.

According to Hashemi, enhancing interactions between the private sectors is among the top priorities. “We are interested in developing operational cooperation in large language models (LLMs), the development of an AI joint platform in the agriculture sector, and the establishment of innovative centers to utilize AI in different fields,” he said.
Highlighting the importance of securing critical infrastructure in the years ahead and India’s capacity in training specialized human resources, Hashemi announced Iran’s readiness to share experiences in cyber threats, combating emerging malware, and strengthening the security of financial infrastructure.
The ICT minister also proposed developing a joint fund to support Iranian and Indian startups, holding joint technological events, and talent exchange programs, allocating special zones in the technology parks of the two countries, and facilitating the issuance of ‘tech visas’ for IT professionals as practical ways to foster cooperation.
For his part, Prasada underscored expanding collaboration between the two sides, saying that India is willing to expand ties with Iran via sharing expertise in AI and cybersecurity, holding workshops on training specialized human resources, and kicking off operational cooperation in collaborative technological projects.
“Establishing joint innovation centers and exchanging experts would help accelerate technological development in both countries, strengthen digital infrastructure, and improve data security,” Prasada noted.

Lebanon's team of tradies win in all-time great finish at World Cup

2026-11-01

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
analysis
Wild finish to Rugby League World Cup classic between Lebanon and France
Rugby league fans had been salivating over what might transpire at Western Sydney Stadium on November 1 for months.
It was the first fixture of the World Cup to sell out weeks ago.
Everyone was hyping it up as the moment we would see this tournament catch fire and the international men's game ascend to higher levels than ever seen before.
And that all transpired, except it came a game early.
There was a triple header here, the Jillaroos against Wales, followed by Lebanon and France, to whet the appetite before the main event of Tonga and Samoa.
What no-one anticipated was that Lebanon and France, two minnows who were already well out of contention for the semifinals, would dish up what is roundly being called one of the greatest finishes in the international game.
One that has proven that just because this sport does a World Cup a little differently from the rest, it doesn't diminish its meaning.
Tradies' time to shine
The vast majority of players spread through the teams in this tournament were born in Australia or New Zealand, choosing to represent the country of their heritage.
The French are a rare exception, and after humbling defeats in their first two pool games, they were the underdogs against a Lebanese squad almost entirely consisting of Australian-born players.
But this was no mismatch.
Trailing by two late, France was denied a match-winning try when Lebanon just grounded the ball in the in-goal.
France's Arthur Mourgue then kicked a two-point field goal to send it to golden point shortly after, and in the first period of extra time, Cesar Rouge slotted a one-pointer.
The scenes were beautiful, joyous, crushing, devastating, a chaotic melting pot of emotions savoured by the growing crowd of largely Tongan and Samoan fans.
But it was disallowed for an escort. And so it went on.
The Cedars' Alex Conti missed a long-range penalty goal, which was collected by Mourgue.
He should've held onto it. A more experienced player under this sort of pressure would've taken the tackle, and the quick breather.
But he went for glory, a chip and chase that could've been his crowning glory.
Instead it became his never-ending nightmare.
Abbas Miski gleefully grabbed the goodies, and strolled the short distance to unleash mayhem unlike anything else we've seen at this tournament so far.
Most of the 30,000 tickets for this game were snapped up by Tongan and Samoan fans.
But a healthy contingent of Sydney's huge Lebanese diaspora turned up, and they were in a heady delirium, as the players danced dazed but delighted, alongside Lebanese drummers on the sidelines.
"It was the saddest I've been this whole tournament and then the happiest I've been this whole tournament. I don't even know what to feel," Lebanon captain Alex Twal told Channel 7.
"We've got plumbers, electricians, foreman, builders … these blokes came here just to have a crack and they're playing against some of the best in the world.
"Abbas, he's a winger, he's never played back row. For him to come up with a play like that, it's true Lebanese spirit.
"I've got goosebumps. I love being Lebanese."
Twal was born a stone's throw from this stadium at Westmead. He played his junior footy for the Parramatta City Titans and his entire NRL career has been with Wests Tigers.
Born and raised in Australia, he has a Jordanian father and Lebanese mother.
It is a story similar for so many children of migrants in Australia. An identity that is multidimensional, not having to remain in one neat box, but able to feel connection to many places, roots spread near and far.
And so often sport is the powerful vehicle that helps drive that message home.
That is why even though this game was a dead rubber, a result that ostensibly wouldn't change the world, it still meant something more than footy.
Because for people who have sometimes felt like they're between worlds, between cultures, there is somewhere they belong.
The hundreds of Lebanese fans who sang and marched to the beat of their traditional drums to the stadium today felt it, and no doubt many more in Australia's sizeable Lebanese community.
This may be the end of the line for the Cedars, in the short term at least.
They are ineligible for future tournaments having been downgraded to an affiliate member by the International Rugby League.
Meaning, for now, their greatest World Cup moment may very well be their last.
And the French must take heart from showing fight till the very end.
They were a team always up against it when facing players who have had league in their blood from birth.
And there will be hope they can try to inspire some sort of renaissance in the sport in the Northern Hemisphere, where it is currently on life support.
But rising from the ashes is what rugby league does best.

Explainer-How US news organizations will make midterm race calls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:12:01 UTC
20:12:01 KST

Explainer-How US news organizations will make midterm race calls
Nov 1 - On Tuesday night, newsrooms across the US will call winners in one of the country's most closely contested midterm election cycles in recent years, long before all the votes are counted.
Most television networks and digital outlets rely on two providers for vote counts: the Associated Press or election-data firm Decision Desk HQ.
Some news outlets such as the Wall Street Journal and MS NOW will rely on the AP for race calls, while others like Fox News and CBS News will make their own projections based on the AP vote count, exit polls, early-vote totals and their own statistical modeling.
The first calls will start soon after polls begin to close in the United States, first with Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. ET (2300 GMT), and shortly after in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia at 7 p.m. (0000 GMT on November 4). In certain races there may be an instant call if much of the voting has already taken place.
Low public trust complicates race calls for news outlets. While more than 60% of Americans have some confidence in news organizations to report accurate election results, only 32% have high confidence, with Democrats more trusting than Republicans, an October poll for the Medill Local News Initiative and the Alliance for Trust in Media found.
While most of the major TV networks all use the same AP vote count tabulation to make their calls, the ones who decide to call winners use a proprietary mix of their own data analysis, historical models, exit poll interviews and expert judgment to call races when they determine that they've become a statistical certainty.
Here's how it works:
AP COUNTS AND RACE CALLS
The AP, a nonprofit newsroom supported by member newspapers, has counted votes in every US election since 1848, working with a national network of reporters and election officials to verify results.
For the 2026 midterms, the AP said it would deploy more than 4,000 reporters at county election offices and local polling locations, gathering and providing data to the decision desks at ABC News, CBS News, Fox, CNN and NBC News. ABC, CBS, CNN and NBC also rely on research firm SSRS, which acquired exit-polling company Edison Research in 2025.
When making calls, the AP uses vote totals and estimates how many votes remain uncounted based on past voting patterns and early-vote data. It calls a race only when the trailing candidate cannot catch up.
DDHQ COUNTS AND RACE CALLS
DDHQ collects vote counts from official state sources, usually secretaries of state or state election departments.
The firm uses statistical analysis, modeling and expert review to project election winners. Its clients include NewsNation, the Hill and Newsmax, and it recently signed up X, the social network owned by Elon Musk.
It uses automated software to repeatedly check official election websites and collect newly posted vote totals in addition to using reporters on the ground. DDHQ says roughly 80% of all votes are processed by pulling data directly from official election sites, or by manually monitoring election sites. The remaining counts are collected by reporters.
It calculates the percentage of ballots counted by dividing the votes reported by election officials by its estimated total turnout for a race. It determines remaining votes by subtracting reported votes from this overall turnout estimate, which is refined on election night using actual data.
Final projections require unanimous team agreement and a sign-off from the head of data science, Scott Tranter. "We’re preparing to have several thousand people working on election night to gather data," Tranter told Reuters.
RACE PROJECTIONS CAN BE WRONG
Retractions are rare, but both the AP and DDHQ have withdrawn calls in the past.
In 2025, DDHQ withdrew a projection in the Seattle mayor's race. Earlier this year, DDHQ withdrew its call in the Democratic primary for a special election in New Jersey's 11th Congressional District after Election Day vote counts shifted the race away from its initial projection.
In 2018, after a projected winner fell behind in California's 21st Congressional District, AP posted on its race-call account that it was retracting the call because Democrat T.J. Cox had taken the lead in the vote count.
THE NEWS OUTLETS MAKING RACE CALLS
Fox's decision desk will be making its own calls in all statewide races as well as the calls for control of the House and control of the Senate. It uses the AP vote count and applies its own analysis.
MS NOW, covering its first midterms since separating from NBCUniversal's cable portfolio, will rely on the AP's race calls and a review by its elections team.
The New York Times relies on AP calls for most contests but independently reviews competitive races using precinct-level data and its Needle model. It may make a call before or after the AP.
Bloomberg does not make its own race calls. For election results, it uses established third-party sources. Reuters will also be citing the race calls from other news organizations.
The Washington Post did not respond to requests for comment on how it will call races. REUTERS

Trump heads to Iowa, Kansas for rallies before midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:07:09 UTC
20:07:09 KST

Republicans get boost from Michigan Democrat's endorsement, face legal setback in Alaska
WASHINGTON/ANCHORAGE, Alaska, Nov 1 - Two days before Tuesday's midterm elections, President Donald Trump's Republicans got an unexpected boost in Michigan from a prominent Democratic endorsement but suffered a setback in Alaska where a federal judge dismissed a legal challenge.
US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democrats' Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed in a bitterly contested race, on Sunday publicly backed Republican candidate Mike Rogers, threatening to worsen divisions in a state viewed as crucial to Democratic hopes of retaking the US Senate.
"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," Stevens said in a video posted to social media.
Thirty-five Senate seats and all 435 House of Representatives seats are on the ballot on Tuesday. Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. Polls show Democrats are favored to win a majority of the House and are locked in a tight battle for control of the Senate, where a handful of races are likely to determine the outcome.
Trump, en route to a Sunday rally in Iowa, told reporters that he would reach out to Stevens to thank her for the endorsement, which he called "a smart thing to do because El-Sayed would destroy our country."
But the Trump administration's attempt to intervene in Alaska's Senate race faltered on Sunday when a federal judge dismissed the US Justice Department's lawsuit seeking to block certification of the results if Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan narrowly loses.
The Justice Department argued voters may be confused by the presence of a challenger named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the same ballot.
If Democrats take control of the House or Senate, they could block Trump's legislative agenda for his final two years in office and launch investigations of an administration that has so far faced largely compliant Republican majorities. The White House has been preparing to implement portions of Trump's agenda without the aid of Congress.
More than 52 million Americans have already voted in person or by mail, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, a record for a midterm and up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day in 2022.
MICHIGAN RIFT
In Michigan, Stevens' endorsement of Rogers came on the same day she was supposed to appear with El-Sayed in a show of party unity. But the planned event unraveled after Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group's ad that she said blames Israel for high grocery prices.
"We can't stand with hate," Stevens told reporters on Sunday, standing alongside Rogers after joining him at a Detroit church service.
El-Sayed's campaign recently asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day so as "not to distract from the central issues of the campaign," a person familiar with the matter said.
Republicans sought to take advantage of Stevens' move. "This is courage in politics in America today," Rogers said. "When you see a party, and at least a sliver of the party, veering off into the virulent hate that they have been spewing toward a group of people, it gets dangerous."
Later on Sunday at the Iowa rally, Trump repeated previous claims that El-Sayed is a "jihadist."
El-Sayed, who has been subjected to a campaign of racist and Islamophobic attacks, has rejected such accusations and called questions about his loyalty to the United States “shameful.”
He declined to directly address Stevens' endorsement on Sunday, saying he was focused on other issues.
"I want to get money out of politics," El-Sayed told reporters. "I want to put money back in pockets."
It was unclear whether the move would affect the outcome of the race. Polls indicate that El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support. He holds a nearly 4-point lead against Rogers according to the Real Clear Polling estimate.
A number of Stevens' congressional staff resigned over the endorsement, according to reports from CNN and The Hill.
Stevens' longtime chief of staff, Justin German, could not immediately be reached to verify the reports, which quoted a statement from him saying, "as of this morning, many members of our team have resigned, including myself." The statement described him as "shocked and heartbroken" by Stevens' endorsement.
ALASKA RULING
In Alaska, a federal judge rejected a Trump administration lawsuit against the state.
The Department of Justice had asked the court to block certification and order an investigation if the outcome indicated that voters may have voted for challenger Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. when they intended to vote for the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan.
The issue has roiled the campaign over the last several days after the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. into the race as a spoiler.
The senator said on Sunday he would accept the results of Tuesday's election even as the Trump administration presses a criminal investigation into the issue. But Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, has suggested he may not certify a victory by Peltola, and the incumbent Sullivan declined to say whether he would support efforts to refuse certification.
He joined his party colleagues in accusing the other Sullivan of trying to confuse voters with his similar name.
"They got the decoy guy on the ballot," the senator told CNN's "State of the Union" program. "I'm sure I'm going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery. So what I say to Alaskans is, 'Don't let them get away with the tricks.'"
Peltola has denied involvement, and Sullivan Jr. has denied coordinating with Peltola's campaign. REUTERS

Trump White House maps path to govern without Congress if Democrats win
