Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:32:46 UTC
19:32:46 KST

Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
A remarkable 18-million-year-old fossil discovered in Egypt suggests that the evolutionary roots of humans and other modern apes may lie in an unexpected part of Africa.
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center (MUVP)
- Summary:
- A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.
- Share:
An ancient ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging a long-standing theory about where the ancestors of modern apes, including humans, first evolved. The remarkable find suggests that a crucial chapter of our evolutionary history may have unfolded much farther north than scientists previously believed.
The newly identified species, named Masripithecus moghraensis, lived approximately 17 to 18 million years ago during the Early Miocene. Its fossilized remains were recovered from Wadi Moghra in northern Egypt, making it the first definitive fossil ape ever discovered in North Africa.
The discovery, described in a study published March 26, 2026, in Science, comes from an international team at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center (Egypt) and the University of Southern California (USA). Their findings suggest that northern Africa and the Middle East may have played a central role in the emergence of the evolutionary lineage that eventually gave rise to all living apes.
A Missing Piece of the Ape Evolutionary Puzzle
For decades, scientists believed that early apes and their close relatives were concentrated primarily in regions farther south in Africa. Fossil sites in North Africa had produced remains of ancient monkeys from the Early Miocene, but researchers had never found definitive evidence of apes from the same period.
That gap helped shape prevailing theories about ape evolution. Although younger ape fossils have been discovered across Africa, Europe, and Asia, their evolutionary relationships and geographic origins remain subjects of scientific debate.
The newly discovered Egyptian fossil may help explain what was missing from this picture.
"We spent five years searching for this kind of fossil because, when we look closely at the early ape family tree, it becomes clear that something is missing -- and North Africa holds that missing piece," said Hesham Sallam, a paleontologist at Mansoura University and senior author of the study.
The discovery is especially important for understanding the origins of crown Hominoidea, the evolutionary group that includes the last common ancestor of all living apes and its descendants. Today, that group encompasses gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and humans.
Scientists suspect that the incomplete geographic distribution of ancient fossils has obscured important details about when and where this group first emerged.
An 18-Million-Year-Old Ape With Unusual Teeth
The fossils were uncovered during expeditions in 2023 and 2024 by researchers from the Sallam Lab at Wadi Moghra, a well-known fossil site in northern Egypt.
The team named the species Masripithecus moghraensis. Its genus name combines Masr (مصر), the Arabic name for Egypt, with píthēkos, the Greek word for ape. The species name honors Wadi Moghra, where the fossils were found.
Although the remains consist only of lower jaw material, they contain an unusual combination of anatomical features that distinguishes the animal from other apes of similar age.
The jaw is exceptionally sturdy, with remarkably large canine and premolar teeth. Its molars also have rounded chewing surfaces covered in pronounced textures. These characteristics offer valuable clues about the foods the animal could eat and how it survived in its environment.
Researchers believe Masripithecus primarily consumed fruit but had teeth powerful enough to process tougher foods when necessary. This dietary flexibility may have been an important survival advantage.
"Together, they suggest that Masripithecus was adapted for versatility. The study interprets its chewing anatomy as evidence of a flexible, mainly fruit-based diet, with the ability to process harder foods such as nuts or seeds when needed. This flexibility would have helped Masripithecus to thrive at a time when climatic changes were leading to more pronounced seasonality in northern Africa and Arabia," said Shorouq Al-Ashqar, a researcher at the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center and a first author of the study.
As seasonal differences became more pronounced, the availability of certain foods likely changed throughout the year. An ape capable of eating a wider range of foods would have been better equipped to cope with those fluctuations.
A Discovery That Challenges the Ape Family Tree
The importance of Masripithecus extends well beyond its unusual anatomy. When researchers examined where the species belonged on the evolutionary family tree, they uncovered a surprising result.
Their analysis suggests that Masripithecus was more closely related to living apes than any known ape species from the Early Miocene of East Africa.
To investigate these relationships, the team used advanced statistical techniques known as Bayesian methods. These approaches allow scientists to compare different evolutionary possibilities and estimate how strongly the available evidence supports each one.
The researchers combined anatomical information from living and extinct apes with genetic evidence from living species. They also incorporated the geological ages of fossil specimens, helping them estimate when different evolutionary branches separated.
By bringing these sources of evidence together, the scientists reconstructed relationships among ancient and modern apes and explored where their shared ancestors may have lived.
The results challenge the long-standing assumption that the evolutionary roots of all living apes were centered in or around East Africa.
Could North Africa Be the Birthplace of Modern Apes?
Additional analyses of ancient animal distributions pointed toward northern Africa and the Middle East as the most likely geographic home of the common ancestor of all living apes.
That ancestor is estimated to have lived during the Early Miocene, an interval spanning roughly 23 million to 16 million years ago. This was an important period in primate evolution, when early ape lineages were diversifying, and environments were undergoing substantial changes.
Geography may help explain why this region was so important.
Millions of years ago, Africa, Arabia, and Asia were moving toward a new geological arrangement. As the African and Arabian tectonic plates traveled northward and approached the final stages of their collision with Asia, the connections between these landmasses began to change.
Sea levels also rose and fell, periodically reducing the stretches of water that separated different regions. At certain times, these changes made it easier for animals to move between Africa and Eurasia.
Northern Africa and the Middle East therefore occupied a potentially crucial position in the movement and evolution of ancient mammals, including apes.
The discovery of Masripithecus helps connect previously separated fossil records from Africa and Eurasia. Its presence suggests that apes were already evolving into distinct forms in this region before new land connections made it possible for them to expand into Europe and Asia.
Rather than being a peripheral location in ape evolution, the region may have been an important center of evolutionary diversification.
Scientists Rethink Where Our Ancient Ape Ancestors Lived
The findings have even prompted some of the researchers to reconsider ideas they held throughout their careers.
Erik Seiffert, a paleontologist at the University of Southern California and co-author of the study, explained how the evidence has changed his understanding of ape origins.
"For my entire career, I considered it probable that the common ancestor of all living apes lived in or around East Africa. But this new discovery, and our new and novel analyses of hominoid phylogeny and biogeography, now strongly challenge that idea. And, importantly, the likelihood of this scenario doesn't depend on Masripithecus -- but it is very much consistent with it."
Importantly, the researchers are not claiming that Masripithecus was a direct ancestor of humans or even necessarily the direct ancestor of living apes. Instead, its position on the evolutionary family tree provides evidence about where the broader ancestral lineage may have originated.
The distinction matters because humans emerged much later in evolutionary history. The Egyptian fossil offers clues to an earlier stage, when the distant ancestors shared by humans and other living apes were evolving.
The team's findings also suggest that the traditional emphasis on East African fossils may have provided an incomplete view of this much older evolutionary story.
More Evolutionary Secrets May Be Hidden in Egypt
Although the discovery offers compelling new evidence, scientists still have much to learn about Masripithecus and the early history of modern apes.
Only part of the animal's jaw has been recovered, leaving important questions about its overall appearance, body size, movement, and behavior unanswered. Additional fossils could provide a more complete picture of how this ancient species lived and how it relates to other early apes.
The researchers believe that further exploration of North Africa and the Middle East could reveal additional species and help clarify when and where the major branches of the modern ape family tree began to emerge.
For now, Masripithecus moghraensis offers a striking reminder that even fundamental ideas about our distant evolutionary past can change when scientists uncover evidence in places that have received relatively little attention.
A fossil jaw preserved for nearly 18 million years may be helping scientists piece together a chapter of evolutionary history that was missing all along.

7 Best Travel Mugs (2026): Insulated, Leakproof, and Self-Heating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:31:00 UTC
19:31:00 KST

If there’s one thing WIRED staffers love almost as much as tech gear, it’s caffeine. We take our coffee so seriously that we don't suffer fools when it comes to travel mugs. Through painstaking testing that's yielded spilled lattes, lukewarm brews, and dented thermoses, WIRED testers have pinpointed the very best travel mugs available. Whether you need a sturdy option that can survive the chaos of an NYC morning commute or a self-heating tumbler for all-day sipping, consider yourself covered.
Want more help leveling up your morning brew? Be sure to check out our guides to the Best Coffee Subscriptions, Best Coffee Grinders, Best Espresso Machines, Best French Presses, Best Portable Coffee Makers, Best AeroPress Coffee Makers, and How to Make Better Coffee at Home.
Updated November 2026: We've added the BrüMate Strova and Ember Tumbler 2, and information on what to look for in a travel mug. We've also updated links and prices throughout.
The Best Travel Coffee Mug
The Hydro Flask Coffee with Flex Sip Lid is my go-to travel mug. It’s low-maintenance and built like a tank, making it a forgiving choice for the clumsiest of sippers. The brand's powder coating can handle clammy hands, and the 16-ounce tumbler fits into most car cup holders.
It's also a multipurpose mug that isn't limited to housing just your steaming morning brew. Because Hydro Flask wide-mouth lids are conveniently interchangeable, you can swap in a straw lid for cold beverages (or anything else you'd like to drink). And if you purchase the travel mug directly from Hydro Flask, you can get it engraved with text or a graphic, in addition to picking from the 10-plus available color options.
A Mug That Can Handle Your Mornings
Imagine sitting by a campfire under the stars, sipping hot cocoa, then waking up at sunrise to a cup of coffee by the lake. A handleless mug just doesn't do that scene justice. Hydro Flask's travel coffee mug brings that camp aesthetic to life. It also just feels great to hold in any setting—including for morning dog walks or while you get yourself ready for your day at home. The slider lid keeps out curious bugs and helps to slow the release of heat, but it’s not leakproof.
I also appreciate the mug's stainless steel rim that's smooth to sip from sans lid. Just note that it’s not TPU powder-coated like most Hydro Flask bottles, so it's a bit less grippy and you’ll have to hand wash it.
Best Value
If you’re a fan of the Owala FreeSip’s spout, then the lightweight SmoothSip Slider will not disappoint. Its triple-layer insulation helps to keep drinks hot for around six hours or cold for 24. The slider lid works fine for everyday use and didn't leak when I flipped it upside down. But I still wouldn’t toss it into a bag because of how easy it is to unlock. Alongside being available in fun colors, Owala also releases limited-edition designs you can shop. Also notable is that Owala bottles are lead-, BPA-, and phthalate-free.
Best Flippable
After an unfortunate entanglement with a coffee mug and my computer, there was a period of time when the only bar where everybody knew my name was the Genius Bar. Now, lid security is my top priority for any liquid I tote around. For that singular concern, BrüMate's cupholder-friendly Strova gets a W from me. The brand claims its patented BevLock lid is fully leakproof, and after putting the mug through its paces—flipping, shaking, and dropping it—before I even considered placing it in my purse to intermingle with my water-sensitive electronics, I came to trust the promise: I couldn't make a single drop of coffee slip through the closed-mouthpiece edges or perimeter of the lid. Further, the mug's ceramic-lined interior both protects the temperature and taste of whatever you're drinking, and it comes in more than a dozen colors and designs any aesthete would be happy to show off.
The compromise you'll have to make is that the Strova is a bit awkward to sip. The mouth opening is quite small, running in a thin, tight line, like an expressionless face, as opposed to larger, easier-to-sip options that might conjure more of an open-mouthed cackle. The construction means you have to tip the mug up past your nose to sip when it's half full or less. This may look a bit aggro while you're drinking, but it’s frankly a small price to pay for confidently avoiding spillage. —Alexis Berger
Best Self-Heating
A long morning commute can be a slog. Add in successive underwhelming sips of tepid coffee, and you're less and less likely to walk into work bright-eyed and bushy-tailed. For owners of the Ember Tumbler 2, that vignette is mere fiction. This travel tumbler, from the brand that normalized spendy warming mugs, holds a generous 16 ounces, fits into a car cupholder, and—most importantly—keeps your beverage hot. It claims to have a battery life of three-plus hours, but I noticed my brew losing its steam after about two. You can control the temperature on the tumbler itself by pressing a button on the bottom that toggles between five heat levels, or you can choose a precise temp via the Bluetooth-connected app. But if you're driving, you'll probably just want to default to the hottest temperature of 145 degrees Fahrenheit before you depart.
The Tumbler 2's slim profile is easy to pick up with one hand while you keep the other firmly on the steering wheel. Do keep the tumbler upright in that cupholder when you're not sipping, though. It dripped when I flipped it upside down, even with the sipping lid's slider closed, so I certainly wouldn't throw it into a purse or computer bag. (The tumbler also comes with a screw-off, top-handle lid, which is less leaky, but also less useful.) Drips aside, the drinking experience is nice, with the lid's smooth texture and curved lip allowing for easy, natural sips.
If cupholder compatibility isn't your priority, you might consider the new 16-ounce Ember Mug 3 ($160), the first edition of the brand's classic line that's available in this larger capacity. It's not formally a travel mug, but it does come with a sipping lid that helps your drink stay warm longer, making it a nice option for the work-from-home crowd. Both the Mug 3 and Tumbler 2 are conveniently top-rack dishwasher safe. —Alexis Berger
Best for Iced Coffee and Matcha Lattes
Fellow nailed it with the Carter Move. This sleek mug has a ceramic-coated interior that doesn't hold scent or taste, meaning your matcha today won’t taste like yesterday’s coffee. A 270-degree twist locks the lid effectively; I’ve tossed it in my bag without a second thought and have never experienced annoying leaks or regrettable spills. The included splash guard keeps ice cubes from smacking your teeth and protects against drips and splatters while you walk and drive. Fellow also drops limited-edition colors and sometimes releases design collaborations with artists. The mug fits into most car cup holders and is conveniently compatible with the Cold Lid + Straw ($12) and the Carry Lid ($12), allowing flexibility in how you drink and tote it.
The Carter Move fits most standard drippers but isn’t compatible with the AeroPress Coffee Maker or Prismo AeroPress Attachment. If that's a deal-breaker, you might consider the Carter Wide ($30), a great alternative to the Move that works with most manual coffee brewers. In that case, you'll have to compromise on a splash guard, which I really like in the Move.
Best Budget Mug With a Handle
For less than $25, the Ello Campy delivers a nostalgic charm, harking back to the enameled camp cups that ooze 20th-century Americana. The Campy isn’t enameled—just painted to look like it—but it pulls off the effect well. The cork-lined handle stays cool even when piping-hot brew fills the mug, while the vacuum insulation retains your drink’s heat. The screw-on plastic lid is designed to avoid heat conduction, and the mug also features a sliding lever for sipping. It’s not spill-proof, but if you hold it upright, it should keep its contents contained. However, it doesn't fit into cupholders, which may be a deal-breaker for drivers, and the paint is likely to chip off with wear.
Honorable Mentions
Some travel mugs are perfectly good enough—just not as great as the top picks above.
KeepCup 12-ounce Coffee Cup for $31: This double-walled, insulated mug aims to replicate (and replace) paper cups from coffee shops. It's a solid option if you're looking for a glass cup (the rubber grip is plastic, though). That said, it’s not the best at preserving the temperature of your drink, and the lid is a tad wobbly.
Oxo Good Grips Thermal Mug for $29: WIRED reviewed this bottle in 2022, and it earned high marks for its sturdy build and dishwasher-friendliness. But since it's older, it now fluctuates in and out of stock.
REI Co-op Camp Mug for $23+: REI's stainless steel cup is decent enough, but it doesn't particularly stand out in the wider category of travel mugs. Our tester says the exterior coating was tough enough to show no scratches, even after knocking it over a few times outside.
Zojirushi Stainless Steel Mug for $40: In addition to having a lid lock that's effective for avoiding accidental spillage, the mug is also a great option for temperature control: A reviewer once left tea in it for 18 hours (unintentionally) and discovered the drink was still hot when she finally opened the lid. The downside is that the cover has three separate parts—a mouthpiece, a gasket, and a lid—that are deeply ridged and annoying to clean.
Avoid These Mugs
They can't all be winners. These two cups fell short compared to our favorites.
Greens Steel Beast 20-Ounce Insulated Tumbler for $23: The Beast Tumbler has more than 81,000 positive reviews on Amazon, but the rubber seal around the lid easily comes out of place. That meant it leaked like a sieve.
Toaks Titanium Double Wall 450-Milliliter Cup for $40: More often than not, we at WIRED champion Toaks gear as an affordable source of titanium camp cookware. But this mug costs $12 more than the Hydro Flask pick above, and has a rougher finish.
Frequently Asked Questions
What to Know About Lead Soldering
Since WIRED editors began testing reusable water bottles and travel mugs, we've discovered that some brands use lead soldering to seal their insulated bottles. While exposure is unlikely (you'd have to drop or damage the bottle or mug to detach the lead pellet), we still believe it's an unnecessary risk, especially since many of our top choices use safer sealing methods. We've removed mugs from brands that have admitted to using lead in their products.
What to Look for in a Travel Mug
There's no shortage of travel mugs available to buy. Narrowing down the best options for you depends on your priorities and how a given mug can satisfy them. Here are key considerations for selecting a great travel mug:
- Leakproof design: When you're buying a mug with the express purpose of toting it around with you, I'd argue that its most important quality should be holding the beverage without leaks or spills. Some travel mugs feature patented locking technology that promises no drips at all, while other models are less intensely engineered—and sometimes the latter works perfectly well. For example, if you're using your mug to sip a coffee during your morning walk or while taking in the sunrise during a camping trip, you might not need the same promise of leakproofing as someone who tosses their mug into their laptop bag.
- Material: Travel mugs are often made from stainless steel, ceramic, or BPA-free plastic—and often a combination of all three. Glass mugs are also available, though less common.
- Stainless steel is a common material in travel mugs. It's effective for retaining heat, especially options that are double-wall–insulated, which basically means the mug will keep your drink hot from the inside without burning your hand from the outside. Stainless steel mugs are often dishwasher-safe, but not microwave-safe, and can sometimes give off a bit of a metallic taste into beverages.
- Some mugs have a smooth, ceramic lining on the inside, which helps to preserve the taste of the beverage—i.e., your afternoon tea won't have a hint of yesterday's coffee—and protect against that metallic hint of a stainless-steel option.
- Plastic appears often in travel-mug lids. Prioritize options that are free of bisphenol A (BPA), a known endocrine disruptor.
- Glass, like ceramic, provides a neutral taste, but it can be heavy and is typically less durable than other materials, opening you to the messy risk of a shattered mug.
- Shape: If you're commuting in a car with your travel mug, you'll want to ensure it fits into your cupholder, and if you're carrying it with you on walks, you'll likely want it to have a handle.
- Price: Our top-pick travel mugs currently span in price from less than $20 to nearly $200. If having precise temperature control of your coffee at any given moment matters to you, a spendy mug may be worth the investment. Most of the picks, though, hover around $30. —Alexis Berger
How I Tested
I’ve been running on caffeine since I was 12 (sorry, Mom and Dad) because I took middle school way too seriously. Fifteen years later, caffeine is basically part of my personality, and I’ve been unofficially testing travel mugs for most of my life.
To officially test the mugs in this guide, I, along with other editors, drank both coffee and tea at piping-hot and ice-cold extremes, rating heat retention and taste, ensuring no picks have any hint of metallic notes. Shape and design matter, too: How comfortable is it to hold a given mug? Does it fit into a car cup holder? Does it offer additional features worth considering? I aggressively shook the mugs that promised to be leakproof and dropped those that claimed to be durable from about 4 feet high onto both wood and concrete surfaces to evaluate how well they held up. Finally, travel mugs can be a pain to scrub, so I factored in ease of cleaning.
Simply put, I need a travel mug that pulls its weight. If it didn't keep my coffee warm, my bag dry, and make my life a little easier, it didn’t make the list.

Chatbots Are Leading Hikers Astray, With Dangerous Consequences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

This story originally appeared on High Country News and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
By the time the three hikers called for help from a rocky face on Mount Shasta in Northern California, they’d made a series of bad decisions. They didn’t bring enough food, and they’d overestimated their fitness. Instead of turning back in late afternoon when they hadn’t yet reached the top, they summited at 7:30 pm and had to descend in the dark. Their lack of preparation and poor planning, as they admitted later, came partly from relying on Google’s artificial intelligence chatbot Gemini. By morning, they were lost on a gnarly part of the mountain, and one hiker had banged up his knee.
“We get plenty of people who come unprepared or don’t do any research at all. To these guys’ credit, they did try,” said Nick Meyers, US Forest Service program manager of the Mount Shasta Wilderness Climbing and Avalanche Center, which responded to the call. “But I think they kind of turned their brains off.”
The three 20-year-olds aren’t the only ones making missteps in wild spaces with the help of artificial intelligence. Another Mount Shasta visitor pitched her tent near a “No Camping” sign, insisting she had a right to do so because AI told her she could, Meyers said. His team also encountered a man wandering around at a trailhead with an AI-generated map that showed prominent features on the wrong side of a nearby mountain. In British Columbia, a helicopter crew rescued a 16-year-old hiker from a ledge in the Widowmaker Arete on the back of Crown Mountain. The teen had used Anthropic’s chatbot Claude to help him plan his trip. News stories focused on that fact went viral across Canada and the US, though the hiker said later that he also consulted Google Maps and the popular hiking app, AllTrails.
Grand Teton National Park in Wyoming has also seen a marked uptick over the past year in the percentage of visitors who report using AI for travel information, said Park Superintendent Chip Jenkins. “It went from zero to 26 percent. And I’m guessing that curve is not going to flatten.”
It remains to be seen whether increasing AI use will lead to an increase in backcountry accidents and search and rescues, Meyers said. His office, which oversees a massive wilderness area in Northern California, averages a dozen rescues each year, and 2026 is shaping up to be an average year. Calls to search and rescue in Wyoming have actually gone down compared to 2025, with only 312 calls so far in 2026 compared to a total of 466 in 2025 and 377 in 2024.
Some search and rescue veterans say that AI chatbots are just the latest tools giving people new ways to get into trouble. Roughly a decade ago, when hikers, backpackers, climbers and other outdoor enthusiasts began to source their destinations, inspiration, and information from Instagram and other social media sites, they faced sometimes deadly consequences. Before that, hikers and other recreationists were led astray by their reliance on Google Maps or smartphone connectivity.
“Over the last two decades, there’s been a phenomenal push in the media to get more people outdoors, and consequently we have more people outdoors and recreating,” said Jim Moss, a Colorado-based recreation attorney and search and rescue volunteer. It’s still unclear how questionable advice from a robot will influence all those people, he added.
Turning to an AI chatbot for guidance does come with unique risks. Chatbots can “hallucinate” persuasively presenting misinformation as real, and their use can lead to a phenomenon called “cognitive surrender,” said Chris Flathmann, a human-centered computing professor at Clemson University in South Carolina who has studied AI and search and rescue.
“When humans work with AI systems, they can get so deep into it they give up thinking critically for themselves,” he explained. When AI pretends to be an expert on an unfamiliar topic, “you can’t call BS on that because you don’t have the expertise.” And once you stop thinking critically, it can be hard to start again, especially in a stressful backcountry situation.
Chatbots also tend to tell users what they want to hear and to do so with authority regardless of whether the sources they’re consulting are reliable, Flathmann and others said. Claude or ChatGPT might answer a query with extensive directions and advice that sound credible but are actually scraped from Reddit threads and out-of-date YouTube videos—and might even be entirely fabricated.
TikTok and Instagram may offer a viewer inspiration, but AI tends to offer instructions—right or wrong—as well as encouragement, Flathmann said. “AI isn’t trying to trick people into going up mountains, but I think it’s the natural evolution of what happens when you get a tool like this.”
Regardless of the resources recreators use, experts have the same advice: When you’re headed to a new place, make sure you double-check your information against reliable, authoritative sources like up-to-date public-land agency maps and websites, trail association websites, or guidebooks. Even better, talk to a real-live guide, a national forest official, or a park ranger.
“If you’re going to go into places that will kill you,” Meyers said, “you should take your planning seriously.”

BJP targets Rahul Gandhi, Congress over 1984 violence as INDIA bloc holds Delhi rally
NEW DELHI: BJP on Sunday organised a protest march in West Delhi's Hari Nagar, demanding an apology from the Congress and its leader Rahul Gandhi for the 1984 anti-Sikh violence, as the INDIA bloc held its 'Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao' rally at Ramlila Maidan.Leading the march, Union minister Hardeep Singh Puri described the killings of Sikhs in 1984 as a “well-planned” massacre rather than a riot or spontaneous outbreak of violence. He cited official figures showing that 2,733 Sikhs were killed in Delhi during the violence.
“It was a well-planned massacre and a genocide and crime against humanity as pointed by the courts, not any spontaneous riot. Congress leaders should think seriously about it,” Puri said, addressing protesters before the march, according to news agency PTI.Delhi chief minister Rekha Gupta, Delhi BJP president and Union minister of state Harsh Malhotra, Delhi Minister Manjinder Singh Sirsa and senior advocate H S Phoolka were among those who participated. Several Sikh leaders and members of the community also joined the march from the Sikh-majority areas of Hari Nagar towards Tilak Nagar.Protesters wearing black headbands raised slogans against the Congress and Gandhi, demanding an apology for the killings.
Puri recalls 1984 violence, questions Congress over apology
Puri said he was in Geneva when the violence broke out in 1984 and recalled how his Hindu friends protected his parents, who were living in Delhi.He rejected the description of the killings as spontaneous violence following the assassination of then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi on October 31, 1984.
“When mobs were arriving at the houses of our Sikh brothers in Delhi, they were not carrying ordinary voter lists. Because on a voter list, a name might say Harnam Singh and Harnam Singh could be from Madhya Pradesh, or Haryana, could be a Jat, a Rajput, or wearing a safa [turban]… no! The preparations were made for it,” he said.Puri also referred to the Delhi High Court's observations on the violence and said the killings should not be described as riots.“Even now, a term is often used referring to it as ‘riots’ or ‘a riot.’ These were not riots. Riots are when two groups fight each other. Here, one group… 2,733 people were killed in cold blood in Delhi. Narsanhar [massacre/carnage] is the right word. In English, narsanhar means ‘genocide.’ And as far as I recall, the Delhi High Court specifically used the term: ‘This is a crime against humanity.’ Genocide and a crime against humanity,” he said.He questioned the INDIA bloc's decision to hold its rally on November 1, saying the wounds of the violence had not healed.“Even today, I believe our community and our nation have not fully accepted or forgiven what happened in 1984. Nor did they ever apologise for it properly. Did they really have to choose this very day?” Puri said.He added that it was the responsibility of citizens to remember the violence to ensure that such incidents did not recur.
Rekha Gupta targets Gandhi family over 1984 killings
Gupta, who wore a black headband during the march, accused the Congress and the Gandhi family of failing to acknowledge the suffering of Sikh families affected by the violence.“The Sikh community in India is asking those who carry a copy of the Constitution in their pockets and invoke democracy today: what about what happened in November 1984? Was that not a murder of democracy, a murder committed by the Gandhi family itself?” she said.
She also referred to the Emergency imposed by Indira Gandhi in 1975 and accused the Congress leadership of repeatedly undermining democratic institutions.“Thousands of Sikh families are weeping tears of blood, still grieving the loss of their loved ones in that Congress-sponsored massacre... yet they have never received justice. Has the Gandhi family ever uttered even a few words about them?” Gupta said.Malhotra also criticised the INDIA bloc for holding its rally on November 1, alleging that the timing hurt the sentiments of the Sikh community.“Congress has not apologised to the country or the Sikh community for this incident to date,” he said, adding that the rally was an attempt to disrupt normal life in Delhi.The 1984 anti-Sikh violence followed the assassination of Indira Gandhi on October 31 that year. According to official figures cited by Puri, 2,733 people were killed in Delhi.
BJP's protest march was held alongside the INDIA bloc's demonstration against alleged irregularities in electoral rolls during the Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.The opposition alliance has demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.The two political events prompted heightened security arrangements across the capital, with police and paramilitary personnel deployed along the rally routes and at key locations.

Thousands joined a protest led by opposition politicians in India's capital on Sunday, renewing demands for the country's election chief to resign over an overhaul of voter lists they say unfairly benefits the ruling party.
The nationwide revision of electoral rolls has sparked political disputes and street protests in the world's largest democracy over the last month.
The Election Commission says the initiative is necessary to ensure accurate voter lists, but the opposition claims it is being manipulated to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Both the Election Commission and the BJP deny the accusations.
On Sunday, protesters led by opposition Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi chanted "vote thief, leave your seat" and beat drums while marching from central parts of New Delhi to Ramlila Maidan, a large outdoor venue.
"I have been a voter since I was 18 and now I find myself struck off the list," protester Nandita, 46, told AFP, giving only one name.
"It's important to be here because of the way things are going. The cost of living is going up... The only option is to take to the streets peacefully."
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online youth-led protest movement, has also thrown its weight behind the campaign against the voter-roll revision.
The overhaul of India's voter rolls has resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings.
Critics say the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.
Members of Hindu-nationalist BJP have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighbouring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India's electoral rolls.
Election authorities say the revision was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries, and that eligible voters remain entitled to apply for inclusion on the roll.
Human Rights Watch has said the removal of voters was "arbitrary and deeply flawed".
"The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India's most marginalised people their right to vote and other government services," it said in a statement this week.
The Cockroach movement has been heavily involved in the pushback to the voter-roll revision and several of its leaders were temporarily detained by police during protests last month.
The CJP has gained millions of followers on social media since it was launched in May.
Earlier protests organised by the CJP in July over exam irregularities forced the resignation of the education minister, marking a rare climbdown by Modi's administration.

Ukraine flies the first drone rescues of wounded troops
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:13:19 GMT
19:13:19 KST

Ukraine has carried out the world’s first medical evacuations by heavy uncrewed aircraft, lifting wounded soldiers out of positions that could not be reached from the ground, and is developing evacuation drones as a dedicated capability of its own, according to the Ukrainian defence ministry.
Brave1, the defence innovation cluster working with the Ministry of Defence, set the requirement in 2024 after working with the military to define what such an aircraft would have to do. The criteria given to the defence technology market were that the aircraft must reliably carry 130 kilograms over a distance of at least fifteen kilometres and must carry an integrated communication system with at least three alternative types to survive in an electronic warfare environment, with lidar, optical stabilisation and navigation that works without satellites listed as options.
The first of those evacuations took place in October, when an infantryman of the 30th Separate Mechanised Brigade was lifted out of a position the enemy had blocked. A Heavy Shot Ayudag-6 hexacopter built by a Brave1 participant flew the mission, an aircraft weighing 98 kilograms with a payload capacity of 130 kilograms, and it covered more than fifteen kilometres on the outbound leg.
Preparation ran to months and drew on the experience of the uncrewed ground vehicle company of the 92nd Separate Assault Brigade. Equipment had been dropped to the soldier in advance and he had to secure himself to the aircraft’s winch without help, while adjacent units launched bomber drones to pull enemy interceptors away from the rescue aircraft.
A second system, Stargate, was built specifically for evacuation at the request of assault troops. It deploys in ten minutes, carries 150 kilograms at speeds up to 105 kilometres an hour and holds a medical module with a stretcher, and its software can plot a route and return to a safe area without help if navigation is completely jammed.
Assault troops of the CODE 9.2 regiment used it twice in a single week to bring out severely wounded soldiers from the grey zone five kilometres from the Russian border, where terrain, water obstacles and first person view drones ruled out any ground rescue. The aircraft flew nearly thirty kilometres each way and came back with the casualties aboard while under electronic attack, relying on artificial intelligence alone for navigation, with heavy strike drones suppressing enemy positions to cover the run.
Conventional casualty evacuation has become close to impossible along much of the front because the density of drone coverage turns any vehicle movement into a target, and uncrewed ground vehicles took over much of the work at the cost of speed. Survival after serious trauma depends heavily on reaching surgical care quickly, and a crawling robot moving along a mined route can take many hours to cover ground a helicopter would cross in minutes.
Ukraine’s Defence Procurement Agency has contracted three times as many uncrewed systems of all types this year as it did last year.

Pro-EU Polish PM brings ‘Russian bots’ into court showdown

Pro-EU Polish PM brings ‘Russian bots’ into court showdown
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has accused his political opponents of receiving support from an “army of Russian bots”amid an escalating constitutional crisis in Warsaw. The pro-EU leader offered no proof for his claim, which came after a government-backed judge moved to oust two key officials supported by his rival, right-wing President Karol Nawrocki, from the Constitutional Tribunal, triggering public outrage.
Unrest erupted on Friday when Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge elected by Tusk’s governing majority, ordered the suspension of Constitutional Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski and his deputy Bartlomiej Sochanski, both linked to the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. The tribunal’s existing leadership rejected the suspensions, declaring that all those participating in the attempted takeover “are committing the crime of a coup d’état.”
The development triggered street protests around the court building and a heavy police deployment. Nawrocki, who canceled a planned trip to Senegal, personally pushed his way into the tribunal to confront Korwin-Piotrowska and her allies, telling them that “you are not judges of the Constitutional Tribunal.”
In a televised address on Saturday evening, Tusk scrambled to defend his actions, accusing his rivals of “seeking to destroy democracy and the rule of law.” The Polish PM, a strong supporter of EU integration who served as president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019, has long criticized PiS judicial reforms – which he said undermined judges’ independence – as well as Nawrocki’s refusal to administer the oath to five Constitutional Tribunal judges elected by the current parliamentary majority.
“Is it greed, stupidity or treason?” Tusk asked, claiming that the opposition was receiving support from “pro-Russian forces worldwide.”
“In this conflict, they’re using an army of Russian bots online. In fact, they’ve even received public compliments from the Kremlin’s chief ideologue,” the prime minister claimed, without providing further proof or elaborating.
Moscow has repeatedly said it does not interfere in other countries’ domestic affairs. While Russian officials have yet to respond to Tusk’s allegation, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov in July denied that Russia was responsible for cyberattacks on Polish energy infrastructure.
Responding to Tusk’s address, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, called the prime minister a “pathological liar” and accused him of setting Poland ablaze while pretending to extinguish the fire. “It’s hard to find a single word, expression, or sentence that would be true, that would reflect the actual or legal reality,” he added.
Tusk’s accusation comes after several Western media outlets, anti-Russia hawks, and Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky propagated the claim that Kiev’s drone strikes, which damaged several data centers operated by Russian technology giant Yandex, crippled alleged Russian bot networks supporting Western right-wing movements, including Germany’s AfD and US President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement.
However, several independent investigations by cybersecurity and research firms quickly debunked the narrative. Experts in particular pointed out that one viral graph supposedly showing a collapse in AfD-related activity was found to contain fabricated or unverifiable figures.
Commenting on the chaos, former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev described it as a “constitutional coup.” He suggested that “Brussels’ protégé Tusk” was persecuting PiS conservatives over the latter’s hostility toward Ukrainian Nazi collaborators. Medvedev concluded by sarcastically invoking an old schoolyard joke, saying, “And these are the people who scold my brother and me for picking our noses.”

Portuguese police clash with housing protesters, arrest 13

Portuguese police clash with housing protesters, arrest 13
- Police stormed protest camps in Lisbon and Porto, arresting 13 people and injuring dozens during clashes over Portugal’s housing crisis.
- Protesters said police used batons and dogs, while police said some demonstrators threw bottles and paint and refused orders to disperse.
- Activists oppose plans to ease evictions and remove rent caps on new leases, warning they will raise housing costs and make tenants more vulnerable.
AI generated
LISBON – Riot police with dogs stormed protest camps in Lisbon and Porto early on Nov 1, charging demonstrators with batons, arresting 13 people and leaving dozens injured in the latest confrontation over Portugal’s housing crisis.
Clashes quickly broke out as dozens of officers moved in on an encampment in Lisbon’s Rossio Square and a smaller camp in Porto’s Dom Joao I Square at around 4.30am local time.
Protesters shouted “smells like a dictatorship”, while the police said some hurled bottles and paint at officers as they tried to take down the tents.
The police said in a statement that six people were arrested in Lisbon and seven in Porto for refusing orders to disperse. It said 13 police were injured in the process, with eight taken to hospital.
In Porto, the police said three plain-clothes officers monitoring the protesters were assaulted after being spotted by a group.
One of the officers displayed his firearm as a deterrent, police said.
An unspecified number of civilians were also injured during the operation, which was carried out “with rigour, balance and respect for citizens’ rights”, the statement read.
Porto protest organisers said 38 people were injured, including three seriously, while Lisbon organisers reported more than 30 injured.
Activist group Acampada Lisboa said more than 30 protesters were injured, including 10 who required hospital treatment, and called a fresh rally in the capital on the afternoon of Nov 1 to protest against the police operation.
“We will not be silenced,” it said in a statement posted on social media, alongside photographs of protesters with bruises or bleeding from injuries it blamed on “police violence”.
Some protesters carried red carnations, a symbol of Portugal’s 1974 revolution, evoking the peaceful military-led uprising that ended nearly five decades of dictatorship.
Police said they seized 69 tents in Lisbon and 30 in Porto.
The camps had been set up late on Oct 31 after peaceful marches through the two cities against soaring housing costs.
Officers have repeatedly dismantled encampments that have sprung up across Lisbon and Porto in recent weeks.
‘Dark night’
After police cleared protest camps in the two cities last weekend, Amnesty International said it was “deeply concerned by the excessive and disproportionate use of force by police”.
A lawyer representing protesters at Lisbon’s housing camps, Ricardo Sa Fernandes, said on Nov 1 he would file a criminal complaint against Interior Minister Luis Neves and the national police chief for abuse of power.
“This is a dark night in the history of Portuguese democracy. This is absolutely intolerable and has crossed all limits,” he told reporters outside a police station in Lisbon where some of those detained were taken.
Neves has defended the police response to the protests, insisting that the encampments must end and warning that officers will use force when necessary to restore public order.
“I feel deep sadness about what happened again last night. Nobody takes any pleasure in seeing this outcome,” he said on Nov 1.
Protesters want the minority centre-right government to abandon plans to ease evictions and remove rent caps on new leases, warning the measures would push up housing costs and leave tenants more vulnerable.
Prime Minister Luis Montenegro has acknowledged that property prices have doubled in a decade, but blames the crisis on previous left-wing governments for failing to build enough homes and pursuing what he calls an overly permissive migration policy.
Portuguese protesters have taken inspiration from a similar movement in neighbouring Spain, where tents have been set up in central Madrid and other cities for weeks. AFP

UK police arrest Palestine Action supporters ahead of hearing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:02:33 UTC
19:02:33 KST

Breadcrumb
UK police say 325 people were arrested at Palestine Action demo
British police said Sunday they had arrested 325 people at a London protest in support of Palestine Action the previous day, ahead of a court appeal over the government's contentious ban of the group.
Demonstrators staged a "mass action" outside the US embassy ahead of the Supreme Court holding a two-day hearing from Wednesday on the UK government's July 2025 decision to outlaw Palestine Action under anti-terror legislation.
The United States also designated Palestine Action as "terrorist" in August, as the administration of President Donald Trump intensifies its campaign against left-wing movements.
The British designation puts the group on a blacklist that also includes entities like the Palestinian group Hamas, and makes membership of, or support for, Palestine Action a crime punishable by up to 14 years in prison.
It has resulted in more than 4,000 people, including many senior citizens and Holocaust survivors, being arrested for showing their support for the group, according to campaigners and police tallies.
"In total, 325 people were arrested yesterday," London's Metropolitan Police said in a Sunday update.
"The vast majority of arrests, 320, were for expressing support for a proscribed organisation under the Terrorism Act."
A smaller number of protesters also rallied outside the US consulate in the Scottish capital Edinburgh on Saturday, but no arrests were made there at the time.
"Enquiries are ongoing to identify people seen wearing t-shirts and holding banners showing support for a proscribed organisation," Police Scotland said in a statement shared with AFP on Sunday.
"Evidence is being reviewed and further action will be taken as appropriate."
Many of those arrested, including senior citizens and Holocaust survivors, have displayed signs at rallies reading: "I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action."
In July, hearings related to more than 2,000 of those cases were postponed until later this year.
"It is truly dystopian that there have now been over 4,000 arrests under terror laws for peaceful vigils," Protest organisers Defend Our Juries said in a statement.
The group's co-founder Huda Ammori has legally challenged the ban, arguing it was "disproportionate" and infringed human rights.
The Supreme Court is set to hold a two-day hearing on the high-profile case from Wednesday, after the Court of Appeal ruled in the government's favour in June.
'Losing faith'
Saturday's London protesters held banners bearing slogans such as "How is trying to stop a genocide a crime?" and "We are protesters, not terrorists."
Attendee Angie Zelter, 75, told AFP she had already been charged at least eight times at previous rallies but wanted to protest again ahead of the Supreme Court hearing.
"I am hoping they will come to their senses and agree PA (Palestine Action) should not have been proscribed," she said.
Marji Mansfield, 70, a retired financial adviser, said she had previously been arrested about 10 times.
"I am losing faith in the judicial system," she told AFP.
"If they lift the ban, it would be a way out for the government," Mansfield added, while noting there was currently "no sign" of the ban's reversal.
Bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney has entered the controversy, with her publisher Faber revealing this month it can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for the group.
Set up in 2020, Palestine Action's stated goal on its website, blocked to UK internet users, is to end "global participation in Israel's genocidal and apartheid regime".
It gained visibility after the outbreak of Israel's genocidal war in October 2023.
Palestine Action has mainly targeted weapons factories in Britain, especially those belonging to the Israel-based defence group Elbit.

Call for two attack submarines at sea at all times
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:01:21 GMT
19:01:21 KST

Two of the five Astute class submarines should be fully deployable and operational at all times, one patrolling northern waters or the Channel and a second working alongside the deterrent patrol, according to a briefing paper published by the 878 Institute.
The recommendation appears in the first of a planned series on the condition of the Royal Navy. It reads: “To ensure that two of the five Astute-class submarines are fully deployable and indeed operational at all times: one actively patrolling the North Sea, the Greenland-Iceland-UK (GIUK) Gap, or English Channel to deter increased Russian submarine activity around British waters; a second always patrolling alongside the CASD.”
It follows the paper’s account of the summer, which states: “Despite maintaining a fleet of five vessels, it was reported that not a single Astute-class submarine was operationally deployed through summer 2026, and that all five remained laid-up in British harbours. Only HMS Agamemnon (one of the two planned additions to the five in service) is at sea conducting trials.
“This is deeply concerning, given both the rise in Russian sub-surface activity around British waters, but perhaps more worrying because of the lack of available escorts for Britain’s nuclear deterrent.” The Ministry of Defence does not comment on submarine operations.
A linked recommendation asks for more money for the class, and warns of what follows without it. It reads: “To increase resource allocation for the troubled Astute-class submarines, all of which were in docks for a period from June 2026. Increased resources are needed to alleviate maintenance backlogs, industrial bottlenecks, and dockyard infrastructure limitations. Without this, the Astute-class must be said to be failing, and with it, Britain’s nuclear deterrent risks being left defenceless at sea or dependent upon allies for support, eroding the UK’s ‘sovereign’ nuclear deterrent.”
Setting a standing requirement of two boats available continuously would mean two fifths of the in-service class at sea at any moment. Sustaining that demands considerably more than two hulls, because the conventional planning assumption across submarine operating navies runs at roughly three boats for every one deployed, allowing for deep maintenance, work-up and crew training, so the recommendation implies six or seven available boats against a class of five with two more coming.
The Astute class carries two primary roles, hunting other submarines and protecting the Vanguard boats, and the paper describes both when it says the class exists for “anti-submarine warfare, as well as fleet protection for the nuclear-armed Vanguard-class.”
Devonport holds the only licence in Britain to refit nuclear submarines, and ministers told Parliament this week that the programme rebuilding the submarine berths there is being recovered after design difficulties, with construction still to start. The refit of HMS Vanguard at the same yard ran to seven and a half years against an original plan of three and a half.
Russian activity around British waters has risen, and the paper records that the Royal Navy spent twenty-one days in July alone monitoring Russian ships, and tracking operations rose twenty-five per cent on the previous year. The Defence Committee reported this month that availability among destroyers, frigates and attack submarines raises questions about whether Britain can meet its commitments in the High North, and that the department has accepted an anti-submarine warfare gap in northern waters.
The 878 Institute published a broader paper on British deterrence gaps in August, which UKDJ reported at the time.

10:00:59 GMT
19:00:59 KST

Britain’s attack submarine fleet spent the summer tied up in harbour while Russian activity around British waters increased, and the availability of escorts for the ballistic missile boats that carry the nuclear deterrent is among the consequences raised, according to a briefing paper published by the 878 Institute.
The paper, the first in a planned series on the condition of the Royal Navy, opens by saying: “The Royal Navy is gripped by a critical but needless decline in strategic capacity, as demonstrated by a steep reduction in both mass and readiness.
“This comes at a time of intensifying maritime competition and growing threats to British national interests. These threats are most acute in and around British waters, as Russia’s submarines, warships and even its shadow-fleet carrying illicit Russian oil across the globe, are all increasing their operations off Britain’s coasts.”
It records that the Royal Navy spent twenty-one days in July alone monitoring Russian ships, that operations to track Russian activity rose twenty-five per cent on the previous year, and that Russian warships made repeated voyages through the Dover Strait and the North Sea. Ministers have confirmed that Moscow uses commercial proxies to threaten undersea infrastructure, and the paper cites analysis uncovering five hundred incidents of Russian civilian vessels loitering above cables.
Concerns about the frigate and destroyer fleets are set out alongside the navy’s transition to automation through the hybrid navy concept, before the paper turns to its main subject. It says: “However, it is in the submarine fleet that we see an especially stark vulnerability and where, due to its purposes, creates unique threats to Britain’s security.”
On the Astute class, which numbers five in service with two more being readied, the paper states: “Despite maintaining a fleet of five vessels, it was reported that not a single Astute-class submarine was operationally deployed through summer 2026, and that all five remained laid-up in British harbours. Only HMS Agamemnon (one of the two planned additions to the five in service) is at sea conducting trials.
“This is deeply concerning, given both the rise in Russian sub-surface activity around British waters, but perhaps more worrying because of the lack of available escorts for Britain’s nuclear deterrent.” That finding draws on reporting by Navy Lookout, and the Ministry of Defence does not comment on submarine operations.
Turning to the four Vanguard boats, the paper acknowledges that deployment cycles are not discussed publicly and then sets out what it describes as widely understood. It says: “Due to the nature of their deterrent, HM Government rightly does not comment on their deployment cycles or current state. However, it is widely understood that the fleet has been in a poor state for some years.”
Designed for patrols of three to four months, the boats have run planned patrols of under a hundred days well past that mark. The paper says: “Most SSN- and SSBN-operating navies view 100-day patrols as the sensible maximum; at least the last ten deterrent patrols all exceeded five months in duration, up until April this year, with the last coming in at over 200 days, apparently becoming the new normal.”
On the four Dreadnought boats due in the early 2030s, the paper argues that work on their successor cannot wait, since each is designed for thirty years of service and the build alone takes twenty. The Ministry of Defence accepted the Strategic Defence Review’s recommendation to begin early definition and requirement-setting during this parliamentary term, a pledge affirmed in July, and the paper says: “However, this pledge was only affirmed in July 2026, and there have been no major announcements since; with only two full Parliamentary years left before the next General Election must be called, the Government needs to properly commit to Dreadnought’s successor at the earliest opportunity.”
The sharpest warnings concern SSN-AUKUS, where steel cutting on the first British boat is scheduled at Barrow-in-Furness in 2027. The paper says: “Given the likely concurrent Astute and Dreadnought programmes, the sole UK submarine construction site in Barrow-in-Furness risks facing acute labour shortfalls as soon as SSN-AUKUS begins. In the meantime the site has added only about 500 workers against a required 2,500 to run the parallel Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS build lines.
“The projected build-timeframes for SSN-AUKUS are also deeply concerning. Astute-class boats averaged 128 months to build; SSN-AUKUS are projected to take only 18 months each. This feels unrealistic, and risks cost overruns, delays, supply-chain over-stretch, and potentially an even bigger ‘submarine gap’.”
Describing the programme as Pillar One of AUKUS and saying it must not fail, the paper adds: “However, without guarantees of resource from HM Government that are currently absent, and instead a vague pledge of total vessels built, a lack of political leadership and gaps in the defence-industrial base, Britain risks being the weak link in the partnership.”
Four recommendations follow, covering a firm commitment to twelve SSN-AUKUS boats at the spring Spending Review in 2027, increased resources for the Astute class to clear maintenance backlogs and dockyard constraints, a standing requirement for two of the five Astutes to be deployable and operational at all times, and the commissioning of the Dreadnought successor definition phase by the close of 2027.
The 878 Institute published a broader paper on British deterrence gaps in August, which UKDJ reported at the time, covering land, space and naval capability with a foreword by General the Lord Dannatt. The Defence Committee reported this month that Britain has allowed its under-ice submarine capability to lapse and that the department has accepted an anti-submarine warfare gap in northern waters, and the Defence Investment Plan commits £63 billion over four years to the nuclear enterprise.

A Newly Discovered Trail of Cosmic Debris Illustrates How the End of the Solar System Could Look
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Astronomers at the European Southern Observatory (ESO) have discovered a debris disk around a white dwarf, consisting of the remnants of the solar system that once orbited it. For researchers, these structures could offer a clue as to what the end of our solar system will look like once the sun runs out of fuel.
The white dwarf J1328−1450 is located about 1,600 light-years from Earth. Astronomers were already aware of it thanks to star-mapping catalogs, but new observations taken with ESO’s Very Large Telescope (yes, that’s its real name) revealed that it is surrounded by a disk of debris with an unusual structure: Two distinct rings of gas separated by a gap.
According to the observatory, this disk of material is likely the remnant of the planetary system that once orbited J1328−1450. As it passed through a red giant phase and subsequently became a white dwarf, the star may have destroyed some of its planets and left other rocky bodies exposed to an extreme environment. Some of the released material ended up forming a disk of gas and dust around the dead star.
The process that shaped this system could repeat itself in our own. In about 5 billion years, the sun will exhaust its fuel and expand into a red giant. During this phase, it could engulf nearby bodies, like the closest planets. It will then shed its outer layers, leaving behind a white dwarf. Any rocky bodies that survive this transformation could break apart and form a debris disk around the dead star, like the one astronomers are now observing in J1328−1450.
But the white dwarf’s two debris rings hint at another possibility. Their structure appears to be shaped by bodies that astronomers have not yet been able to identify directly. The data suggest that, following the star’s transformation, at least two planetary objects may have survived among the remnants of that system.
Researchers believe these two bodies could be very different in size. The one closest to the white dwarf would measure just a few kilometers in diameter, while the more distant one could be as large as Pluto or even the moon. Their interaction with the surrounding material would explain the formation of the two rings, although it has not yet been confirmed that they exist as separate objects. An alternative possibility is that the structure originates from different parts of a single planet-like body, such as its crust and core.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Dezeen's favourite furniture and homeware from October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Dezeen’s favourite furniture and homeware from October
The first piece of furniture by architecture office Studio Hagen Hall and a pleated cabinet by Didi Ng Wing Yin feature in this roundup of design pieces spotted by Dezeen’s Jane Englefield over the last month.
SHH-001 table by Studio Hagen Hall
Louis Hagen Hall of London-based Studio Hagen Hall has made his first foray into furniture with this sculptural coffee table, delivered as two legs and a weighty glass tabletop that require no mechanical fixings.
Hagen Hall originally designed the asymmetric piece for Pine Heath, a modernist Hampstead renovation with a corner sofa that required a bespoke coffee table to offset the negative space left by the seating.
Cherry veneer legs are paired with recyclable brown smoked glass to create the made-to-order piece, informed by the design philosophy of modernist American architect John Lautner.
Exo 01 vase by Flora Lechner
Austrian, Netherlands-based designer Flora Lechner originally caught the attention of London’s Max Radford Gallery with her alternative aluminium chandeliers that look like ornate robots
Lechner has now translated her distinctive style into an unusual vase, composed of aluminium clips held together by stainless steel bolts. Stems can be slotted into the clips, which are supported by a base that can be filled with water.
“Exo 01 approaches the vase more as a support structure than as a container,” explained Lechner. “Inspired by braces used to hold and align parts of the body, the work applies this principle to flowers.”
Low-relief table by Anne Holtrop
Anne Holtrop is known for his rough-hewn furniture pieces, which conjure images of volcanic craters and mountainous landscapes.
For his inaugrual exhibition with Carpenter’s Workshop Gallery in London, the Dutch architect and designer is showing off his Low-relief collection of tables made from cast glass.
Their unrefined legs were informed by stone reliefs Holtrop visited in Aswan, Egypt.
Pleats Cabinet No 1 by Didi Ng Wing Yin
Helsinki designer Didi Ng Wing Yin is known for his distinctively pleated wooden furniture, which he makes from locally sourced Finnish timber.
Last week, the designer debuted his first cabinet at Paris’s Spazio Nobile Gallery. Made from a mixture of fir and pine, finished with tung oil, the cabinet features a delicately pleated door made using Ng’s combined splitting, brushing and carving technique.
“I wanted to explore the dynamic contrast between form and texture,” Ng told Dezeen.
“The chunky pedestal base is built from straightforward architectural beams that retain their natural knots and raw characteristics, providing a heavy, structural anchor for the light, organic silhouette of the pleated cabinet door.”
OBJ-05 Chair by Manu Bañó
One of many design events in October was PAD London, a collectible fair that takes place annually in Mayfair’s Berkley Square.
Among this year’s exhibitors was Mexico-based Manu Bañó, who showed a duo of striking patinated brass chairs formed from stacked, sculptural slabs of metal.
The chairs are a continuation of Bañó’s existing brass and stainless steel furniture, and were presented as part of the Objects with Narratives exhibition.
Ballon furniture by Seungjin Yang
South Korean designer Seungjin Yang has been making playful furniture shaped like balloons for years, using colourful epoxy resin.
At PAD London, Yang showed his most recent balloon-like creations in the form of a sofa, two armchairs and two stools.
The designer coats real balloons in resin, painstakingly building their strength. Each piece is complete after around two weeks of delicate testing.
Don’t be misled by the intriguingly delicate appearance of Yang’s finished pieces, which are solid enough to be sat on.

Greece receives second FDI frigate HS Nearchos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:57:10 UTC
18:57:10 KST

- Naval Group delivered HS Nearchos, Greece’s second FDI frigate, at Lorient on Oct. 30, ten months after the first ship, HS Kimon.
- The third Greek frigate is due by the end of 2026, and a fourth, ordered in November 2025, is scheduled for 2028.
Naval Group handed over HS Nearchos, the second of Greece’s new French-built defense and intervention frigates, to the Hellenic Navy at its shipyard in Lorient, France, on Oct. 30, ten months after Greece received the first ship of the class.
Greek Defense Minister Nikos Dendias and French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin attended the ceremony. The third Greek frigate, HS Formion, is due by the end of 2026, which would give the Hellenic Navy three of the ships within a year, the company said. Naval Group did not say when Nearchos will sail for Greece or enter operational service.
“Only ten months after the delivery of HS Kimon, it is an honour to deliver the second FDI frigate for the Hellenic Navy, HS Nearchos, in the presence of Catherine Vautrin and Nikos Dendias, whom I would like to thank for their renewed trust,” said Pierre Éric Pommellet, chairman and CEO of Naval Group.
The FDI, short for Frégate de Défense et d’Intervention, is a French design of about 4,500 tons and 122 m (400 feet) built for air defense, anti-ship and anti-submarine warfare. Greece’s version, known as the FDI HN or Kimon class, carries a heavier weapons fit than the French Navy’s ships, with Thales Sea Fire radar and up to 32 Aster 30 long-range air defense missiles. Greece is also buying Schiebel CAMCOPTER S-100 drones to fly from Kimon, Nearchos and Formion for surveillance and anti-submarine work.
The first ship, HS Kimon, was delivered on Dec. 18, 2025, and arrived in Greece in January. In March, Greece sent it to Cyprus to help defend the island against Iranian attacks, alongside a Hydra-class frigate and F-16 fighters, its first operational mission. At the time, Kimon was the only Greek warship able to provide long-range air defense, Naval News reported.
Greece agreed in September 2021 to buy three of the frigates, with an option for a fourth, in a package worth about €3 billion including weapons, and the program started in 2022. It exercised the option in November 2025, ordering a fourth ship, HS Themistokles, along with maintenance and upgrades for the whole fleet. That ship is due in 2028.
More than 75 Greek companies are involved in Naval Group’s frigate and submarine programs for Greece, supplying parts ranging from electronic maps to pre-outfitted hull blocks and complex mechanical and electronic systems, the company said. Naval Group has committed to 25% local content on the fourth frigate. It has also won the initial in-service support contract for the Greek FDIs, which it will carry out with its Greek subsidiary, Naval Group Hellas, and local partners.
The Greek ships are part of a larger order book. Thirteen FDIs have now been ordered for three NATO navies, five for France, four for Greece and four for Sweden, and Naval Group says its Lorient yard can now deliver two of the frigates a year.

Japan’s Economic Diplomacy: A Compass in a Divided World
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:52:00 UTC
18:52:00 KST

During the second term of U.S. President Donald Trump, protectionist measures – including unilateral trade actions and reciprocal tariffs – have re-emerged as central pillars of U.S. foreign policy. With this fundamental structure shift in trade policy of the United States, once the preeminent champion of open markets, Japan has arrived at a critical strategic juncture. Tokyo must bolster its economic “strategic autonomy” and diversify its international economic partnerships, even as it maintains its core alliance with Washington.
To be clear, the foundational importance of the U.S.-Japan alliance remains unaltered. Strategic diversification does not imply distancing Tokyo from Washington. Rather, expanding Japan’s economic options and building national resilience alongside this indispensable alliance ultimately fortifies bilateral stability. Simultaneously, Japan must differentiate itself from Washington’s protectionist drift by steadfastly anchoring an international economic order based on predictable, rules-based trade.
Beijing views these shifts in U.S. policy as an opening, positioning itself as a defender of globalization while expanding ties across the Global South. The high-profile U.S.-China summit in late 2026 illustrated this shifting dynamic: while the spectacle drew international headlines, the meeting produced minimal structural adjustments in their underlying economic rivalry, leaving regional partners navigating persistent uncertainty.
In this volatile environment, Japan’s imperative is not to compete with China for regional hegemony. Instead, Tokyo should collaborate with a broad coalition (which includes the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, and key Indo-Pacific partners) to co-create an international economic climate that remains open, rules-bound, and inclusive.
CPTPP and the European Connection
The symbolic inflection point of America’s retreat from multilateral trade leadership occurred in 2017 with its withdrawal from the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP). Taking the helm among remaining signatories, Japan led the negotiations that brought the 11-nation Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) into force in 2018. The CPTPP moved beyond conventional tariff elimination, introducing high-standard 21st-century discipline on digital commerce, state-owned enterprises, intellectual property, and service liberalization.
With the formal accession of the United Kingdom, the CPTPP now encompasses roughly 15 percent of global GDP. As additional economies seek entry, upholding the agreement’s rigorous standards, particularly regarding non-market policies and state subsidies, remains vital to preserving the integrity of both the accord and the broader multilateral system.
Concurrently, the institutional architecture underpinning Japan-EU ties has seen significant development. Building on the 2019 Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), the comprehensive Strategic Partnership Agreement (SPA) is now in effect, consolidating broad cooperation rooted in shared norms. Meanwhile, following Brexit, the U.S.-UK CPTPP connection and bilateral EPAs have established a strategic alignment linking Europe and the Indo-Pacific.
This momentum reached a new milestone at the Japan-EU Summit, where both sides established the Japan-EU Competitiveness Alliance. Designed to enhance mutual resilience, this framework deepens cooperation in supply chain security, critical minerals, semiconductors, and emerging technologies, while reinforcing joint leadership to revitalize the World Trade Organization (WTO).
Constructing “Open, Predictable, and Resilient Trade”
A critical conceptual task is to refrain from casting open trade and economic security as mutually exclusive. In today’s interconnected yet fragmented economy, maintaining open markets while mitigating single-source dependencies and fortifying supply chains are complementary objectives. What Japan must advocate is not a simple return to pre-crisis free trade, but the construction of “Open, Predictable, and Resilient Trade.”
While the post-World War II economic architecture developed under American leadership, Washington’s stepping back from its traditional role is accelerating multipolarity and fragmentation. In this emerging landscape, Japan occupies a unique position.
However, Tokyo should not seek to impose its own template. Japan’s principal asset lies in its capacity to connect diverse nations across varying developmental stages, identify overlapping strategic interests, and build practical, durable coalitions.
This approach is indispensable in engaging the Global South. Rigidly demanding compliance with external standards without addressing local realities will not cultivate lasting support for a rules-based order. What is required is a pragmatic strategy that respects national sovereignty, supports tangible development needs, and delivers shared economic benefits.
By sustaining its vital alliance with the United States and preserving pragmatic economic ties with China, while simultaneously deepening multi-layered partnerships across Europe, Asia, and emerging economies, Japan can chart a stable path forward. This multi-layered diplomatic network offers a compelling alternative to stark binary choices, providing a clear compass for navigating an increasingly fractured global economy.

Man, 84, walks 6 km to escape Kherson
An 84-year-old man from Kherson has walked almost 6 km (nearly 4 miles) to leave the city, where he had been living in isolation for six months because of Russian attacks.
Source: Kherson City Military Administration
Details: Vasyl Zaichenko had lived in Kherson for 60 years. He and his wife built a family home, planted an orchard and grew flowers on their plot of land. But for almost the past six months Vasyl had been living in near-total isolation, existing on humanitarian aid delivered to him by drones.
"The attacks became intense, and there was no heating. In winter the temperature was around +8°C. Everyone was evacuated, but I chose to stay. I lived on what I grew in the garden," Vasyl said.
When he finally decided to evacuate, he had to walk to reach a safer area. He covered about 6 km in an hour and a half, taking only a torch and a phone charger with him.
Volunteers met Vasyl, and his daughter and grandson picked him up from a transit centre. He will now live with his family in Nikopol, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast.
Vasyl will celebrate his 85th birthday on 22 November. He says his greatest wish is for victory and to return home.
"This story once again shows how important it is not to delay evacuation. We urge people living in dangerous areas of Kherson to leave in good time while they still can," the city administration stressed.
