NATO turns 5G towers into sensors in Baltic battlefield experiment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:48:48 UTC
18:48:48 KST

- NATO linked a Maven system to a national system in hours using agentic AI and ran a Lithuania-to-Latvia counter-drone engagement during DiBaX 2026.
- The Oct. 19-30 experiment in Latvia also tested military use of commercial 5G networks, jam-resistant communications and 5G-based object detection.
NATO linked a Maven targeting system to a national military system in a matter of hours using agentic artificial intelligence and ran a cross-border counter-drone engagement during a two-week experiment in Latvia, the alliance’s top transformation commander said on Oct. 30.
Adm. Pierre Vandier, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, described the results at Ādaži Military Base near Riga at the close of the Digital Backbone Experimentation, known as DiBaX 2026, which ran from Oct. 19 to 30. He said some tests failed along the way and that the alliance had deliberately accepted that risk.
“We have connected systems that were never designed to communicate with each other, using artificial intelligence to overcome interoperability barriers. It’s the first time that we have, for example, a Maven system that is speaking to a national system, and that has been fixed in hours with Agentic AI,” said Vandier.
NATO bought its own version of Palantir’s AI-enabled Maven Smart System in 2025 to help commanders pull together intelligence and speed up decisions, and has been rolling it out across its headquarters. Vandier did not say which country’s system Maven was connected to. Agentic AI refers to software that can carry out multistep tasks on its own, in this case working out how two systems exchange data.
The counter-drone test crossed a national border. A drone took off in Lithuania, flew into Latvia and was engaged there by a counter-drone system, Vandier said. It was one of several trials under NATO’s Layered Counter-UAS Initiative, which looks at how sensors and weapons from different countries and companies can work together as one layered defense against drones.
“Even if it didn’t work this morning, it has been done this week. So we had a drone taking off from Lithuania, arriving here and being engaged by a counter system,” said Vandier.
DiBaX itself tested three ways to keep NATO forces connected. In the first, organizers set up a private slice of a host country’s commercial 5G network, reserved and secured for military use, so arriving NATO forces could have command and data links from their first day before their own infrastructure arrived. The second tested automatic switching between communication paths when one is jammed, including radio across different frequencies, satellite links such as 5G direct-to-device, and troposcatter, which bounces radio signals off the lower atmosphere to reach beyond the horizon. The third used ordinary 5G cell towers as passive sensors to detect objects moving through their coverage, particularly in cities with dense tower networks. Vandier said a team of medics in the field also sent patient biodata over the network to doctors in the United States.
The scenarios were built around grey-zone incidents below the threshold of NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense clause, such as drone incursions and damage to undersea cables in the Baltic Sea. A third track, Next Generation Targeting, tested AI-enabled decision support to shorten the time between collecting information and acting on it, and Vandier said the targeting process ran noticeably faster by the end of the week than at the start.
“For us, as a NATO member of the Alliance Eastern Flank here in Latvia, we cannot afford to treat technological innovation and adaptation as a distant objective for us,” said Lt. Gen. Kaspars Pudāns, commander of the Latvian National Armed Forces.
Latvia, Lithuania, Germany, the United States, Canada, Finland and other allies took part, along with NATO bodies including the DIANA innovation accelerator and the NATO Communications and Information Agency. More than 60 technology companies joined, among them Ericsson, Nokia, Thales and Portuguese drone maker TEKEVER, with Latvian telecom company LMT acting as technical integrator. This was the fifth year in a row the experiment has been held in Latvia.
The event closed with NATO FUSE on Oct. 29 and 30, which included live field demonstrations. NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, visited Latvia on Oct. 30 and met President Edgars Rinkēvičs. European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis used the event to announce two pilot European Drone Technology Hubs, one in Latvia and one in the Netherlands, to open in 2027 and speed up development and testing of drone and counter-drone technology in cooperation with NATO.
“The next challenge, and it’s the most difficult, is adoption,” said Vandier.

A group of chefs in Guatemala broke the Guinness World Record for preparing the biggest fiambre salad in history in late October.
To achieve that milestone, the Guatemalan chefs chopped two tons of fresh meat, vegetables, eggs, sausages, corn, peppers and more. The Guatemalans traditionally serve the fiambre salad in late October just before All Saints Day and All Souls Day.
The salad was weighed 1,962.2 kg by a Guinness World Records adjudicator and served to the crowd at the event.

Turkey moves Kurdish militant leader as part of peace process
Improving prison conditions for Abdullah Ocalan, who heads the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, has been a key Kurdish demand since his capture in 1999
Turkey has moved the country’s Kurdish militant leader to a newly built part of an island prison where he has been incarcerated since 1999 as part of efforts to end decades of conflict, a senior Kurdish official said.
Improving prison conditions for Abdullah Ocalan, who heads the Kurdistan Workers’ Party, or PKK, has been a key Kurdish demand in the push to end the 42-year-long conflict between the militant group and Turkish authorities.
Ocalan has been imprisoned in a penitentiary on the island of Imrali in the Marmara Sea – which links the Black Sea to the Aegean Sea – since he was captured in 1999.

Damp and mould in barracks cleared in three weeks
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:43:17 GMT
18:43:17 KST

Damp and mould reported in Single Living Accommodation takes an average of 20.94 days from the report being made to the work being completed, according to an answer given in Parliament.
James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat member for Lewes, asked what the average time is between damp and mould being reported in Single Living Accommodation and works being completed to rectify it.
Calvin Bailey, Parliamentary Under-Secretary and Minister for Veterans and People, said: “As of 23 October 2026, the average time between damp and mould being reported in Single Living Accommodation and works being completed was 20.94 days.”
An average of twenty-one days covers cases cleared within a few days and others that run considerably longer, and the department has told Parliament separately that it cannot supply the longest outstanding waiting time without disproportionate cost. Damp and mould in service accommodation became a political issue after the death of Awaab Ishak in Rochdale in 2020 led to Awaab’s Law, which imposes fixed timescales on social landlords in England for investigating and repairing hazards of this kind.
Service accommodation falls outside that regime because the Ministry of Defence is not a registered social landlord, and the department instead applies the Decent Homes Standard to family housing and a Defence Minimum Standard of its own design to the blocks. The blocks were last assessed against that standard in 2023, when 72 per cent met or exceeded it.
There have been 31,540 urgent reactive call-outs to Single Living Accommodation since the start of January, and forty-three buildings are currently scheduled for refurbishment. Capital spending on the blocks reached £299 million in 2024-25, and the Defence Investment Plan sets aside £1.4 billion for them over this Parliament.
An independent review of Single Living Accommodation and the overseas estate began in January 2026 and is expected to report this autumn.

North Korea tests cluster-bomb warhead for ballistic missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:36:31 UTC
18:36:31 KST

- North Korea tested a “Standard Type 2” cluster-bomb warhead for tactical ballistic missiles on Oct. 31, claiming it can destroy 12 to 13 hectares.
- The Missile Administration said units will be able to use four types of cluster warheads by the end of the year.
North Korea tested a cluster-bomb warhead for its tactical ballistic missiles on Oct. 31 and said it will let its military units choose from four types of cluster warheads by the end of the year, state news agency KCNA reported on Nov. 1.
The Missile Administration, which runs North Korea’s missile development, said the test assessed the warhead’s combat readiness and destructive power. Its Ballistic Missile System Institute and Warhead Institute said they confirmed that the “Standard Type 2” cluster warhead can destroy a target area of 12 to 13 hectares, about 30 to 32 acres. Kim Jong Sik, a member of the ruling Workers’ Party’s Central Military Commission and first vice director of a Central Committee department, oversaw the test. Leader Kim Jong Un was not reported to have attended.
KCNA did not name the missile or give its range, altitude or launch site. The missile was fired at an uninhabited island target in the West Sea, also known as the Yellow Sea, South Korea’s JKN reported, and analysts said it appears to be the first time North Korea has fired a cluster-armed missile from a wheeled mobile launcher.
“We classify the cluster-bomb warheads into four categories according to special and standard purposes. Within this year we will enable units to select and use all those types according to operational aims and specific features of targets,” said the general director of the DPRK Missile Administration.
A cluster warhead opens in the air and scatters dozens or hundreds of small bomblets over a wide area, making it effective against troops, vehicles, artillery positions and airfields rather than a single hardened target. Neither North Korea nor South Korea has joined the international convention banning cluster munitions.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff did not announce the launch on the day it happened, a break from its usual practice of reporting North Korean ballistic missile launches in real time. The military said on Nov. 1 that it had tracked related activity before the launch in close information sharing with the United States and maintained a readiness posture. Because the missile flew a short range at low altitude, the military wanted to complete its analysis before confirming it was a ballistic missile, Financial News reported.
North Korea has tested cluster warheads on its tactical missiles before. In April, it tested a Hwasong-11A short-range ballistic missile with a cluster warhead alongside other new weapons, and later that month Kim Jong Un watched the launch of Hwasong-11 Ra missiles fitted with cluster bomb and fragmentation mine warheads, which state media also claimed could devastate an area of about 13 hectares.
The test came two days after North Korea fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the Wonsan area during a firepower demonstration tied to a drone exhibition, where Kim called for “absolute superiority” in drone technology. The Missile Administration described the Oct. 31 launch as part of regular research work to improve the power of its weapon systems.

‘Deeply shameful’: Tharoor slams UK over colonialism omission in slavery apology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:22:34 UTC
18:22:34 KST

Shashi Tharoor slams UK PM over proposed slavery apology, questions omission of colonialism. (File photo)
NEW DELHI: Congress MP Shashi Tharoor has criticised British prime minister Andy Burnham for considering an apology for Britain's role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade while leaving out its colonial past.The Thiruvananthapuram Lok Sabha MP described the omission as “inexplicable and inexcusable”, arguing that Britain must also acknowledge the suffering caused by its colonial rule.Tharoor's remarks followed Burnham's announcement that his government would consider issuing a formal apology for Britain's involvement in the slave trade as part of efforts to strengthen ties with countries in Africa and the Caribbean.
In an article published in The Guardian on Saturday, Burnham said Britain needed to confront its “complicated history” to protect the future of the Commonwealth, a grouping of 56 independent countries that largely emerged from the former British Empire.Burnham is scheduled to visit Antigua and Barbuda this week for a meeting of Commonwealth leaders.
Tharoor says colonialism cannot be left out
Responding to Burnham's remarks in a post on X on Saturday, Tharoor said he had long maintained that putting a monetary figure on the damage caused by British rule was difficult.
"But moral atonement for the ravages of colonialism is indispensable. I am glad to learn that Prime Minister Burnham is prepared to offer a formal apology on behalf of the British state for the horrors of slavery. But the omission of colonialism from his apology is inexplicable and inexcusable," the MP from Thiruvananthapuram said.
Tharoor's remarks followed Burnham's remark over Britain's involvement in the slave trade.
He also said Britain had never formally apologised for the destruction and exploitation carried out during its colonial rule."It remains deeply shameful that Britain has never said a simple 'sorry' for the loot, pillage, death and destruction perpetrated during the colonial era on millions of innocent victims of British imperialism," he said.
Burnham pitches for 'honest conversation' on slavery
In his article, Burnham said countries affected by the trans-Atlantic slave trade had repeatedly sought an acknowledgement of its lasting consequences.“For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery,” Burnham was quoted as saying by media reports. “By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function.”Tharoor, who has written extensively about British colonial rule, is the author of Inglorious Empire: What the British Did to India. The book examines how British rule led to the systematic exploitation and plunder of India's wealth.

DGCA mandates twin pilot operations from Monday, chopper operators threaten to suspend Char Dam flights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:19:46 UTC
18:19:46 KST

Chopper operators on Char Dham routes have threatened to suspend operations from Monday over DGCA's mandatory twin-pilot rule, citing unviable costs, after a crash killed six people.
NEW DELHI: Chopper operations on Char Dham routes could come to standstill from Monday. Following a chopper crashing soon after take off from Badrinath on Friday (October 30), killing all six people on board — a pilot and five passengers, the DGCA has made it mandatory for choppers operating on Char Dham to be manned by two pilots starting Monday (Nov 2), in a bid to improve safety. However chopper operators have termed the move unviable and threatened to suspend these sorties from Monday “until the matter is reviewed and a mutually workable solution is arrived at.Chopper operators on Saturday sent their “collective objection to the implementation of mandatory twin-pilot operations and intimation of suspension of operations from Nov 2, 2026,” to Directorate General of Civil Aviation chief Vir Vikram Yadav. “… (we) collectively place on record our serious concern and reservation regarding the mandatory requirement of twin-pilot operations for charter services (in) the new operational restrictions communicated by DGCA proposed to be implemented with effect from the first take-off on Nov 2, 2026.”“The mandatory deployment of two pilots on every charter sortie will substantially increase operating costs, crew requirements, accommodation and logistical expenses, and overall operational commitments.
Given the existing commercial structure, prevailing charter rates and limited operational margins, these additional costs cannot be reasonably absorbed by the operators. Nor is it commercially feasible to pass on the entire additional burden to customers,” it says.“… all operators have consistently complied with applicable DGCA regulations and have invested considerable resources in maintaining safe, efficient and reliable operations in the challenging Himalayan terrain…. any additional safety-related measures must be practical, proportionate, commercially sustainable and developed in consultation with the operating stakeholders. Accordingly, after due consideration and mutual consultation, all operators collectively express their inability to accept the mandatory twin-pilot requirement in its present form,” it says.
"In view of the above, we wish to formally convey that all participating operators are proposing to suspend their Char Dham charter operations with effect from Nov 2, 2026, until the matter is reviewed and a mutually workable solution is arrived at by the concerned authorities in consultation with the operators. Under the proposed framework, continuing operations would result in unsustainable financial and operational commitments, leaving the operators with no commercially viable alternative,” it said.Operators have DGCA and Uttarakhand Civil Aviation Development Authority (UCADA) to "reconsider the mandatory twin-pilot requirement, engage with all stakeholders on an urgent basis, and explore an alternative operational framework that adequately addresses safety concerns while ensuring the commercial viability and sustainability of helicopter operations in the region. We remain committed to aviation safety, regulatory compliance and the continued development of helicopter services in Uttarakhand. We hope that the matter will receive urgent consideration and that a constructive resolution can be reached before the proposed implementation date.”

Drone strike hits power station in northern Sudan as attacks on energy facilities mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:19:15 UTC
18:19:15 KST

A drone strike hit a power station in northern Sudan early on Sunday, sparking a fire and triggering loud explosions, witnesses told Anadolu.
The attack targeted the Abu Hamad power station in River Nile state, about 334 miles (538 kilometres) north of the capital, Khartoum, according to witnesses.
They said loud explosions were heard around the facility as flames engulfed parts of the station.
Videos circulated by activists on social media showed a large fire at the power station.
The latest strike brought to 12 the number of power stations targeted by drone attacks across six Sudanese states since Monday.
The affected states include Khartoum, Gezira, Sennar, Gedaref, River Nile and Red Sea.
There was no immediate comment from Sudanese authorities on the attack or the extent of casualties and damage.
Power infrastructure targeted in series of drone strikes
The latest attack followed another drone strike on Saturday targeting the Hayya power station in Red Sea state, a facility still under construction.
The attacks on power infrastructure come amid the ongoing conflict between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
The two sides have been fighting since April 2023, when disagreements over the integration of the country's military forces escalated into armed conflict.
The war has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, amid a worsening humanitarian and hunger crisis.

El Nino, weak monsoon behind Hong Kong’s warmest October since records began
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:15:58 UTC
18:15:58 KST

El Nino, weak monsoon behind Hong Kong’s warmest October since records began
All three monthly temperature averages broke October records, with the average high reaching 30.5 degrees Celsius
Hong Kong sweltered through its warmest October on record, as an extremely strong El Nino, a weak northeast monsoon and a persistent anticyclone aloft over southern China combined to drive temperatures to unprecedented levels, the weather forecaster has said.
The Hong Kong Observatory said on Sunday that the mean maximum temperature last month was 30.5 degrees Celsius (86.9 Fahrenheit), the mean temperature 27.6 degrees and the mean minimum 25.8 degrees – all the highest for any October since records began in 1884.
“Aside from the impact of climate warming, we are experiencing an extremely strong El Nino event,” the weather forecaster said.

AUCKLAND, New Zealand, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's Fifa Laopakdee successfully defended his Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship title at Te Arai Links' South Course in New Zealand on Sunday, with his six-under 278 beating runner-up Zack Swanwick of New Zealand by three strokes.
With the win, Laopakdee earns an invitation to the 2027 Masters Tournament and an exemption into The 155th Open at St Andrews. He made his debut in each major earlier this year at Augusta National Golf Club and Royal Birkdale Golf Club.
"I feel like I'm more proud of myself this year because I never stopped believing in myself, and even though I had a tough year," said Laopakdee. "I literally didn't win a single thing since March. I just keep telling myself that I've still got it. This win means a lot because I'm able to prove to myself that I've still got it."
Swanwick carded a final-round 75, but a closing birdie on No. 18 moved him into solo second place. His runner-up finish is the best by a New Zealander in the Championship's 17-year history.
"It was a special week," said Swanwick, who felt the encouragement from the spectators on site at Te Arai Links. "Back in your home country, playing on a nice course, family out. A little disappointing but it's tough to be sad walking away from the week."
Australia's Kayun Mudadana ranked third with a two-under 282 after a final-round 67, followed by New Zealander Cooper Moore in fourth at one-under 283. New Zealander Ryan Xie rounded out the top five at even-par 284.
China's Li Zhi carded a final-round 74 to finish 10th with a four-round total of 288, making him the highest-ranked Chinese player in this year's tournament.
Li gave himself a score of 85 out of 100 for his first appearance at the tournament. "I played a pretty steady round today. My long game was good, and my putting was also good. I just had a minor issue or two," he said. "It was a challenging week with strong winds on the course, but I think my overall performance was quite mature. I also really liked the course and the overall atmosphere."
The 2027 Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship will be played from October 28 to 31 at Hoiana Shores Golf Club in Hoi An, Vietnam. ■

Iran designates Britain's navy, air force, MI6 as "terrorist, hostile" entities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
17:09:18 CST
18:09:18 KST

TEHRAN, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The Iranian Foreign Ministry on Sunday announced that Tehran had designated Britain's Royal Navy, Royal Air Force and Secret Intelligence Service (MI6) as "terrorist and hostile" entities over the British government's anti-Iran actions over the past year.
The decision, effective Sunday, was based on a resolution adopted by Iran's Supreme National Security Council, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry condemned the British government's anti-Iran policies and actions as contrary to the principles of the United Nations Charter and international law, particularly those concerning respect for national sovereignty and the prohibition of unlawful measures against other states.
It reaffirmed Iran's determination to safeguard its national security and interests, citing several "hostile" actions by the British government, including its participation in the war against Iran by making military bases and facilities on British territory available for use, as well as its designation of the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps as a "threat to national security."
The ministry said the measures were adopted in accordance with international law and the principle of reciprocity, adding that the British government would bear responsibility for their consequences. ■

YAOUNDE, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- At least 25 people were killed and 22 others injured in intercommunal clashes in a border area between Chad's western provinces of Hadjer-Lamis and Barh el Gazel, authorities said late Saturday.
In a statement posted on social media, the Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralization said the clashes involved two "sister communities." A total of 39 people arrested in connection with the violence had been transferred to the capital, N'Djamena, for further judicial proceedings.

Shen unveils five-point labor platform at Taipei labor rally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:08:04 UTC
18:08:04 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) outlined five labor policy proposals at an outdoor event in front of Taipei City Hall on Sunday, responding to calls from labor groups for candidates to prioritize grassroots workers' rights, per Mirror Daily.
The Taipei City Confederation of Trade Unions and the Taipei City Government Environmental Protection Bureau Enterprise Union organized the event. Both Shen and Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) were invited to present their labor platforms and sign commitments addressing workers' concerns.
Shen's five proposals include providing workers with AI support, helping middle-aged and older employees transition to new careers, implementing reduced working hours for parents alongside subsidies for substitute workers, offering six free psychological counseling sessions, and subsidizing one dose of shingles vaccine for Taipei residents aged 50 and older.
Shen said workers should not be pressured to master an ever-growing range of AI tools. Instead, he proposed having “AI coaches” accompany employees on the job for three to six months, observe their work, and consult with unions and the Taipei City Government before developing tools suited to their needs, per CNA.
He also proposed helping middle-aged and older workers change careers, noting that the city could help address some industries that have shortages of part-time employees. The reduced-hours and substitute-worker subsidy proposal would be coordinated with central government policies and implemented nationwide, he said.
In response to labor groups' demands, Shen outlined three areas of commitments: workplace safety, labor protections, and support services. His workplace safety proposals include strengthening labor inspections, adding inspectors, subsidizing vehicle replacements, and providing cooling vests for outdoor workers.
Other commitments include ending the outsourcing of existing work and reviewing additional compensation and retention measures for municipal employees.
Shen said his late mother had worked as a cleaner and sold drinks, giving him a firsthand understanding of workers' conditions and long hours. He said that experience had informed his labor policy proposals, per CNA.

Culture Wars bet on themselves with Taipei show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
09:07:51 UTC
18:07:51 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Austin-based band Culture Wars is scheduled to perform at Taipei's Legacy next Friday.
For Culture Wars frontman Alex Dugan, a good gamble can pay off in more ways than one.
During the pandemic, Duggan and his bandmates discovered that nearly empty Las Vegas casinos were willing to offer free hotel rooms to blackjack players. They took full advantage, spending stretches of time at the Wynn, writing music in their rooms during the day and heading downstairs to gamble at night.
“We would live in Vegas for like two weeks at a time for free, essentially,” Dugan recalled in a conference call with Taiwan News. “We would write all day, go down and gamble, and get everything for free pretty much.”
He estimates he spent six weeks at the hotel across three separate stays. Blackjack eventually gave way to craps and baccarat, but the bigger bet was still to come.
After building an audience through singles, streaming, and social media, Culture Wars is spending the past year proving it can sell tickets without relying on festival slots or support appearances.
The results have been encouraging, selling out medium-capacity rooms not only in their hometown but also in Warsaw and Stockholm despite promoters' initial reservations.
The band also sold out two nights at Los Angeles' historic Troubadour, a venue Duggan had long wanted to play.
“Everything we have been doing this last year is doing our own stuff and proving that we are capable of holding our own and having our own shows,” he said.
That makes the Nov. 13 concert at Taipei's Legacy especially important. It is the band's only headline show during its Asia tour, and Taiwan is one of its biggest markets for both streaming and social media.
Duggan calls the concert a test and “a very big stake in the ground," a chance to show promoters that the band's online following can translate into a live audience.
The band released its debut album “Don't Speak” this year after putting out singles one at a time to build an audience. Duggan said he wanted each song to have its own chance to find listeners before the album arrived.
That patient approach also applies to the music. Culture Wars puts melody and songwriting ahead of a signature sound or a flashy riff. “If we're gonna do this, the songs themselves have to be good,” Duggan said. “Let's not hide behind a sound or a cool riff.”
He wants the band to develop its own songwriting skills rather than depend on outside writers, arguing that strong songs give musicians more freedom to experiment and offer a better path to longevity.
The band's connection with its audience is another part of the plan. Members regularly stay after shows to sign records and shirts and talk with fans, sometimes for as long as two hours. Duggan said those conversations help the band understand how people are discovering its music, whether through Instagram or Spotify.
Touring has also produced its share of mishaps. One crew member was ticketed in Malaysia after packing a giant novelty sex toy intended as a prank for the drummer, apparently unaware the item was prohibited. On another tour, a bus driver failed to secure the trailer properly, and it detached from the bus.
Through it all, the band keeps moving. Duggan, who recently became a father to a baby boy, is already looking ahead to a second album and hopes to set aside several months for writing.
For now, the next wager is Taipei. Culture Wars has seen the numbers online and sold out rooms in Europe and the US. On Nov. 13, the band gets to find out whether that momentum holds on the other side of the world.

Romania scrambles four fighter jets due to drone incursion
Radar surveillance systems operated by Romania's Ministry of National Defence detected two unmanned aerial vehicles that had entered the country's airspace without authorisation on the evening of 31 October.
Source: Romania's Ministry of National Defence, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Romania scrambled four F-16 fighter jets and an IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter to monitor the situation and manage the response after two unmanned aerial vehicles violated the country's airspace.
Alerts were issued in six Romanian counties due to the airspace violation: Iași, Neamț, Vaslui, Botoșani, Bacău and Suceava.
One of the two drones left the country's airspace, while the other was last spotted in the area between the counties of Vaslui and Bacău.
No drone crashes were reported.
Background:
- On the same day, a drone violated Moldovan airspace during Russian aerial attacks on Ukraine.
- On 23 October, Moldova's Foreign Ministry condemned the violation of the country's airspace by a drone and blamed Russia for the incident.
- After a drone was found in the village of Chiștelnița, just 100 m from a residential building, the ministry stated it would declare a Russian Embassy employee in Chișinău persona non grata.
- Romania is reportedly holding talks with Moldova on the joint development of counter-drone programmes.

Bulgaria votes in presidential runoff after tight first round
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:52:15 UTC
17:52:15 KST

Bulgaria's acting President Iotova takes lead in presidential runoff vote, exit polls show
SOFIA, Nov 1 - Exit polls showed Bulgaria's acting President Iliana Iotova led a low-turnout runoff vote for the largely ceremonial role on Sunday, putting her on course to become the country's first elected female head of state.
Iotova, 61, led with about 51% versus 43% to 45% for former caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov, 50, according to two exit polls published as voting ended at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT).
The final official result is expected on Monday as the ballots are counted.
The exit polls put voter participation at about 27% to 29%, a bit higher than the first-round race on October 25, which had a record-low turnout of 23%.
The presidential vote comes against the backdrop of a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast in the past month, which have sparked international condemnation and concerns about the growing reach of the war in Ukraine.
About two dozen seafarers are feared dead, and the strikes have prompted the government to seek allied assistance to bolster maritime security. On Wednesday, a Greek container ship sank after being hit by sea drones.
Both leading presidential candidates have condemned the attacks. Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who backs Iotova, said the strikes' outcome "benefits the Russian Federation". The two candidates have both called for a diplomatic end to the war.
Iotova became acting president in January after Radev resigned to enter — and win — a parliamentary race on what many political analysts considered a Kremlin-friendly ticket.
"I voted for Bulgaria to be a strong state in a strong Europe, but for Bulgaria to have its own foreign policy and a voice when it needs to stand up for what matters most — the national interest," Iotova said on Sunday.
Gyurov, who served as caretaker prime minister this year, is supported by pro-Western, reformist parties and has long expressed support for Ukraine.
"Today I voted for a secure, stable and European Bulgaria," he said after voting.
He signed a security cooperation agreement with Kyiv during his time as premier.
A host of right-leaning political figures, among them ex-premier Boyko Borissov, have expressed support for Gyurov. REUTERS

After annulled vote: Serbia holds re-voting in 53 polling stations
The early parliamentary elections in Serbia on October 25, which were won by the Student List with an absolute majority, are being repeated today in 53 polling stations.
One of the busiest polling stations in the UK is the one at the Bulgarian embassy. Last Sunday, 415 people cast their votes there.

designboom radar: exhibitions to see around the world this november
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:45:50 UTC
17:45:50 KST

designboom radar: exhibitions to see around the world this november
explore our monthly round up of must-see art, design, and architecture exhibitions to check out around the world.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
november exhibitions from DESIGNBOOM RADAR
November’s designboom exhibition radar begins with an unlikely reunion in Paris, where two Alexander Calder mobiles return to public view after decades. In Zurich, 125 familiar lamps become a walk-through tunnel, while a new gallery in Hong Kong transfers the grain of wood into cast aluminum. Elsewhere, a house lost to Mexico City’s architectural history returns through an imagined botanical setting, and a new museum in Western Sydney opens with exhibitions on flight and water.
Some of the exhibitions highlighted in earlier radars and listings on our dedicated events guide remain on view, giving designboom readers more time to encounter them around the globe.
mariko mori: all that shines
Visitors can enter Mariko Mori‘s Wave UFO, an interactive work that incorporates brainwave feedback, as part of All That Shines at Tokyo’s Mori Art Museum. Developed between 1999 and 2002, the large, futuristic installation connects neurological activity with visual experience. It appears in a retrospective of approximately 40 works spanning more than three decades of the Japanese artist’s practice.
The exhibition begins with Mori’s early performance-based photography and science-fiction-inspired imagery, including her experiments with cyborg identities in the 1990s. Later works turn toward Buddhist concepts of consciousness and questions about the cosmos, using sculpture and technology to approach subjects that resist direct representation. Together, the installations and moving-image works trace Mori’s changing ideas about the relationship between human perception and technological experience.
name: Mariko Mori: All That Shines
artist: Mariko Mori
museum: Mori Art Museum
location: Tokyo, Japan
dates: October 31st, 2026 — March 28th, 2027
hella jongerius: whispering things
More than 400 objects trace the experimental practice of Dutch designer Hella Jongerius at the Museum für Kunst und Gewerbe Hamburg. Whispering Things, organized by the Vitra Design Museum, brings together furniture, textiles, ceramics, and early prototypes to examine how she has approached the making of objects over three decades.
The exhibition moves from commercially produced designs for companies such as Vitra and IKEA to more sculptural investigations of material and color. Sketches, collages, and films reveal the processes behind the finished work, including experiments that resist the predictability of industrial production. Throughout her career, Jongerius has returned to the relationship between craftsmanship and manufacturing, considering how objects can retain the irregularities and physical traces of their making.
name: Hella Jongerius: Whispering Things
designer: Hella Jongerius
museum: Museum für Kunst und Gewerbe Hamburg
location: Hamburg, Germany
dates: October 23rd, 2026 — June 13th, 2027
charlotte perriand: free to rethink the world
A reconstruction of Charlotte Perriand‘s 1929 domestic prototype, Équipement intérieur d’une habitation, appears at Barcelona’s Fundació Joan Miró in Free to Rethink the World. Produced by Cassina in collaboration with Perriand’s daughter, architect Pernette Perriand-Barsac, the installation revisits a project developed with Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret during Perriand’s early career.
The exhibition follows four decades of work through ten sections, extending from her Parisian interiors to her encounters with Japanese craftsmanship. Photographs and archival documents reveal her interest in creating spaces around the changing needs of their occupants. The presentation also revisits her friendship with architect Josep Lluís Sert, whose building for the Fundació Joan Miró opened in 1975, with Perriand attending its inauguration the following year.
name: Charlotte Perriand: Free to Rethink the World
designer, architect: Charlotte Perriand
museum: Fundació Joan Miró
location: Barcelona, Spain
dates: October 9th, 2026 — February 28th, 2027
no ordinary light: akari at 75
A monumental paper lantern measuring roughly two meters across takes its place at the Noguchi Museum in New York for No Ordinary Light: Akari at 75. The exhibition traces the development of Isamu Noguchi‘s Akari light sculptures, first conceived in Gifu, Japan, in 1951. Over the following decades, Noguchi developed more than 200 variations of the familiar illuminated forms.
Among the works identified for the presentation is the large-scale 200D, created around 1985, alongside archival sketchbooks and examples of Noguchi’s sculpture in other materials. The exhibition revisits Akari’s appearance at the home of Charles and Ray Eames in 1951 and its later presentation at the 1986 Venice Biennale, following the movement of these paper forms between sculpture and the domestic interior.
name: No Ordinary Light: Akari at 75
artist, designer: Isamu Noguchi
museum: The Noguchi Museum
location: New York, USA
dates: November 4th, 2026 — September 5th, 2027
sabine marcelis: light and color
At the Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, 125 circular IKEA lamps form an eleven-meter-long tunnel in Sabine Marcelis: Light and Color. A mirrored wall with a color gradient extends the installation visually, turning a familiar household object into an illuminated passage. The Dutch designer’s first museum exhibition brings together recent projects and new works conceived for the museum’s Toni-Areal location.
Another room contains eight Mathmos lava lamps, each nearly three meters tall, multiplied through surrounding mirrors. In Sunbeam Captured, developed with Boris Acket, mechanical waves move across a thin layer of water as a shifting light source follows the path of the sun. Material studies accompany the installations, revealing how Sabine Marcelis works with transparency and reflection.
name: Sabine Marcelis—Light and Color
designer: Sabine Marcelis
museum: Museum für Gestaltung Zürich
location: Zurich, Switzerland
dates: October 30th, 2026 — April 4th, 2027
misha kahn: all intensive purposes
A sprawling cast-metal dining table, complete with a sculpted torn napkin and scraps of food, appears among the new works in Misha Kahn‘s All Intensive Purposes at Friedman Benda in New York. Its glass-and-stone surface introduces a surprising degree of order to an object assembled from seemingly accidental gestures. Elsewhere, an onyx table adopts the appearance of a far more roughly constructed piece.
The exhibition marks ten years of collaboration between Kahn and the gallery, following his interest in the unpredictable paths of making. New upholstered furniture incorporates exaggerated forms and graphic surfaces, while multilayered plywood becomes the basis for sculptural objects. The title deliberately alters the familiar phrase ‘all intents and purposes,’ placing the emphasis on experimentation itself.
name: Misha Kahn: All Intensive Purposes
designer: Misha Kahn
gallery: Friedman Benda
location: New York, USA
dates: October 29th, 2026 — December 12th, 2026
calder: françois premier
Two major Alexander Calder mobiles return to public view at Hauser & Wirth Paris in Calder: François Premier, an exhibition devoted to the artist’s years in France during the early 1950s. The presentation brings together Les Granettes (1953), a large standing mobile exhibited for the first time in 72 years, and The Putney Mobile (1954), making its public European debut.
The show takes its name from a seventeenth-century stone house in Saché, where Calder lived and worked after returning to France in 1953. Ink and gouache paintings from this period accompany the sculptures, tracing a particularly productive chapter in his career. There is a geographical coincidence, too: the Paris gallery occupies a historic building on rue François Premier.
name: Calder: François Premier
artist: Alexander Calder
gallery: Hauser & Wirth
location: Paris, France
dates: October 19th, 2026 — December 19th, 2026
dan flavin: some light
Green fluorescent tubes stretch across several meters in Dan Flavin‘s greens crossing greens (to Piet Mondrian who lacked green), one of the works presented in Some Light at the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao. Made in 1966, the installation arranges ordinary industrial fixtures into two illuminated sections, bringing color directly into the surrounding architecture.
The exhibition draws on the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum‘s holdings, with works dating from the 1960s through the 1980s and particular attention to Flavin’s early experiments. Beginning in 1963, the American artist used commercially available fluorescent lights to construct corners, barriers, and corridors. Their arrangement changes the appearance of the gallery itself, allowing visitors to experience color through the spaces the light occupies.
name: Dan Flavin: Some Light
artist: Dan Flavin
museum: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
location: Bilbao, Spain
dates: November 11th, 2026 — April 4th, 2027
powerhouse parramatta
With architecture by Moreau Kusunoki, Powerhouse Parramatta opens in Western Sydney on November 7th with five inaugural exhibitions devoted to art, design, science, and technology. Among them is Task Eternal, an ambitious exploration of aviation and space designed by OPEN Architecture. Its more than 850 objects include drawings of flying machines by Leonardo da Vinci and a NASA Moon rock, alongside a new light installation by James Turrell.
Elsewhere, Overflow brings together seven Aboriginal organizations to examine the living systems of Water Country. The Mall, developed with OMA/AMO, investigates the shopping mall as an architectural and cultural form, while Es Devlin presents five immersive installations in The Turning. A fifth exhibition, The Dark, creates an imaginative environment for children. Together, they introduce the museum’s extensive new program.
museum: Powerhouse Parramatta
participants: multiple artists, designers, architects, and First Nations organizations
location: Parramatta, Australia
dates: from November 7th, 2026
tai shani: m.i.a.s.m.a.
British artist Tai Shani brings M.I.A.S.M.A. to Jupiter Artland outside Edinburgh, transforming the gallery through sculpture and sound. The exhibition revisits the ancient Greek tragedy Antigone, asking how mourning becomes a form of resistance and whose lives are allowed to be remembered. Its expanded title, Moral Injury in the Apocalyptic Sunsets of Modernity disAssociation, gives some indication of the political and emotional territory Shani is exploring.
Developed as an international co-commission, the project was first presented at Kunsthalle Bern earlier this year. Jupiter Artland’s presentation combines imagery with architectural elements to construct an environment shaped by feminist mythology. Visitors can also encounter Shani’s separate installation The Spell or The Dream in the sculpture park’s orchard, where its setting changes with the approaching winter.
name: Tai Shani: M.I.A.S.M.A.
artist: Tai Shani
gallery: Jupiter Artland
location: Edinburgh, UK
dates: October 30th, 2026 — April 11th, 2027
paul r. williams: architect for living
Previously unexhibited drawings and photographs offer a closer look at the career of Paul R. Williams in Architect for Living at LACMA in Los Angeles. Working from the 1920s through the early 1970s, Williams designed buildings across Southern California during a period of extraordinary urban expansion. His commissions ranged from private residences to major civic projects.
The exhibition explores this breadth through archival material, tracing a practice that moved between different architectural languages and types of clients. Williams became particularly well known for his houses for Hollywood figures, while his larger body of work included public housing and hotels. Presented alongside related exhibitions at the Getty Research Institute and USC Fisher Museum of Art, the LACMA survey places his architecture within the wider development of Los Angeles.
name: Paul R. Williams: Architect for Living
architect: Paul R. Williams
museum: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
location: Los Angeles, USA
dates: November 15th, 2026 — May 31st, 2027
sophie calle: matrimoni, rotture e funerali inclusi
An attempt to capture her mother’s final breath is among the personal investigations revisited in Sophie Calle’s Matrimoni, Rotture e Funerali inclusi at MAXXI in Rome. Bringing together eight projects made between 1978 and 2026, the exhibition follows the French artist’s longstanding interest in the rituals people invent around intimacy and loss.
Photographs and written accounts guide visitors through experiences shaped by separation, absence, and the passage of time. Calle’s projects often begin with a self-imposed rule, whether documenting the end of a relationship or recording encounters with people seeing the sea for the first time. The presentation extends beyond the museum with a new permanent installation at Rome’s Non-Catholic Cemetery for Foreigners, adding another setting to her exploration of how personal histories are remembered.
name: Sophie Calle: Matrimoni, Rotture e Funerali inclusi
artist: Sophie Calle
museum: MAXXI
location: Rome, Italy
dates: October 16th, 2026 — February 7th, 2027
álvaro urbano: helen
A vanished house in Mexico City becomes the starting point for Álvaro Urbano’s Helen at Museo Jumex. The exhibition revisits Casa Cueva, the home and garden created by architect Juan O’Gorman and inhabited with his wife, artist and botanically minded writer Helen Fowler O’Gorman. Built in the rocky landscape of Pedregal de San Ángel, the house brought architecture into close contact with its surroundings.
Urbano draws on Fowler O’Gorman’s 1961 book Mexican Flowering Trees and Plants, imagining the botanical world that once occupied the property. References to Juan O’Gorman’s stone murals and later interventions by artist Helen Escobedo add further layers to the presentation. Through an atmospheric architectural reconstruction, Urbano considers how a building’s history can survive through fragments, images, and the people who lived there.
name: Álvaro Urbano: Helen
artist: Álvaro Urbano
museum: Museo Jumex
location: Mexico City, Mexico
dates: October 16th, 2026 — February 7th, 2027
jeonghwa seo: precise play
Wood grain appears on the surface of cast aluminum in Precise Play, an exhibition by South Korean designer Jeonghwa Seo at Carwan Gallery‘s new Hong Kong space. Seo uses sand casting to transfer the texture of wood into metal, producing objects that retain traces of the organic material used in their making. The exhibition inaugurates the gallery’s new location.
Bringing together established pieces and newly commissioned works, the presentation moves between sculptural furniture and lighting. Seo also works with resin and natural rush, combining materials with different physical qualities in precisely constructed forms. His objects invite a second look at the relationship between surface and structure, particularly when a metallic piece appears to preserve the grain of timber or a functional object adopts an unexpected sculptural form.
name: Jeonghwa Seo: Precise Play
designer: Jeonghwa Seo
gallery: Carwan Gallery
location: Hong Kong, China
dates: November 20th, 2026 – February 20th, 2027
yu nishimura: towards a sea
A sea glimpsed through a train window or partially hidden behind trees runs through Yu Nishimura’s Towards a Sea at Lafayette Anticipations in Paris. The Japanese painter’s first institutional solo exhibition in France brings together approximately 50 works from the past decade, including new pieces made for the presentation.
Working in oil and tempera, Nishimura moves between landscape and portraiture, allowing familiar subjects to become blurred or partially obscured. A bicycle wheel might appear alongside a human face, while the boundary between water and sky remains difficult to locate. The exhibition follows the artist’s interest in how places are recalled through imperfect images. His compositions borrow from the language of photography and cinema, and give ordinary scenes the elusive quality of something remembered.
name: Yu Nishimura: Towards a Sea
artist: Yu Nishimura
museum: Lafayette Anticipations
location: Paris, France
dates: October 21st, 2026 — January 3rd, 2027
giuseppe penone: the inner flow of life
Trees and other natural forms enter the architecture of the National Museum of Qatar in Giuseppe Penone: The Inner Flow of Life. Installed across the museum’s Baraha and Old Palace, the exhibition brings together sculptures and architectural interventions by the Italian artist, whose practice has explored the physical relationship between human bodies and the natural world for more than five decades.
The presentation moves between early works and recent pieces, including Rovesciare i propri occhi from 1970 and Vene di bronzo from 2026. Penone uses materials such as wood and bronze to investigate the forces that shape living matter, often bringing the traces of touch or growth into sculpture. A newly installed public artwork, Idee di Pietra, extends the project to Doha Old Port.
name: Giuseppe Penone: The Inner Flow of Life
artist: Giuseppe Penone
museum: National Museum of Qatar
location: Doha, Qatar
dates: October 26th, 2026 — February 13th, 2027
Rashid Johnson: A Poem for Deep Thinkers
More than 70 works spanning nearly three decades of Rashid Johnson’s practice come together at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago in A Poem for Deep Thinkers. The survey brings together photographs, large-scale installations, and films, including his black-soap Cosmic Slops paintings and the expressive faces of the Anxious Men and Broken Men series.
Throughout his career, Johnson has drawn on Black intellectual culture and art history to explore questions of identity, anxiety, and freedom. His 2024 film Sanguine turns toward his own family, examining relationships with his father, brother, and son, and incorporating a poem by writer and activist Amiri Baraka.
name: Rashid Johnson: A Poem for Deep Thinkers
artist: Rashid Johnson
museum: Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago
location: Chicago, USA
dates: November 7th, 2026 — April 25th, 2027
global antiquity
An ancient Indian ivory statuette discovered in Pompeii offers a glimpse into the far-reaching connections explored in Global Antiquity at Fondazione Prada in Milan. Bringing together more than 150 artworks and artifacts, the exhibition examines cultural exchange across Afro-Eurasia between approximately 600 BCE and 1000 CE. The presentation occupies the foundation’s Podium building, with exhibition design by Rem Koolhaas and AMO/OMA.
Curated by Salvatore Settis, Anna Anguissola, and Chiara Ballestrazzi, the exhibition considers how objects traveled through systems of trade and political contact long before the modern idea of globalization. Their places of discovery become as revealing as their origins. Together, the artifacts trace connections between distant societies across 1,700 years.
name: Global Antiquity: Cultural Interactions in Afroeurasian Space, 600 BCE–1000 CE
curators: Salvatore Settis, Anna Anguissola, Chiara Ballestrazzi
exhibition design: Rem Koolhaas and AMO/OMA
museum: Fondazione Prada
location: Milan, Italy
dates: November 5th, 2026 — March 1st, 2027

Cambodia sees rise in drug arrests, drop in seizures in first 10 months of 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:22:35 CST
17:22:35 KST

PHNOM PENH, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia reported a rise in drug-related arrests but a drop in overall narcotics seizures during the first 10 months of 2026, according to an Anti-Drug Department (ADP) report released on Sunday.
The Southeast Asian nation detained 25,360 drug suspects during the January-October period, a 16.3 percent increase compared to 21,800 during the same period last year. Foreign nationals made up 1,248 of the detainees, representing 25 different nationalities.
Of the total suspects, 48.3 percent were classified as drug traffickers, manufacturers, possessors, or transporters, while 51.7 percent were recorded as drug users.
"Authorities confiscated 4.26 tons of illicit drugs and 537 kilograms of dry cannabis between Jan. 1 and Oct. 31, 2026," the report said, adding that this marked a decrease from the 5.48 tons of narcotics and 516 kilograms of dry marijuana seized during the same timeframe in 2025.
Other seized evidence included 73 pistols and 27 homemade rifles, the report said, adding that the confiscated narcotics largely consisted of ketamine, ecstasy, heroin, crystal methamphetamine, methamphetamine pills, cocaine, and cathinone.
Cambodia does not impose the death penalty for drug offenses. Under national law, individuals convicted of trafficking more than 80 grams of illicit drugs can face life imprisonment. ■

Protocol upgrading China-Peru FTA takes effect
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
16:22:31 CST
17:22:31 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The protocol upgrading the China-Peru free trade agreement (FTA) took effect on Sunday, according to China's Ministry of Commerce (MOC).
China and Peru launched negotiations on the upgrade in November 2018 and signed the protocol on Nov. 14, 2024. The original FTA was signed in 2009 and took effect in 2010.
The protocol improves seven existing chapters of the original FTA, covering rules of origin, customs procedures and trade facilitation, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, intellectual property rights, trade in services, temporary entry of business personnel, and investment, the MOC said in an online statement.
The protocol also adds five new chapters on standards and conformity assessment cooperation, competition policy, e-commerce, global supply chains, and environment and trade.
The two sides also set out future provisions for negotiations on negative lists for trade in services and investment, aimed at further raising openness in these areas, according to the statement.
The China-Peru FTA was the first comprehensive free trade agreement China signed with a Latin American country.
China is Peru's largest trading partner, largest export market and largest source of imports, while Peru is China's fourth-largest trading partner in Latin America and an important investment destination, said an MOC official.
Under the protocol, the new chapter on global supply chains encourages multimodal transport and the development of foreign trade logistics corridors and infrastructure, an innovative arrangement that signals the two countries' commitment to keeping supply chains stable and unimpeded.
The chapter on standards and conformity assessment cooperation establishes a dedicated cooperation mechanism and sets out an intended cooperation list, creating a platform for mutual recognition of standards that is expected to reduce trade costs for enterprises.
The two sides agreed to launch negotiations on negative lists for trade in services and investment within two years after the protocol takes effect, in a bid to further raise the level of openness in these areas and continue to tap the potential of bilateral trade and investment, the official added.
Since the original FTA came into force in 2010, it has played an important role in promoting bilateral economic and trade cooperation. Two-way trade rose from 6.4 billion U.S. dollars in 2009 to 50.4 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, an increase of nearly seven times, official data show.
The protocol is expected to help tap further opportunities for bilateral trade and investment cooperation, provide a better business environment for enterprises of both countries and inject new vitality into bilateral economic and trade relations, the MOC said. ■

Chinese research ships map Taiwan’s undersea infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
08:22:25 UTC
17:22:25 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China has ramped up undersea mapping operations in waters east and south of Taiwan to advance its ability to seize it, according to a Wall Street Journal report.
Chinese research vessels are surveying the subsurface landscape to help its submarines and underwater drones, which could be used to blockade or halt US intervention, Bryan Clark, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, said.
Surveying around Taiwan increased following an announcement by Japan and the Philippines in May of plans to hold discussions on overlapping maritime boundaries in waters east of Taiwan. The two countries have stepped up defense cooperation in response to what they see as threats from Beijing.
“China is capitalizing on the boundary talks as a pretext for what it likely wanted to do anyway: that is, to ratchet up the pressure on Taiwan,” said Allen Zhang, a Heritage Foundation research assistant. “Beijing has long sought legal cover for its gray-zone tactics—coercive activities short of lethal force—and research vessels fit that mold quite well,” Zhang added.
Su Chih-chieh (蘇志杰), an associate professor at National Taiwan University’s Institute of Oceanography, said, “They are launching research ships as fast as dropping dumplings into a pot. Taiwan is having a really hard time catching up right now.”
Taiwan has only five ships actively carrying out its own maritime research. It added two ships in August.
Chen Chung-ling (陳璋玲), president of the National Academy of Marine Research in Kaohsiung, said Taiwanese research efforts demonstrate Taiwan’s commitment to security, WSJ reported. “The more you understand the ocean, the more you can get from it,” she said.
However, Liao Te-yu (陳璋玲), director general of the Taiwan Ocean Research Institute, warned that Taiwan’s research ships are more academically focused and do not necessarily align with defense needs. “We actually understand very little about the waters surrounding us,” Liao said.
China also uses research vessels to locate telecommunications cables, which are another target in a conflict, WSJ cited analysts as saying.
“They’re trying to see what the undersea infrastructure looks like, because they probably want the ability to cut off Taiwan from outside communications if they can as part of a coercion campaign,” Clark said.
WSJ cited a Center for Strategic and International Studies report as saying China-linked research vessels “spent a disproportionately large share of their observed time near critical infrastructure compared with research vessels from 47 other countries.”

Judge rules on Trump’s $10 billion WSJ-Epstein lawsuit
A federal judge has permanently dismissed US President Donald Trump’s $10 billion amended defamation case against the Wall Street Journal and media mogul Rupert Murdoch over a report about his letter to the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
In July 2025, the WSJ published an article describing a sexually suggestive note, which Trump allegedly presented to the disgraced financier for his 50th birthday in 2003. It reportedly appeared in a book of congratulatory letters put together by Ghislaine Maxwell, who is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence for her participation in Epstein’s sex-trafficking scheme.
The note, which, among other things, said: “Happy Birthday – and may every day be another wonderful secret,” contained several lines of typed text framed by a hand-drawn outline of what looks to be a nude woman. A signature resembling the one used by Trump appeared in the area where the figure’s pelvic region might be.
Following the publication, the US president vigorously denied the authorship of the raunchy birthday card, claiming: “This is not me. This is a fake thing. I never wrote a picture in my life. I don’t draw pictures of women.”
Trump’s initial defamation case against the Wall Street Journal and Murdoch’s News Corp., which owns the outlet, was rejected by US District Judge Darrin Gayles in Miami in April. However, he allowed the president’s team to fix the legal defects that he had identified and file another complaint.
On Saturday, the same judge threw out Trump’s second attempt to sue the WSJ and Murdoch, saying that “as with his first attempt, he has failed” to prove that the defendants acted with actual malice when they reported on the birthday card.
Gayles disagreed with Trump’s lawyers, who argued that the outlet should have dropped the story as soon as the president denied his involvement with Epstein. “That is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment,” he wrote in a 20-page ruling.
The judge dismissed the case “with prejudice,” meaning that it cannot be refiled again.
A spokesperson for the WSJ’s publisher, Dow Jones & Co., said in a statement that it’s “pleased with the court’s decision.”
The representative of Trump’s legal team insisted that “the president will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions.” A source told CBS News that the ruling by Gayles will likely be appealed.
Trump has repeatedly denied having been friendly with Epstein, who died in a New York jail in 2019 while awaiting trial on federal sex-trafficking charges. However, the US president’s name is mentioned on at least 3,000 occasions in a massive trove of files related to the investigation of Epstein’s case, which had been released by the US Department of Justice last year.

India’s new high-altitude combat tank was designed to go where its heavier armoured fighting vehicles cannot: the thin mountain air, narrow roads and small bridges along its disputed border with China.
In its base configuration, the Zorawar weighs some 25 tonnes – light enough to be flown all the way to the Line of Actual Control – but a push to make it strong enough to withstand high-calibre autocannon fire could add an extra seven tonnes to that loadout.
Reports of renewed stand-offs between Indian and Chinese troops at the border, including one carried by The Hindu newspaper on October 23, have injected fresh urgency into the debate surrounding how much the tank should weigh.

Australia's latest World Cup smash-up helps nobody
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:53:51 UTC
16:53:51 KST

Fri, 18 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Tigers 0, Raiders 6
analysis
Australia's 124-6 win over Wales in the women's Rugby League World Cup helps nobody
Gallows humour was the order of the day for Australia's World Cup match against Wales, which was only fitting given it trudged towards its inevitable conclusion like the condemned to the executioner's block.
The Jillaroos ran out 124-6 winners in a game where the only element of contest was whether the reigning world champions could bring up the century.
They did it easily in the end, smashing their own record for biggest World Cup win, with Jaime Chapman's sixth try in the shadows of the full-time siren eclipsing France's 116-0 victory over Serbia in 2023 in the most lopsided result in women's international rugby league history.
In the first half, as they ran up a 60-0 lead, Australia scored 10 tries and Wales played the ball just 15 times. Five-eighth Jesse Southwell finished with 44 points on her own.
The Jillaroos did not make a tackle from the fifth minute until after the half-time siren and Australian halfback Tarryn Aiken did not make a tackle until 10 minutes before full-time.
After Australia scored its 15th try of the match it started getting booed by the sparse Parramatta Stadium crowd, who reserved their biggest cheer of the day for Welsh second rower Paige Travis's score that narrowed the gap to 100-6.
It was the sole bright spot of the match but the punters soon returned to an idle stupor as Australia added four more tries in the final seven minutes.
All World Cups are going to have their blowouts and rugby league's more than most. But they must serve a wider purpose and this one did not.
It benefited nobody and served to damage the tournament's credibility and its only legacy can be like Australia's 110-4 win over Russia in the men's 2000 World Cup, which is to say as a historical oddity for the trainspotters.
As the women's World Cup reckons with what has been an uneven tournament at best, marred by the same enormous scorelines of the men's edition but with few of the strong crowds, questions must be asked as to why a game like this could happen at all.
The uninterested and meagre turn-out for this match was proof it did not maximise the product, which very much felt like a curtain-raiser to the two men's matches that followed. Nor does it aid development.
It stuffed some stat sheets and gave ammunition to the bad-faith actors who are always on the hunt for an opportunity to take a shot at women's sport.
The Jillaroos are the best team in the world by an order of magnitude and have been for years. They gain nothing by putting the cleaners through Wales, who exist in a different universe.
That's why the Welsh should be spared any blame for how this went down. When the criticism comes it should not fall on them.
They qualified fair and square but they did not ask for this and there's no way to say it without sounding patronising but they did their best in the face of impossible odds.
While they have Canterbury halfback Tayla Preston and North Queensland winger Sian Williams as well as a smattering of Super League talent in Bethan Daiton, Carys Marsh and Agnes Wood, most of their players ply their trade in the women's second division in England.
It's a competition that can still have the draw disrupted by forfeits and a far cry from the semi-professional existence most of the Australians lead.
Cardiff plays the same sport as the Sydney Roosters, but the two teams live in different worlds.
Some of the Welsh players had only played a handful of rugby league games before this tour and their entire coaching staff is filled by volunteers.
As Australia moves on to the semi-finals, Wales heads home with a few bumps and bruises and perhaps a few stories to tell.
It is part of the developing arm of a developing sport and while it has its place on the international scene it is not across from an Australia side who are so dominant it's starting to become a problem.
They are overwhelming against everyone they play, let alone a team from the sport's frontiers packed with players who have never taken on athletes like Chapman, Tamika Upton or Jess Sergis in their lives.
Even so, lopsided results are not an issue on their own, so long as they serve a wider purpose.
The progress of Samoa, Fiji and Papua New Guinea through this World Cup would not have happened if they were not exposed to teams like Australia and New Zealand, even if there were growing pains.
Hours later, in the same stadium, Tonga and Samoa played out the most eagerly anticipated clash of the men's World Cup, one which could have sold out the ground twice over.
None of that happens without some blow-outs along the way.
But there are limits to what can be found amid the wreckage when a team who shouldn't be there are thrown into the fast lane.
Total obliteration leaves nothing behind. This was not a building block; this was a massacre that left no survivors.

Safety or 'intimidation'? Launch of police unit with military-style rifles sparks human rights fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:48:13 UTC
16:48:13 KST

IN BRIEF
- The NSW Police's new Armed Response Command officially commenced operations on Sunday.
- Rights advocates have raised concerns that the unit may be used to "intimidate or suppress peaceful protest".
Human rights advocates and political opponents are warning that the NSW Police unit now patrolling Sydney hotspots with military-style rifles could lead to overpolicing and "intimidation".
The $94.3 million, "high-visibility, intelligence-led" Armed Response Command (ARC), which was officially launched on Sunday, was among a range of reforms introduced by the NSW government after the Bondi Beach terror attack on 14 December 2025.
Authorities have said the ARC — a first-of-its-kind rapid response unit in Australia, inspired by similar units in the United Kingdom and Germany — would deter crime, increase community safety, and increase police capacity to respond rapidly to serious threats.
NSW Premier Chris Minns has said: "The security challenges facing our state have changed, and our policing model needs to change with them."
"This is about being prepared for the worst and making sure we can keep the community safe," Minns said when unveiling the ARC in early October.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
NSW Police has said the ARC will increase police presence in "high-risk" areas, including "priority locations, major events, crowded public spaces, sporting matches and places of worship".
The ARC is comprised of 250 "carefully selected officers" who have undergone six months of specialist training, including "rifle proficiency, active armed offender response, advanced driver training and tactical medical care", according to a statement from late October.
The unit, which was announced in late February, will patrol the streets in purpose-built vehicles, fitted with specialised gun safes.
Officers will carry Australian Combat Assault Rifles. Measuring over 70cm long and with a range of more than 500 metres, NSW Police say the weapons were deemed "the most suitable" after "extensive field and endurance testing".
NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon has said the ARC will be "a deterrent for those who wish to commit harm, incite hatred or cause fear".
"The environment in NSW has changed, so the way we police the community has changed and what the community expect from us, has changed," he said on 8 October.
While giving evidence at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion, the NSW Police's deputy commissioner said officers responding to the attack at Bondi Beach with standard-issue 9mm Glock pistols were outgunned.
Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Alex Ryvchin has also said police didn't have the resources to properly respond.
"On December 14 our police were clearly not given the means to promptly stop the attack, and two officers were among the seriously injured as a result," he said.
"No Australian wants to see officers with military weapons on our streets, but the sight of body bags is far worse."
He said the NSW community should "be grateful to the police and state government" for increasing preparedness, which will "hopefully deter terrorists or end attacks quickly".
ARC an 'escalation of state violence'
However, the unit has also sparked concerns from human rights advocates and some members of the NSW parliament.
Amnesty International Australia has said it has "serious concerns about the increasing militarisation of policing" and is calling for "robust safeguards to protect human rights, particularly the right to peaceful protest".
"People must be able to exercise their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly without fear of intimidation or excessive force," Amnesty International Australia strategic campaigner Andrew Witheford said.
"The NSW Government must provide clear assurances that the Armed Response Command will not be used to intimidate or suppress peaceful protest, and ensure its operations are subject to rigorous human rights safeguards and independent scrutiny."
"Any expansion of police powers and capabilities must be accompanied by clear, publicly accessible rules, robust independent oversight and accountability," he said, adding that the "use of force by police must always comply with international human rights standards".
Sue Higginson, a NSW Greens upper house member and the party's spokesperson for justice, described the ARC as an "intimidation unit" and an "escalation in state violence".
She said police "wav[ing] weapons of death" around Sydney streets would only increase already existing fears of police violence.
"To believe you can intimidate your way to community cohesion is authoritarian and draconian," she added.
"I'm alarmed by the commentary of Commissioner Mal Lanyon that the threat of being shot by police should act as a deterrent to 'harm' or 'hatred'. I am astounded by the attitude of our most senior police officer."
Higginson also raised concerns about how the ARC may seek to use long-range rifles at peaceful protests.
She said that, while political speech has been deemed constitutionally protected from anti-protest laws, it should not be deterred "with guns".
In response to questions about the presence of the ARC at protest events, ARC commander Detective Superintendent Andrew Evans said the NSW Police's Public Order and Riot Squad were "the experts when it comes to public order management, not the Armed Response Command".
However, he added that he was "not in a position to say we will never be there".
"If there's information that a particular group might be the target of an active armed offender incident, we will have rifles around the corner," he said at a press conference on Sunday.
NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley said the ARC was a "sensible" and "measured" response to events like the Bondi massacre and "nobody is better to deploy this than the New South Wales Police and the officers that we have who are expertly trained".
She added that, since the Bondi attack, there hadn't been "much of a backlash" from the deployment of officers with long-armed rifles at large public events, such as New Year's Eve celebrations in Sydney and Melbourne and at the Sydney Cricket Grounds for the final Ashes Test match in January.
Declining trust in NSW Police
NSW Police has experienced a significant decline in community trust since 2019, according to data from the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research.
Community confidence in the police's ability to bring offenders to justice dropped from 82 per cent in 2019 to 73 per cent in 2025.
Only 49 per cent of respondents felt police dealt with cases promptly, compared to 66 per cent in 2019.
Over the same period, confidence that police officers respected the rights of people accused of crimes declined from 75 to 69 per cent.
Meanwhile, belief that accused persons are treated fairly fell from 77 to 69 per cent and trust that police meet victims' needs dropped from 70 per cent to 56 per cent.
Evans told ARC officers during their attestation that he hoped the unit would improve the community's trust in police.
"When a member of the public sees an ARC vehicle, I want them to feel reassured," he said.

Bolivia declares state of emergency due to Super El Niño

Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz announced that he is introducing a state of emergency in the country due to droughts and floods related to the Super El Niño phenomenon, which is causing significant damage in various parts of the world this year, Agence France-Presse reported.
The measure will allow for the allocation of additional financial resources and the dispatch of rescue teams to the most affected areas.
"We have made enormous efforts to protect the environment and minimize the consequences of this year's Super El Niño phenomenon," Paz said in an address to the nation.
The drought has affected more than 78,000 families in six of the country's nine departments. According to the latest figures from the civil defense ministry, as of this week, it has also caused the loss of more than 75,000 livestock.
"This phenomenon will cause extremely severe damage as a result of both drought and flooding, so we need the cooperation of all institutions," the president noted.
This year's El Niño could reach unprecedented intensity and exceed the limits of measurement scales used over the past four decades, the United Nations warned this week.
In neighboring countries like Peru, El Niño has led to rising temperatures and the spread of forest fires that have already claimed at least 12 lives. It has also been a factor in the spread of dengue, a tropical disease that has killed 81 people this year. As a result of the impact of El Niño in Chile, the capital Santiago recorded its wettest October on record, AFP recalls.
