====================================================================================================

India is running out of time on fifth-generation fighter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:33:59 UTC
16:33:59 KST

India is running out of time on fifth-generation fighter
Despite India’s increased defense spending, robust government support for domestic arms and military technology manufacturers, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s personal focus on the development of the military-industrial complex, experts warn that the Indian Air Force faces a critical squadron decline that may influence its ability to counter potential adversaries.
This paradox stems from India’s procurement policies, which do not prioritize the acquisition of advanced aircraft for the air force. Apparently, segments of India’s business elite and military leadership, possibly influenced by Western companies, are lobbying for contracts that offer questionable benefits to the country’s armed forces.
While India’s geopolitical and military rivals (China and Pakistan) invest in cutting-edge technology – such as the fifth-generation J-20 and J-35 multi-role fighters – India continues to acquire fourth-generation aircraft like the Rafale and Tejas fighters. However, such aircraft cannot address modern combat challenges or threats effectively.
The situation looks even more dire considering that the Rafale and Tejas fighters are not superior to the Su-30MKI, the primary fighter in service with the Indian Air Force, and may even fall short when it comes to certain tactical specifications. The Su-30MKI boasts significant advantages in speed, maneuverability, payload capacity, and operational range.
This raises a crucial question: why are substantial financial resources from the Indian budget allocated for the purchase of expensive aircraft (Rafale fighters cost about €160 million each) directly from the French private firm Dassault Aviation, when the state-owned Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) offers the option to procure Su-30MKI aircraft assembled under license from Russia at a considerably lower cost?
Real threats
Clearly, the rivalry between Pakistan (and China, which stands behind it) and India is not going to fade anytime soon. In fact, competition will likely intensify in the foreseeable future. A critical factor in preventing the most dangerous scenarios lies in maintaining a balance of military capabilities and defense potential between the opposing sides. So, what does the power balance look like today?
Islamabad and Beijing are heavily investing in fifth-generation multirole fighters. By 2030, Pakistan is expected to field no fewer than 40 J-35AE fighters, while the Chinese Air Force could deploy up to 500 J-20s and J-35 fighters. Additionally, the Chinese Navy may have over 50 carrier-based J-35s. In total, this amounts to about 600 fifth-generation fighters – each one of them superior to any fourth-generation aircraft.
Armed with highly effective long-range air-to-air weapons, Pakistan and China’s stealthy fifth-generation fighters will be able to launch missile attacks without being detected by Indian Air Force radar systems. Under such circumstances, India’s military aviation could face a devastating defeat, leading to humiliation and a prolonged recovery process. This is inevitable, since fifth-generation fighters surpass fourth-generation aircraft.
The strategy of overwhelming the enemy with sheer numbers and concentrating an extensive air force over specific combat zones, is fundamentally flawed: no number of Rafale or Tejas fighters can match the combat capabilities of J-20 and J-35 aircraft.
The air forces of Pakistan and China possess cutting-edge technologies like stealth capabilities, advanced radar systems capable of covertly tracking opponents, and long-range missiles that significantly outdistance those in the arsenals of Rafale and Tejas fighters.
However, if the Indian Air Force were to acquire Su-57E fighters, equipped with stealth technology, the modern N-036 Byelka radar, long-range RVV-BD missiles, and other state-of-the-art munitions, India’s ability to confront its neighbors in the above-mentioned scenarios would change dramatically.
Why Russia?
For over 70 years, Soviet and Russian aviation technology has been in service with the Indian military, demonstrating remarkable efficiency and reliability. Russia has proven to be a dependable partner in military-technical cooperation.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has praised the quality and effectiveness of Russian weapons, particularly highlighting their successful deployment during Operation Sindoor in May 2025. Moscow is eager to continue the mutually beneficial collaboration with New Delhi in the defense sector. This includes maintaining the joint Su-30MKI program and potentially organizing licensed assembly of the fifth-generation Su-57E fighter at facilities operated by India’s HAL.
The ongoing modernization of the Pakistani Air Force and the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Air Force with advanced aircraft has prompted India to take decisive actions to restore parity and the balance of power. Given the current circumstances, a swift acquisition of 50 Su-57E fighters from Russia under a fast-track mechanism, along with plans for licensed production of an additional 450 units in India, seems like the most prudent course of action. This could involve the latest two-seat variant, the Su-57D. Over the next few decades, such a project would effectively address the challenges and threats that India faces.
More than just a prototype
The Su-57 fighter jet has already entered service with the Russian Air Force and has participated in combat operations.
India contributed to the development of the fighter that served as the basis for the Su-57. In 2010, the Indian Ministry of Defense initiated the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) program to create an indigenous fifth-generation fighter. However, after more than 15 years, this program has yet to reach the flight testing stage. Serial production is not likely to commence before 2035.
Alexander Mikheev, head of Rosoboronexport, and Vadim Badekha, head of the United Aircraft Corporation (UAC), confirmed that the Su-57 aircraft – specifically its export version, the Su-57E – is already being delivered abroad. The Su-57E is available for friendly countries collaborating with Russia on defense projects. If India approaches Moscow regarding the supply of this combat aircraft, Russia would likely respond in a positive manner.
Moreover, advanced Russian technologies transferred to India under a licensing agreement will assist Indian specialists in refining and successfully implementing several national projects, including the AMCA.
Unlike American F-35s – which have struggled to maintain supersonic speeds in sustained cruise mode – the Su-57 meets all the criteria expected of a fifth-generation fighter.
For New Delhi, the Su-57 offers multiple advantages, especially since it was designed at the same bureau that developed the Su-30MKI – the Indian Air Force’s primary combat aircraft as of 2026. This continuity provides valuable benefits in terms of operational procedures, maintenance, repair, and logistical support, leveraging existing airfield, storage, and training infrastructures.
Indigenous programs
Prime Minister Narendra Modi highly supports India’s national defense industry initiatives. He made history as the first prime minister of India to fly in the cockpit of a supersonic fighter jet.
Professional pilots who have flown the Tejas aircraft praise its performance, noting it surpasses the MiG-21, which the Tejas was designed to replace under the Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) program that began in 1983. However, the mission was not fulfilled; the project has faced significant delays, and by the time the Tejas was deployed in 2015, the vast majority of the 874 MiG-21s acquired by the Indian Air Force between 1963 and 1987 had already been retired due to wear and tear. Instead of 20 squadrons of MiG aircraft, by 2026, the Indian Air Force had just two Tejas squadrons consisting of 30 single-seat and six two-seat models. Field tests are being conducted to identify and rectify issues on aircraft from the initial production batch.
The 18th Squadron, formed in 2020, has already lost two Tejas planes in accidents – one in March 2024 and another in November 2025. The latter incident involved a fatal failure during a demonstration flight at an airshow in Dubai. The initial variant (Mark I) will no longer be produced, as it proved unreliable and technically inadequate.
Like many Indian projects, Tejas is plagued by delays which result in technological obsolescence by the time of production. Consequently, the substantial financial investments in such programs fail to deliver the expected returns or strengthen India’s defense capabilities.
Indian manufacturers also developed a naval version of the Tejas. Testing began in 2020 aboard the INS Vikramaditya aircraft carrier (built by Russia under Project 11430) and continued three years later on the indigenously constructed INS Vikrant. The compact design of the Tejas offers advantages for hangar storage; however, with a standard combat load, it can only operate within a few hundred miles. During combat operations, the carrier would need to approach the target closer, increasing the risk of retaliatory strikes from the enemy.
After conducting evaluations, the Indian Navy concluded that such an aircraft was not suitable for carrier operations. The official reason for rejecting the LCA-Navy was its low thrust-to-weight ratio, which prevented full utilization of the aircraft’s potential when taking off from an aircraft carrier. In response to requests from Indian industry, further tests were conducted on an upgraded version, but its performance still fell short of naval requirements.
Coming to terms with the LCA-Navy’s inability to meet expectations, Indian aerospace engineers proposed a completely new aircraft – the Twin Engine Deck Based Fighter (TEDBF), which bears a striking resemblance to the French Rafale-M. This move signifies a concession by the creators and advocates of the Tejas, acknowledging their defeat in the competition for carrier aviation. Work on the TEDBF began in 2020. The prototype’s first flight is scheduled for 2032 and serial production is anticipated in 2038.
Meanwhile, last year, the People’s Liberation Army Navy received its third aircraft carrier, the Fujian, equipped with fifth-generation J-35 fighters. Construction has also begun on the fourth Type 004 aircraft carrier. It will likely have a displacement of around 100,000 tons and accommodate an air wing of 100 aircraft, including the J-35.
Dependence on the US
In coordination with the main contractor, Indian industry continues Tejas Mark IA testing, which started in spring 2022. Without waiting for these trials to conclude, the Indian Air Force has placed two successive orders totaling 141 single-seat and 41 two-seat aircraft, scheduled for delivery between 2027 and 2032. Production will take place at two facilities in Bangalore and Nasik.
Following this, production of the Tejas Mark II is expected to commence. The first test flight has faced multiple delays and is now expected no earlier than 2028. While no firm order has been placed for this new model, the Air Force leadership hopes to eventually have 18 squadrons of Tejas aircraft, including 10 Mark II variant squadrons.
The idea to direct resources into producing fourth-generation fighters for the next decade seems imprudent, given that China has mastered mass production of fifth-generation aircraft and is set to begin transitioning to sixth-generation models in the coming years. Deliveries of Chinese J-35 fifth-generation fighters to Pakistan are underway, while existing JF-17s are being upgraded with systems and munitions developed for the J-35.
However, a far more pressing issue is the potential deepening dependence on the United States. Throughout the practical implementation of the LCA program, the technical specifications of the aircraft have been repeatedly adjusted, primarily by replacing certain Indian components with foreign ones, which gradually increases the foreign share in the cost of mass-produced products. Among the imported items, the most expensive was the US engine, which had to replace the GTX-35VS Kaveri engine which faced challenges in meeting technical criteria.
Negotiations for a licensed production agreement for the F414 engine have been challenging, largely because Washington is reluctant to share advanced General Electric technologies developed with Pentagon funding. The US is only willing to share some of the technology, omitting the most sensitive components.
The reluctance to fully share F414 engine technology can be explained by one factor: Washington seeks to maintain leverage over New Delhi by controlling the pace of the licensed production of engines for India’s frontline air force.
The second most costly imported component is the onboard radar system. Development of an indigenous MMR radar was halted due to unsatisfactory test results, leading to a preference for foreign alternatives. The prototype aircraft utilized the Ericsson-Ferranti PS-05 radar, originally designed for the Swedish JAS-39 Gripen. Delays in the LCA program rendered the PS-05 obsolete, resulting in its discontinuation. It has since been replaced by the EL/M-2032, which now equips Mark I variants.
It’s worth noting that Elta’s product is also outdated; it was developed in the 1980s for the Israeli Lavi fighter jet (canceled in 1987). The obsolescence is particularly evident in its use of mechanical beam scanning, while the Russian N-011M radar on the Su-30MKI, which was introduced into the Indian Air Force in 2002, boasts more advanced electronic scanning technology.
Recently, Elta proposed the EL/M-2052 with an active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar configuration. The manufacturer promises to refine it by the time Mark IA aircraft (formed in 2015) are delivered to the air force, projected for late this year or early next year. Various publications have diligently presented Israeli radars as a “temporary solution” for the Tejas program, but as seen with General Electric engines, “temporary” solutions often end up being used much longer than expected.
Strategic decision-making
The practical implementation of the LCA program has resulted in yet another fourth-generation supersonic fighter jet emerging on the global stage. However, the Tejas does not surpass its foreign counterparts. Technically, the Tejas Mark I barely matches the Chinese FC-1, which was adopted by the Pakistan Air Force as the JF-17 in 2007. At best, the Tejas Mark II might reach the level of the JF-17 Block III (with AESA, operational since 2023) and the J-10CE, which Pakistani pilots effectively utilized to fend off an Indian airstrike in May 2025.
With the Indian Air Force already operating a substantial fleet of over 300 Su-30MKIs and Rafale aircraft, which are far better suited for the interception of aerial threats and air superiority missions, the Tejas Mark I may only serve effectively in ground attack operations and pilot training. Fortunately, being a lightweight, single-engine aircraft means it has low fuel consumption. Nevertheless, its limited thrust-to-weight ratio, outdated radar, reduced payload capacity, and narrow selection of munitions (lacking long-range air-to-air missiles), along with the absence of critical stealth technologies naturally confine the aircraft to its own niche. The Su-57E is in a different class altogether.
Consequently, the Tejas cannot be viewed as a viable alternative to the Su-57E. Continuing the LCA program in its current form hampers the decision-making process, since the program competes for budget resources. Moreover, there’s another contender for state funding – the AMCA, with its first flight planned for 2034 and serial production slated for 2036.
In selecting a fifth-generation fighter program, decision-makers in India will need to consider numerous factors and criteria that can sometimes be conflicting and contradictory. Among these is the inherent bias towards domestic projects (i.e. AMCA, LCA, etc.), even if they may not be technically or technologically superior compared to the best foreign alternatives.
The desire to produce everything domestically is understandable, but there are many compelling arguments in favor of purchasing the best foreign technologies or producing them under license. The advanced Su-57E, a premier frontline fighter, is one of such example. For India, Russia remains a reliable partner as decades of effective military-technical collaboration have proven.

Bulgaria's presidential runoff kicks off

SOFIA, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Bulgarians go to the polls on Sunday to vote in the second round of the country's elections for president and vice president.
Nearly 6.6 million voters are eligible to choose between incumbent President Iliana Iotova, running with Kiril Valchev as her vice-presidential candidate, and Andrey Gurov, who is seeking the presidency with Georgi Kandev as his running mate.
The Iotova-Valchev ticket, backed by the ruling Progressive Bulgaria party and the Bulgarian Socialist Party, among others, came on top in the first round on Oct. 25 with 34.76 percent of the votes.
The Gurov-Kandev ticket, supported by the parties We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria, came second among the 27 candidate pairs with 31.95 percent.
The first exit polls are expected to be released at 8:00 p.m. (1800 GMT), immediately after the close of the polls. Official results are due no later than Wednesday.
The Bulgarian president and vice president are elected directly by voters for a five-year term. Iotova's term is set to expire at the end of January 2027.
Iotova, 62, was elected vice president twice, in 2016 and 2021, serving alongside President Rumen Radev. In accordance with the country's Constitution, she succeeded Radev as head of state after he resigned in January this year. Before that, she served on the National Council of the Bulgarian Socialist Party from 2000 to 2016, as well as in the Bulgarian National Assembly and the European Parliament.
Valchev is director general of the Bulgarian News Agency.
Gurov, an adjunct professor of finance at the American University in Bulgaria, has less political experience than Iotova. He served as Bulgaria's caretaker prime minister for 78 days in the first half of this year and chaired the parliamentary group of We Continue the Change in two legislatures from December 2021 to February 2023.
Kandev is a former career police officer who served as acting secretary general at the Ministry of Interior for several months this year. ■

World Insights: Yerevan Pathway charts course for biodiversity action, but challenges remain
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:25:46 CST
16:25:46 KST

YEREVAN, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) concluded in Yerevan on Saturday after negotiators secured agreement on the conference's main decisions, including the Yerevan Pathway aimed at accelerating global biodiversity action.
This encouraging outcome came at a critical time for global biodiversity protection. Halfway between the adoption of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and its 2030 deadline, countries face a widening gap between their commitments to protect nature and the action to fulfill them. Whether the Yerevan Pathway can help close that gap will depend on financing, national policies and sustained international cooperation.
A PATHWAY TO ACCELERATE ACTION
The conference's main task was to conduct the first global review of collective progress in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which sets out 23 targets for 2030.
The assessment presented governments with a clear warning: Without a rapid acceleration of implementation, the framework's 2030 targets and mission would not be achieved, putting its longer-term goals for 2050 at risk.
The Yerevan Pathway is part of the response to that assessment. Rather than setting new targets, it focuses on how countries can step up efforts to meet those already agreed upon.
Embedded in the global review decision, the pathway identifies several priorities for the period through 2030: accelerating implementation, broadening the coverage of national targets, strengthening financial and other support, engaging governments and societies more widely, and improving monitoring and knowledge.
Negotiators also adopted decisions covering protected areas and forest biodiversity, sustainable wildlife management, invasive alien species, marine and coastal biodiversity, synthetic biology and other areas.
Alongside the negotiations, nearly 2 billion U.S. dollars in new biodiversity funding was announced, according to the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). This included 560 million dollars under the ninth replenishment of the Global Environment Facility and its Global Biodiversity Framework Fund, 500 million dollars through the Species Recovery Alliance, and more than 330 million dollars through the Value Nature Fund.
Together, the decisions and funding announcements provide a basis for further action. However, the effectiveness of the pathway will depend on whether international agreements lead to changes in national priorities and concrete action on the ground.
FINANCE DIVIDE TESTS DELIVERY
Finance remains one of the main obstacles to implementation, both in terms of how much funding is available and how the responsibility for providing it is shared.
The global report found that developed countries had failed to meet their commitment to provide at least 20 billion dollars annually in biodiversity finance to developing countries by 2025. This shortfall was a major point of contention in negotiations over funding for the next stage of implementation.
Some developed countries called for broadening the contributor base, bringing into focus a longstanding dispute over the relationship between countries' financial capacity and their obligations under the CBD.
Article 20 of the convention requires developed-country parties to provide new and additional financial resources, while allowing other parties to assume such obligations voluntarily.
The new funding announcements offered some encouragement, but the broader challenge of securing predictable support on the scale needed remains. For developing countries, efforts to strengthen conservation, restore ecosystems and monitor progress continue to depend heavily on access to finance and technical assistance.
Nor did the conference resolve every issue. Negotiations on cooperation and strategic review, along with two items under the Nagoya Protocol, remained unfinished and were deferred to the next ordinary meetings.
"Every diluted clause, every deferred target, is a step towards irreversible loss," Guido Broekhoven, interim global director of multilateral policy at the World Wide Fund for Nature International, told a press conference before the closing session.
His remarks underscored a central challenge facing the negotiations: while consensus is essential to international cooperation, biodiversity loss continues as governments work to reach agreement.
CHINA'S ROLE IN ADVANCING IMPLEMENTATION
Turning commitments into concrete results was also a key theme in discussions of China's contribution, including its support for the global review, sharing experience in domestic conservation and financing for biodiversity projects in developing countries.
The global review decision specifically thanked China for hosting the Kunming dialogue to support preparations for the review. It also acknowledged financial support provided through the China Trust Fund via the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP).
In an interview with Xinhua during the conference, COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan said China had made important contributions to advancing the talks, from preparatory work to the formal negotiations.
Such cooperation has practical relevance as countries seek ways to overcome implementation barriers, Matevosyan said, adding that national experiences can help identify approaches that others may adapt to their own circumstances.
Astrid Schomaker, executive secretary of the secretariat of the CBD, said the progress reflected in China's seventh national report was encouraging and highlighted its ecological conservation red lines as an example of how biodiversity protection could be incorporated into national planning and development.
Financial support is another important part of turning the framework into action.
Inger Andersen, executive director of the UNEP, recognized China's continued leadership through the establishment of the Kunming Biodiversity Fund following its COP15 presidency. She emphasized the importance of helping developing countries access the financing needed to implement the agreement.
These contributions point to the task now facing all parties: ensuring that international cooperation is backed by the funding, institutions and policies needed to deliver results.
The Yerevan conference preserved a common direction at a difficult moment for biodiversity protection. The next four years will determine whether governments can turn their commitments into measurable progress before the 2030 deadline.
As Schomaker put it: "Ultimately, the test is not what governments agreed in Yerevan, but what they change when they return home." ■

Economic Watch: New Zealand firms seek to deepen China market engagement via import expo
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
15:25:41 CST
16:25:41 KST

WELLINGTON, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- From established exhibitors who were present for many consecutive years to innovative businesses making their debut with independent booths this year, New Zealand companies are participating in the China International Import Expo (CIIE) in increasingly diverse ways.
The CIIE is the world's first national-level exhibition dedicated to imports, and its ninth edition will take place in Shanghai from Nov. 5 to 10. For many New Zealand companies, this annual event has become an important gateway to the Chinese market.
GATEWAY TO HUGE CHINESE MARKET
For Sanchia Yonge, chief executive of New Zealand Trade and Enterprise, the international business development agency of the New Zealand government, China is an important market for New Zealand exporters.
The CIIE provides New Zealand exporters a valuable opportunity to showcase their products to buyers and consumers, understand the evolving Chinese market, strengthen brand awareness, and connect with customers, commercial and government partners who can support their long-term growth in China, Yonge stressed.
"We perceive CIIE as the most important exhibition or event for foreign companies to enter the Chinese market," said Roy Van Den Hurk, CEO of Milk New Zealand Dairy Ltd.
"It's a central point where all the buyers come to see you," he added.
For many years, Van Den Hurk personally traveled to Shanghai for the expo almost every year. From a very small booth when the company first joined it to its current independent 200-square-meter exhibition space, the company has achieved tangible business growth through the platform.
Blis Technologies, a New Zealand biotechnology company, is experiencing a new milestone this year, as it will have its own independent booth at the Shanghai expo. In just two years, sales of its oral probiotics products in China have exceeded 100,000 orders.
"First and foremost, China is a very large market. You've got to be very targeted in what you do," said Scott Johnson, CEO of Blis Technologies. "We also believe that the Chinese consumer is taking a more proactive approach to their health."
"TASTE OF NEW ZEALAND"
Sanchia Yonge said that more than 80 New Zealand exporters will be showcasing a diverse range of New Zealand products and services at the CIIE this year. Products and services on display will include food and beverages, dairy, fruit, meat, wine, honey, wool, pet food, consumer goods, health supplements, healthcare and technology.
Some New Zealand companies are participating collectively under the organization of business associations. The China Chamber of Commerce in New Zealand, in cooperation with New Zealand Trade and Enterprise, has taken the lead in organizing the "Taste of New Zealand" exhibition group. This year, it has brought 35 New Zealand exhibitors to the CIIE, with the exhibition group covering an area of 1,170 square meters.
The New Zealand Pavilion will bring together distinctive exhibitors to present a more complete tapestry of New Zealand products. These include king salmon from mountains and glacial waters on the South Island, manuka honey associated with native plants and Maori culture, avocado oil from the Bay of Plenty on the North Island, Hawke's Bay wines, as well as dairy products, ice cream and nutritional supplements.
Together, the exhibitors will showcase different aspects of the industries, from planting and farming to food processing.
Throughout the week, the New Zealand Trade and Enterprise team in China will connect exporters with buyers, partners and media, support customer meetings and networking, livestreaming, product launches and stand by as business agreements are signed.
"We want to help New Zealand exporters turn conversations at CIIE into lasting commercial partnerships in China to support their ongoing growth," said Yonge.
TARGETING SHIFTING CONSUMER DEMANDS
For New Zealand exhibitors, the CIIE is not only a platform for bringing products into the Chinese market, but also an opportunity to gain a closer understanding of the market and consumer demand.
"Going up there each year for the CIIE, you can actually feel how it changes. It's quite big changes actually that you notice," said Van Den Hurk.
To attract Chinese consumers, companies must keep up with the pace of the Chinese market, the CEO stressed, adding that they must come to China in person and engage face-to-face with consumers, the market and distribution channels.
For this reason, the company also introduces new products at the CIIE every year.
"We try to bring new products every year. And I think overall it's very successful," Van Den Hurk said, adding that the company will bring new formulations again for milk powder products, which are going to help the elderly.
He noted that his company's products, packaging and promotional channels are all being updated in response to changing Chinese consumer demand, and the CIIE is an important channel for the company to keep up with the pace of the Chinese market.
"It's the opportunity for businesses like Blis and other New Zealand companies and other global companies to showcase their products in China, with a whole lot of people coming together at one event," Scott Johnson said, adding that it also helps get feedback and understand more about the Chinese consumer and the market up there, so that "we can actually get better and improve our offering because it's always evolving".
"It's even more important to be up there on a regular basis because it's changing so quickly," he added. ■

Bulgaria votes in presidential runoff amid political instability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
07:05:28 UTC
16:05:28 KST

Bulgarians return to the polls on Sunday to elect their president in a runoff between acting President Iliana Yotova and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov after neither candidate secured a majority in the first round.
Yotova and her running mate, Kiril Valchev, received 34.8 percent of the vote, while Gyurov and Georgi Kandev secured 32 percent, according to the Central Election Commission.
Turnout in the October 25 vote stood at around 22.5 percent, the lowest recorded in the country's post-communist history.
A total of 27 candidates contested the first round.
A candidate must receive more than half of the valid votes, with turnout exceeding 50 percent of registered voters, to win in the first round under electoral rules. If those conditions are not met, the two leading candidates advance to a runoff.
The vote comes amid political instability in Bulgaria, which has held eight parliamentary elections since April 2021, including seven early elections.
Disagreements
The repeated parliamentary votes followed difficulties among political parties in securing the support needed to form stable governments.
Disagreements over coalition arrangements led to the collapse of successive attempts to establish regular governments, resulting in caretaker Cabinets and further early elections.
The latest parliamentary election, held in April, saw Progressive Bulgaria, led by former President Rumen Radev, win 131 of the National Assembly's 240 seats, giving the party an outright majority.
Yotova, who served as Radev's vice president, assumed the presidency after he resigned in January. Backed by Radev's Progressive Bulgaria party, she is seeking a full presidential mandate.
A victory would make Yotova Bulgaria's first elected female president, whose duties include representing the country, serving as commander-in-chief of the armed forces and exercising a veto on legislation.
Gyurov, an economist and former deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank, served as caretaker prime minister before the parliamentary elections in April. He is backed by opposition parties.
The campaign has included debate about Bulgaria's foreign policy and its relations with Russia, Ukraine and Western allies.
Polling stations are scheduled to open at 7 am (0500GMT) and close at 8 pm (1800GMT).

Youth protests in more than 30 German cities against the possible introduction of compulsory military service and in support of better education and social justice have escalated into clashes with police and riots. Several police officers were injured, and in Frankfurt demonstrators smashed shop windows, ransacked shops and stole goods. This is reported by DPA.
The protests were organized at the call of the youth movement "Generation Z Takes Charge" (Gen Z regelt). According to organizers, more than 100,000 people took part in the demonstrations across the country. Participants expressed dissatisfaction not only with the possible return of compulsory military service, but also with insufficient funding for education, the rising cost of living, the lack of sufficient measures against climate change and social inequality.
Although most demonstrations were peaceful, tensions escalated in several major cities and clashes with law enforcement.
The most serious unrest was recorded in Frankfurt, where the protest began peacefully in the early afternoon along the Main River. Police said up to 8,000 people took part in the march, while organizers said around 9,000.
However, in the evening, the situation in the city center became more tense. Some of the demonstrators began throwing stones, bottles and firecrackers at the police, which forced the police to end the demonstration. The police used water cannons and pepper spray to disperse the crowd. Several police officers were injured, one of whom may have suffered more serious injuries, said Roman Pozek, the interior minister of the state of Hesse. According to him, about 100 representatives of left-wing extremist circles took part in the attacks on the police.
BTA/AP
The violence continued after the demonstration was dispersed. Groups of rioters smashed the windows of several commercial establishments and looted shops in the city center. Sports shoes and other goods were stolen, and among the attacked establishments was a specialized firearms store. According to police, Molotov cocktails were even thrown at law enforcement officers and emergency services teams.
The situation around Zeil, one of the main shopping streets in Frankfurt, was particularly tense, with a significant police contingent stationed there.
There were also riots in Hamburg. Several thousand people joined the protest march there, and some of the participants, dressed in black and some with masks on their faces, tore down plastic barriers from a road repair area and set them on fire near a subway station. Police intervened with pepper spray, and the fire was extinguished with a water cannon. According to organizers, between 6,000 and 7,000 people participated in the demonstration.
In Berlin, fireworks were also used during a protest in the central Mitte district. About 700 people gathered at Rosenthaler Platz, from where they headed to the Prenzlauer Berg district. Police warned demonstrators not to use fireworks and to refrain from violence. According to law enforcement, representatives of left-wing political circles and pro-Palestinian movements were among the participants.
Due to the previously announced demonstrations, German authorities had taken enhanced security measures. Additional police forces, water cannons and drones were deployed in a number of cities.
BTA/AP
The protests showed that discontent among some young Germans spans a wide range of issues, from the prospect of compulsory military service to education, social policy and the cost of living. Despite the largely peaceful nature of the demonstrations, clashes and subsequent vandalism in Frankfurt and other cities marked the day of protests.

Ukrainian drone forces commander reports monthly record: one target hit every 41 seconds
In October, units from the Unmanned Systems Forces hit a Russian asset every 41 seconds on average and a Russian soldier every 159 seconds. The month set a record for the number of Russian personnel losses inflicted by the grouping.
Source: Robert "Magyar" Brovdi, Commander of Unmanned Systems Forces, on Telegram
Details: Brovdi said that in October, units from the Unmanned Systems Forces hit 64,807 targets, and Russian military personnel losses inflicted by them amounted to 16,796.
The figure for Russian personnel losses was a record for the Unmanned Systems Forces since the start of the full-scale war – 52.55% higher than in August and 24.71% higher than in September.
The daily average was 542 Russian soldiers. The highest daily figure, 701, was recorded on 24 October.
In total over the month, the group's units carried out 255,605 combat missions, of which around 151,500 were strike missions and 104,000 reconnaissance missions.
Around 69.5% of Russian personnel losses were recorded on the Dobropillia-Pokrovsk, Oleksandrivka and Huliaipole fronts.
Brovdi stressed that these figures relate solely to units from the Unmanned Systems Forces and did not include data from other components of Ukraine's defence forces. He said all the results had been verified in the Delta situational awareness system.

Slender-billed nutcracker spotted by amateur photographer in Landen: “Rare phenomenon underway”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:44:00 UTC
15:44:00 KST

In Landen (Flemish Brabant), amateur photographer Eddy Koninckx managed to photograph a slender-billed nutcracker. The little bird is rare and has been in the area for several days now. It has also been spotted in nearby Heverlee (Flemish Brabant) and Averbode (Flemish Brabant).
Slender-billed nutcracker spotted by amateur photographer in Landen: “Rare phenomenon underway”
“The bird was remarkably easy to spot and certainly not shy. At one point, it came within a good 5 metres,” says Eddy.
The thin-billed nutcracker is related to the crow. It has dark brown plumage with distinctive white markings. Its sturdy beak is also striking. The bird is a rare sight in Belgium. It is mainly found in Scandinavia and Eastern Europe.
Invasion of nutcrackers
According to environmental organisation Natuurpunt, a rare phenomenon is currently taking place: an invasion of nutcrackers. “Since October, they have been appearing in unusual numbers across Flanders, whereas they are normally seen here only extremely rarely. These are birds that have undertaken an enormous journey from the taiga, the forested region in the far north-east of Europe. We have to go back decades to find a comparable, large-scale invasion.”
Not enough seeds
The birds are probably looking for food. “They mainly eat pine seeds. But some years, the trees produce few seeds, forcing the birds to seek alternative sources. That was the case this year in the north-eastern breeding grounds. These nutcrackers are then forced to move to temperate regions where they can find sufficient food. In many cases, that means Western Europe,” says Natuurpunt.
And so, the thin-billed nutcracker has also ended up in Landen, though it has already been spotted in Heverlee, Averbode and Merksplas (Antwerp Province), amongst other places. In Landen, it is already attracting many birdwatchers.
“Armed with binoculars and large cameras, they’re trying to catch a glimpse of the bird. The locals are quite pleased about it too, and some just pop round for a chat and even call it ‘their bird’. It’s lovely, isn’t it?”, says Eddy.

Protocol upgrading China-Peru FTA takes effect
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:32:33 CST
15:32:33 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- The protocol upgrading the China-Peru free trade agreement (FTA) took effect on Sunday, according to China's Ministry of Commerce (MOC).
China and Peru launched negotiations on the upgrade in November 2018 and signed the protocol on Nov. 14, 2024. The original FTA was signed in 2009 and took effect in 2010.
The protocol improves seven existing chapters of the original FTA, covering rules of origin, customs procedures and trade facilitation, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, intellectual property rights, trade in services, temporary entry of business personnel, and investment, the MOC said in an online statement.
The protocol also adds five new chapters on standards and conformity assessment cooperation, competition policy, e-commerce, global supply chains, and environment and trade.
The two sides also set out future provisions for negotiations on negative lists for trade in services and investment, aimed at further raising openness in these areas, according to the statement.
Since the original FTA came into force in 2010, it has played an important role in promoting bilateral economic and trade cooperation. Two-way trade rose from 6.4 billion U.S. dollars in 2009 to 50.4 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, an increase of nearly seven times, official data show.
The protocol is expected to help tap further opportunities for bilateral trade and investment cooperation, provide a better business environment for enterprises of both countries and inject new vitality into bilateral economic and trade relations, the MOC said. ■

China Focus: China's resident-led renewal efforts give old neighborhoods new life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:32:27 CST
15:32:27 KST

HANGZHOU, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Amid the ongoing urban renewal drive in China, residents in an east China neighborhood have spearheaded a new model by raising funds for rebuilding their dilapidated residential block.
Unlike the government-led model that typically offers residents new apartments and cash compensation, this project saw its 548 homeowner households raise 499 million yuan (about 74.32 million U.S. dollars), more than 80 percent of the reconstruction bill, with the government covering the rest.
The compound with 13 previously run-down buildings, known as Zhegong Xincun, sits in the downtown Gongshu District of Hangzhou, capital of the affluent Zhejiang Province. These six-story walk-ups were transformed into seven mid-rise buildings, surrounded by green spaces and shared facilities, in February last year.
Hangzhou was an early adopter of this approach. It is among initiatives piloted across Chinese cities, from Harbin in northeast China's Heilongjiang Province to Shenzhen in south China's Guangdong Province, to avoid large-scale land acquisition and heavy investment from developers.
Such pilot projects address long-standing hurdles for urban regeneration in China. Small scattered plots often deliver slim returns for commercial developers, and matching residents' compensation expectations has frequently stalled renewal plans, said Wu Songtao, professor at the School of Architecture and Design of Harbin Institute of Technology.
According to a State Council executive meeting held in May, China is shifting from the stage of large-scale incremental expansion to a stage focused on improving the quality and efficiency of existing urban stock.
"Instead of large-scale demolition, the goal now is to revitalize existing buildings, factories, neighborhoods and public spaces," said Zheng Degao, vice president of the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design.
Zheng added that all beneficiaries, namely government, businesses and property owners alike, should share both the costs and the benefits.
But translating this vision into practice was no easy task. Renewing old neighborhoods involves many interests and is prone to disputes, said Li Yin, an official with Gongshu District.
Previous attempts to renew Zhegong Xincun all failed due to residents seeing only limited benefits and strains on public finances.
Built in the 1980s and 1990s as faculty housing for Zhejiang University of Technology, the compound sits in a prime location in central Hangzhou, surrounded by shopping areas, metro stations and a large hospital.
However, over the years, safety hazards mounted. Stiff windows were difficult to close, and building settlement warped door frames and locks, sometimes forcing residents to climb over walls to enter their homes.
"The plaster crumbled at the slightest touch. We lived in fear every day," said a resident surnamed Yu.
The university once carried out reinforcement work, but the effect was limited. Because the buildings continued to tilt and crack due to ongoing building settlement, such measures offered only temporary relief.
A previous housing-relocation plan failed to win broad support. According to residents, a 2014 survey on demolition and reconstruction, and another attempt in 2018, both came to nothing.
"The old idea was that the government should cover everything, from relocation to renovation," one resident said. "But as previous plans kept falling through, we realized we had to do it ourselves."
The turning point came in April 2023, when the subdistrict community office reached out to residents for their opinions on starting a resident-led renewal project.
With support from local policies on renovating old urban neighborhoods, Gongshu District developed and adopted a resident-led renewal model for the compound. The initial stage of the renewal project was launched in mid-2022. The district set up a special task force to coordinate departments, study relevant policies and win public support via explanations.
Local officials said that the harder part was reaching a consensus. "The core of the entire project lies in community engagement, shifting residents' mindset from being asked to renovate to wanting to renovate," Li said.
A voluntary committee of 13 representatives was formed. After consulting all households, it submitted an application and entrusted local authorities to coordinate and initiate the renewal.
By late August 2023, all but one of the compound's 548 homeowner households had signed agreements, bringing the signing rate to 99.82 percent, thus paving the way for the renewal plan to move forward.
In May 2024, the last household came forward to sign before delivery. "This last resident later told me, 'I watched for a long time, and I could see the project is fair,'" Li said.
Yu calculated that her original 76-square-meter apartment, plus an additional 19 square meters and a parking space, brought her total payment to nearly 980,000 yuan.
"I originally bought the apartment for 1.51 million yuan. Even with this expense, my total cost remains below the market price, and I have more living space. I am also a beneficiary," she said.
The project, though, has benefited from the community's demographics. Experts noted that although Zhegong Xincun is an aging community, its residents, mostly Zhejiang University of Technology faculty members and their families, are relatively better off, a factor that helped the project move forward.
When the project was launched, the community also had a large elderly population, with 208 residents aged 80 or above and 36 aged 90 or above. Some feared a long construction period might keep them from returning, while others with children overseas faced the daunting task of relocating alone.
To address these concerns, the working group provided comprehensive support. Ambulances were arranged to escort several residents over 90 on the moving day. Transitional housing was secured and rented to elderly residents, refurbished with age-friendly features such as shower seats and toilet grab bars.
The compound was handed over last year, with about 70 percent of households having moved in, and they have begun renovating their new homes.
The approach of Zhegong Xincun aligns with China's grand roadmap to advance urban renewal as the country endeavors to create safer, greener and more comfortable cities, while fostering new growth momentum.
Under the urban renewal plan during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China aims to renovate 500,000 units of dilapidated urban housing and 115,000 old urban residential communities. It supports resident-led renewal and on-site demolition and reconstruction of old housing, while exploring sustainable operation models.
"This resident-led renewal model has opened a new path for urban renewal in China," said Xu Lin, a professor at Zhejiang University, noting that as China's urbanization enters a new phase, cities are no longer expanding through large-scale demolition and construction, but focusing on improving living conditions for residents.
"At the end of the day, it's about giving people a better life," said Xu. ■

Researchers discover first fully marine stem amphibian in Late Triassic fossils
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
14:32:23 CST
15:32:23 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- A group of international researchers has reported the first fully marine species of stem amphibian, Gerrothorax maritimus, in a recent research article published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution.
Based on two nearly complete skeletons measuring at least 737 millimeters from the Late Triassic (about 237 million years ago) discovered in southwest China's Guizhou Province, the researchers reconstructed the appearance of Gerrothorax maritimus: a flattened body covered with heavy bony armor, a broad and flat head, a wide mouth, and sturdy, well-developed gill arches, according to a report by China Science Daily.
More than 8,000 amphibian species exist today, but none of them lives entirely in the sea. Amphibian skin is permeable, which aids respiration but causes water loss in seawater, where high salinity adds physiological challenges.
Some living amphibians can tolerate brackish habitats where freshwater meets seawater, and fossils of ancient species have been found in coastal sediments. But previous evidence was insufficient to confirm that any amphibian ever had a fully marine lifestyle.
Gerrothorax maritimus is therefore recognized as the first stem amphibian known to date to have lived entirely in a marine environment, said Jiang Dayong, the article's corresponding author.
The researchers suggested that Gerrothorax maritimus's flattened body suited life on the seafloor, allowing it to hide in sediments.
The species' heavy bony armor helped prevent water loss through the skin, while adults retained their gills and could breathe underwater, possibly without needing to surface to breathe air with their lungs.
The researchers of this study come from the Geological Museum of Guizhou, Peking University, and the University of California, Davis. ■

NEW DELHI: External affairs minister S Jaishankar has said Prime Minister Narendra Modi discussed the Ukraine conflict with Russian President Vladimir Putin in New Delhi and earlier in Bishkek, as India continues diplomatic engagement with Moscow, Kyiv and Washington on measures to protect civilian shipping, restore grain exports and safeguard energy infrastructure.Speaking exclusively to news agency ANI on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Atlanta on Saturday, Jaishankar said India had held discussions with Russia, Ukraine and European countries on three key aspects of the conflict."Prime Minister himself had a discussion with President Putin in Delhi and before that in Bishkek," he said, referring to India's diplomatic engagement.
Jaishankar said he had also discussed the conflict with Russian and Ukrainian officials, including during visits to Moscow and Kyiv, and in talks with Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov.
"We have also been coordinating this with the Americans because they have their own peace mediation initiative. So Secretary Rubio knows properly what is going on here," he said.
India focuses on civilian shipping, grain exports and energy security
Explaining the three areas under discussion, Jaishankar said India was first seeking to ensure that civilian vessels and seafarers were not targeted in the conflict.The second priority was to restore grain exports from Russia and Ukraine, both major suppliers to international markets.
He said shipments through the Black Sea had fallen sharply because of the conflict."One not to attack civilian shipping and seafarers. The second is to find a way by which the grain exports from both Russia and Ukraine. Then these are two major exporters of grains for the global markets. Find a way of restoring that flow because that flow has cut down very sharply in the Black Sea," he said.The third area concerned energy infrastructure and shipments. Jaishankar said this was the most complicated issue because the concerns differed among the parties involved."Non-attack on energy is probably the most complicated piece because it means different things to the different players," he said, referring to refineries, electricity grids and ships carrying fuel.He added that India was trying to bring the parties together to address these concerns but could not publicly disclose the current status of the discussions.
Jaishankar calls for diplomatic solutions to global conflicts
At the G20 meeting, the external affairs minister reiterated India's position that major international conflicts required diplomatic engagement rather than military escalation."Look, there are big conflicts today, two major conflicts which are having global ramifications," he said, adding that "there are no military solutions; we have to find a diplomatic pathway."Jaishankar also flagged the impact of disruptions in energy markets and fuel distribution on developing economies."This distortion of the energy markets, the politicisation of energy flows, this is something which is very harmful," he said, adding that the Global South was bearing the brunt of energy shortages.He also raised concerns over disruptions to grain shipments through the Black Sea and fertiliser shortages linked to tensions along the Persian Gulf and Red Sea corridors.On supply chain resilience, which was the focus of the G20 meeting's concluding plenary session, Jaishankar called for greater diversification of global production and manufacturing networks."Today we need more diversified supply chains," he said, advocating "more globalised, you know, more diversified production, more diversified manufacturing."In a post on X after the session, he said securing resilient supply chains was central to the well-being of the global economy. He also called for promoting the "right to industrialise", resisting "predatory practices" and pursuing the "de-politicisation of markets".
Jaishankar meets Russian, Polish and South Korean counterparts
On the sidelines of the G20 meeting, Jaishankar held separate discussions with his Russian, Polish and South Korean counterparts on the Ukraine conflict, West Asia, bilateral ties and multilateral issues.After meeting Lavrov, Jaishankar said the two sides had discussed the Ukraine conflict, the Gulf situation and multilateral issues.He also met Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, with discussions focusing on the Ukraine conflict, India-European Union ties and the G20."My meeting with DPM & FM Radosław Sikorski @sikorskiradek of Poland focused on the Ukraine conflict, India-EU ties and the G20," Jaishankar said.Poland is participating in this year's G20 meetings as a full participant following an invitation from the United States. It has also expressed interest in securing permanent membership of the grouping.
Jaishankar separately met South Korean foreign minister Cho Hyun to review bilateral cooperation and discuss G20-related and other multilateral issues."Appreciated the stocktaking with @FMChoHyun of the Republic of Korea of our bilateral cooperation, as also the discussion on G20 and multilateral issues," he said.Earlier on Saturday, Jaishankar also participated in the Quad Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Atlanta with US secretary of state Marco Rubio, Japanese foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi and Australian foreign minister Penny Wong.The US is holding the G20 presidency this year. After two days of discussions, Jaishankar and other foreign ministers attended a college football game between the Florida Gators and the Georgia Bulldogs at the Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta.

From 1909 to Today: Celebrating the Day of the National Awakeners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:26:56 UTC
15:26:56 KST

A calm start to election day in the country
Спокойно начало на изборния ден в страната, отчитат Областните дирекции на МВР.
We celebrate the Day of the People's Awakeners. It is dedicated to the work of our writers, educators and fighters for national liberation , who have preserved the spiritual values of the nation and its morality over the centuries - Joasaph Bdinski, Grigoriy Tsamblak, Konstantin Kostenechki, Vladislav Gramatik, priest Peyo, Matei Gramatik, St. Ivan Rilski, Neofit Bozveli, the brothers Dimitar and Konstantin Miladinovi, Georgi S. Rakovski, Vasil Levski, Hristo Botev, Ivan Vazov, Stefan Karadzha, Hadji Dimitar, Lyuben Karavelov, Dobri Chintulov and hundreds of other champions of national consciousness and Bulgarian identity.
The celebration of the Day of the People's Awakeners this year coincides with the second round of the presidential elections, which will be held on November 1.
For the first time, the Day of the People's Awakeners was celebrated in 1909 in Plovdiv. In 1922, Stoyan Omarchevski, Minister of Education, submitted the proposal to mark November 1 as the holiday of the people's awakeners. Stoyan Omarchevski was Minister of Education in the government of Stamboliyski (1920-1923). He was associated with a number of educational reforms in secondary and higher education. He introduced compulsory and free primary education lasting seven years and initiated the construction of new schools in the country, the number of which increased from 561 to 1,676 in two years.
On November 1, 1923, by decree of Tsar Boris III, the day was declared a national holiday in memory of deserving Bulgarians. It was banned in 1945. Its celebration was resumed with the Law on Supplementing the Labor Code, adopted by the 36th National Assembly on October 28, 1992, when it was officially declared the Day of the People's Awakeners and a day off for all educational institutions in the country.

Foreign media on Kazakhstan: Nuclear power, landmark Türkiye visit and major construction plans
As President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev calls for faster construction of nuclear power plants, receives a ceremonial welcome from Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and proposes declaring 2027 “the Year of Large-scale Construction” to develop public infrastructure nationwide, Qazinform News Agency presents its weekly review of Kazakhstan coverage in foreign media.
Euronews: Kazakhstan's Tokayev calls for faster construction of nuclear power plants
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for a national uranium reserve and faster construction of two nuclear power plants in his annual state-of-the-nation address, Euronews reports.
“I believe it is possible, and perhaps even necessary, to begin construction of the Balkhash NPP as early as next year,” he said, also urging an agreement to advance the Moyynkum project.
Tokayev described an electricity surplus as essential for digitalization and artificial intelligence, while criticizing costly winter electricity imports followed by cheap summer exports.
He also urged Kazakhstan to capitalize on growing demand for overland transport.
“Kazakhstan must seize this historic opportunity to truly become a leading logistics hub for Eurasia,” he said.
The Aral-Caspian Highway is expected to shorten the Trans-Caspian route by 1,000 kilometres, while the Bakty-Ayagoz railway will add a third crossing with China.
Tokayev designated next year as the Year of Nationwide Construction, prioritizing public infrastructure.
Milliyet: President Erdoğan welcomed President Tokayev of Kazakhstan with an official ceremony
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan welcomed Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev with an official ceremony at the Presidential Complex in Ankara before bilateral and delegation-level talks, Milliyet reports.

According to Türkiye’s Directorate of Communications, the leaders discussed bilateral relations and regional and global issues.
Erdoğan said the two countries would strengthen their enhanced strategic partnership through further cooperation in trade, investment, energy, transport and the defense industry.
He also pledged close coordination with Kazakhstan during Türkiye’s chairmanship of the Organization of Turkic States.

According to Anadolu Agency, Türkiye will deepen defense industry cooperation with Kazakhstan through joint production and mutually beneficial partnerships, Turkish defense industry chief Haluk Gorgun said on Wednesday.
His remarks followed talks in Ankara, where President Recep Tayyip Erdogan hosted Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.
Gorgun described Türkiye as a reliable, long-term partner offering competitive defense products and policies supporting joint production.
"We will diversify and deepen our areas of cooperation with friendly and brotherly Kazakhstan within the framework of a win-win approach," he said.
He added that combining the two countries’ expertise would contribute to the security and prosperity of the Turkic world.
Hürriyet: Turkic world leaders gather in Ankara for landmark summit
Ankara is hosting the 13th Organization of Turkic States summit on October 29-30 as Türkiye celebrates the republic’s 103rd anniversary, Hürriyet reports.
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev was the first leader to arrive, receiving a ceremonial welcome from President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan before bilateral talks.

Healthcare Minister Akmaral Alnazarova outlined plans for nearly 70 healthcare facilities, including perinatal centers, children’s hospitals and rehabilitation branches. The projects would add or modernize 9,200 hospital beds.
Euronews: Gold market and central banks: Russia and Kazakhstan sell as Poland and China buy
Kazakhstan plans to reduce gold’s share of its reserves from around 78% to 75% by year-end, after ranking among the world’s biggest buyers in the first eight months of 2026, Euronews reports.
“Kazakhstan has been buying gold for a long time, so it will now be selling at a significant profit,” says Adam Stroniawski, managing director of Polish precious metals dealer Mennica Skarbowa.
He believes the limited reduction and gradual sales will have little impact on global prices. Russia has also reduced its holdings, while Poland continues buying.

Kazakhstan is seeking access to both American and Chinese AI ecosystems as rivalry between the two powers puts pressure on countries to choose sides, AP reports.
AI Minister Zhaslan Madiyev joined the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative in June, and then travelled to Shanghai three weeks later as Kazakhstan became a founding member of China’s World AI Cooperation Organization.
Kazakhstan hopes to attract investment, enter global AI supply chains and influence standards.

Companies promised AI gains— here's how the payoff showed up in earnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:00:01 UTC
15:00:01 KST

Some companies are beginning to report financial benefits from artificial intelligence investments, as interest in the technology shifts from hype to measurable returns in the latest quarter.
Corporate AI investment has surged as companies look to boost efficiency and become more profitable, reaching $581.7 billion in 2025, up 130% from the previous year, according to the Stanford HAI 2026 AI Index report.
As CEOs tout the tech's benefits and hyperscalers like Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Meta are expected to spend $700 billion combined this year on its infrastructure, investors are looking for measurable gains.
Now, with third-quarter earnings season underway, some companies are beginning to put numbers around those benefits.
Santander puts a number on AI gains
Spanish banking giant Santander said Wednesday that it saw AI initiatives generate 194 million euros ($216 million) in business value in the first nine months of 2026.
Santander Chief Financial Officer José García Cantera told CNBC that AI is helping the bank reduce low-value tasks so employees can focus on higher-value work.
"This affects both revenue and costs, so we are actually in the quarter where we can actually link directly to AI a positive contribution," Cantera said.
"AI is being embedded in all the processes that we are conducting at the bank, so it's really difficult to just say how much comes from AI, but clearly AI is improving the quality of our services to clients."
Novartis and Standard Chartered see AI in results
Swiss pharmaceutical giant Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan told CNBC that AI was beginning to contribute to the company's bottom line.
Novartis reported third-quarter core operating income of $6.04 billion, up 10% year on year at constant currencies. The company did not quantify how much of that was attributable to AI but Narasimhan told CNBC: "I think this is the first quarter I've really seen AI start to improve actually our P&L on a tangible basis."
"We're working on R&D [research & development] to see if it can really increase R&D productivity," Narasimhan said on "Squawk Box Europe" on Tuesday.
"We're already seeing some of the productivity you saw in the bottom-line performance of what we can do with AI from M&S [marketing & sales]."
Meanwhile, Standard Chartered Chief Financial Officer Manus Costello told "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday that the company is seeing AI "appear everywhere across the business."
The bank reported third-quarter operating income growth of 14% at constant currency, excluding notable items.
"I think you can see it in the top line growth that we're delivering, and you can see it in that operating leverage that I talked about," Costello said, adding that AI is helping managers build better customer relationships and generate more income.
"We're also seeing that strong operating leverage that I talked about, where income is growing much faster than costs, and some of that is because we've been able to deploy AI tools to improve core processes and enable us to scale those up very efficiently," he added.
Carlsberg says benefits are not yet at scale
Carlsberg CEO Jacob Aarup-Andersen said on "Squawk Box Europe" this week that it's not seeing AI benefits at scale, but the technology has impacted internal processes, cost efficiency, commercial and pricing processes, marketing and its supply chain.
The company's revenue grew 4.9% in the third quarter.
Big Tech points to AI-driven growth
Elsewhere, tech firms are also reporting gains. Meta said in its Oct. 21 earnings that its AI investments were delivering "substantial incremental advertising revenue," while total revenue jumped 26% in the quarter ended Sept. 30.
While Alphabet's Google Search revenue growth slowed amid concerns about AI competition, Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to nearly $31 billion in the third quarter, it reported on Wednesday.

Scrapped marine rope recast as stools that rock like buoys
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
06:00:00 UTC
15:00:00 KST

Scrapped marine rope recast as stools that rock like buoys
Rotterdam studio The New Raw has used discarded rope salvaged from the city’s harbour to create a series of 3D-printed public seating for its waterfront.
Called Buoy, the urban furniture project is shortlisted for a 2026 Dezeen Award in the sustainable design category.
To create the stools, The New Raw founder Foteini Setaki collected a series of plastic ropes from Rotterdam harbour, which were formerly used for managing boats and would’ve otherwise gone to waste.
The ropes were then transported to Maastricht, in the south of the Netherlands, where they were cleaned, shredded and mechanically recycled into pellets.
After returning to The New Raw’s Rotterdam studio, the recycled plastic pellets were melted and 3D-printed to create the stools, layer by layer.
“The material fuses as it is deposited, so no separate binder is needed,” Setaki told Dezeen.
Setaki explained that marine ropes are challenging to recycle because they contain a cocktail of materials that accumulate various residues over time.
Careful selection is essential to determine the ropes with the highest polypropylene content to be transformed into recycled plastic pellets, she explained.
While no virgin plastic is used in the creation of the stools, a small percentage of additives support the furniture’s long-term outdoor use, including UV protection.
“These additives are compatible with recycling the material again,” said Setaki.
Each seat features a subtly different hue, which is determined by the colour of the original rope rather than additional pigments or coatings.
The stools were also designed with spinning top-style pointed bases, so that they rock when the user sits down.
This gentle rocking motion was chosen to mimic real buoys bobbing along on the water.
“We wanted the seats to carry a recognisable link to their maritime origin, through both their shape and the slow movement of floating buoys,” explained Setaki.
“Borrowing that movement brings a playful quality to sitting, and the connection to the harbour becomes something you can feel.”
Each unique stool was engraved with its batch and production number, and then placed by Rotterdam harbour.
The project was created as an example of how designers can seek out local, surplus resources in an effort to contextualise their practice with the place that they work.
“Working with a local waste stream is a way of strengthening the relationship between the city and its harbour,” said Setaki.
“The material’s journey and the experience of sitting make that relationship tangible. This approach could also be adapted to other harbour cities, starting with their own discarded materials and local networks.”
Founded in 2016, The New Raw is run by Setaki and Panos Sakkas. The studio 3D prints locally sourced plastic waste to create furniture.
Buoy is nominated alongside a vibrant shortlist of sustainable design projects, including a cement-free architectural material made of waste date pits and lighting for an Australia bookshop made of its own faulty publications rejected due to printing errors.

Bulgaria elects seventh president: Everything important about voting by machine and ballot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:57:53 UTC
14:57:53 KST

On November 1, Bulgarian citizens will once again go to the polls to elect a president and vice president of the country. In the second round of the presidential elections, the presidential candidate pairs Andrey Gyurov – Georgi Kandev and Iliyana Yotova – Kiril Valchev will face each other . Nearly 6.6 million Bulgarians have the right to vote. Voting will be mainly by machine, with paper ballots being used in cases specified by law.
Election day began at 7:00 AM and will end at 8:00 PM. 
How to check where you vote, what documents are needed and how the vote is marked - step by step.
All Bulgarian citizens who have reached the age of 18 on or before election day, are not under guardianship and are not serving a prison sentence, have the right to vote.
Where do you vote by machine and where by paper ballot?
In all polling stations with 300 or morevoterson the list, voting is by machine.
You can vote by paper ballot only:
- In sections with fewer than 300 voters on the list.
- In sections with a mobile ballot box.
- In medical facilities, nursing homes and specialized social institutions.
- On vessels flying the Bulgarian flag.
- In certain sections outside the country where there are under 300 applications submitted or under 300 voters in previous elections.
- When machine voting is suspended for technical reasons on election day.
In machine voting stations , voters cannot choose whether to vote by machine or by paper ballot.
- Upon entering the polling station, you present your ID card to a member of the polling station election commission (PEC). You receive a special card with the inscription "Voter", which activates the machine.
- You insert the card into the machine.
- The card is inserted into the device with the chip facing up. The electronic ballot with the candidate pairs for president and vice president appears on the touch screen. In the runoff, the choice will be only between two pairs: Gyurov - Kandev and Yotova - Valchev.
- You touch the box next to the names of your preferred presidential and vice presidential candidates.
- You press the "View" button. The screen displays the selection you made. If you made a mistake, you can go back and change your selection.
- If everything is correct, you click the "Vote" button, which finally confirms your vote.
- After confirmation, the machine displays a message that the voting is complete and prints a control receipt reflecting the choice made.
- You check whether the correct choice is marked on the receipt. You hand it to a member of the SIC, who stamps it. Then you drop the receipt into the special box for machine voting.
- You return the card marked "Voter", sign the voter list, receive your ID back, and leave the polling station.
Important: After the final confirmation of the election, you cannot vote again.
The control receipts from the machines are collected in a separate box, different from the one for paper ballots. After the end of the election day, the section commission carries out a control count of the receipts to verify the reported results.
How to vote with a paper ballot - step by step?
- After you present your identification document, a member of the SIC tears the ballot from the cob, puts a stamp on the back, and hands it to you.
- You can check if the control slice number matches the cob number.
- With a blue pen, place an "X" or "V" in the box opposite the names of the selected candidate pair.
- You must not put any other marks, write words, letters, numbers or draw anything on the ballot. This may invalidate your vote.
- After marking your choice, you fold the ballot so that it is not visible who you voted for.
- You hand the folded ballot to a member of the sectional committee. He places a second stamp on the back, tears off the control strip, and returns it to you.
- Before that, you check if there are two seals on the back.
- You sign the voter list, receive your ID back, and leave the room.
Important: There are no preferences in the presidential elections. The president and vice president are elected together, as a candidate pair, with one common mark on the ballot.
How to check which section you should vote in?
Every voter can check the number and address of the section in which he is included in the electoral list.
The check can be done:
Online through the GRAO website – https://grao.government.bg/elections/ , where there is an option to check by personal identification number or address.
By phone at the toll-free number 0800 1 4726.
Through the website of the relevant municipality, where the electoral lists are published.
At a place in the municipality or city hall, where the lists are announced in a prominent place.
As a rule, voters vote in the section at their permanent address.
If you find that you are not included in the electoral list, you can request an addition from the section election commission on election day. This is possible if you have the right to vote and are not included in the list of deleted persons.
You can't vote with a driver's license.

Russia attacks Ukraine with 433 drones: hits recorded at 16 locations

Source: Ukraine's Air Force

Hits were recorded at 16 locations and the fall of downed aerial assets (debris) was reported at 14 locations.
Background: Russian forces destroyed Kramatorsk City Council's executive committee building in an airstrike late on 31 October.

Rioters smash, loot storefronts amid cost of living protests in Germany
Masked rioters smashed storefronts and looted goods late Saturday in Frankfurt, Germany amid a protest against the rising cost of living.
The largely peaceful demonstrations were led by a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" - roughly translated to "Gen Z's got this" - rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.
Tensions peaked in the evening as some groups of protesters refused to disperse, sparking clashes and violence in major cities including Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.
in Frankfurt's financial hub, masked protesters hurled stones, fireworks and pepper bombs, according to police.
Authorities also said looters stole weapons from a gun store, which were later retrieved. Some rioters also threw Molotov cocktails at police after pummeling them with stones and bottles earlier in the day, Frankfurt police said on X.
In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police responded by using water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.
Earlier in the day, demonstrations had been largely peaceful. In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.
"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection - in short, in our future - because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.
