How do you score 171 out of 170 in a Harvard Exam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:38:04 UTC
14:38:04 KST

In a recent conversation with 
The Times of India
, Impact Catalyst Aruna Lohia Goenka unveiled YASHA
, her five-pillar framework for Viksit Bharat 2047: Yuva, Anna, Shiksha, Hunar and Abundance, shaped by nearly 30 years of engagement in national development.
The 
knowledge series
, under the overarching theme of Viksit Bharat 2047, now takes that conversation further. Across five interviews, Sanjiv Kaura, CEO-CSR, The Times of India, explores the experiences, convictions and ideas behind each pillar of the YASHA framework.
We begin with 
S for Shiksha
.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 As we approach a world in which machines may become more intelligent than human beings, what is the greatest danger facing our children?
Aruna Goenka:
 The danger is not that machines will become more intelligent. It is that humans may stop thinking and become like robots: programmed to respond, but forgetting how to feel, empathise and connect.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 Can you share an example of an educational intervention that reflects this philosophy?
Aruna Goenka:
 In the tribal district of Bastar, Chhattisgarh, we taught children 
how to think, rather than 
what to think. That was in the 1990s. The greatest moment is not when a child says, "I know the answer." It is when the child asks, "But why?" Today, 30 years later, I feel blessed to be associated with the AM/NS India Times Critical Thinking Championship, which reaches 1 million children each year across 28 states and 8 Union Territories in 14 languages. The scale has changed enormously, but the underlying conviction remains the same.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 If AI can become a personal tutor to every child, will we still need teachers?
Aruna Goenka:
 More than ever! AI may explain Einstein’s and Newton's laws, but can it recognise the child who has stopped believing in herself? A machine can deliver a lesson, but a great teacher can change a life. AI should be our children's co-pilot, not their autopilot.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 Are we sometimes confusing marks with intelligence?
Aruna Goenka:
 (Laughs) We give children marks for answering questions correctly. Perhaps we should reward them much more for asking questions nobody else thought of! And who says 100% is the ceiling? Let me tell you a fascinating story. In December 2018, an IIT alum and IAS officer, Ankur Garg, studying at Harvard Kennedy School, scored 171 marks out of 170 in a macroeconomics examination conducted by the world-renowned economist Professor Jeffrey Frankel. Yes, you heard that correctly. 171 out of 170! Now, isn't that wonderful?
For me, that is a beautiful metaphor for education and life. Never allow someone else's definition of the maximum to become the limit of your potential. And why restrict this philosophy to examinations? Whether it is knowledge, kindness, compassion or service, give more than is expected of you. After all, a
100% cent may be the examiner's limit. It need not be the limit of human potential.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 Socrates famously argued that the unexamined life is not worth living. Are we losing sight of that larger purpose of education?
Aruna Goenka:
 Absolutely, Socrates was reminding us that a meaningful life must be examined, not merely lived. For him, the pursuit of wisdom was inseparable from virtue. Compassion, honesty, courage, self-discipline and consciousness are not optional extras in education. They are at its very heart.
And education is not confined to degrees. Think of the extraordinary wisdom ancient Bharat produced: the 
Upanishads
, 
Tirukkural, Yoga Sutras
, 
Charaka Samhita
, and 
Panchatantra
. Consider Gautam Buddha's teachings on compassion and mindfulness; Lord Mahavira's Anekantavada, which reminds us that truth has many facets and no single viewpoint captures its entirety; Kabir's fearless questioning of dogma; Guru Nanak's message of equality and service; Tulsidas's 
Ramcharitmanas
, with its timeless reflections on duty and devotion, and Kahlil Gibran's timeless wisdom on love, self-discovery and nurturing of independent minds across centuries and civilisations, these extraordinary minds explored not merely how much we can know, but how wisely we can live. Their insights continue to inspire humanity even today. I believe we must cultivate the awareness to discover the possibilities present in the Universe; otherwise, surrounded by information and technology, we risk becoming intellectual zombies!
Sanjiv Kaura:
 You come from a family blessed with Lakshmi (prosperity), yet your affection for Saraswati (knowledge) seems just as profound!
Aruna Goenka
: (With a twinkle in her eyes) I come from a family of geniuses and wizards! My elder brother has one of the world's largest collections of handwritten books/manuscripts. Imagine the centuries of knowledge, imagination and wisdom preserved in those pages. I have never seen 
Lakshmi
 and 
Saraswati as rivals but as two complementary forces within us. 
Lakshmi
 symbolises the subconscious mind, where dreams are born, while 
Saraswati represents the conscious mind, which gives direction to the dreams. And remember, 
Lakshmi
 does not stay where 
Saraswati is neglected. Wealth without wisdom never creates lasting abundance.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 We sometimes celebrate the 
silver spoon
. But listening to you, I wonder whether a 
Silva Mind
 is the greater inheritance.
Aruna Goenka:
 (Laughs) Interestingly, I have seen the Silva Mind technique being used by my elder brother for decades – I saw him reading a book about it when he was just fourteen! The power of visualisation fascinated me. I believe it helped him envision extraordinary possibilities and turn them into reality, including the remarkable library he eventually built. But I like your comparison. A silver spoon may feed the body, but a silver mind feeds curiosity. And I must say, there is something wonderful about knowledge. It is perhaps the only inheritance that becomes richer the more you give it away.
Sanjiv Kaura: Which are some of your favourite books?
Aruna Goenka: Oh, Sanjiv, that's like asking a mother to choose her favourite child! (Laughs) But a few have stayed with me. 
Autobiography of a Yogi
 opens our minds to spirituality, consciousness and life's infinite possibilities. Then there is Thoreau's 
Walden
, which reminds us that a rich life need not be a complicated one. And I love Ralph Waldo Emerson's essay 
Self-Reliance
, with its powerful message about trusting one's own judgment rather than blindly following the crowd. Another favourite is 
Critical Thinking
 by Richard Paul. And here's a lovely coincidence! Only recently, I discovered that my younger brother has been reading it since the early 1990s! Imagine - all these years, we have been travelling along similar intellectual paths without even realising it.
Sanjiv Kaura:
 Aruna ji, your closing thoughts?
Aruna Goenka:
 Literacy teaches us to read, education teaches us to understand, and wisdom teaches us to question. Literacy opens the book. Education opens the mind. Wisdom opens the heart. And above all, dream big! But why confine your dreams to the night? Dream during the day, with your eyes wide open, and work to turn those dreams into reality. Imagine 1.4 billion people, each with a dream for Bharat, and each determined to make it happen! When 1.4 billion dreams become 1.4 billion actions, Viksit Bharat 2047 will not be just a vision. It will be our reality!

Fat-dissolving claims land FatX Solution in regulatory trouble; CDSCO cancels registration

CDSCO finds over 160 drug samples as 'not of standard quality' for December
NEW DELHI: Promising to dissolve fat cells may sound like an attractive pitch for a slimming product, but it has landed FatX Solution in trouble with the country's drug regulator. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has cancelled the product's registration after finding that it was being promoted with claims that are not permitted for cosmetics.In an order dated October 28, CDSCO said Delhi-based importer Tekno Midas Aesthetics was marketing FatX Solution on its website as a product that could dissolve fat cells and reduce their size. The regulator said these were drug-related claims and did not fit the definition of a cosmetic under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.The action followed a scrutiny of the company's application and website, during which CDSCO found differences between the claims being made online and those mentioned on the approved product label.Under the Cosmetics Rules, 2020, cosmetic products cannot make false or misleading claims. The rules define cosmetics as products meant for cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering appearance.
Claims to dissolve fat cells go beyond this definition, the regulator said.CDSCO had issued a show-cause notice to the company on August 10, citing violations of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and the Cosmetics Rules. The company submitted its response on September 1, but the regulator found it inconclusive and unsatisfactory. The firm also requested that its registration certificate be voluntarily surrendered.
Rajan Bhatnagar of Tekno Midas Aesthetics told TOI that the product had been registered as a cosmetic more than four years ago. "At that time, the licence was granted because the product was registered as a cosmetic. The authorities have now changed their interpretation of the category under which the product falls. Earlier, it was considered a cosmetic, but now they say it falls under another category," he said.He said the company had decided not to contest the matter after receiving the notice. "We did not want to get into any dispute or challenge the notification. We voluntarily requested the surrender of the licence, and the authorities cancelled it," he said.The Central Licensing Authority subsequently cancelled the registration certificate, RC/COS-003300, which was issued in July 2022 and was valid until July 14, 2027. The cancellation took effect from October 28.

North Korea tests cluster warhead for tactical ballistic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:36:51 UTC
14:36:51 KST

North Korea conducted a test of a cluster warhead for a tactical ballistic missile to assess its combat applicability and destructive power, state media reported on Sunday.
The Missile Administration carried out the test on Saturday, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
The test was overseen by General Kim Jong-sik, a member of the Central Military Commission of the ruling Workers' Party of Korea and first deputy director of a department of the party's Central Committee.
North Korea's Ballistic Missile Systems Research Institute and Warhead Research Institute said the test confirmed that the country's "Type-2 standard cluster warhead" could devastate a target area of about 12 to 13 hectares (29 to 32 acres) at what they described as an "ultra-high density."
The head of the Missile Administration said North Korea classifies its cluster warheads into four categories, including special-purpose and standard types.
He said Pyongyang plans to make all four types available to military units by the end of this year, allowing them to select warheads according to operational objectives and the characteristics of targets.
The Missile Administration described the test as part of regular scientific research aimed at increasing the destructive power of its weapons systems.

Two Palestinian infants have died of severe burns after a fire tears through a displacement tent in Al Mawasi, west of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, as families cook over open flames amid shortages under Israel’s blockade.
Habiba Mohammed Zanoun, two months old, and Aseel Abu Suhayban, seven months old, died on Saturday morning at Nasser Medical Complex, which identifies them. Both are admitted to intensive care after flames break out on Friday afternoon while relatives are gathered at the tent.
Habiba was due for her two-month vaccinations on the day she dies.
Sources tell Anadolu the fire started while food is being cooked inside the tent. They said severe shortages of cooking gas and basic supplies force displaced families to prepare meals over open fires.

‘Why is all this happening to us?’
The girls’ grandmother told Anadolu that her daughter had come to visit the family when the fire erupted. Habiba was her daughter’s baby, she said, and neither infant could withstand the severity of her injuries.
“Why is all this happening to us?” she asked. “Every day there are accidents, bombings and fires, and people are dying in so many ways.”
“For three years, we have been living like this, amid displacement, anguish and pain,” she added.
Cooking without safe alternatives
Sources said the blaze is one of three fires reported on Friday in displacement tents in central and southern Gaza.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned in June that cooking inside tents is a leading cause of fires. It said blankets, old fabric, cardboard and plastic sheeting used to reinforce shelters let flames spread rapidly and make fires harder to control.
OCHA also reported that Israeli authorities denied entry on August 26 and September 2 to a previously approved shipment through the Egyptian corridor. The shipment contained 36,960 pieces of timber and 660 emergency shelter kits.
The Gaza Government Media Office previously said more than 800,000 displaced Palestinians live in tents unfit for human habitation. It estimates that 162,000 of Gaza’s 270,000 displacement tents need immediate replacement.

Interview: Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building provides key insights for political parties worldwide, says Tajik expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
13:35:44 CST
14:35:44 KST

DUSHANBE, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building provides important guidance for political parties in different countries to strengthen their organizational foundations and enhance their governance capacity, a Tajik expert has said.
"Political parties in various countries are facing new risks and challenges in today's world," said Suhrob Raufzoda, editor-in-chief of "People's Tribune," the newspaper of Tajikistan's ruling People's Democratic Party, in an interview with Xinhua.
In his view, steadily strengthening organizational foundations and enhancing governance capacity are important guarantees for a country's long-term stability and development, and the Communist Party of China's (CPC) experience in advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance provides useful guidance for political parties in other countries.
Raufzoda attaches particular importance to China's efforts in personnel training. He said that modern state governance requires high-caliber officials with firm political conviction, professional expertise and a strong sense of responsibility. Therefore, cultivating officials and building such a cadre represent important investments in China's long-term development, he added.
In Raufzoda's view, strengthening the Party's organizational system, advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance, and cultivating high-caliber officials characterized by loyalty, integrity and a sense of responsibility are interconnected and mutually reinforcing.
The Tajik expert believes that an important objective of Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building is to further strengthen the CPC so that it always remains a vibrant Marxist governing party and the strong leadership core of the cause of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
"The experience of the Communist Party of China has attracted the attention of many countries, as it demonstrates practical experience in continuously improving institutional development, strategic planning, the training of highly qualified personnel and mechanisms of state governance," Raufzoda said.
He stressed that every country has its own historical traditions, political system and development path. At the same time, continuously enhancing governance capacity, strengthening institutional development, cultivating highly qualified personnel and building public trust are common tasks facing many countries, he said.
Raufzoda also noted that China's achievements in areas such as poverty alleviation, personnel training, state governance, scientific and technological innovation, and modernization can provide useful guidance for countries of the Global South as they seek development paths suited to their national conditions.
"A deeper study of China's concrete practices can help provide a more objective and comprehensive understanding of the CPC's ideas on state governance and its experience in governance," he said. ■

Bulgaria Marks the Day of the National Enlighteners as Voters Head to a Presidential Runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
05:16:00 UTC
14:16:00 KST

Bulgaria Marks the Day of the National Enlighteners as Voters Head to a Presidential Runoff
Bulgaria marks the Day of the National Enlighteners on Sunday, November 1. The holiday honors the writers, teachers, clergy and revolutionaries who kept Bulgarian language, faith and historical memory alive during the centuries of Ottoman rule and shaped the national revival that led to the country’s liberation in 1878. This year the date coincides with the presidential runoff between incumbent Iliana Yotova and Andrey Gyurov, so many Bulgarians will lay flowers at monuments and cast ballots on the same day.
The Bulgarian name, Den na narodnite buditeli, is difficult to translate. A buditel is literally an “awakener,” someone who wakes others up and English-language sources variously call the holiday Enlighteners’ Day, Awakeners’ Day or the Day of the Leaders of the National Revival. The idea behind all of them is the same: a nation that had lost its state and much of its written culture had to be reminded of who it was before it could fight for independence.
Who the awakeners were
The figure most often placed at the start of the list is Paisius of Hilendar, a monk at the Hilendar monastery on Mount Athos who in 1762 completed his Slavo-Bulgarian History. The book urged Bulgarians to take pride in their past and their language at a time when Greek dominated the church and education. Its manuscript was copied by hand and passed between villages and monasteries for decades.
Sophronius of Vratsa, who copied and spread Paisius’s work, belongs to the same tradition, as does Neofit Rilski, often called the patriarch of modern Bulgarian education. Later generations of the revival built schools, reading rooms and printing presses across the Bulgarian lands, and their work fed into the political and revolutionary movement of the 19th century, whose best-known figures, Vasil Levski and Hristo Botev, are also honored on November 1.
The holiday also has a religious link. Before Bulgaria adopted the Gregorian calendar, the Orthodox Church honored St. Ivan of Rila, the country’s patron saint and founder of the Rila Monastery, on October 19. Under the new calendar that date falls on November 1.
A holiday that was banned and restored
The day was first celebrated in Plovdiv in 1909. In 1922, Education Minister Stoyan Omarchevski proposed making November 1 a national day of tribute to the enlighteners, and on December 13 of that year the 19th National Assembly adopted the idea as an amendment to the Holidays Act, according to the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA). A decree issued by Tsar Boris III on February 3, 1923, formally set the date as a day to commemorate distinguished Bulgarians.
The communist authorities banned the holiday in 1945, and it was absent from the official calendar for almost five decades. On October 28, 1992, the 36th National Assembly restored it through an amendment to the Labour Code. Since then it has been an official holiday and a non-attendance day for all schools and universities, although it is a working day for most other Bulgarians.
How the day is marked
The president traditionally opens the day with a flag-raising ceremony in front of the Presidency in Sofia and greets the guard of honor. Schools, universities and the network of chitalishta, the community cultural centers that were themselves products of the national revival, hold events through the week. Wreaths and flowers are laid at monuments to Paisius, Levski, Botev and other revival figures across the country. Over time the holiday has widened to honor people working in education, science and culture today, and many institutions hand out awards around November 1.
A holiday on election day
This year the commemoration falls on a Sunday that also decides who will be Bulgaria’s next president. In the first round on October 25, Yotova received 34.76% and Gyurov 31.95%, according to the final count of the Central Election Commission, on a turnout of 22.98%, a historic low for a presidential vote. Because no candidate won a majority with turnout above 50%, the two meet again on November 1.
The coincidence has not been lost on commentators. The revival figures honored on the day spent their lives persuading their compatriots to take part in the life of their nation and the runoff will show how many Bulgarians accept that invitation more than two centuries after Paisius first made it.
Bulgarians Mark St. Demetrius’ Day and the Traditional Start of Winter
The Bulgarian Orthodox Church celebrates St. Demetrius’ Day (Dimitrovden) on October 26, honoring the Holy Great Martyr Demetrius the Myrrh-streaming and the Venerable Dimitra of Dorostol, while Bulgarian folklore associates the feast with the arrival of
St. John of Rila Celebrated as Bulgaria's Patron and Physicians' Protector
The Bulgarian Orthodox Church marks October 19 as the feast day of St. John of Rila the Wonderworker, the country's most revered saint and patron, while Bulgaria also celebrates the Day of the Bulgarian Physician in his honor

The Bulgarian government has approved an additional transfer of more than €4.8 million to Burgas Municipality to prepare for and host the 71st Eurovision Song Contest in May 2027, with the funding covering a test event and technical work at Arena Burgas

Equality cannot be reversed; to ensure everyone can truly live in peace, we still need to continue our efforts in our daily lives,” said Lai.
As president, Lai said the government must protect everyone's dignity, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, or gender identity, and ensure equal opportunities and the freedom to pursue happiness.
He added that respect for these principles extends to the exercise of public authority. Law enforcement agencies should act within the law, respect privacy, and treat everyone equally so that no one is intimidated or targeted because of their identity.
Lai said the world sees Taiwan's rainbow and how its people use democracy and freedom to bring different voices together in public spaces. He said Taiwanese people cherish these freedoms and should take seriously every voice reminding them that the country can do better.

Kazakhstan to modernize airport infrastructure under 3-year plan through 2029
Kazakhstan is set to implement large-scale projects to modernize airport infrastructure by 2029, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the Civil Aviation Committee of the Ministry of Transport.
Vice Minister Talgat Lastayev chaired a meeting with the representatives of all regional administrations and airports across the country to discuss infrastructure modernization issues.
The meeting was convened in line with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s State-of-the-Nation Address delivered on October 28, 2026. Participants reviewed the progress of implementation of the projects on the construction and reconstruction of runways, the modernization of passenger terminals, and the development of airport infrastructure.
Under the three-year airport infrastructure development plan through 2029, runways are to be modernized at seven airports. The plan includes the construction of three new runways in Astana, Shymkent and Aktobe, as well as the reconstruction of four existing runways in Almaty, Zhezkazgan, Taraz, and Uralsk.
The plan also provides for the construction and reconstruction of passenger terminals at seven airports in Aktobe, Atyrau, Ust-Kamenogorsk, Zhezkazgan, Semey, Pavlodar, and Urjar.
The meeting also discussed the timely preparation of design and cost estimate documentation, the identification of funding sources, and compliance with project implementation deadlines.
Following the meeting, the relevant government agencies, local executive bodies and stakeholders were instructed to step up their efforts and ensure the timely implementation of the infrastructure projects.
Earlier, it was reported that Kazakhstan’s Aviation Administration (AAK) and the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) had signed a Statement of Intent to deepen cooperation in civil aviation, strengthen bilateral ties, and increase passenger and cargo traffic.

China Focus: China's new rules to protect children's health, safety take effect
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:41:41 CST
13:41:41 KST

BEIJING, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Four new or revised mandatory national standards and regulations to better protect children's health and safety took effect in China on Sunday, covering classroom lighting, youth sports training, and children's products and toys.
The rules aim to reduce health and safety risks in children's daily learning, physical activities and play, with a greater emphasis on prevention and clearer safety requirements.
BETTER LIGHTING TO PROTECT EYESIGHT
A revised national standard on classroom lighting and daylighting sets stricter requirements for the lighting environment in primary and secondary schools, as China steps up efforts to curb myopia among children and adolescents.
The standard addresses aspects such as natural light, lighting uniformity, blue-light hazards and flicker, aiming to enhance the comfort of classrooms for students who spend long hours reading and writing. It also calls for regular inspections and upkeep of lighting equipment.
The revised standard will also apply to secondary vocational schools, while extracurricular training institutions serving school-age children are encouraged to follow its requirements.
Liu Yiwei, a lecturer at Capital Normal University, said the new standard sets more detailed mandatory requirements for classroom lighting, providing a measurable and enforceable framework to support efforts to prevent myopia among young students.
It incorporates the principle of putting health first into educational settings and places greater emphasis on preventing myopia before it develops, Liu added.
MORE STANDARDIZED SPORTS TRAINING
A new code of conduct for youth sports training sets requirements for training venues, class sizes, instructor qualifications and safety management, addressing concerns over unsafe facilities and uneven coaching standards in a rapidly growing market.
It is essential for training providers to tailor courses to align with the ages, physical conditions, and varying levels of athletic ability of children. Instructors must hold recognized qualifications, while people with specified criminal records, including those involving sexual abuse or physical assault, are prohibited from working in the sector.
The rules also establish limits on class sizes and require additional first-aid support for high-risk sports, helping create safer conditions for children to participate in physical activities.
Huang Haiyan, dean of the School of Management at Beijing Sport University, noted that the code upgrades the regulatory framework and is a necessary step toward higher-quality development of the industry.
The code should serve as a basis for further clarifying the respective oversight responsibilities of education, market regulation and public security authorities, helping improve the overall governance of the industry, Huang said.
SAFER CHILDREN'S PRODUCTS, TOYS
A new mandatory national standard on the general safety of children's products establishes baseline requirements for products used, worn or played with by children under 14, covering product categories that previously lacked mandatory safety standards.
The standard covers risks such as sharp edges, detachable small parts that could cause choking, and cords that could pose strangulation hazards. It also sets limits on potentially harmful chemicals, including heavy metals and formaldehyde.
Meanwhile, revised mandatory toy safety standards expand controls on hazardous substances and strengthen requirements concerning physical safety and fire risks.
The revisions pay particular attention to products that have drawn public concern, including popular novelty toys such as squishy toys and slime. They introduce additional limits on substances such as formaldehyde, plasticizers and boron, helping reduce the risk of harmful chemical exposure.
Together, the new requirements are the country's latest move to fill the safety gaps for certain products used in children's everyday lives, making safety standards more comprehensive as the range of children's goods continues to expand. ■

Roundup: Another wave of protests sweeps Europe over various grievances
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
12:41:38 CST
13:41:38 KST

People participate in a protest at Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, Germany, Oct. 31, 2026. Another wave of protests swept across major European cities on Saturday, with demonstrators voicing grievances over issues ranging from living conditions to disputes involving public institutions. Meanwhile, calls for gatherings on social media prompted police to step up security in several cities. Public services, the cost of living and housing affordability remained key concerns in many of the protests. (Xinhua/Zhao Jiantong)
MADRID, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Another wave of protests swept across major European cities on Saturday, with demonstrators voicing grievances over issues ranging from living conditions to disputes involving public institutions. Meanwhile, calls for gatherings on social media prompted police to step up security in several cities.
Public services, the cost of living and housing affordability remained key concerns in many of the protests. In France, around 320,000 people took part in a new round of protests on Saturday, including about 70,000 in Paris, according to Interior Ministry figures. Organizers put the nationwide turnout at nearly 500,000, including 200,000 in the capital.
Around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed nationwide. Most marches passed off peacefully, although clashes with police and other disturbances were reported in several cities. French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters that, according to a preliminary tally, 422 people had been arrested nationwide.
In Germany, demonstrations took place in more than 30 cities on Saturday. Protesters called for greater investment in public services, measures to address the rising cost of living, and opposed compulsory military service. By late afternoon, organizers reported more than 68,000 participants, based on figures from 12 cities.
As in France, the demonstrations in Germany were largely peaceful, but clashes broke out in several cities in the evening. German news agency dpa reported that police officers were injured in Frankfurt, barricades were set ablaze in Hamburg, and officers came under attack in Bremen.
In Italy, protesters remained camped near Rome's Colosseum on Saturday following nationwide demonstrations over living costs and public services. Workers and other groups had joined rallies in more than 60 cities on Friday during a general strike called by Unione Sindacale di Base (USB), Italian news agency ANSA reported. The union estimated 1.5 million people took part, while the Interior Ministry put the figure at about 255,000.
In Portugal, housing protests drew more than 1,000 people each in Lisbon and Porto on Saturday. In Lisbon, demonstrators marched toward Rossio Square, where they planned to camp overnight. Police had dispersed protest encampments in both cities on Oct. 25.
Political grievances also dominated protests in various countries. In Albania, protests demanding better education, improved living conditions and Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation continued for a 19th consecutive day in Tirana on Saturday, according to the Albanian Telegraphic Agency. Some protesters threw stones and Molotov cocktails at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons. The opposition Democratic Party backed the movement.
In Poland, an escalating dispute over the composition and leadership of the Constitutional Tribunal brought demonstrators onto the streets of Warsaw. Protestors gathered outside Warsaw's Constitutional Tribunal from Friday evening into Saturday, with police reporting four detained during overnight operations around the building, local media reported. Polish President Karol Nawrocki returned early from a foreign trip and announced urgent political consultations.
Elsewhere, social media calls for gatherings prompted heightened security measures. In the Netherlands, police dispersed a crowd near The Hague Central Station on Saturday afternoon and urged the public to avoid the city center. Local police reported 34 arrests during the day.
The gathering followed online calls for demonstrations in several Dutch cities, some of which encouraged looting and vandalism. Some businesses boarded up their storefronts ahead of the planned gatherings.
In Spain, police stepped up security in cities including Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia on Saturday following online calls for gatherings, local media reported.
The deployments aimed to prevent a repeat of the previous weekend's unrest in Barcelona, which left 15 officers injured and led to 128 arrests. Spanish news agency EFE reported on Friday that police had arrested 10 people nationwide on suspicion of inciting unrest and violence through online channels. ■

Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
04:33:36 UTC
13:33:36 KST

Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
- Date:
- November 1, 2026
- Source:
- University of Southampton
- Summary:
- A mysterious particle overlooked for decades may hold the key to why matter survived the Big Bang, allowing stars, planets, and life to exist. Scientists believe this forgotten neutrino reshaped the early universe and may have left detectable gravitational wave signals that could help unlock the cosmos’s deepest mysteries.
- Share:
Scientists have proposed a surprising new explanation for why the universe exists, and it centers on a mysterious particle that physicists have largely overlooked for decades. Their theory suggests this forgotten particle may have played a crucial role in shaping the early cosmos and allowing matter to survive after the Big Bang.
The research addresses one of the most fundamental mysteries in physics: why does the universe contain matter instead of nothing at all? Scientists believe matter and antimatter were produced in nearly equal amounts in the early universe. When these opposites encounter one another, they annihilate and release energy. If they had existed in perfectly equal quantities, virtually all matter could have disappeared, leaving no material to form stars, planets, or life.
Now, researchers from the University of Southampton and the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur believe they may have found an important piece of the puzzle. Their explanation involves a little-understood relative of the neutrino, an extremely lightweight particle that rarely interacts with ordinary matter.
A Forgotten Particle With a Powerful Role in the Early Universe
The team focused on a type of particle known as a 'decoupled' heavy neutrino. Unlike ordinary neutrinos, this hypothetical heavier relative has generally been considered too weakly connected to other particles to significantly influence the universe.
However, the researchers found that its unusually long lifetime could have made it far more important than previously thought. According to their calculations, the particle may have survived long enough to temporarily dominate the universe's energy density as the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang.
That brief period of dominance could have altered how the early universe evolved, influencing the conditions that ultimately allowed matter to outnumber antimatter.
Dr. Rishav Roshan of the University of Southampton, an author of the study, explained:
"This decoupled heavy neutrino has long been dismissed as an irrelevant background detail in particle physics.
"However, it decays incredibly slowly. As the cosmos cooled after the Big Bang, the particle lived long enough that it temporarily took over the energy density of the universe and triggered a matter-dominated period."
The findings were published in Physical Review Letters, a scientific journal of the American Physical Society.
How a Heavy Neutrino Could Explain Why Matter Survived
Previous attempts to explain why matter prevailed over antimatter generally left out the decoupled heavy neutrino. Because it interacts so weakly with other particles, scientists assumed it would have little influence on the processes responsible for creating the imbalance.
The new research challenges that assumption. The team found that even a particle with extremely weak interactions could indirectly affect the conditions under which matter gained its crucial advantage.
This imbalance, known as matter and antimatter asymmetry, is essential to understanding our existence. For reasons physicists are still trying to explain, the early universe ended up with slightly more matter than antimatter. That small difference allowed some matter to remain after most particles and their antiparticles annihilated one another.
"The fact that we are here at all proves that an asymmetry between matter and antimatter occurred," added Dr. Roshan.
"The decoupled neutrino shifted the temperature in the early universe at which fundamental particles - like electrons and other leptons - interacted with their anti-particles with the help of Standard Model Higgs boson.
"This temperature acts like a switch that shapes how the matter-antimatter imbalance was built up."
The Higgs boson is a fundamental particle associated with the mechanism that gives many elementary particles their mass. In the researchers' proposed scenario, the heavy neutrino changed the temperature conditions governing important particle interactions involving the Higgs boson.
By shifting when these interactions occurred, the particle could have influenced how the imbalance between matter and antimatter developed. In other words, something long considered insignificant may have helped determine why the universe contains matter at all.
Ancient Gravitational Waves Could Reveal the Answer
The theory could also have important implications for understanding how the universe expanded in its earliest stages.
Study co-author Dr. Sudipta Show of the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur said the findings suggest that the forgotten particle may have dramatically altered the expansion history of the young cosmos.
He added: "It offers us a new explanation for how matter won.
"The dramatic shift in the early expansion of the cosmos leaves distinct but detectable imprints of changes, for example on primordial gravitational waves.
"These gravitational wave signatures open up new avenues for us to unravel the evolution of the early universe after the Big Bang."
Gravitational waves are ripples in the fabric of space and time. Scientists believe processes in the extremely early universe may have generated primordial gravitational waves that carry information about conditions from that distant era.
According to the new theory, the temporary dominance of the heavy neutrino could have left recognizable signatures in those ancient signals. Detecting such patterns could eventually provide a way to investigate whether the proposed particle really influenced the universe's earliest evolution.
For now, the explanation remains theoretical. But it offers physicists a new possibility for solving one of cosmology's deepest mysteries: how matter survived when its encounter with antimatter could have left the universe almost entirely empty.

Materials provided by University of Southampton. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

- Rishav Roshan, Sudipta Show. Delayed Charged Lepton Yukawa Equilibration in Minimal Seesaw. Physical Review Letters, 2026; 137 (11) DOI: 10.1103/nfkx-q6z7

Ahead of the INDIA bloc's rally at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan on Sunday, the BJP released a poster titled "Thago Ka Mela' (Fair of Thugs)", targeting Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and several other opposition leaders.Designed in the style of a film poster, the graphic, released by BJP Delhi, features Rahul Gandhi, Congress general secretary Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, Trinamool Congress chief Mamata Banerjee and Shiv Sena (UBT) chief Uddhav Thackeray, among other INDIA bloc leaders.

Guangzhou reclaims crown as China’s busiest airport after US$8 billion mega expansion
A new terminal, runway and links with major international trading partners have helped it overtake Shanghai in passenger numbers
Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport has reclaimed its position as China’s busiest airport, handling more than 67 million passenger trips in the first nine months of 2026 following a major expansion last year, the municipal government announced.
The airport overtook Shanghai Pudong International Airport, which handled 66.58 million passenger trips during the same period, official data showed. Baiyun had fallen behind Pudong in 2024 and 2025.
The expansion took half a decade to complete and includes a new third terminal and fifth runway. It cost 53.77 billion yuan (US$8.1 billion) and broke long-standing bottlenecks by increasing Baiyun’s annual passenger capacity to 120 million, the municipal government said on its official WeChat account. Authorities projected it would handle 90 million passenger trips this year.

AI-designed virus given to a human patient for the first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
03:47:30 UTC
12:47:30 KST

AI-designed virus given to a human patient for the first time
The viruses, known as bacteriophages, infect and kill bacteria. Unlike antibiotics, they can target specific bacteria while leaving beneficial bacteria largely untouched.
The treatment was developed by Radical Numerics, a company that uses AI to study and design biological systems. Its AI model, Omnii-1, helped create virus variants selected to target the bacteria causing the patient's infection.
Laboratory tests showed that a mixture of the AI-designed viruses eliminated the patient's bacteria. Doctors then administered the experimental treatment under a special permission process for patients with serious conditions who have no satisfactory treatment alternatives.
The company has not disclosed the patient's condition after treatment or other clinical details to protect their privacy. It also stressed that the treatment has not been approved for wider medical use and that one patient's case cannot establish its safety or effectiveness.
The approach could offer another option for patients whose infections no longer respond to antibiotics. However, researchers must still develop reliable ways to design and test treatments for individual infections before the method can become more widely available.

Vietnam reduces gasoline special consumption tax to zero through March 2027
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:45:32 CST
12:45:32 KST

HANOI, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam has reduced the special consumption tax on all types of gasoline to zero percent from Sunday through March 31, 2027, under a new government resolution issued on Saturday, local daily VnExpress reported.
Under the special consumption tax law, which took effect on July 1 this year, the tax rates are set at 10 percent for regular gasoline, 8 percent for E5 biofuel and 7 percent for E10 biofuel.
The tax was previously reduced to zero percent from late March to June 2026 to help stabilize the domestic market.
Meanwhile, the environmental protection tax on gasoline and oil products remains at zero Vietnamese dong per liter.
These products are also exempt from value-added tax declaration and payment under a policy extended through the end of 2026, the report said. ■

Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
11:45:16 CST
12:45:16 KST

LIMA, Oct. 31 (Xinhua) -- Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz signed a decree Saturday declaring a national state of emergency to address the impacts of El Nino.
Paz said he signed the decree to tackle drought affecting several regions of the country and prepare for potential flooding in the coming months.
The president said the measure aims to mobilize financial and human resources, strengthen coordination among government agencies and seek international cooperation to assist affected families and mitigate the impact of climate-related disasters on people's lives and economic activities.
Paz said 63 communities in Bolivia have already been affected by drought, while the livestock sector is also struggling with shortages of animal feed.
Bolivia's Vice Ministry of Civil Defense said Wednesday that nearly 80,000 families across six of the country's nine departments had been affected by water shortages, with drought killing more than 75,000 head of livestock.
El Nino is a climate phenomenon characterized by unusually warm surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, often causing abnormal weather patterns in many parts of the world. ■

Three Chinese-language newspapers in Hong Kong have raised their retail prices by HK$3 (40 US cents) this month, marking the first sector-wide adjustment in two years.

Two financial broadsheets will follow suit on Monday. The Hong Kong Economic Times (HKET) will raise its price from HK$12 to HK$15, while the Hong Kong Economic Journal (HKEJ) will increase its price by 20 per cent from HK$15 to HK$18.

Fri, 11 Sept, 7:50 pm, Final score, Rabbitohs 10, Knights 20
Rugby League World Cup: Tonga beats Samoa after Lebanon steals one from France in extra time
Tonga has held on for a 20-18 victory over Samoa in a the Rugby League World Cup contest that more than lived up to the hype.
The clash between Pacific rivals was ultimately decided by goal-kicking as Samoa scored four tries to Tonga's three, but Isaya Katoa's boot (3/3 conversions, 1/1 penalty goal) got the Mate Ma'a over the line and into the semifinals for just the second time.
Tonga will face New Zealand in the first men's semifinal at Newcastle's Hunter Stadium on Saturday, before the Kangaroos take on Samoa in Sydney on Sunday.
Both sides will fancy their chances in the final four after producing a scintillating Test brimming with as much skill as it was physicality.
The teams were deadlocked until some brilliance from Haumole Olakau'atu and Rob Toia saw Tonga strike first after 26 minutes, with Katoa adding a penalty goal soon after.
But, just before half-time, Samoa stayed in the contest with winger Brian To'o's first try off a brilliant Stephen Crichton offload.
Tonga looked the better team to start the second half and got the rewards when Jojo Fifita dove in after a Samoan error, but then came Samoa's reply.
To'o got his second off another brilliant pass, this time from Chanel Harris-Tavita, but it proved to be the five-eighth's last impact on the game as he left the field after grabbing at his hamstring immediately after missing the conversion.
Samoa kept pressing and added tries to Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow and Harris-Tavita's replacement, Ronald Volkman, who potted Samoa's only successful conversion of the match to make it 18-14 heading into the final 10 minutes.
But prop Addin Fonua-Blake was the hero for Tonga as he skipped through a tired Spencer Leniu tackle to score soon after and Katoa's final conversion gave Tonga the decisive lead.
Samoa thought Sua Fa'alogo had pinched the win in the shadows of full-time, but replays showed him just stepping on the touchline before he crossed.
The two-point thriller came after a chaotic golden-point win for Lebanon against France as a group stage littered with enormous blowouts wrapped up with two of the tournament's most exciting showdowns at Western Sydney Stadium.
The two men's games were in stark contrast to the first game of the Parramatta triple header, when the Jillaroos scored a record-breaking 124-6 victory over Wales.
The Australian women will meet Fiji in the semis on Sunday, with New Zealand and Samoa playing the first semifinal on Saturday evening in Newcastle.

Key Event
Kiwis to be without Mulitalo after nasty high tackle
— reporting by AAP
New Zealand have been dealt a blow ahead of their do-or-die Rugby League World Cup semifinal, with Ronaldo Mulitalo handed a one-game ban.
The Kiwis' 78-0 thumping of Fiji on Saturday on the Gold Coast came at a cost, with the star winger sent off for a shoulder charge on Ronald Philitoga in the 52nd minute.
It led to a melee between Fiji and New Zealand players, which culminated in halfback Brandon Wakeham punching Mulitalo in the head. The action earned the Fijian his marching orders as well.
On Sunday, the judiciary deemed Mulitalo's tackle careless and charged him with a grade-two offence.
But much to his relief he was only given a one-game suspension if he takes an early plea, meaning the winger would be eligible to return for the grand final if New Zealand win their semi next Saturday in Newcastle.
Multialo's ban will hurt the Kiwis, because he has scored three tries and been typically busy under the high ball.
New Zealand face a challenge to qualify for the final, playing either Samoa or Tonga.
Wakeham also avoided a heavy ban, handed a one-game suspension, although that won't matter because Fiji have been eliminated from the global showpiece.

Key Event
REPORT: Jillaroos thrash Wales in record-breaking World Cup win
— reporting by AAP
Australia have broken the record for the biggest victory in women's rugby league by scoring 21 tries in a 124-6 thumping of Wales.
Both Jess Sergis and Jaime Chapman, who scored a double-hat-trick at Western Sydney Stadium on Sunday, recorded more running metres than the entire Welsh side.
Winger Chapman's six-try haul equalled the record for most tries in a game for the Jillaroos, who will face Fiji in a semifinal next Sunday at the Sydney Football Stadium.
The one-sided result surpassed France's 116-0 win over Serbia in 2023 as the heaviest victory in the history of the international women's game.
Australian five-eighth Jesse Southwell was almost perfect on the kicking tee, slotting 20 conversions from 21 attempts.
Coupled with a try, the five-eighth's 44 individual points are a new Jillaroos record.
A clunky opening for the Aussies was put to bed when Olivia Kernick crossed for the first points of the afternoon before Chapman burned Wales on the outside for the next two tries — all three scored without Wales touching the ball.
The Welsh did not have another possession for the entire first half as Australia cruised to a 60-0 half-time lead.
Whilst suffering a historic defeat, the Welsh also put on the first points scored against the Jillaroos all tournament.
Wales got themselves on the board in the 59th minute when Tayla Preston grubbered through to Paige Travis for a much-celebrated try.
Sergis had four tries, while Keilee Joseph, Abbi Church and Tamika Upton crossed for doubles.
Kernick, Southwell, Kezie Apps, Sariah Paki, and Keeley Nizza had a try each.
Ruthless Jillaroos dissect dismantling
Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner and captain Isabelle Kelly have spoken to the media after their thumping win over Wales.
Skinner said despite the lopsided nature of the Jillaroos' pool games, there are positive signs for the future of the game.
"I love women's international rugby league, and I think our Pasifika crew are really building nicely to that.
It would be really great to get some investment there in the Northern Hemisphere.
We know what it took Wales to get here and the work that they've done. Our jersey was there not too long ago as well.
So a way that we did that was our [Pacific Championships] concept. We built NRLW as well. That was probably the biggest one for us.
So it'd be really good to see even the Super League to get a little bit more investment and stronger support over there. And I think that'll help that region a lot.
And not taking anything away. This is a World Cup, and Wales has done the work to be here. They've qualified to be here unfortunate result for them today. But we're playing every game to to put our best foot forward to win this thing."
Kelly had similar sentiments.
"I've been really impressed with Samoa this year. I think what they're doing and girls going back and pledging their allegiance to their nations has been incredible.
I think they're leading that, and I think how well they're doing is only going to inspire other girls to do so.
We don't go out there and say that we want to put a certain amount of points on team.
We go out there to be competitive and play the best footy that we can. So I think it's going to take time, but it's definitely starting to happen now."
Key Event
The records which the Jillaroos set today
Highest score in an international match men or women: 124
- The previous high score was a men's Test in 2003, when France defeated Serbia 120-0.
Highest score in a Rugby League World Cup match men or women:124
Previous records were:
- Men's: Australia 110-4 Russia in 2000
- Women's: Australia 92-0 France in 2022, and New Zealand 92-0 France 2026
Largest margin in a women's international: 118
- The previous record was France's 116-0 win over Serbia in 2023
Most tries scored in a women's international: 21
- The previous record was 20 during France's 116-0 win over Serbia in 2023
Most goals kicked in a women's international: 20
- The previous record was 18 during France's 116-0 win over Serbia in 2023
Most individual goals kicked in rugby league international men or women: 20 (Jesse Southwell)
- The previous record was 18 by Ryan Girdler during Australia's 110-4 win over Russia in 2000
Most individual tries in a women's international: 6 (Jamie Chapman)
- Equals the record with Fuarosa Time (New Zealand, 2003), Honey Hireme (New Zealand, 2017), and Julia Robinson (Australia, 2024)
The Cedars fans are here
While most of the build up to this day has focused on Samoa v Tonga, shortly Lebanon and France will face off in the second match of this triple header.
And some of Sydney's huge Lebanese community has turned out on a beautiful afternoon in Parramatta to cheer on the Cedars.
I joined several hundred fans on their march to the stadium, with drummers leading the way, Lebanese music blaring, and lots of dancing and revelry.
It's been great to see how Australia's multicultural communities have embraced this tournament and been able to celebrate their culture through rugby league.

Binance’s US$6b crypto heist: Five things to know about North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
03:23:00 UTC
12:23:00 KST

Binance’s US$6b crypto heist: Five things to know about North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers
- North Korea’s TraderTraitor hackers are blamed for a record US$6 billion Binance crypto theft. US authorities say the group is linked to Lazarus and Pyongyang’s cyber warfare programme.
- TraderTraitor uses fake job offers and malware to steal data and digital assets. The FBI says hackers have also hit DMM Bitcoin, Atomic Wallet, Alphapo, CoinsPaid and Bybit.
- Stolen crypto is laundered through mixing services and private exchanges, then used for weapons research and procurement. Analysts say cybercrime gives North Korea fast money despite sanctions.
AI generated
SEOUL – North Korea’s TraderTraitor hacking group has been blamed by the US authorities for stealing more than US$6 billion (S$7.7 billion) in virtual assets from Binance, in what is believed to be the largest crypto heist in history.
The Oct 29 attack is the latest in a string of high-profile cyberthefts linked to Pyongyang, which has built a formidable hacking operation, generating funds believed to help finance its weapons programme.
Here are five things to know about the group and its place in North Korea’s cyberwarfare programme:
Who are they?
TraderTraitor is the name given to a North Korean hacking operation linked to the broader Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it hacked Sony Pictures in retaliation for The Interview, a satirical film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
Pyongyang has invested heavily in developing its cybercapabilities since at least the mid-1990s, building a force that South Korean intelligence estimated in 2024 comprised around 8,400 personnel.
“North Korea has built a capable cyberforce, funnelling many of the country’s top students into computer science and IT training,” the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on its website.
Much of the hacking activity is known to have been directed by Pyongyang’s Reconnaissance General Bureau, its primary foreign intelligence agency.
“The top two students in my class were recruited to the hacking unit,” South Korean MP Park Choong-kwon, who studied at the North’s elite National Defense University before his defection, told AFP in a 2024 interview.
How do they operate?
TraderTraitor actors have been known to pose as recruiters offering lucrative jobs to trick victims into downloading malicious software.
The malware can allow hackers to infiltrate victims’ computer systems and steal sensitive information and digital assets.
In a 2024 heist involving the theft of US$308 million from Japanese cryptocurrency exchange DMM Bitcoin, a North Korean hacker posing as a recruiter on LinkedIn contacted an employee of a separate virtual currency wallet software company.
They sent the employee what appeared to be a pre-employment test, which actually contained a malicious line of code.
That allowed the hacker to compromise their system and impersonate the employee, the FBI said.
What have North Korean hackers done?
High-profile cyberattacks attributed to North Korean hackers include the theft of US$81 million from Bangladesh’s central bank in 2016 and the WannaCry ransomware attack that disrupted computers worldwide in 2017.
In 2022, the US authorities blamed Lazarus-linked hackers for stealing some US$620 million from the Ronin blockchain network.
The FBI subsequently attributed three more cryptocurrency heists in 2023 to TraderTraitor actors, involving the theft of nearly US$200 million from Atomic Wallet, AlphaPo and Coinspaid.
The scale of the thefts increased dramatically in February 2025, when the FBI blamed TraderTraitor for stealing around US$1.5 billion in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit.
“TraderTraitor actors are proceeding rapidly and have converted some of the stolen assets,” the FBI said at the time.
How does North Korea use stolen funds?
The North Korean regime launders stolen cryptocurrency and converts it into cash “through mixing services or private exchanges”, Lim Eul-chul, a professor at the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University, told AFP.
“The proceeds are then channelled directly into military research, the illicit procurement of weapons components and the defence industry,” he added.
A 2024 United Nations report said proceeds from North Korean cyberattacks “reportedly helped to fund the country’s development of weapons of mass destruction”.
Why cybercrime?
Analysts say Pyongyang’s illicit cyberactivity is driven by its ability to obtain vast sums of money quickly and at “minimal cost”.
“While international sanctions severely restrict North Korea’s ability to earn foreign currency through conventional trade, cybertheft allows it to acquire billions of dollars with minimal personnel and resources,” said Lim.
“Hacking offers Pyongyang a way to obtain funds outside conventional banking channels, taking advantage of the pseudonymous and borderless nature of digital assets to bypass financial restrictions,” he added. 
AFP

Bolivia declares state of emergency over El Nino
- Bolivia declared a state of emergency on 31 October to release resources and send more rescue teams as El Nino brings floods and drought.
- President Rodrigo Paz said the crisis will have “very severe impacts” and needs “the cooperation of all institutions”.
- A government report says drought affects 78,000 families in six departments and has killed more than 75,000 cattle, with UN warnings of “unprecedented” strength.
AI generated
LA PAZ – Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz declared a state of emergency on Oct 31 to free up resources for dealing with the impact of the El Nino weather phenomenon, wreaking havoc around the world.
The decree calls for deploying more rescue teams in hard-hit areas as Bolivia grapples with both flooding and drought because of El Nino, Paz said in an address to the nation.
“This phenomenon will have very severe impacts in terms of drought and floods, and we need the cooperation of all institutions,” he said.
Drought is affecting 78,000 families in six of the country’s nine departments and has led to the loss of more than 75,000 head of cattle, according to a government report this week.
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
The United Nations warned this week that the El Nino could have “unprecedented” strength that would bring havoc to Latin America, eastern and southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific.
Among Bolivia’s neighbours, Peru has seen increased temperatures and wildfires, which have already claimed the lives of at least 12 people.
Chile has experienced the rainiest October ever recorded in Santiago, the capital. AFP

Kazakhstan established diplomatic relations with all UN member states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Kazakhstan established diplomatic relations with all UN member states
Kazakhstan and Nauru have established diplomatic relations, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of the Kazakh Foreign Ministry.
The Joint Communiqué on the Establishment of Diplomatic Relations between the two countries was signed by Kazakhstan's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Kairat Umarov, and the Permanent Representative of the Republic of Nauru to the United Nations, Lara Erab Daniel.
Nauru became the 194th country with which Kazakhstan has established diplomatic ties.
Thus, Kazakhstan has completed the process of establishing diplomatic relations with all United Nations member states, including Nauru, as well as the two Observer States at the Organization. This marks an important milestone in the history of Kazakhstan’s diplomacy.
The signing of the document laid the foundation for the development of bilateral cooperation based on the principles of the UN Charter and international law, including mutual respect for national sovereignty and territorial integrity, equality of States, and non-interference in each other’s internal affairs.
During the meeting, the two sides discussed prospects for developing political dialogue and expanding trade, economic and humanitarian ties. Trade, sustainable development, digitalization and human capital development were highlighted as potential areas of cooperation.
Particular attention was paid to strengthening cooperation within the United Nations and other multilateral forums. The two sides emphasized the importance of maintaining regular dialogue on current issues on the international agenda and developing partnerships between Kazakhstan and countries of the Pacific region.
The establishment of diplomatic relations with Nauru reflects Kazakhstan’s consistent policy of expanding international cooperation, strengthening friendly ties and fostering constructive dialogue with countries around the world.
Earlier, Kazakhstan proposed closer coordination among 5 nuclear-weapon-free zones and Mongolia at the forum on “Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zones: From the Comprehensive Study to Practical Cooperation" at the United Nations.

Economic Watch: China's "super seller" role expands, benefiting more consumers, businesses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-01
10:48:50 CST
11:48:50 KST

GUANGZHOU, Nov. 1 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese-made heat pump that could save European households hundreds of euros a year. Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered teaching tools reaching classrooms in Vietnam. Industrial machinery helping developing countries expand production.
The 140th China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, is offering a window into how China's exports are giving consumers more choices and businesses access to technology and equipment.
When Gree Electric Appliances first attended the Canton Fair 31 years ago, it mainly exported household air conditioners. This year, the Zhuhai-based company is showcasing low-carbon energy solutions covering home appliances, industrial equipment, energy storage and cold-chain technologies.
One heat pump system designed for the European market can cut annual electricity use by about 50 percent. At an average European Union electricity price of 0.3 euros per kilowatt-hour, it could save a household in a 150-square-meter home around 800 euros a year, or more than 1,000 euros in countries such as Germany, according to Gree.
The company's products now reach more than 200 countries and regions, serving around 600 million consumers.
"For Gree, the story of going global is very simple," said Zhu Lei, Gree's vice president and chief marketing officer. "We have one fundamental goal -- to meet consumers' needs and provide them with the best products and services."
The potential savings for European households illustrate what Chinese Premier Li Qiang described as the benefits of China's role as a "super seller."
"As a 'super seller,' China brings benefits to its trading partners," Li said at the Canton Fair's opening ceremony.
He said quality and affordable Chinese goods had raised consumers' actual purchasing power, improved their quality of life, and helped countries strengthen their capacity for industrial development.
China exported 23.2 trillion yuan (about 3.46 trillion U.S. dollars) worth of goods in the first nine months of 2026, up 16.4 percent from a year earlier, according to the General Administration of Customs.
Its exports range from 300,000-tonne oil tankers and industrial robots to miniature ice makers and portable filming equipment. China's manufacturing supply chains allow businesses to turn ideas into customized products.
From 2012 to 2025, China exported about 39 billion U.S. dollars' worth of textile machinery to developing countries, helping some countries in Southeast and South Asia become major textile producers and exporters, according to Chinese industry figures.
Marking its 70th anniversary this year, the Canton Fair reflects how China's exports have evolved, offering a wider range of products and technologies to consumers and businesses worldwide.
At the first fair in 1957, agricultural products and handicrafts, including silk, tea and porcelain, accounted for 63.9 percent of export transactions by value. Machinery and electronic products became the largest product category in 1999. Today, consumer electronics, AI-powered devices and energy storage equipment are among the products on display.
More than 32,000 Chinese and overseas companies are participating in this year's fair, held in three phases in Guangzhou from Oct. 15 to Nov. 4. The first phase drew a record 189,000 overseas buyers from 214 countries and regions.
About 64 percent of exhibitors have adopted technologies such as the industrial internet and AI. New products account for 23.2 percent of exhibits and green products for 26 percent, both record shares.
At the fair's new energy vehicle exhibition area, GAC Group showcased models that included the AION i60, aimed at overseas consumers concerned about travel costs and driving range.
Wei Haigang, president of GAC International, said the company is expanding overseas while building charging and energy storage networks to support local customers.
Chinese companies are also bringing technology and services to overseas schools. At the booth of Guangzhou-based CVTE, AI-powered displays turn abstract lessons into visual presentations. Another AI system helps teachers prepare lesson plans, slides and classroom activities.
Xiao Hang, president of CVTE's overseas business group, recalled a project in Vietnam in 2024. Rather than simply installing equipment, the company sent a seven-member team to work with local users for three days.
"When the children came out of their classrooms, they gathered around us, greeting us in English, Vietnamese and even imperfect Chinese, eager to give us high-fives," Xiao said. "At that moment, we realized this was not just a business, but also a responsibility."
Pascal Lamy, former director-general of the World Trade Organization, said the Canton Fair had become a major meeting point for Chinese producers and businesses worldwide, connecting "supply and demand, producers and consumers, ideas and markets."
Lamy said China had been one of the greatest beneficiaries of the opening of the world economy over recent decades, while also contributing to the global economy through production, innovation, investment and trade. ■

Government will not promise net savings in budget update, even as rate rise looms
In short:
The finance minister and treasurer have refused to confirm December's budget update will contain more savings than new spending, even as pressure mounts on the federal government to tighten its belt.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher told ABC Insiders pressures on the budget were growing, and decisions were still being made for the mid-year update.
What's next?
The mid-year economic and fiscal outlook will be delivered in December.
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update, even as Australians brace for another interest rate rise amid ongoing high inflation.
On Wednesday Treasurer Jim Chalmers also refused to commit to net savings in the mid-year budget update following a worse-than-expected inflation figure of 4.3 per cent over the year to September, which lifted expectations of another rate hike when the Reserve Bank meets on Tuesday.
The finance minister told ABC Insiders despite pressure being put on the government to rein in its spending, she would not pre-commit to overall savings.
"I can't, I don't want to pre-empt the [Expenditure Review Committee] process. We will go through that ... but there is enormous effort being placed, particularly by Jim and myself on the savings side," Senator Gallgher said.
"We are doing a lot of work on the savings side but I can’t get ahead of decisions that haven’t been made yet."
The minister rejected suggestions the pressure to find savings was causing tension inside cabinet, saying it was healthy for ministers to have "robust" debate and bring different perspectives.
Senator Gallagher added that the government's record in each of its previous budgets and mid-year updates had been to deliver overall improvements to the budget, and that in recent budgets its policy decisions had also found more savings than new spending.
The Reserve Bank's chief economist said last week that government spending remained a contributor to ongoing inflation, even if the government points to the war in Iran as the "primary driver".
The treasurer has previously warned that the cost of borrowing would add billions of dollars in additional costs to the budget, as long-term expectations that global interest rates would remain higher for longer were priced into bonds.
Senator Gallagher said other pressures on the budget were also growing, including in health and aged care.
She said the government's spending measures in those pressure areas were necessary to rescue a Medicare system "in freefall" and clear processing backlogs for veterans.
"If you go back to … the Howard era, you know, they were not dealing with AUKUS, they were not dealing with aged care," Senator Gallagher said.
"They weren't dealing with Medicare falling over there, all of these pressures that are coming. So there has to be some acknowledgement of that. We are living in a different world."
The government maintains that the budget is helping to tackle inflation.
However ahead of his departure to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese acknowledged that the Reserve Bank only had a single "blunt instrument" in the inflation fight.
The remaining levers to reduce demand in the economy rest with federal and state governments.
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor told radio station 2GB that the government could do more to avert further rate rises.
"The government can commit tomorrow to take pressure off interest rates and inflation, that would send a strong signal to the Reserve Bank [that] they don't need to raise," Mr Taylor said.
"But they won't do it."
The Reserve Bank's chief economist Sarah Hunter said last week that state and federal government spending was "definitely" contributing to demand pressures in the economy, before adding that it was not the RBA's place to advice government on its spending.
Frontbench minister Murray Watt told News24 demand growth in the economy tripled in the private sector last financial year, while government demand growth halved.
"The substantial portion of the growth in spending in the economy is happening in the private sector rather than in the public sector. Now, I'm not being critical of people who are spending money, going to restaurants, buying a car, whatever it is that they're they're spending money on. But that's where most of the spending [growth] is happening," Senator Watt said.
"And that, of course, is contributing to inflation, as is fuel prices."
